Report  of  Acting  Master  Griswold,  U.  S.  Navy,  executive  officer  of  TJ.  S.  bark  Restless. 

U.  S.  Bark  Restless, 

j Bull’s  Bay ,  South  Carolina ,  October  7:2,  1862. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  submit  the  following  report  of  the  capture 
of  the  schooner  Elmira  Cornelius ,  of  New  York,  by  the  boat  under  my 
command,  by  your  order: 

On  leaving  this  vessel  I  proceeded  toward  Bull’s  Baj^  with  all  possible 
speed,  hoping  to  reach  the  mouth  of  the  narrow  channel  by  which  the 
schooner  was  trying  to  run  the  blockade,  but  she  was  too  fast  for  us, 
for,  finding  that  the  boat  gained,  she  set  her  mainsail  and  gaff-topsail. 
As  there  was  a  strong  breeze  blowing  at  S.  S.  W.,  she  went  through 
the  water  at  a  furious  rate,  the  pilot  evidently  well  acquainted  with 
the  channel.  On  her  reaching  Bird  Island  Passage  she  entered  it 
beautifully,  and  under  all  sail  fairly  flew  through  the  water  toward 
Harbor  Creek,  seeing  which  I  tried  to  cut  her  off  by  crossing  the  shoals 
close  to  the  island  (Bird),  but  it  was  of  no  use.  Suddenly,  however,  she 
took  the  ground,  and  by  the  time  she  floated  again  1  was  within  a  quarter 
of  a  mile  of  her;  fired  a  rifle  at  her,  but  no  notice  was  taken  of  it.  She, 
still  under  all  sail,  tried  to  reach  the  mainland;  again  she  took  the 
ground.  Those  on  board  finding  that  she  was  hard  and  fast  and  the 
boat  close  on  them,  gave  it  up  and  hoisted  an  American  ensign  in 
the  fore-rigging',  port  side,  union  down.  The  captain  said  that  the  flag 


384  SOUTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 

had  been  there  all  the  morning,  but  we  could  not  Bee  it  till  close  on 
her.  It  might  have  been  there,  however,  as  they  could  not  have  chosen 
a  better  place  to  have  hidden  it  from  us.  On  boarding  her  I  found 
the  water  up  to  the  cabin  floor,  but  on  trying  the  pumps  found  tnat 
she  could  be  kept  free  by  pumping  ten  minutes  in  the  hour;  tried  to 
get  her  off  that  tide,  but  could  not,  on  account  of  the  water  that  was 
fn  her;  lost  the  port  anchor  in  the  attempt.  At  12:20,  or  near  that 
time,  Mr.  Chisholm,  acting  master,  from  the  Flag ,  came  on  board  in 
charge  of  two  boats  to  aid  in  getting  the  vessel  off.  At  my  request 
he  sent  his  boat  to  the  ship  with  captain,  crew,  and  papers  ot  schooner 
in  charge  of  Master’s  Mate  Wells,  of  the  Flag.  On  the  morning  of 
the  12th,  there  being  a  heavy  tide,  got  her  ofl.  Not  considering  it  sate 
to  trust  her  in  deep  water  immediately,  as  the  weather  was  threaten¬ 
ing,  I  came  to  an  anchor  near  Bird  Island,  binding  that  she  was  not 
damaged  materially  on  the  flat,  I,  at  1  p.  m. ,  got  my  anchor  and  at  7 . 30 
came  to,  near  this  vessel.  I  am  happy  to  report  that  the  conduct  ot 
Acting  Ensign  Henry  Eason,  who  boarded  shortly  after  myself,  was- 
highly  efficient. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

W.  N.  Griswold, 

Acting  Master ,  Executive  Officer.

Statement  of  John  Simonson,  master  of  the  prize  schooner  Elmira  Cornelius. 

U.  S.  Ship  Vermont, 

Port  Royal,  S.  C. ,  October  %8,  186%. 

Sir:  While  lying  in  this  harbor  in  the  month  of  August  last  I  called 
at  the  custom-house  at  Hilton  Head,  and  there,  in  course  of  conversa¬ 
tion,  stated  to  the  oflieial  present  that  I  had  some  misgivings  as  to  the 
intentions  of  the  charterer  of  my  schooner,  but  I  had  no  means  of 
arriving  at  any  positive  conclusion.  I  deemed  it  my  duty  to  commu¬ 
nicate  this  fact  to  him  for  his  guidance  in  the  premises.  As  this  state¬ 
ment,  made  by  me  while  lying  in  this  harbor,  proves  that  I  had  no 
interest  other 'than  a  lawful  charter,  I  will  thank  you  for  permission 
to  obtain  a  written  evidence  from  the  official,  which  I  can  do  by  calling 
at  the  custom-house  at  Hilton  Head,  if  }Tou  will  kindly  permit  me  to 
do  so  under  guard  from  this  ship. 

The  schooner  is  my  own,  the  hard  earnings  of  years  of  service  and 
hard  work.  I  am  innocent  of  any  collusion  with  the  charterer.  I  had 
entered  a  protest,  cleared  for  New  York,  so  as  to  have  the  protest 
extended  on  my  arrival  in  New  York.  These  are  facts  which  refute 
any  idea  of  my  intention  of  carrying  any  cargo  to  any  port  against  the 
laws  of  the  United  States  custom-house,  and  I  would  be  very  thankful 
to  you  to  grant  me  a  hearing  and  see  what  you  think  of  my  case.  If 
there  is  one  scratch  of  a  pen  wrong  in  my  papers,  and  anything  else 
can  be  proved  against  me,  I  will  give  in  that  I  am  in  the  wrong. 

John  Simonson, 

Captain  Schooner  called  the  Elmira  Cornelius. 

[Rear-Admiral  S.  F.  Du  Pont.]

Report  of  Commander  Strong,  B.  S.  Navy,  of  the  capture  of  the  David  Crockett  by  the  U.  S 

schooner  America,  October  13,  1862. 

U.  S.  S.  Flag, 

Off  Charleston,  October  /■£,  1862. 

Sik:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  to  you  that  last  evening  at  11: 05 
p.  m.  I  discovered  a  sail  under  the  land  bearing  about  N.W.  by  N.  At 
11: 15  the  U.  S.  schooner  America  fired  two  guns,  burned  a  blue  light, 
and  sent  up  a  rocket.  I  immediately  called  all  hands,  went  to  quarters, 
slipped  the  port  chain,  and  stood  in  for  the  America  (about  three-fourths 
of  a  mile  distant).  As  we  approached,  the  America  tired  two  more 
guns,  when  the  vessel  anchored  and  lowered  her  sails.  I  sent  a  boat 
to  the  America  for  the  crew,  who  had  been  taken  on  board  from  the 
prize,  and  had  them  brought  on  board  this  vessel,  viz,  captain,  mate, 
four  seamen,  and  two  passengers. 

She  proved  to  be  the  schooner  David  Crockett ,  of  and  from  Charles¬ 
ton,  bound  for  Bermuda,  with  a  cargo  of  175  barrels  spirits  of  turpen¬ 
tine  and  10  barrels  rosin. 

The  captain  of  the  vessel,  William  Thompson,  admits  having  run 
the  blockade  several  times  during  this  rebellion. 

1  herewith  enclose  the  muster  rolls  of  the  officers  and  crew  of  this 
ship  at  date  of  said  capture. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

J.  H.  Strong, 

Commander.

Report  of  Commander  Downes,  U.  S.  Nary,  commanding  U.  S.  S. 
■  Huron,  of  his  arrival  at  Boston  and  the  condition  of  his  vessel. 

U.  S.  Gunboat  Huron, 
Boston,  October  12,  1862. 

Sir:  In  compliance  with  the  orders  of  Captain  Godon,  commanding 
the  South  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron,  a  copy  of  which  is  herewith 


388 


SOUTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


enclosed,  I  have  the  honor  to  report  to  you  my  arrival  in  this  port 
with  the  Huron  under  my  command,  and,  I  regret  to  inform  you,  with 
the  crew  and  officers  suffering  severely  from  fever  and  general 
debility. 

Though  we  have  been  employed  a  great  part  ot  our  time  upon 
blockading  duties  and  upon  healthy  stations,  lately  the  health  of  the 
ship’s  company  has  been  in  an  unsatisfactory  state,  and  after  a  few 
days’  experience  of  the  climate  of  the  North  Edisto  River  fever  broke 
out  on  board  with  such  violence  that  in  a  week,  having  twenty  men  and 
officers  on  the  sick  list  with  it,  on  the  6th  instant,  I  felt  compelled  to 
leave  my  station  for  relief,  and  made  the  best  of  my  way  to  Charles¬ 
ton  where  I  reported  1113"  condition  to  the  senior  officer,  who  ordered 
me  to  Port  Royal,  whence  I  was  immediately  ordered  north,  leaving 

on  the  evening  of  the  7th.  .  . 

The  vessel  requires  a  thorough  breaking  out,  cleansing,  painting, 
and  frosting,  and  I  would  respectfully  suggest  that  something  be  done 
to  improve  the  ventilation  below  generally,  as  to  the  want  of  it  I  am 
inclined  to  attribute  the  general  unsanitary  condition  on  board. 

The  men  have  now  been  closely  confined  on  board  this  small  vessel 
more  than  eight  months,  and,  I  think,  require  a  short  run  on  liberty. 

I  enclose  herewith  a  correct  muster  roll  of  the  ship’s  company. 

I  am,  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

’  John  Downes, 

Commander. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy,  Washington .

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  forward,  for  the  information  of  the  Depart¬

steamer  Ouachita  on  the  14th  instant,  on  his  way  to  join  my  squadron. 

The  steamer  when  overtaken  was  disabled  in  her  boilers  by  her

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant,

U.  S.  S.  Memphis, 

At  Sea,  October  15,  1862. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  that  on  the  morning  of  14th  instant, 
at  daylight,  in  latitude  33°  03'  N.,  longitude  76°  26'  W.,  a  steamer  was 


SOUTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON.  889 

discovered  standing  to  the  westward.  On  steering  for  her  she  altered 
her  course  to  the  eastward. 

The  pursuit  was  continued  until  3:30  p.  in.,  when  two  shots  were 
fired  in  her  neighborhood,  which  brought  her  to.  She  hoisted  English 
colors;  was  boarded,  and  proved  to  be  the  Ouachita,  from  Bermuda, 
with  a  clearance  for  Havana  and  regular  papers.  The  captain  reported 
but  6  tons  of  coal  left,  and  that  he  had  stopped  her  steaming. 

I  placed  her  in  charge  of  Acting  Master  Curtis,  executive  officer  of 
this  vessel,  with  five  men,  and  took  her  in  tow. 

When  first  seen  she  had  but  her  lower  mast  standing,  under  fore- 
and-aft  sails.  During  the  chase  she  sent  aloft  a  large  square-sail  yard 
and  set  the  sail.  Before  we  overhauled  [her]  we  passed  a  large  box 
floating  in  her  wake. 

Her  second  officer  and  four  of  her  crew  were  brought  here  in  order 
to  make  room  for  our  crew.  These  men  reported  that  the}7'  had  been 
busy  from  10  a.  m.  till  2  p.  m.,  throwing  overboard  cargo;  that  many 
of  the  boxes  were  long  fiat  ones,  with  rope  beckets  fitted  in  the  ends, 
and  heavy;  that  they  had  been  kept  supplied  with  liquor,  as  the  con¬ 
dition  of  those  on  board  reported  by  Mr.  Curtis  confirmed;  also,  that 
the  boilers  were  damaged  by  the  excess  of  pressure  [in  their]  efforts 
to  outsteam  us. 

I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Bend  G.  Watmough, 

Acting  Lieutenant,  Commanding . 

Rear-Admiral  S.  F.  Du  Pont, 

Commanding  South  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron.

Letter  from  the  Secretary  of  the  Navy  to  Captain.  Dahlgren,  TJ.  S. 
Navy,  Chief  of  Bureau  of  Ordnance,  regarding  his  application  to  be 
assigned  to  command  the  naval  forces  to  enter  Charleston,  S.  C. 


Navy  Department,  October  If  1862. 

Sir:  Your  communication  of  the  11th  instant,  placed  in  my  hands 
yesterday  by  yourself,  has  caused  me  both  surprise  and  regret,  it  is 


390  SOUTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 

» 

not  necessary  that  I  should  repeat  to  you  that  in  tendering  you  leave 
of  absence  and  the  command  of  an  armored  ship  in  the  proposed  expe¬ 
dition  against  Charleston  I  had  no  intention  to  inflict  on  you  “painful 
humiliation,”  but  on  the  contrary  my  object,  as  you  well  know,  was  to 
confer  a  special  favor,  and  that  against  my  wishes,  for  you  can,  in  my 
opinion,  nowhere  be  more  useful  than  in  the  Ordnance  Bureau. 

I  do  not  propose  to  discuss  the  point  whether  in  my  past  action  or 
in  the  permit  granted  there  is  anything  to  justify  the  imputation  of 
designing  to  inflict  on  }7ou  “painful  humiliation.”  I  am  confident 
you  would  not  so  misapprehend  me. 

You  requested  a  squadron  and  a  rear-admiral’s  appointment,  or  the 
command  of  the  expedition  to  capture  Charleston.  Regard  for  others, 
for  the  service,  and  for  yourself  forbade  this,  not  that  I  questioned 
your  ability  and  merits,  but  there  are  others,  some  of  them  on  that 
station,  whose  services  and  position  could  not  thus  be  set  aside.  I 
could  not  move  Admiral  Du  Pont  from  his  command,  nor  have  I  been 
disposed  to,  but  had  he  been  withdrawn  your  appointment  to  the  squad¬ 
ron  would  have  been  cause  of  dissatisfaction. 

The  honors  bestowed  upon  you  have  greatly  exceeded  those  of  any 
of  your  contemporaries  or  any  officer  of  equal  grade  from  the  organi¬ 
zation  of  the  Government.  You  were  placed  in  command  of  a  navy 
yard  when  only  a  commander,  and  the  law  was  altered  that  you  might 
be  continued  in  the  position  which  had  been  confided  to  you  in  a  great 
and  trying  emergency.  Some  of  your  seniors  took  exceptions  to  my 
action  on  that  occasion,  and  for  the  same  reasons  as  you  now  do  to  my 
conferring  an  independent  command  on  one  who  is  your  junior,  but 
whom  you  admit  to  be  admirably  adapted  to  the  command  that  is  given 
him.  On  each  occasion  I  was  satisfied  of  the  rectitude  of  the  course 
pursued  and  that  what  was  done  was  for  the  best  interests  of  the  coun¬ 
try.  This  and  this  alone  has  controlled  me  in  every  appointment  and 
every  selection  I  have  made  since  my  connection  with  the  Department. 
1  have  no  partialities  to  gratify,  no  prejudices  to  influence  me. 

On  no  consideration  would  I  withdraw  Admiral  Du  Pont  from  the 
command  of  the  South  Atlantic  Squadron  or  commit  to  another  the 
capture  of  Charleston.  That  object  constituted  originally  the  great 
feature  of  his  command,  and  the  country  expects  and  demands  that 
achievement  of  him.  No  man  would  be  justified  in  depriving  him  of 
that  service,  nor  do  I  see  how  he  can  relinquish  it  without  dishonor. 

Individual  aspirations  can  not  be  permitted  to  intrude  in  such  a 
matter  in  a  crisis  like  this.  In  declining  to  substitute  yourself  or 
any  other  officer  for  that  duty  1  would  not  be  understood  as  denying 
your  or  their  merits,  but  according  to  my  own  convictions  of  duty  I 
owe  it  to  the  country  to  retain  Admiral  Du  Pont  in  command  of  that 
squadron. 

You  ask,  however,  that  the  Department  will  at  least  authorize  you 
to  hoist  the  flag  of  a  rear-admiral  in  the  squadron  under  the  command 
of  Rear-Admiral  Du  Pont.  This  is  inadmissible.  There  has  been 
sufficient  embarrassment  on  the  subject  of  these  acting  appointments 
without  further  complication. 

Only  officers  in  actual  command  of  squadrons  have  received  these 
appointments,  and  they  from  public  necessity,  in  order  that  our  naval 
officers  commanding  squadrons  might  have  relative  rank  with  officers 
in  corresponding  positions  in  the  Army  or  with  naval  officers  of  other 


SOUTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


891 


countries.  While  on  duty  with  the  former  they  are  often  called  to 
cooperate,  and  with  the  latter  they  come  in  contact. 

It  has  been  the  service  and  the  country,  rather  than  the  individual, 
that  have  been  consulted  and  considered  in  these  appointments.  I 
should  not  feel  myself  justified  in  recommending  an  appointment 
called  for  by  no  such  public  necessity,  whatever  may  be  the  merits  or 
however  distinguished  the  services  of  any  individual. 

You  can  not,  I  think,  have  fully  considered  the  effect  and  bearing 
of  your  request,  were  it  to  be  complied  with.  If  the  argument  which 
you  urge  in  regard  to  the  selection  of  one  junior  to  yourself  to  the 
command  of  the  Mississippi  squadron  is  legitimate,  then  every  other 
officer  who  is  his  senior  may,  like  yourself,  take  exceptions,  and  the 
Department,  if  governed  by  that  consideration,  would  be  compelled 
to  disregard  merit  and  qualification  and  rely  on  length  of  service  alone. 
Besides,  if  you  are  grieved  by  that  selection  because  you  are  his  senior, 
it  would  only  aggravate  the  error  as  regards  every  officer  on  the  active 
list  senior  to  yourself  were  you  to  receive  an  acting  rear-admiral’s 
appointment,  and  that,  too,  when  the  service  requires  no  such 
appointment. 

I  will  not  pursue  this  subject,  already  too  extended,  and  which 
nothing  but  my  sincere  regard  for  you  personally  and  my  high  appre¬ 
ciation  of  you  as  an  officer  would  have  induced  me  to  make.  It  has 
been  with  great  reluctance  that  1  yielded  to  your  earnest  desire  often 
expressed  before  you  made  your  late  written  application  for  duty 
afloat.  In  no  position  can  you  so  well  serve  the  country  as  in  the 
department  with  which  your  name  is  identified  and  on  which  must  rest 
your  enduring  fame.  But  you  were  sensitive,  not  without  reason, 
perhaps,  under  the  remarks  that  you  were  not  actively  participating 
in  the  war  in  the  strict  line  of  your  profession.  I  appreciate  the 
wound  these  remarks  and  these  opinions  have  inflicted  on  a  sensitive 
mind  filled  with  the  laudable  ambition  of  attaining  the  highest  rank 
in  his  profession. 

It  was  this  which  prompted  me  to  tender  you  leave  of  absence  for  a  few 
weeks  and  the  command  of  an  armored  vessel  in  one  of  the  most  impor¬ 
tant  demonstrations  of  the  war.  I  regret  that  my  object  should  have 
been  misunderstood  or  should  have  caused  you  a  moment’s  pain.  I  am 
satisfied  that  nowhere  else  can  you  render  so  great  service  to  the 
country — if  that  be  your  aim,  as  it  certainly  should  be  the  first  object 
of  each  of  us— as  in  the  position  you  now  occupy,  and  to  which  not 
only  the  Department  but  the  President  and  the  Senate  assigned  you. 
We  are  wanting  for  effective  service  a  great  amount  of  ordnance,  and 
on  you,  who  have  made  ordnance  a  specialty,  devolves  beyond  anyone 
else  the  duty  of  meeting  this  great  necessity.  It  is  with  reluctance 
that  I  acquiesce  in  your  absence  from  ordnance  duty  even  for  a  brief 
period,  and  in  so  acquiescing  upon  your  own  application  I  had  not  the 
remotest  conception  of  humiliating  or  paining  you,  but  supposed  that 
at  some  sacrifice  to  myself  and  to  the  service  I  was  rendering  you  a 

special  favor.  . 

To  prevent  further  misapprehension  after  this  explanation  I  desire 
to  sav  to  you  that  my  letter  of  the  8th  instant  was  not  intended  to  be 
mandatory  and  is  in  no  sense  to  be  considered  as  an  order  to  you,  but 
is  a  permit  or  leave,  if  you  desire  it,  not  otherwise,  for  special  service 
for  a  few  weeks,  and  to  be  accepted  or  not  at  your  own  option.  If 


392  SOUTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 

* 

you  do  not  desire  the  duty,  I  do  not  wish  you  to  accept  of  leave,  for 
in  no  position  can  you  render  the  country  so  great  service  as  in  the 
Ordnance  Department,  and  in  these  times  it  becomes  everyone  to 
sacrifice  all  personal  considerations  for  the  good  of  the  country. 

I  am,  respectfully,  etc., 

Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  Navy. 

Captain  John  A.  Dahlgren, 

Chief  of  Bureau  of  Ordnance.

to  be  used  upon  discovery  of  vessels  attempting  to  run  thy  blockade  at 
night. 

U.  S.  S.  Canandaigua, 

Off  Charleston ,  October  17,  1862. 

Sir:  Hereafter  any  vessel  of  the  blockading  force  off  this  port  dis¬ 
covering  a  vessel  during  the  night  attempting  to  run  the  blockade  will 
tire  one  or  more  rockets  or  guns  as  a  signal  that  the  attempt  is  being 
made,  and  immediately  after  burn  a  white  light  (either  Coston  No.  2 
or  signal  light)  if  the  Vessel  is  outward  bound,  or  red  (Coston)  No.  5 
if  the  vessel  is  inward  bound,  the  lights  to  be  repeated  after  an  inter¬ 
val  of  ten  minutes  should  the  chase  be  continued. 

Continuous  and  rapid  firing  of  guns  will  be  understood  as  a  signal 
that  assistance  may  be  required  by  the  vessel  firing  the  guns,  and  the 
nearest  vessel  to  her  will  proceed  to  her  assistance,  but  will  not  be 
absent  from  her  station  for  a  longer  time  than  is  absolutely  necessary.

cate  that  all  of  the  vessels  employed  on  the  blockade  are  to  repair  to 
the  locality  where  the  signals  are  made.

J.  F.  Green,

Report  of  Captain  Green ,  U  S.  Navy ,  regarding  the  visits  of  II.  B. 

M.  S.  Racer ,  in  Charleston  Ilawor. 

U.  S.  S.  Canandaigua, 

Off  Charleston ,  October/'  19,  186 ‘2. 

Sir:  I  have  to  report  to  you  that  Id.  M.  S.  Racer ,  Captain  Lyons, 
arrived  off  this  port  from  Hampton  Roads  on  the  17th  instant,  and 
requested  permission  to  proceed  into  the  bar  in  order  to  communicate 
with  the  English  consul,  which  request  I  granted,  provided  he  would 
show  no  lights  nor  communicate  with  the  shore  during  the  night.  She 
remained  at  anchor  off  the  bar  near  the  entrance  to  the  Swash  Chan¬ 
nel  until  the  19th  instant,  when  she  sailed  for  Hampton  Roads,  having- 
had  communication  with  Charleston  twice  by  steamer  under  the 
English  flag  and  a  flag  of  truce. 

I  received  information  from  Captain  Lyons  that  General  Lamar  had 
recently  died  at  Charleston,  and  that  yellow  fever  prevailed  there  to  a 
great  extent,  but  that  not  many  deaths  had  occurred;  also  that  a  salute 
tired  from  the  batteries  on  shore  a  few  days  since  was  on  account  of 
General  Bragg  having  gained  a  great  victory  over  General  Buell. 

In  connection  with  the  visit  of  the  Racer  off  this  port  1  would  state 
that  several  officers  who  have  been  employed  a  long  time  on  this 
blockade  remarked  to  me  on  her  arrival  that  an  attempt  to  violate  the 
blockade  was  generally  made  immediately  after  her  departure.  The 
recent  attempt  was  made  on  the  night  of  the  day  of  her  sailing,  and 
Commander  Strong  informs  me  that  he  took  the  bearing  of  the  Racer 
at  dark,  and  at  about  8  p.  m,  saw  three  bright  white  lights  in  her 
direction. 

I  would  propose  that  she  be  followed  a  reasonable  distance  on  her 
departure  should  she  visit  this  port  again. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

J.  F.  Green, 

Captain  and  Senior  Officer  off  Charleston. 

Captain  S.  W.  Godon, 

Comdg.  South  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron,  Port  Royal ,  S.  C.

Flagship  Wabash, 

Port  Royal  Harbor ,  S.  C. ,  October  28,  1862. 
Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  to  the  Department  that  on  the  morn¬ 
ing  of  the  20th  instant,  between  the  hours  of  2  and  3  o’clock,  a  steamer 
succeeded  in  running  the  blockade  off  Charleston.  She  passed  to  the 
northward  of  the  Rattlesnake  Shoal,  and  was  first  discovered  by  the 
schooner  Blunt,  who  made  the  usual  signal  and  fired  at  her,  but  could 
not  pursue  as  there  was  no  wind.  The  Blambeau  was  on  the  alert,  and 
soon  after  discovering  the  steamer  Lieutenant-Commander  Upshur 
slipped  his  chain  and  commenced  firing,  but  though  he  discharged 
nine  shell  at  her,  did  not  succeed  in  arresting  her  progress.  He  pur¬ 
sued  her  until  his  own  vessel  was  under  the  fire  of  the  rebel  batteries. 
In  the  morning  it  was  discovered  that  the  steamer  had  run  aground 
close  to  Fort  Moultrie  and  was  apparently  bilged. 

By  the  Charleston  papers,  since  received,  it  appears  that  this  steamer 
was'the  Minho,  that  she  will  perhaps  become  a  wreck,  as  there  is  much 
water  in  the  hold,  and  part  of  the  cargo  floating  about  in  the  vessel. 
So  much  of  the  cargo,  it  is  stated,  as  may  be  destroyed  by  water  will 
be  nearty  a  total  loss. 

I  regret  the  escape  of  this  vessel,  but  under  the  circumstances,  owing 
to  the  darkness  of  the  night  and  the  haziness  of  the  atmosphere,  ren¬ 
dering  it  difficult  to  discover  a  vessel  only  a  short  distance  off,  I  can

attach  no  blame  to  the  officers  on  the  blockade.  I  enclose  Lieutenant-

[Enclosure.] 

U.  S.  S.  Flambeau, 

Off  Charleston ,  S.  C.,  October  20,  186 2. 

Sir:  I  have  to  report  that  at  2: 40  this  morning,  while  at  our  anchor¬ 
age  inside  the  Rattlesnake  Shoal,  I  discovered  that  the  schooner  Blunt 
was  firing  guns  and  had  already  discharged  a  rocket,  apparently  toward 
Sullivan’s  Island. 

We  immediately  beat  to  quarters,  but  for  at  least  ten  minutes  noth¬ 
ing  suspicious  could  be  observed.  Finally,  at  2:52  a.  m. ,  discovered  a 
strange  vessel  to  the  northward  and  eastward,  stealthily  gliding  under 
shadow  of  the  land.  W  e  immediately  slipped  our  chain,  got  underway, 
and  backed  our  engine  until  we  found  ourselves  in  16i  feet  of  water. 
We  then  fired  at  the  approaching  vessel  from  our  after  gun  twice  in 
succession.  Finding  that  the  strange  object  was  still  moving  onward, 
we  wore  ship  and  brought  our  forward  and  midship  guns  to  bear.  We 
then  fired  repeatedly  and  as  rapidly  as  possible  five  additional  shell 
from  our  30-pounders  and  howitzer,  at  the  same  time  giving  chase  to  the 
northward  and  westward,  within  a  very  short  distance  of  Breach  Inlet 
batteries.  By  this  time  the  stranger  had  reached  a  point  under  cover 
of  the  said  batteries  and  appeared  for  a  few  moments  to  have  grounded 
there.  We  then  gave  her  three  more  shell  from  our  30-pounders,  but 
immediately  afterwards  discovered  that  the  strange  steamer  was  again 
underway  and  rapidly  eluding  us.  It  was  now  impossible  to  chase  any 
farther,  as  we  were  already  close  under  the  shore.  At  this  moment 
heard  report  of  a  gun  from  the  harbor,  and  judging  that  the  stranger 
had  reached  a  point  of  safety,  we  dropped  our  remaining  anchor  under 
foot  and  waited  until  daylight,  when,  perceiving  that  we  were  within 
easy  range  of  the  batteries,  we  steamed  out  a  short  distance.  By  this 
time  we  were  enabled  to  notice  that  the  chase  was  lying  close  to  Fort 
Moultrie  and  apparently  in  an  injured  condition,  whether  from  our 
shot  or  from  having  run  on  the  piles  there  implanted,  we  know  not. 
Unable  to  act  further  in  the  matter,  we  then  weighed  anchor  and 
steamed  in  search  of  the  one  which  had  been  slipped. 

I  am,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

J.  Id.  Upshur, 
Lieutenant-  Commander. 

Captain  J.  F.  Green, 

Commanding  U.  S.  Steam  Sloop  Canandaigua. 


Report  of  Captain  Green ,  U  S.  Navy ,  of  the  breach  of  blockade  by  the 
steamer  Minho ,  October  20,  1862. 

U.  S.  S.  Canandaigua, 

Off  Charleston ,  October  23 ,  1862. 

Sir:  I  have  to  inform  you  that  a  steamer  succeeded  in  running  the 
blockade  and  reaching  the  anchorage  off  Fort  Moultrie  between  2  and 


SOUTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


397 


3  o’clock  in  the  morning  of  the  20th  instant.  She  passed  in  to  the 
northward  of  Rattlesnake  Shoal  within  sight  of  the  schooner  George  IF 
Blunt,  stationed  off  the  extremity  of  the  shoal  extending  from  Dewees 
Inlet,  and  the  Flambeau ,  stationed  in  the  neighborhood  of  the  western 
Rattlesnake  buoy.  The  former  vessel  discovered  her  first,  made  the 
usual  signals,  and  fired  at  her  so  long  as  she  was  in  sight,  but  could  not 
pursue  her  in  consequence  of  there  being  no  wind.  The  latter  vessel, 
on  discovering  her,  fired  repeatedly  at  and  pursued  her,  but  failed  to 
arrest  her  progress  toward  the  harbor. 

At  daylight  the  strange  steamer  was  discovered  about  three-quarters 
of  a  mile  distant  from  Fort  Moultrie,  flying  English  and  Confederate 
colors,  and  at  8  o’clock  it  was  discovered  that  she  was  aground. 
Whether  she  had  been  run  aground  accidentally  or  in  consequence  of 
damage  received  from  shot  can  not  be  ascertained.  Steamers  from  the 
city  immediately  proceeded  to  her  assistance,  but  she  still  remained 
aground,  apparently  bilged  and  a  complete  wreck. 

I  enclose  herewith  Lieutenant-Commander  Upshur’s  and  Acting 
Master  Beers’*  reports  of  their  proceedings  in  endeavoring  to  capture 
her. 

I  regret  exceedingly  that  this  vessel  should  have  succeeded  in  pass¬ 
ing  the  blockade.  On  reviewing  all  the  circumstances  attending  it, 
particularly  the  haziness  of  the  atmosphere  at  the  time,  rendering  it 
difficult  to  discover  a  vessel  only  a  short  distance,  the  uncertainty  at 
night  of  the  time  and  direction  of  the  approach  of  a  vessel  attempting 
to  run  The  blockade,  combined  with  the  perplexities  of  navigation  in 
shallow  waters,  I  think  the  efforts  made  to  intercept  and  capture  her 
were  creditable,  although  not  successful.  1  am  of  the  opinion,  how¬ 
ever,  that  if  the  Flambeau' s  head  had  been  toward  Fort  Moultrie,  and 
inclined  toward  the  mainland  instead  of  seaward  at  the  time  of  her 
discovery  of  the  steamer,  which  passed  inside  of  her,  the  probabilities 
of  capturing  or  heading  her  off  would  have  been  greater. 

I  beg  leave  to  repeat  the  suggestion  made  to  you  verbally  on  your 
recent  visit  off  this  port,  that  the  blockading  force  would  be  much  more 
effective  by  the  addition  of  two  or  more  light-draft  steamers  and  the 
employment  of  two  fast  and  economical  steamers  in  cruising  off  the 
northern  and  southern  approaches  to  Charleston. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

J.  F.  Green, 

Captain  and  Senior  Officer  off  Charleston ,  S.  C. 

Rear-Admiral  S.  F.  Du  Pont, 

South  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron ,  Port  Royal ,  S.  C.

Report  of  Commander  Woodhidl ,  TI.  S.  Navy ,  commanding  TJ.  S.  S. 

Cimarron ,  of  the  destruction  of  salt  works  at  Cedar  Point ,  Fla., 

and  regarding  general  affairs  in  St.  John’s  Rive?'. 

U.  S.  S.  Cimarron, 

St.  John's  River ,  Florida ,  October  21,  1862. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  inform  you  that  I  have  had  the  prize 
steamer  Governor  Milton  armed  with  two  24-pounder  howitzers,  and 
up  to  this  time  she  has  proved  very  useful. 

Yesterday  I  fitted  out  an  expedition  composed  of  50  men,  and  all 
the  marines  of  this  vessel,  which  proceeded  on  board  the  Milton,  in 
charge  of  Lieutenant-Commander  Bushrod  Taylor,  to  Cedar  Point, 
the  purpose  of  which  was  to  destroy  the  salt  works  in  that  locality. 
I  am  happy  to  inform  you  of  the  entire  success  of  the  undertaking. 
The  works  were  found  to  be  of  larger  proportions  than  generally 
believed.  Everything  was  totally  destroyed,  consisting  of  six  cast- 
iron  (8  feet  in  diameter)  boiling  pans  and  a  large  17-foot  tubular  boiler, 
with  furnaces,  all  complete. 

Since  the  departure  of  the  Paul  Jones  I  have  kept  the  Hale  and  the 
Milton  constantly  cruising  between  this  anchorage  and  the  point  above 
Yellow  Bluff;  so  far  everything  appeared  to  be  quiet. 

The  coal  vessel  has  been  discharged,  ballasted,  and  will  proceed  to 
sea  this  morning.  Her  bill  of  lading  calls  for  225  tons  of  coal,  but  all 
we  can  account  for  having  received  from  her  is  something  less  than 
200  tons,  viz,  80  tons  to  the  Paul  Jo?ies ,  81  to  this  vessel,  and  33  or  34 
to  the  Hale.  I  do  not  think  the  difference  is  chargeable  to  the  captain 
of  the  schooner,  but  very  much  doubt  if  the  full  quantity  named  was 
put  on  board  at  the  shipping  port.  I  have  endorsed  on  the  bill  of 
lading  the  amount  really  received. 

The  Neptune  arrived  this  morning,  and  part  of  my  crew  are  being- 
employed  loading  her  with  lumber  and  a  number  of  valuable  articles 
found  at  the  Mayport  Mills.  I  hope  to  get  her  off  by  to-morrow. 

I  really  think  if  it  is  desirable  to  hold  this  river  throughout  its 
whole  extent,  we  should  have  more  force.  This  vessel  and  the  Hale 
are  not  sufficient  for  the  purpose.  The  Milton  can  not  be  much  relied 
upon,  and  I  fear  to  trust  her  beyond  signal  distance. 

I  shall  use  all  the  vigilance  in  my  power  and  do  all  I  can  to  prevent 
the  enemy  from  giving  us  further  trouble;  more  than  that  I  do  not 
think  the  force  I  have  can  accomplish.

Report  of  Commander  Steedman,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  commanding  II.  S.  S.  Paul  Jones. 

U.  S.  Gunboat  Paul  Jones, 

Port  Royal ,  S.  C.,  October  27,  1862. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  submit  the  following  report: 

On  Tuesday,  October  21,  Captain  Godon,  the  senior  officer  com¬ 
manding  in  your  absence,  placed  me  in  command  of  the  gunboats 
which  were  to  accompany  and  cooperate  with  General  Bran  nan's 
forces.  The  accompanjdng  paper,  a  copy  of  which  was  furnished 
each  commander  of  gunboats  and  transports,  gives  the  names  of  ves¬ 
sels,  the  number  of  troops  each  was  to  carry,  the  order  in  which  to 
move,  and  the  directions  to  prevent  any  accidents  if  possible;  the 
commanders  of  the  gunboats  were  also  assembled  on  board  the  Ver 
mont  by  Captain  Godon  and  the  proposed  movement  fully  explained. 
At  sunset,  by  signal  from  the  Vermont ,  I  got  underway  and  pro¬ 
ceeded  up  the  mouth  of  Broad  River,  where  1  came  to  anchor,  the 
other  vessels  following  and  taking  their  stations  in  line.  After  anchor¬ 
ing  General  Bran  nan  called  on  board  for  the  purpose  of  consultation, 
and  at  his  request  the  three  launches  of  the  Wabash  and  one  from  this 
vessel  were  dispatched  up  the  river  in  tow  of  a  small  tug  carrying 
100  men  of  General  Terry’s  command  for  the  purpose  of  surprising 
the  picket  guards  of  the  enemy  at  Mackay’s  Point  and  Cuthbert’s 
Landing.  The  orders  were  that  the  tug  should  proceed  up  within  2 
miles  of  these  points,  when  the  troops  were  to  be  taken  on  board  the 
launches  and  continue  up  cautiously  to  effect  the  object  in  view.  I 
will  here  inform  you  that  owing  to  the  ignorance  of  the  contraband 
guide  who  accompanied  the  Wabash'’ s  launches  the  party  failed  in 
their  object  of  capturing  the  picket  guard  at  Mackay’s  Point;  the 
party  in  the  Paul  Jones’s  launch,  in  charge  of  Acting  Master  Ormond, 
being  more  fortunate  in  having  a  good  guide,  was  successful  in  every 
respect. 

At  12:30  a.  m.  of  the  22d,  the  signal  for  getting  underway  was 
made,  and  allowing  thirty  minutes  for  the  rest  of  the  vessels  "to  get 
ready,  this  vessel  weighed  and  stood  up  the  river,  following  a  tug  in 
charge  of  Lieutenant  Preston,  who  was  [so]  kind  [as]  to  show  the  way 
above  the  flats.  To  this  officer  I  am  much  indebted  for  the  valuable 
assistance  he  afforded  me  in  starting  the  expedition.  The  Ben  De 
Ford ,  with  General  Brannan  on  board,  followed  closely.  Proceed¬ 
ing  slowly  up  the  river  (making  but  six  revolutions),  I  arrived  and 
anchored  just  above  Mackay’s  Point  at  4:30  a.  m. ,  accompanied  only 
by  the  Ben  De  Ford.  I  regret  to  say  that  at  daylight  not  a  vessel  of 
the  expedition  was  in  sight,  nor  did  they  make  their  appearance  until 
some  time  after  sunrise;  the  cause  of  this  can  be  explained  by  their 
respective  commanders.  I  have  since  learned  from  Commander  Wer- 
den,  of  the  Conemaugh,  that  the  signal  for  getting  underway  was  not 


SOUTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


401 


seen  by  him,  and  when  he  moved,  owing  to  his  having  no  copy  of 
the  order  of  sailing  and  directions  for  passing  the  lights,  his  vessel 
grounded  by  passing  on  the  wrong  side  of  one  of  them.  The  Cone- 
maugh,  the  third  vessel  in  line,  in  not  getting  underway,  and  then 
grounding,  I  am  satisfied  was  the  principal  cause  of  the  disarrange¬ 
ment  and  delay  of  the  other  vessels,  with  the  exception  of  the  Mar¬ 
blehead  and  Water  Witch ,  which  ran  afoul  of  each  other,  got  out  of 
line,  and  did  not  leave  the  anchorage  until  daylight.  Upon  anchor¬ 
ing,  the  disembarkation  of  troops  was  at  once  commenced  from  the 
Ben  De  Ford  and  continued  from  the  other  vessels  as  they  came  up. 
I  must  here  say  that  the  commanders  of  the  gunboats  deserve  praise 
for  their  activity  and  energy  in  assisting  the  disembarkation.  By 
10  o’clock  a.  m.  the  whole  force  was  landed  and  moved  on  to  meet  the 
enemy.  At  the  request  of  General  Brannan  the  Uncas  was  ordered  to 
proceed  up  the  Pocotaligo  and  the  Patroon  and  Vixen  up  the  Coosaw- 
hatchie  rivers,  the  latter  vessels  to  cover  the  landing  of  Colonel 
Barton’s  command  on  board  the  Planter.  These  vessels  rendered  effi¬ 
cient  service,  and  I  take  much  pleasure  in  commending  the  conduct  of 
their  officers  and  crews.  The  three  howitzers  of  the  Wabash,  in 
charge  of  Lieutenant  Phoenix  and  Ensigns  W allace,  Pearson,  and 
Adams,  by  request  of  General  Brannan,  were  landed  and  placed  under 
his  orders.  The  good  services  rendered  by  these  guns  and  the  gallantry 
and  skill  of  the  officers  and  men  in  handling  them  are,  as  I  am  informed 
by  the  general,  beyond  praise.  From  this  time  until  sunset  nothing 
occurred  worthy  of  note  within  my  observation.  At  about  5  o’clock 
p.  m.  I  received  a  message  from  the  general  announcing  his  intention 
of  falling  back,  and  requesting  me  to  keep  a  good  lookout  in  case  the 
enemy  should  attempt  to  harass  his  rear.  I  made  arrangements  accord¬ 
ingly.  Having  received  a  message  from  Captain  Coryell,  of  the  quar¬ 
termaster’s  department,  requesting  the  services  of  our  surgeons,  I 
directed  all  of  them  to  proceed  on  shore  at  once  and  report  to  the 
medical  director,  which  was  promptly  done,  and  I  am  happy  to  say 
that  the}'-  rendered  very  valuable  aid  in  attending  to  the  wounded. 

The  next  day  (23d  instant)  the  troops  were  embarked,  and  as  each 
vessel  received  its  quota  on  board  proceeded  down  the  river  to  Hilton 
Head,  this  vessel,  the  Marblehead,  and  the  Vixen  remaining  to  cover 
and  bring  up  the  rear.  By  sunset  the  whole  force  was  reembarked, 
and  by  10  o’clock  p.  m.  the  last  of  them  arrived  oft'  Hilton  Head. 

To  Ensign  Johnson,  who  accompanied  me  as  aid  and  signal  officer, 
I  am  much  indebted.  It  is  not  for  me  to  say  anything  in  praise  of  the 
general  in  command  of  the  expedition,  except  that  I  shall  always 
esteem  myself  fortunate  in  having  served  on  two  separate  occasions 
with  that  gallant,  able,  and  courteous  gentleman. 

It  will  afford  you  gratification  to  learn  that  the  utmost  cordiality 
existed  between  the  two  branches  of  the  service.  In  conclusion,  I  must 
express  my  high  appreciation  of  the  good  conduct  of  the  officers  and 
men  on  board  of  this  vessel. 

Enclosed  you  will  find  Lieutenant  Phoenix’s  report. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Charles  Steedman, 

Commander ,  U.  S.  Navy. 

Rear-Admiral  S.  F.  Du  Pont, 

Commanding  South  Atlantic  Squadron.

will  he  the  signal  to  get  underway. 

2d.  Entering  Broad  River,  vessels  will  pass  on  — - hand  of  the 

first  red  light  (on  Karnak ),  on  the  port  hand  of  second  red  light  (in 
small  boat),  and  on  the  starboard  hand  of  third  red  light  (on  schooner 
America). 

3d.  No  masthead  lights  will  be  carried;  all  other  lights  must  be  care¬ 
fully  concealed. 

4th.  Each  vessel  will  follow  carefully  in  the  wake  of  its  immediate 
leader  and  keep  as  close  to  him  as  practicable. 

5th.  Ben  De  Ford  tows  flat  No.  1,  with  horses  and  artillery.

Report  of  Lieutenant  Phoenix,  IJ.  S.  Navy,  U.  S.  S.  Wabash. 

U.  S.  S.  Wabash, 

Port  Royal ,  8.  C. ,  October  1862. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  that  three  12-pounder  boat  howitzers 
from  the  Wabash ,  under  my  charge,  were  landed  on  the  morning  of  the 
22d  at  Mackay’s  Point.  The  howitzers,  Nos.  1,  2,  3,  were  respectively 
under  the  immediate  command  of  Ensigns  Wallace,  Adams,  and  Pear¬ 
son.  Assistant  Surgeon  McSherry  accompanied  the  expedition. 

The  men  had  been  pulling  in  the  boat  since  1  o’clock  the  previous 
night,  and  were  by  no  means  fresh  on  the  morning  of  the  landing; 
nevertheless,  they  cheerfully  took  their  places  at  the  drag  ropes  and 
kept  up  their  zeal  and  spirit  throughout  the  expedition.  After  a  march 
of  about  5  miles,  over  part  of  which  we  were  ably  assisted  at  the  drag 
ropes  by  a  detachment  from  the  Third  Rhode  Island  Artillery,  the 
infantry  met  the  enemy  in  the  woods,  while  their  artillery  opened  on 
us  over  the  trees.  The  howitzers  were  immediately  thrown  into  bat¬ 
tery  and  commenced  a  rapid  discharge  of  shrapnel  and  shells.  The 
enemy  having  fallen  back,  we  advanced  with  the  troops,  although  a 


SOUTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


403 


few  rounds  of  canister  were  all  the  ammunition  left  to  us.  On  arriv¬ 
ing-  at  the  position  from  which  the  enemy’s  batteries  opened  lire,  we 
found  part  of  a  rebel  caisson  tilled  with  12-pounder  shell.  After 
filling  our  ammunition  boxes  with  those  we  proceeded  on  as  fast  as 
possible  to  the  front,  where  our  forces  were  already  engaged.  On  the 
road  one  piece  was  detached  and  ordered  to  the  left,  which  was  then 
seriously  threatened.  The  other  two  came  into  action  with  the  center 
and  commenced  firing  with  shells.  This  was  continued  until  all  our 
shells  were  expended  except  two  for  each  gun,  when  the  order  came 
to  cease  firing  and  reserve  our  remaining  ammunition  in  case  the  enenry 
advanced.  The  guns  Avere  accordingly  loaded  with  canister  and  planted 
in  the  road.  Our  position  Avas  shifted  to  the  rear  from  time  to  time, 
as  our  forces  were  ordered  to  fall  to  the  rear.  A  shell  was  occasion¬ 
ally  thrown  into  the  enemy’s  position  as  we  moved  to  the  rear,  but  as 
they  did  not  pursue  this  was  soon  rendered  unnecessary.  When  the 
order  to  retreat  came  the  howitzers  Avere  secured  and  moved  with  the 
rear  of  the  army.  The  retreat  was  commenced  a  little  after  sunset, 
and  after  a  long,  weary  march  of  over  four  hours  we  arrived  at  the 
landing,  from  which  the  boats  took  us  to  the  Paul  Jones.  The  morn¬ 
ing  of  the  23d  was  occupied  by  transporting  troops  in  our  boats  from 
the  landing  to  the  transports.  In  the  afternoon  the  launch  and  first 
cutter  were  ordered  up  the  Pocotaligo  RAer  to  shell  an}^  of  the  enemy’s 
pickets  that  might  show  themselves.  A  party  of  these  avc re  seen 
slowly  advancing  toward  the  ferry,  but  were  soon  dispersed  with  a 
few  shell.  After  remaining  here  until  all  the  troops  Avere  on  board 
the  transports  we  returned  to  the  Paul  Jones  and  from  thence  to  the 
Wabash.  1  regret  to  say  that  DaArid  Moitoav  (seaman)  was  wounded 
in  the  breast,  Oscar  Farenholt  (ordinary  seaman)  seriously  in  the  arm, 
and  John  Bernard  (ordinary  seaman)  slightly  injured  by  the  recoil  of 
a  gun.  The  officers  and  men  behaved  with  the  greatest  gallantry,  per¬ 
forming  every  service  with  the  alacrity  of  sailors,  and  bearing  all  the 
hardships  of  the  march  with  the  utmost  perseverance  and  fortitude.  I 
am  much  indebted  to  Captain  Comstock’s  company  of  the  Third  Rhode 
Island  Artillery  for  the  assistance  rendered  in  dragging  the  pieces. 

Yerv  respectfully, 

Lloyd  Phoenix, 

Lieutenant. 

Commander  Charles  Steedman, 

Commanding  Paul  Jones.

General  order  of  General  Beauregard,  C.  S.  Army. 

General  Orders,  |  Hdqrs.  Dept,  of  S.  C.,  Ga.,  and  Fla., 

No.  46.  )  Charleston ,  March,  26,  1863. 

1.  The  troops  engaged  in  the  action  with  the  enemy  at  Pocotaligo 
on  the  22d  of  October,  1862,  will  have  inscribed  on  their  colors  “Poco¬ 
taligo,  22d  October,  1862,”  in  honor  of  the  veteran-like  steadiness  and 
unsurpassable  courage  displayed  on  that  day  in  their  conflict  with  and 
defeat  of  an  enemy  of  almost  incredible  superiority  in  numbers.  The 
whole  country  has  been  already  informed  of  and  appreciates  the  bril¬ 
liant  events  and  incidents  of  the  battle  of  Pocotaligo,  and  it  has  only 
remained  thus  officially  to  authorize  an  honor  so  brilliantly  won. 
The  field  of  Pocotaligo,  made  memorable  by  those  who  held  it  on  the 
22d  of  October,  1862,  surely  can  not  be  yielded  up  to  any  greater  force 
with  which  the  enemy  may  attack  in  that  quarter.

Report  of  General  Beauregard,  C.  S.  Army,  commanding  Department  of  South  Carolina, 

Georgia,  and  Florida. 

Savannah,  Ga.,  October  23,  1862 — 8  p.  m. 
The  abolitionists  attacked  in  force  Pocotaligo  and  Coosawhatchie 
yesterday.  They  were  gallantly  repulsed  to  their  gunboats  at  Mackay  s 
Point  and  Bee’s  Creek  Landing  by  Colonel  W.  S.  Walker,  command¬ 
ing  district,  and  Colonel  G.  P.  Harrison,  commanding  troops  sent  from 
here.  Enemy  had  come  in  thirteen  transports  and  gunboats.  Charles¬ 
ton  Railroad  uninjured.  Abolitionists  left  dead  and  wounded  in  the 
field.  Our  cavalry  in  hot  pursuit. 

G.  T.  Beauregard, 

General ,  Commanding. 

General  S.  Cooper, 

Adjutant  and  Inspector-  General ,  Richmond ,  Va. 


Report  of  Commander  1  Voodhull,  TJ.  S.  Navy ,  of  the  arrival  of  the 
IT.  S.  S.  Seneca ,  and  explaining  the  delay  in  dispatching  the  steamer 
Governor  Milton  to  Ossabaw  Island ,  Georgia. 

U.  S.  S.  Cimarron, 

St.  Johils  River ,  Florida ,  October  22,  1862. 
Sir:  Yesterday  morning  the  gunboat  Seneca  arrived  off  the  bar.  I 
immediately  sent  a  boat  to  communicate  with  her.  I  did  not  get  your 
dispatch  till  3  p.  m.  I  then  immediately  gave  orders  to  have  the  Gov¬ 
ernor  Milton  got  ready  to  proceed  without  any  unnecessary  delay  as 
you  directed.  There  was  something  to  be  done  to  the  engine,  which 
would  take,  it  is  said,  a  couple  of  hours.  At  the  termination  of  that 
time  steam  was  got  up  and  I  expected  to  see  her  en  route  a  few 
moments  after,  but  unfortunately  something  broke  down  and,  in  con¬ 
sequence,  the  steam  had  to  be  let  off  and  work  recommenced  on  her.  I 
have  had  my  engineers  and  mechanics  at  work  all  night  getting  her  in 
steaming  order  again,  and  I  am  happy  to  inform  you  that  she  left  for 
her  destination  this  morning  at  11  a.  m. 

I  have  put  on  board  of  her  the  Cimarroii’s  12-pounder  howitzer, 
with  sufficient  ammunition  to  aid  in  her  protection  should  an  effort  be 
made  to  intercept  her;  also  a  week’s  provisions  for  all  hands. 

1  gave  orders  regarding  the  scows,  and  it  is  not  practical.  The 
scows  can  not  be  got  through  Sister’s  Creek.  The  captain  of  the  Gov¬ 
ernor  Milton  was  very  desirious  to  accomplish  it,  but  he  assures  me, 
upon  further  inspection  of  the  creek,  that  it  is  impossible  to  be  done. 
I  have  further  the  opinion  of  my  executive  officer  and  pilot,  both  con¬ 
curring  in  the  same  statement.  I  consequently  was  obliged  reluc¬ 
tantly  to  give  it  up.  1  think  the  scows  are  hardly  worth  moving  that 
distance;  they  are  old,  leaky,  water-logged,  and  float  deeply. 

I  regret  that  I  have  been  unable  to  execute  all  your  orders,  but  the 
circumstances  have  controlled  1113-  wishes  to  do  so. 

The  little  steamer  is  a  great  loss  to  us,  as  she  could  be  made  very 
useful  in  various  ways;  besides,  with  the  battery  I  have  placed  on 
board  of  her  (two  24-pounders),  she  could  have  aided  me  much  in  keep¬ 
ing  possession  of  the  river.  There  have  been  seen  at  various  times  in 
the  last  two  days  small  groups  of  guerrillas  wandering  about  in  this 
neighborhood  0:1  both  banks  of  the  river.  They  have  even  approached 


SOUTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


407 


the  vicinity  of  the  entrance  of  the  harbor.  I  have  been  unable  to 
reach  them  as  yet,  as  they,  too,  cautiously  keep  without  the  range  of 
our  guns;  how  large  their  force  may  be  back  of  this  I  am  unable  to 
ascertain.  1  think  we  ought  to  have  an  additional  vessel  if  it  is  desir¬ 
able  to  keep  the  river  open  to  its  whole  extent.  Without  that  addi¬

Letter  from  Rear-Admiral  Du  Pont,  U.  8.  Navy,  to  the  Assistant  Sec¬ 
retary  of  the  Navy  regarding  movements  of  the  blockading  vessels 
during  his  absence  and  his  need  of  reinforcements. 

[Private  and  confidential.]  Flagship  Wabash, 

Peat  Royal  Harbor,  8.  C.,  October  33,  1863. 
My  Dear  Sir:  I  reached  here  last  evening  after  a  pleasant  run, 
calling  off  Charleston.  Two  schooners  had  been  taken  within  a  few 
days  and  a  large  English  steamer  run  on  shore  113-  the  Flambeau  under 
Moultrie.  She  was  on  her  beam  ends  as  I  passed  at  high  water  yester¬ 
day,  but  they  were  doubtless  getting  her  cargo  out,  for  a  tug  was 
alongside  of  her,  and  I  fear  her  engine  will  be  taken  for  one  of  the 
rams. 

The  Racer  had  been  in  and  came  out  that  day.  At  night  some  white 
lights  were  seen  made  by  her;  it  is  thought  to  this  steamer.  She  was 
flushed  b3T  the  Blunt,  but  not  a  breath  of  wind  for  her  to  get  under¬ 
way;  her  fire  made  Upshur  slip.  The  steamer  going  b3T  at  lightning- 
speed,  he  shelled  and  chased,  and  the  fellow  ran  her  up  high  and  dry 
on  the  spit  off  Moultrie. 

I  heard  on  my  arrival  here  that  an  expedition  had  been  sent  up  Broad 
River  of  4,500  men,  with  many  gunboats,  to  cut  the  railroad  bridge 
at  Pocotaligo  and  as  a  feint  for  a  further  expedition  to  the  Ogeechee. 
1  regretted  such  things  were  attempted  in  my  absence  by  General 
Mitchel,  absorbing  my  vessels  from  the  blockade,  which,  of  course, 
could  not  be  refused  him  by  the  senior  officer  present,  and  this,  with 
nothing  pending  or  to  result  from  them  if  successful,  not  an3T  more 
than  burning  a  wood  pile  or  the  wharf,  to  be  replaced  in  a  week. 

It  was  a  complete  failure,  with  heavy  loss;  the  troops  ventured  out 
of  reach  of  the  gunboats,  and,  though  behaving  well,  were  thrashed 
by  an  inferior  force,  well  posted,  full  information  of  the  movement 
having  been  carried  to  the  rebels  by  faithless  or  spy  contrabands.  I

saw  a  portion  of  the  poor,  wounded  fellows  landing,  said  to  bo  400  in

Charleston  instead  of  here  we  would  have  had  that  steamer,  doubtless

A  few  items  now  as  to  my  wants: 

1st.  Do  not  forget  the  tugs  and  ferryboats  and  small  dispatch  har¬

2d.  Please  put  a  200[-pounder]  Parrott  rifle  on  the  Huron  and 
send  her  out  as  soon  as  possible;  had  I  been  here  she  never  would 
have  moved  a  foot;  her  sickness  was  not  yellow  fever,  the  onl}T  con¬

1th.  The  Pacer  told  Green  that  the  defenses  of  Charleston  Harbor

has  one.  You  forget  these  rams,  I  think;  if  we  have  to  divert  two 
ironclads  for  them  not  many  of  your  proposed  force  will  be  left  for

You  had  better  have  some  10,000  men  sent  out  here  at  once,  or 
these  troops,  but  for  the  squadron,  will  be  driven  into  the  sea  and  we 
shall  lose  Beaufort.  Mitchel  is  quite  ready  for  James  Island  when 
the  time  comes,  but  he  has  no  means. 

Respectfully,  etc. , 

S.  F.  Du  Pont,

Capture  of  the  British  steamers  Scotia  and  Anglia ,  October  2 If.  and  27,

Report  of  Rear-Admiral  Du  Pont,  D.  S.  Navy. 


Flagship  Wabash, 

Pcrrt  Royal  Harbor,  S.  C. ,  October  29,  1862. 

Sir:  I  have  the  pleasure  to  report  to  the  Department  the  capture,  on 
the  24th  instant,  of  the  British  steamer  Scotia  by  the  U.  S.  bark 
Restless,  Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  E.  Conroy,  commanding,  off' 
Bull’s  Bay. 

The  steamer  was  discovered  at  daylight  standing  toward  Bull’s 
Island.  Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  Conroy  immediately  got  under¬ 
way  with  his  vessel,  and  at  the  same  time  sent  two  armed  boats  to  the 
leeward  of  the  steamer,  which  forced  her  to  run  ashore.  He  then  ran 
in  with  the  Restless  to  cut  her  off  and  keep  her  from  running  out 
should  she  get  off  before  the  boats  could  reach  her.  When  the  boats 
got  alongside  it  was  discovered  that  the  captain,  an  old  offender  named 
Libby,  with  a  gentleman  and  a  lady  (passengers),  had  left  the  steamer 
in  an  open  boat.  The  crew  were  in  a  state  of  intoxication,  so  that  they 


410 


SOUTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


became  almost  unmanageable,  and  Acting’  Volunteer  Lieutenant  Conroy 
ordered  them  to  be  transferred  on  board  the  Restless  and  put  in  irons. 
Acting- Volunteer  Lieutenant  Conroy  did  not  succeed  in  getting  her  oh 
until  the  morning  of  the  26th,  during  which  time  he  was  obliged  to 
anchor  with  the  Restless  within  gunshot  of  the  prize  to  protect  her, 
and  at  low  tide  his  own  vessel  touched  bottom  several  times,  but  with¬ 
out  sustaining  any  material  injury.  He  reports  the  loss  by  drowning 
of  John  Martin  (seaman),  of  the  Restless,  a, nd  a  fireman  of  the  Scotia 
in  consequence  of  the  swamping  of  a  boat  in  trying  to  get  out  a  hawser. 

In  getting  off  the  Scotia  and  afterwards  in  bringing  her  to  Port 
Royal  the  engineers  of  that  vessel  rendered  every  assistance  in  their 
power,  for  which  Lieutenant  Conroy  promised  that  they  should  receive 
compensation. 

I  have  further  the  honor  to  report  the  capture  at  Bull’s  Bay,  on  the 
27th  instant,  of  the  British  steamer  Anglia  by  the  boats  of  the  U.  S.  S. 
Flag. 

The  Restless ,  then  under  command  of  Acting  Master  Griswold 
(Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  Conroy  being  temporarily  absent  on 
duty  in  the  Scotia ),  had  discovered  the  steamer  entering  Bull’s  Bay 
the'evening  before,  but  she  having  passed  so  far  to  windward  of  her 
the  Restless  could  not  prevent  her  getting  in,  and  having  only  one 
small  boat  belonging  to  the  ship,  Acting  Master  Griswold  did  not  think 
it  prudent  to  send  her  in  pursuit,  but  he  got  the  Restless  in  a  position 
to  command  the  channel  for  the  purpose  of  preventing  the  escape  of 
the  steamer.  On  the  next  day  the  Flag ,  having  Acting  Volunteer 
Lieutenant  Conroy  on  board,  on  his  way  to  join  his  vessel,  arrived  at 
the  anchorage  of  the  Restless ,  and  on  receiving  the  above  information 
Commander  Strong,  under  the  pilotage  of  Acting  Volunteer  Lieuten¬ 
ant  Conroy,  ran  the  Flag  close  to  the  bar,  which  his  vessel  could  not 
cross,  and  dispatched  four  armed  boats,  under  charge  of  Lieutenant- 
Commander  Carpenter  and  Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  Conroy, 
inside  of  Bull’s  Island. 

The  steamer  was  discovered  on  shore  near  Jack’s  Creek,  about  4 
miles  from  the  entrance  of  Bull’s  Bay,  but  was  soon  safely  got  off,  all 
of  her  officers  and  crew  being  on  board  (except  the  pilot  and  six  men 
who  had  gone  to  Charleston  the  evening  previous)  and,  according  to 
Lieutenant-Commander  Carpenter’s  report,  rendered  every  assistance 
in  getting  her  off.  Lieutenant  Conroy  piloted  the  Anglia  out  of  Bull’s 
Bay  and  over  the  bar. 

The  Anglia  when  captured  was  almost  out  of  coal,  and  was  sent 
by  Captain  Godon,  senior  officer  off  Charleston,  to  this  harbor  to  be 
supplied.  She  is  the  same  vessel  which  attempted,  on  the  night  of 
the  19th  of  September  last,  to  enter  Charleston  Harbor  by  Sanford’s 
[Lawford]  Channel,  but  was  headed  off,  though  she  succeeded  in  escap¬ 
ing  in  the  darkness.  I  shall  dispatch  both  of  these  steamers  north  as 
soon  as  practicable. 

Before  closing  this  dispatch  1  can  not  forbear  calling  the  attention 
of  the  Department  to  the  energy  and  activity  shown  on  all  occasions 
by  Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  Conroy,  of  the  Restless. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

S.  F.  Du  Pont, 

Rear-Admiral ,  Comdg.  South  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron.  ' 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  JVavy ,  Washington.

Report  of  Acting  Lieutenant  Conroy,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  TJ.  S.  bark  Restless,  regarding 

the  capture  of  the  steamer  Scotia. 

U.  S.  Bark  Restless, 

Off  BulVs  Bay ,  South  Carolina ,  October  2 6 ,  1862. 

Sir:  1  have  the  pleasure  of  reporting  to  you  the  capture  of  the 
British  steamer  Scotia  by  the  Bestless,  under  ni3r  command,  for  violat¬ 
ing  the  blockade  at  Bull’s  Bay. 

At  daylight,  the  24th  instant,  a  steamer  was  discovered  standing 
toward  Bull's  Island.  I  immediately  got  underway,  at  the  same  time 
sending  two  armed  boats  to  the  leeward  of  the  steamer,  and  forced 
her  to  run  ashore.  I  was  then  obliged  to  run  in  with  the  Bestless  to 
cut  her  off  and  keep  her  from  running  out  should  she  get  off  before 
the  boats  could  reach  her. 

When  the  boats  came  alongside  it  was  discovered  that  the  captain, 
with  a  gentleman  and  lady  (passengers),  had  left  the  steamer  in  an  open 
boat,  and  the  crew  were  in  a  state  of  intoxication,  so  that  they  became 
almost  unmanageable.  1  ordered  them  to  be  transferred  on  board  the 
Bestless  and  put  in  irons. 

In  trying  to  get  the  schooner  afloat  her  engineers  have  done  the 
utmost  in  their  power  to  assist  us,  but  one  of  the  boilers  giving  way 
prevented  us  from  success.  I  was  therefore  obliged  to  anchor  with 
the  Bestless  within  gunshot  of  the  prize  to  protect  her,  which  left  the 
Bestless  at  low  tide  in  a  very  heavy  sea,  touching  bottom  several  times, 
but  as  soon  as  the  tide  ran  in  she  was  got  off  and  anchored  in  deeper 
water.  She  sustained  no  damage,  but  leaks  some. 

The  boilers  and  machinery  having  been  repaired  under  my  personal 
supervision,  I  succeeded  this  morning  in  getting  the  Scotia  oft  and 
brought  her  to  the  fleet  off  Charleston. 

I  regret  to  have  to  report  the  loss  by  drowning  of  John  Martin, 
landsman,  of  the  Bestless ,  and  one  fireman  of  the  Scotia ,  the  boat 
having  swamped  in  trying  to  get  out  a  hawser. 

I  consider  it  my  duty  to  recommend  the  engineers  of  the  Scotia  for 
their  hearty  cooperation  in  getting  her  off  and  bringing  her  to  Charles¬ 
ton,  and  1  could  not  do  otherwise  but  promise  them  compensation. 

1  have  detailed  Acting  Master  J.  B.  Rogers  to  take  charge  of  the 
prize. 

I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Edw.  Conroy, 

Acting  Lieutenant ,  Commanding. 

Captain  S.  W.  Godon, 

Comdg.  Charleston  Blockade ,  TJ.  S.  S.  Frigate  Pcnvhatan.

Report  of  Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  Conroy,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  TJ.  S.  bark  Rest¬ 
less,  regarding  the  capture  of  the  steamer  Anglia. 

U.  S.  Bark  Restless, 

Bulks  Bay ,  South  Carolina ,  October  27 ,  1862. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  of  reporting  to  you  the  capture  of  the  English 
steamer  Anglia  by  the  armed  boats  of  the  U .  S.  S.  Flag ,  under  the 
command  of  Lieutenant-Commander  Charles  C.  Carpenter  and  myself, 
under  the  following  circumstances: 

On  my  return  from  the  Charleston  blockading  squadron  (where  I 
had  been  to  deliver  the  prize  steamer  Scotia ,  captured  by  the  Restless 
on  the  24th  instant)  in  the  U.  S.  S.  Flag ,  we  met  the  Restless  making- 
signals  for  assistance.  Acting  Ensign  Henry  Eason  came  on  board  the 
Flag  and  reported  that  another  steamer  had  run  into  Bull’s  Bay  Chan¬ 
nel  on  Sunday  afternoon,  but  so  far  out  of  the  range  of  our  guns  that 
it  was  impossible  to  bring  her  to.  At  the  time  it  blew  a  heav}-  gale 
from  the  N.  W.,  and  having  only  one  small  five-oared  boat  (the  other 
one  was  lost  in  getting  out  the  Scotia),  Acting  Master  William  N. 
Griswold,  then  in  charge  of  the  Restless,  did  not  deem  it  prudent  to 
send  her  in  for  the  purpose  of  cutting  out  the  steamer. 

He  put  the  ship  in  such  a  position,  however,  [as]  to  prevent  her 
coming  out  during  the  night. 

So  soon  as  Commander  Strong  and  myself  received  this  report,  Com¬ 
mander  Strong  ordered  four  boats  to  be  armed  and  manned  and 
requested  me  to  pilot  the  Flag  inside  the  bar;  but  the  tide  being  ebb, 
the  water  was  too  low  to  admit  the  Flag  entering,  and  we  anchored  as 
near  as  prudent  under  the  circumstances.  The  boats  then  left  the  ship 
in  command  of  Lieutenant-Commander  Charles  C.  Carpenter,  of  the 
Flag,  and  myself.  On  entering  the  inner  channel,  we  found  the 
steamer,  which  proved  to  be  the  Anglia,  from  Nassau,  aground  in 
front  of  Jacks  Creek,  4  miles  inside  from  Bull’s  Island  light-house, 
and  took  possession  of  her. 

The  pilot,  Thomas  Jones  (a  Charleston  pilot),  had  left,  with  some 
passengers,  through  the  inner  channel  for  Charleston.  The  steamer 
was  gotten  off  with  very  little  trouble,  and  1  piloted  her  out  and  came 
to  anchor  under  the  protection  of  the  guns  of  the  Flag  and  the  Rest¬ 
less,  at  7:30  p.  m. 

I  left  the  Anglia  in  charge  of  Lieutenant-Commander  Carpenter, 
reported  myself  to  Commander  Strong,  and  then  repaired  on  board 

the  Restless. 

Enclosed  I  forward  a  copy  of  the  report  of  Acting  Master  William 
N.  Griswold,  whom  I  left  in  command  of  the  Restless  during  the  time 


MOUTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON.  413 

I  went  to  deliver  the  prize  steamer  Scotia  to  the  senior  officer  off 
Charleston. 

1  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  }'our  obedient  servant, 

Edwd.  Conroy,

Report  of  Acting  Master  Griswold,  U.  S.  Navy,  of  the  R.  S.  bark  Restless,  regarding  his 
proceedings  with  reference  to  the  steamer  Anglia. 

U.  S.  Bark  Bestless, 

Bull’s  Bay,  October  25  [27],  1862. 

Sir:  I  submit  to  you  the  following-  report  with  regard  to  my  pro¬ 
ceedings  with  the  steamer  Anglia,  now  a  prize  to  this  bark  and  the 
Flag : 

Yesterday  afternoon  at  4:30  a  sail  was  reported  standing  in;  soon 
made  her  out  to  be  a  steamer;  all  thought  the  Scotia ,  stopping.  We 
concluded  her  machinery  had  given  out.  Soon,  however,  she  started 
again  and  slowly  passing  our  bows,  full  4  miles  distant;  then  I  saw  it 
was  not  the  Scotia ,  though  evidently  a  sister  ship.  Knowing  that  once 
inside  she  was  in  a  trap,  for  there  was  not  enough  of  water  for  her  to 
reach  the  mainland,  I  waited  patiently  till  she  was  well  in,  and  then 
guarded  the  channel;  then  fired  three  guns  as  a  signal  to  the  Flag. 
As  there  was  no  answer,  at  dark  1  sent  up  two  rockets  and  burned 
Coston’s  signals  in  the  maintopmast  crosstrees,  hoping  that  the  Flag 
would  see  them  and  come  to  my  assistance.  Receiving  no  answer, 
concluded  to  wait  until  morning  and  procure  assistance,  for  I  was  with¬ 
out  means  to  cut  her  out,  having  but  one  small  boat  and  hardly  enough 
men  to  handle  the  ship  if  aught  happened  to  her.  With  the  number 
of  prisoners  on  board  I  did  not  think  it  prudent  to  run  the  risk  trying 
to  do  it  alone,  so  this  morning  I  got  the  ship  underway  to  look  for 
assistance.  The  Flag  hove  in  sight  at  11:30  a.  m. ,  and  at  1  p.  m. 
I  sent  an  officer  on  board  to  report  to  you  the  fact  of  the  steamer  being- 
inside.  I  followed  the  Flag  in  and  came  to  anchor  near  her. 

I  am,  sir,  yours,  most  respectfully, 

W.  N.  Griswold, 

Acting  Master  and  Executive  Officer,  U.  S.  Bark  Bestless. 

Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  Edwd.  Conroy, 

Commanding  U.  S.  Bark  Bestless,  Bulls  Bay,  S.  C.

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  to  you  the  capture  of  the  British 
steamer  Anglia,  from  Nassau,  New  Providence,  October  21,  1862, 
yesterday  afternoon  by  the  boats  of  this  ship. 

On  my  way  to  Bull’s  Bay  yesterday  I  met  the  U.  S.  bark  Bestless, 
which  reported  a  steamer  gone  in  at  5  p.  m.  the  previous  evening.

Letter  from  Captain  Dahlgren ,  U.  8.  Navy,  to  the  Secretary  of  the 
Navy ,  accepting  command  of  a  single  vessel. 

Bureau  of  Ordnance,  October  25,  1862. 

Sir:  Permit  me  to  assure  you  that  I  have  not  the  most  remote  idea 
of  imputing  to  you  an  intention  to  inflict  any  humiliation  on  me,  and 
I  regret  that  the  terms  used  by  me  should  have  been  susceptible  of 
such  construction.  Nor  did  1  think  of  seeking-  to  command  the  forces 
that  were  to  enter  Charleston  Harbor,  unless  perfectly  agreeable  to 
Admiral  Du  Pont.  My  application  was  deferred  so  as  to  have  it  con¬ 
venient  for  you  to  consult  him  on  his  return  north  and  you  may  remem¬ 
ber  that  I  suggested  the  enquiry  of  him.  I  beg  leave  to  explain  myself, 
though  briefly,  upon  another  topic  of  my  letter. 

The  Senate  has  virtually  decided  not  to  recognize  by  vote  any  serv¬ 
ice,  even  in  action,  performed  by  commanders  of  single  vessels  of  the 
force  engaged. 

Upon  such  a  vote,  however,  depends  by  law  the  extension  of  the 
term  of  service  on  the  active  list,  and  as  a  consequence  this  is  only 
accessible  to  the  flag-officers  of  the  force. 

As  an  officer  junior  to  myself  had  received  this  opportunity,  with 
the  flag  of  a  rear-admiral,  I  only  desired  a  like  privilege,  which  could 
not  be  conferred  by  the  command  of  a  single  vessel,  and  ventured  to 
suggest  reasons  therefor  which  might  be  of  public  interest. 

It  is  perfectly  correct,  as  observed  by  the  Department,  that  its  oiler 
to  me  of  the  command  of  one  of  the  vessels  that  is  to  enter  Charleston 
Harbor  is  not  an  order,  and  therefore  not  mandatory,  but  it  is  so  in 
effect,  because,  as  before  stated,  it  would  not  become  an  officer  to 
decline  a  tender  of  active  service  under  the  circumstances  even  if  other 
vessels  of  similar  class  on  the  same  service  are  commanded  by  officers 
whose  grades  are  one  or  perhaps  two  below  mine. 

Wherefore  I  feel  constrained  to  accept  the  command  of  that  single 
vessel  whatever  the  personal  sacrifice  may  be. 

It  is  entirely  unnecessary  for  me  to  say  that  my  services  are  alwaj^s 
subject  to  any  disposition  which  may  please  the  Department. 

In  conclusion,  I  hope  you  will  accept  my  thanks  for  the  kindness 
with  which  you  have  been  pleased  to  express  yourself,  and  for  which  I 
am  gratefully  sensible. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  most  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Jno.  A.  Dahlgren. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Nary.

Confidential  report  of  Rear-Admiral  Du  Pont ,  TI.  8.  Navy ,  trans¬ 
mitting  report  regarding  the  construction  of  ironclads  at  Charleston , 

S.  C.,  and  Savannah ,  Ga. 

Confidential.]  Flagship  Wabash, 

Port  Royal  Harbor ,  S.  C. ,  October  25,  1862. 

Sir:  I  enclose  copy  of  a  communication  of  the  21st  instant  from 
Lieutenant-Commander  Scott,  of  the  Sebago,  giving  information 
derived  from  a  deserter  from  Savannah. 

Whatever  inaccuracies  there  may  be  in  the  details  of  such  state¬ 
ments,  there  is  a  general  concurrence  as  to  certain  points  which  should 
be  noted,  viz,  that  three  ironclads  with  rams  are  building  at  Savannah 
and  two  at  Charleston;  2d,  the  Fingal ,  all  agree,  has  a  very  powerful 
engine.  When  she  is  completed  it  is  the  intention  to  take  up  the 
Nashville  and  clad  her. 

This  man  reports  he  overheard  a  conversation  between  General 
Mercer  and  Commodore  Tattnall,  in  which  the  former  said  “They 
are  moving  in  Virginia;  we  ought  to  be  doing  something  here.” 
“Yes,”  replied  Tattnall,  “We  ought;  but  I  am  not  going  to  sea  in 
this  vessel  alone.  I  must  be  joined  by  the  Charleston  vessels.” 

The  idea  seems  to  be  to  open  the  Savannah  River,  then  come  to 
Port  Royal,  and  thence  off  Charleston  and  raise  the  blockade,  etc. 

Since  the  above  was  written,  two  contrabands  have  come  in,  one  a 
stevedore,  who  works  on  the  wharves;  both  more  intelligent  than  the 
white  man.  They  state  the  Fingal  to  be  ready;  think  she  will  draw 
a  great  deal  of  water,  however  (16  feet),  her  roof  nearly  down  to  the 
water’s  edge;  two  others  are  building;  a  third  was  commenced,  but 
the  work  was  stopped  for  some  reason. 

They  confirm  the  report  that  the  Nashville  is  laid  up,  having  been 
entirely  unloaded  of  her  cotton,  and  is  moored  at  the  railroad  bridge, 
15  miles  from  Savannah.  Large  quantities  of  cotton  are  collecting  in 
Savannah,  all  baled  for  storage.  Four  thousand  contrabands  are  at 
work  round  Savannah;  all  would  leave  and  come  to  the  coast  if  they 
dared. 

I  submit  that  the  Ironsides  and  Passaic  should  be  dispatched  at  an 
early  day. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

S.  F.  Du  Pont, 

Rear-Admiral ,  Comdg.  South  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron. 

Hon.  G.  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy,  Washington.

Report  of  Captain  Godon,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  commanding  TJ.  S.  S.  Pow¬ 
hatan,  of  his  arrival  off  Charleston,  S.  C. ,  and  regarding  the  stations 
of  certain  vessels  on  the  blockade. 

U.  S.  S.  Powhatan, 

Off  Charleston,  October  26,  1862. 

My  Dear  Admiral:  I  arrived  here  in  proper  time  yesterday;  the 
Seneca  and  Memphis ,  although  starting  two  hours  before  us,  got  here 
after  the  Keystone  State. 


SOUTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


419 


This  morning  I  moved  the  Quaker  City  much  nearer  in,  as  also  this 
ship,  and  1  have  placed  the  Seneca  where  the  Blunt  was,  making  the 
Blunt  more  of  a  picket  by  putting  her  along  the  reef  three-fourths  of 
a  mile  more  to  the  northward  and  eastward.  The  Memphis  will  run , 
at  night  between  Bull's  Bay  and  the  outside  point  of  the  Rattlesnake 
Shoal.  It  seems  to  me  that  no  vessel  attempting  to  come  in  that  way 
could  do  it  without  making  the  land  to  the  north  and  then  following 
down  the  shoals  along  the  land.  A  vessel  there  underway  can  give 
warning  to  those  inshore  by  firing  and  prevent  the  blockade  breaker 
from  getting  almost  upon  the  vessels  without  being  seen.  The  vessel 
that  ran  on  shore  is  now  lying  on  her  beam  ends,  with  her  masts  almost 
along  the  water.  1  ran  in  with  this  ship  at  low  water  to  quarter  less 
4  fathoms  and  could  see  her  in  that  condition,  bottom  pretty  well  up; 
at  high  tide  she  is  well  covered,  and  the  sand  being  quick,  she  will 
sink  too  far  for  anything  to  be  got  out  of  her.  Steamers  were  not 
even  at  work  near  her.  Green  seems  to  think  that  but  little  could 
have  been  got  from  her  and  nothing  can  be  obtained  now.  I  shall 
hold  on  to  the  Flambeau  until  the  moon  increases  as  she  is  very  neces¬ 
sary  here. 

******* 

This  ship  will  have  to  return  about  the  same  time  to  fill  up,  but  I 
will  not  move  until  the  moon  is  large.  The  Flambeau  must  have 
struck  the  beached  steamer,  otherwise  I  can  not  see  why  she  should 
have  sunk  where  she  now  is.  I  shall  attend  to  the  matter  of  the  Best- 
less  (getting  the  Charleston  paper)  to-morrow.  I  noticed  when  1  stood 
in  to-day  something  like  a  thousand  troops  marching  from  Fort  Moul¬ 
trie  down  toward  the  lower  batteries.  As  it  was  near  sundown,  it 
may  have  been  the  reliefs;  we  could  see  them  quite  distinctly. 

The  tide  is  about  half  an  hour  of  being  full  and  we  are  keeping  an 
awfully  sharp  lookout  about  this  time.  We  don’t  sleep  much  here 


you  know,  except  at  low  water.
