Letter  from  Captain  Rodgers,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  to  Rear-Admiral  Du  Pont, 
U.  S.  Navy,  offering  suggestions  in  regard  to  attacks  upon  forts  by 
mailed  vessels. 

Lb  S.  S.  Galena, 

Off  Newport  News ,  October  29,  1862. 
Dear  Admiral:  I  have  some  diffidence  in  offering  thoughts' in  regard 
to  attacks  upon  forts  by  mailed  vessels.  I  presume  that  generally, 
however,  officers  charged  with  such  great  responsibilities  as  yourself 
are  not  unwilling  to  receive  suggestions  in  order  to  combine  such  as 
may  seem  good  with  your  own  ideas,  leaving  it  to  your  greater  expe¬ 
rience  and  better  judgment  to  modify  or  reject  what  I  offer. 

I  start  with  two  propositions,  first,  that  Fort  Sumter  has  the  most 
formidable  artillery  that  the  Confederacy  can  either  make  or  procure; 
next,  that  you  will  seek  to  conquer  while  receiving  the  least  damage; 
to  run  no  risk  not  necessary  to  success;  to  avoid  every  chance  of  injury 
so  far  as  this  avoidance  comports  with  the  ends  desired. 

If  we  can  find  a  distance  at  which  our  projectiles  will  breach  a  fort 
while  the  fire  of  the  fort  will  be  harmless  against  our  ironclads,  we 
shall  have  solved  a  very  necessary  problem.  If,  upon  studying  a 


422  SOUTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON 

» 

chart,  we  find  that  a  harbor  admits  of  taking  a  position  destructive  to 
the  enemy  and  secure  to  our  vessels,  then,  humanly  speaking,  it  only 
remains  to  make  the  attack  to  insure  victory. 

Experiments  at  iron  targets  representing  the  resistance  of  ships 
throw  valuable  light.  Unhappity  we  are  without  the  information 
which  our  experiments  would  give,  if  we  have  made  any.  The  Eng¬ 
lish  trials,  however,  come  into  play. 

At  Shoeburyness  the  English  Government  has  tried  the  heaviest 
artillery  which  the  manufacturers  felt  inclined  to  ofler  against  a  sec¬ 
tion  of  the  Warrior’s  side — like  that  of  the  Gloire  and  our  own  Iron¬ 
sides,  4i  inches  of  iron  plate,  backed  with  wood.  . 

Sir  William  Armstrong’s  gun  failed  to  pierce  this  targetat600  yards, 
but  the  Whitworth  gun,  at  600  yards,  “  was  found  successful  not  only 
with  shot,  but  even  with  shell.” 

The  only  account  which  I  have  seen  of  the  recent  experiments  at 
Shoeburyness  is  a  very  incomplete  one  from  the  Liverpool  Times..  The 
Liverpool  Times  quotes  the  London  Times  upon  the  same  subject  to 
the  following  effect:  “No  gun  has  yet  been  produced  which  could 
pierce  the  sides  of  a  frigate  like  the  Warrior  at  3,000  yards,  or  even 
half  that  distance.”  I  learn  from  the  article  that  a  gun  can  pierce  44 
inches  of  iron  heavdly  backed  with  wood  at  600  yards’  distance  both 
with  shot  and  with  shell;  but  that  at  1,500  yards  it  is  impenetrable. 

I  think  that  it  will  be  safe  to  assume  that  at  1,200  or  1,300  yards  our 
ironclads  will  be  secure;  but  at  a  distance  somewhat  greater  than  this 
Beauregard  breached  the  walls  of  Fort  Sumter.  The  range  of  5-second 
fuzes  is  about  1,350  yards. 

In  a  line  drawn  from  Fort  Sumter  about  N.’N.  W.,  at  the  distance 
of  1,200  or  1,300  yards,  is  a  point  in  the  middle  of  the  harbor,  about 
2,200  yards  from  Fort  Moultrie  and  the  same  distance  from  Fort 
Johnson. 

Describe  the  arc  of  a  circle,  say  1,250  yards,  from  Fort  Sumter  as 
a  center,  let  one  end  of  the  arc  be  a  mile,  or  1,760  yards,  from  Fort 
Moultrie,  and  the  other  end  the  same  distance  from  Fort  Johnson. 
This  arc,  so  bounded,  will  be  half  a  mile  in  extent,  on  it  the  ships  may 
lie  so  far  apart  that  a  shot  aimed  at  one  can  hit  no  other  vessel.  This 
meets  the  problem  on  the  first  page. 

Lastly,  it  will  be  preferable  to  take  too  great  a  distance  at  first  and 
then  close  in,  rather  than  fall  into  the  opposite  error  of  going  too  near 
at  first  and  then  withdrawing. 

The  exact  distance  which  you  may  decide  to  take  can  easily  be  picked 
up  by  the  ships  by  measuring  with  a  sextant  the  angle  subtended  either 
by  the  height  of  the  fort  or  its  sides  upon  a  given  bearing. 

An}'-  officer  from  the  Naval  Academy  will  calculate  the  necessary 
angle. 

I  should  be  inclined  to  anchor — better  aim,  less  danger  from 
torpedoes. 

All  theoretical  rules  insist  upon  the  concentration  of  force.  In  act¬ 
ual  warfare  this  is  rarely  possible,  except  to  such  genius  as  that  of 
Napoleon.  In  Charleston  it  becomes  so  easy  that  it  would  be  a  pity 
to  neglect  it. 

When  the  ironclads  come  out  overwhelm  them  with  your  whole 
force;  then  take  the  forts  successively  in  quiet. 

I  have  amused  myself  in  attempting  to  place  the  mortar  boats  in 
Charleston  Harbor.  I  was  embarrassed  to  find  a  position  for  them. 


SOUTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON- 


423 


Do  the  creeks  from  Stono  offer  one? 

Any  vessels  you  may  have  to  push  up  the  Cooper  and  Ashley  should 
have  good  protection  from  sharpshooters,  especially  for  the  pilot  and 
helmsman.  This  I  have  learned  in  James  River. 

Of  course  I  do  not  expect  you,  admiral,  to  do  more  than  receive 
this  as  the  honest  conviction  of  one  who  has  a  deep  interest  in  your 
success;  and  who  confides  in  your  own  straightforward  purposes  to 
accept  it  as  an  humble  offering,  to  be  put  in  the  crucible  of  your  judg¬ 
ment  and  come  out  for  what  it  is  worth. 

The  problem  of  distance  is  original  with  me,  though  other  people 
have,  no  doubt,  discussed  the  same  question.  It  is  of  such  high  im¬ 
portance  that  had  I  to  solve  it  I  should  call  in  more  knowledge  than  I 
profess  to  have. 

Captain  Dahlgren  was  on  board  to-day.  I  mentioned  the  subject  to 
him  and  told  him  that  he  was  better  able  to  decide  the  question  involved 
than  anyone  I  knew. 

Yeiy  respectfully  and  affectionately, 

John  Rodgers. 

Admiral  Du  Pont. 


Lett er  from  Lear- Admiral  Du  Pont ,  U.  jS.  Navy ,  to  Commodore 
Bailey ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  regarding  the  defenses  of  Charleston ,  S.  C. 


Wabash, 

Port  Royal,  /S.  C. ,  October  30 ,  1862. 

My  Dear  Bailee:  *  *  *  I  hope  under  Providence  that  I  may 

continue  to  meet  the  expectations  of  my  naval  friends.  I  feel  that 
very  heavv  work  is  before  me,  for  there  seems  a  morbid  appetite  in 
the  land  to  have  Charleston.  It  is  natural  it  should  be  so  for  two  rea¬ 
sons — it  is  the  cradle  of  this  wicked  rebellion;  secondly,  our  armies 
have  been  a  dead  failure,  and  but  for  the  Navy  the  nation  would  now 
be  in  sackcloth  and  ashes,  perhaps  suing  for  peace;  certainly  foreign 
intervention  would  have  been  upon  us.  If  a  single  tithe  of  that  Poto¬ 
mac  army  had  been  sent  to  this  region  after  the  capture  of  the  forts 
here,  Savannah  and  Charleston  would  have  fallen  with  scarcely  any 
loss  of  life  under  a  joint  operation.  The  difficulties  to  be  overcome 
now  have  increased  a  thousandfold  since  then.  English  people  who 
have  been  into  Charleston  call  it  a  Sebastopol,  and  smile  at  the  idea  of 
its  being  taken.  The  Department  thinks  it  can  be  done  with  a  few 
monitors,  and  talks  of  four;  Ingraham  has  two  inside,  so  that  two 
more  are  expected  to  take  nine  forts.  You  are  aware  there  is  “no  run¬ 
ning  by;”  the  harbor  is  a  bog,  or  cut  de  sac,  to  say  nothing  of  obstruc¬ 
tions,  which  ironclads  are  much  less  serviceable  in  removing,  as  you 
know,  than  wooden  vessels  with  their  boats  and  appliances.  I  hope 
and  believe  we  can  do  the  job  as  well  as  most  people.  I  shall  certainly 
try.  All  this  between  ourselves. 

*  *  *  *  *  '*•' 

Most  trulv,  your  friend, 

S.  F.  Du  Pont. 

Commodore  Bailey,  U.  S.  Navy, 

Sackett's  Harbor,  New  York.

Sir:  I  respectfully  report  that  while  up  the  Folly  River,  near  the 
mouth  of  what  is  called  Light-House  Creek,  on  Fiiday,  Octobei  oO,  I 
saw  very  distinctly  from  the  masthead  the  rebel  camps  around  beces- 
sionville  and  theirline  of  fortifications  stretching  over  toward  the  Stono 
River.  They  are  being  constantly  strengthened,  I  judge,  from  the  num¬ 
ber  of  men  seen  working  upon  them,  particularly  that  part  which  com¬ 
mands  Light-House  Creek.  The  embankments  there  seemed  very  heavy 


426

and  of  fresh  earth.  It  was  thought  by  some  of  the  officers  and  by  the 
signal  quartermaster,  who  was  at  the  masthead,  that  there  were  at  least 
500  tents  in  the  encampment.  My  estimate,  or  rather  guess,  did  not 
go  beyond  300.  The  fact  of  the  encampment  is,  of  course,  known  to 
you,  sir,  but  I  thought  it  proper  to  report  the  line  of  strong  and

Navy  Department,  November  1 ,  1862. 


Sir:  Your  communication  of  the  25th  ultimo  was  received.  I  am 
gratified  that  the  misunderstanding  in  regard  to  the  effect  of  the  permit 
given  you  to  take  one  of  the  ironclads  into  Charleston  is  removed.  As 
the  whole  object  and  intention  were  to  gratify  you,  at  some  inconven¬ 
ience  to  the  Department  and  the  service,  and  as  it  is  not  so  received 
and  considered  by  yourself,  but  is  accepted  under  constraint  and  per¬ 
sonal  sacrifice,  I  deem  it  for  the  true  interest  of  the  country  that  you 
should  not  leave,  even  temporarily,  the  important  bureau  and  ordnance 
duties  confided  to  you  and  which  require  your  constant  and  undivided 
attention.  I  therefore  revoke  the  tender  that  was  made  you  of  an 
armed  vessel  in  the  Charleston  expedition. 

I  am,  respectfully,  etc., 


Gideon  Welles,

Abstract  log  of  the  TJ.  S.  S.  Wissahickon ,  Lieutenant- Commander 
I) avis,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  commanding. 

November  2,  1862. — From  12  to  4,  Great  Ogeechee  River:  At  12 
discovered  a  boat  up  the  river  pulling  downstream.  Sent  an  armed 
boat  to  meet  her,  the  strange  boat  having  five  men  in  her.  When  she 
turned  and  pulled  rapidly  upstream,  fired  the  20-pounder  rifle  to  bring 
her  to.  The  boat  continued  on;  got  underway  and  steamed  up  the  river; 
fired  another  shot  but  failed  to  bring  her  to.  She  succeeded  in  getting 
under  guns  of  Genesis  battery;  recalled  the  boat  when  about  2  miles 
off  the  battery.  Let  go  the  port  anchor  to  bring  the  ship  to,  when  we 
fired  another  shot  which  exploded  directly  over  the  battery.  They 
fired  five  shots  in  return,  but  they  fell  short  of  us.  At  1:40  got 
underway  and  steamed  down  to  our  anchorage.

Report  of  Commander  Woodhidl,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  commanding  TJ.  S.  S. 
Cimarron,  regarding  general  matters  in  the  vicinity  of  St.  John  s 

River,  Florida.  r 

U.  S.  S.  Cimarron, 


St.  John! s  River,  Florida,  November  3,  1862. 

Admiral:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  that  up  to  this  time  everything 
remains  quiet  so  far  as  it  is  possible  for  us  to  ascertain.  I  have  main¬ 
tained  a  constant  reconnoissance  of  the  river  as  far  up  as  Jacksom  die. 


428 


SOUTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 

* 

The  inhabitants  of  that  town  seem  to  be  regaining  their  confidence, 
and  it  is  observable  that  a  goodly  number  of  absentees  have  returned. 

The  guerrillas  are  still  in  numbers  on  each  side  of  the  river.  I  have 
given  it  out  that  should  any  of  these  parties  fire  on  any  of  our  steamers 
or  boats,  I  would  retaliate  and  burn  everything  in  the  neighborhood  of 
the  locality. 

We  have  the  nucleus  of  a  white  colony  at  Pilot  Town,  consisting  of 
5  men,  3  women,  and  some  half  dozen  children,  and  a  number  of  blacks, 
fugitives  escaping  from  the  despotism  of  the  rebel  leaders  in  these 
park.  The  new  conscript  law  of  the  Confederates  is  bearing  very 
hard  on  the  people  along  the  border  of  the  river.  I  think  if  we  could 
promise  protection,  we  would  soon  have  an  exodus  of  them,  escaping 
its  rigor. 

It  is  also  said  that  the  reported  intention  of  removing  the  Florida 
troops  to  another  district  and  substituting  Georgia  or  Alabama  troops 
for  them  is  very  unpopular,  and  it  is  believed  that  a  large  desertion  is 
likely  to  occur  in  consequence  among  the  Floridians.  I  have  acted  on 
this  matter  through  my  own  judgment.  I  should  be  pleased  to  know 
your  views,  and  also  your  orders  regarding  the  future  of  the  little 
colony.  They  are  destitute  of  almost  everything  and  express  the  wish 
to  go"  to  one  of  the  Western  States  to  settle  after  the  winter  is  over. 
They  are  all  Southern  born,  and  consequently  dread  the  winter  of  the 
North. 

It  is  reported  to  me  through  several  sources  that  there  is  now  in 
operation  at  Indian  Fiver  an  extensive  salt  works;  it  is  represented 
that  a  large  working  force  is  now  employed  daily  in  the  manufacture 
of  that  necessary  article.  They  have  some  100  pans  and  boilers. 
I  send  you  this  information,  as  I  deem  it  of  importance  that  you 
should  know  it. 

The  engines  of  the  Cimarron  are  daily  becoming  less  trustworthy, 
and  the  critical  condition  of  the  frame  is  more  manifest.  I  really 
think  she  should  have  the  proper  repairs  made  without  further  delay, 
also  the  long-continued  firing  of  her  heavy  guns  in  her  late  operations 
against  St.  John’s  Bluff  has  increased  her  inherent  weakness  of  hull. 
She  requires  and  ought  to  be  strengthened  thoroughly  and  her  rudder 
enlarged  or  altered  to  make  her  an  effective  vessel. 

We  have  only  about  twenty  days’  provisions  and  about  ten  days’ 
coal,  with  only  about  fifty  rounds  of  ammunition  for  our  heavy  guns. 
Will  you  be  pleased  to  give  some  order  as  regards  our  renewal  of 
these  necessities. 

If  we  had  a  small  steamer  in  addition  to  the  Hale  and  this  vessel, 
we  could  do  a  good  many  things  that  we  are  now  debarred  from  the 
execution  of. 

The  officers  and  crews  of  the  vessel  upon  this  part  of  the  blockade 
are  in  good  health. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  veiy  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

M.  WOODHULL, 
Commander ,  II.  S.  Alary. 

Fear- Admiral  S.  F.  Du  Pont,  U.  S.  Navy, 

Ccmdg.  South  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron ,  Port  Royal ,  S.  C.

the  enclosed  bill  of  lading?  Enclosed  is  a  muster  roll  of  the  officers

Report  of  Commander  Woodhull,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  IT.  8.  S. 
Cimarron ,  of  the  capture  of  the  Confederate  pilot  boat  Wave,  Novem¬ 
ber  Jh  1863,  and  regarding  affairs  in  St.  John's  River,  Florida. 

U.  S.  S.  Cimarron, 

St.  John's  River,  Florida,  November  7,  1863.  ' 
Admiral:  I  have  the  honor  to  acknowledge  the  receipt  of  your 
communication  of  the  30th  instant  [ultimo],  and  also  to  inform  you 
that  I  had  arranged  to  carry  out  the  plan  you  proposed  ere  it  came  to 
hand. 


430  SOUTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 

On  the  morning  of  the  4th  I  dispatched  the  Hade  to  Nassau  River 
to  capture  and  bring  away  the  two  vessels  said  to  be  in  that  locality. 

I  now  have  the  pleasure  to  inform  you  of  the  perfect  success  ot  the 
enterprise.  One  vessel,  the  pilot  boat  Wave,  was  found  fully  loaded 
and  ready  for  sea.  She  was  brought  off  safely.  Her  cargo  consists 
of  cotton  and  turpentine.  The  Wave  is  an  old  acquaintance.  She  was 
formerly  known  as  the  Friends,  of  Fernandina.  Phis  vessel  was  found 
in  Lofton  Creek;  she  had  been  fired,  but  not  damaged.  Those  having 
her  in  charge  escaped  too  suddenly  to  make  good  their  efforts  toward 
her  destruction. 

At  Holmes’  Mills  was  found  a  schooner  of  about  50  tons;  she  was  an 
old  vessel,  uncoppered,  without  lading,  and  appeared  to  have  been  out 
of  service  for  sometime  and  laid  up.  Under  the  cii  cumstances  she 
was  burned.  It  is  also  reported  to  me  that  at  Holmes  Mills  is  accumu¬ 
lated  an  immense  quantity  of  fine,  newly  manufactured  lumber,  amount¬ 
ing  to  nearly  a  million  feet.  Ought  it  not  to  be  removed?  Vessels, 
loaded,  drawing  Hi  feet,  can  pass  the  bar  of  Nassau  River.  Five 
good,  low-draft,  empty  coal  vessels  could  accomplish  this,  and  the 
whole  business  (if  a  few  hands  extra  were  sent  on  board  these  vessels 
to  aid  the  loading)  could  be  accomplished  without  risk  or  loss  of  life 
in  a  couple  or  three  days.  These  mills  are  upon  a  small,  island,  easily 
defended.  Most  of  this  lumber  is  suitable  for  decks,  just  the  mate¬ 
rial  most  wanted  and  most  difficult  to  be  obtained  at  our  navy  yards  at 

the  North.  _  . 

I  send  the  Wave  to  Port  Royal  subject  to  your  orders,  deeming  her 
too  small  a  vessel  to  risk  at  this  season  of  the  year  a  voyage  to  New 
York  or  Philadelphia.  The  schooner  appears  to  be  a  stout  little 
affair  and  would  make  a  capital  dispatch  boat. 

Captain  Snell  informs  me  that  twenty-two  contrabands  took  advan¬ 
tage  of  the  presence  of  the  Hale  by  accompanying  her  down  the  river; 
they,  in  boats,  proceeded  by  the  inland  passages  to  Fernandina.  He 
also  says  there  were  no  signs  of  an  enemy  at  any  point  of  the  river  to 
be  seen,  nor  could  he  discover  that  this  river  had  been  used  by  the 
blockade  runners  for  the  past  three  or  four  months. 

Enclosed  I  send  you  the  crew  list  of  the  Ilale,  containing  the  names 
of  all  connected  with  the  capture  of  the  rebel  schooner  Wave. 

All  of  which  I  have  the  honor  to  submit  for  your  consideration. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

M.  WOODHULL, 
Commander,  U.  S.  Wavy 

Rear-Admiral  S.  F.  Du  Pont, 

Comdg.  South  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron,  Port  Royal,  S.  C.

the  Santee,  through  the  energy  and  enterprise  of  Acting  Volunteer

Report  of  Acting  Master’s  Mate  Russell,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  expedition. 

U.  S.  Bark  Restless, 

Bulk’s  Bay ,  South  Carolina ,  November  5,  1862. 
Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  to  you  that  in  accordance  with  your 
orders  I  proceeded  from  Bull’s  Island,  in  a  small  boat,  with  tivo  con¬ 
trabands,  armed,  at  2  p.  m.  of  the  4th,  to  proceed  to  Jewey’s  [Sewee’s] 


432  SOUTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 

Landing,  Palmetto  Point,  South  Carolina,  for  the  'purpose  of  inter¬ 
cepting  the  mail  between  Charleston  and  Georgetown.  I  arrived  at  the 
point  about  5:  30  p.  m.,  and  proceeded  to  the  main  road,  about  5  miles 
distant,  and  learned  from  a  contraband  whom  I  met  on  the  road,  and 
who  was  acquainted  with  the  two  contrabands  with  me,  that  the  mail  was 
expected  that  night.  I  secreted  myself  and  party  in  the  woods,  close 
by  the  road,  to  await  its  coming.  At  10:  30  p.  m.  the  carrier  came 
along  in  a  sulky.  I  immediately  commanded  him  to  halt.  _  He  asked 
by  what  authority.  I  replied,  by  the  authority  of  the  U  nited  States 
Government.  He  at  once  dismounted  and  told  me  he  was  glad,  for  he 
had  long  wished  for  an  opportunity  to  leave  that  place.  After  search¬ 
ing  and  finding  him  unarmed,  I  proceeded  to  search  his  sulky  and 
found  two  mail  bags,  which  I  took  possession  of.  1  then  made  the 
horse  fast  in  the  woods  and  proceeded,  with  the  mail  carrier  and  the 
three  contrabands,  to  return  to  the  boat.  W  hen  within  about  30  yards 
of  the  landing  place  1  observed  four  horses  tied  to  the  landing.  After 
cautiously  looking  around  I  discovered  four  soldiers  (pickets)  on  the 
lookout.  I  then  concealed  myself  and  party  close  at  hand,  where  I 
could  watch  their  movements. 

About  daylight  they  left,  when  I  immediately  proceeded  to  my  boat 
and  returned  to  the  ship,  arriving  at  9:  30  this  a.  m. 

The  mail  carrier  (Milligan),  though  close  at  my  side  when  I  discov¬ 
ered  the  pickets,  manifested  no  disposition  to  leave  or  give  any  alarm, 
but  remained  close  by  me.  The  contraband  (Jack  Graddock)  having 
proved  himself  of  great  service  to  me,  and  expressing  a  great  desire 
to  get  off  to  the  fleet,  I  brought  him  off  with  me. 

I  am,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Jas.  J.  Russell, 

Acting  Master’s  Mate ,  II.  8.  Barit  Restless. 

Edward  Conroy, 

Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant ,  Comdg.  (J.  8.  Barit  Restless. 


Letter  from  Rear-Admiral  Du  Pont,  U.  S.  Navy,  to  Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  Conroy, 
U.  S.  Navy,  regarding  the  services  of  Acting  Master’s  Mate  Russell. 

Flagship  Wabash, 

Port  Royal  Harbor ,  8.  (J. ,  November  10,  18611. 

Sir:  I  take  great  pleasure  in  acknowledging  the  receipt  of  your 
communications  referring  to  the  capture  of  the  steamers  Scotia  and 
Anglia. 

Both  these  vessels  I  sent  to  New  York  for  adjudication.  The  engi¬ 
neers  of  the  Scotia  were  paid  for  bringing  the  steamer  to  this  port,  but 
they  subsequently  refused  to  do  duty  in  taking  her  to  New  York. 

I  must  also  acknowledge  your  communication  of - ,  giving  a 

list  of  vessels  taken  and  destroyed  by  the  Restless  under  your  com¬ 
mand — a  list  which  sufficiently  evidences  the  activity  and  energy  ever 
exhibited  by  you. 

Your  letter  of  the  5th  instant,  enclosing  the  report  of  Acting  Mas¬ 
ter’s  Mate  J.  J.  Russell,  detailing  the  circumstances  of  the  capture  of

Report  of  Commander  Wood  hull,  TJ.  S. Navy,  commanding  U.  S.  S. 

Cimarron,  regarding  affairs  in  the  St.  John's  River ,  Florida. 

U.  S.  S.  Cimarron, 

St.  John's  River,  Florida,  November  [7],  1862. 

Admiral:  I  have  the  honor  to  inform  you  that  everything  is  quiet 
in  this  region.  1  never  allow  a  day  to  pass  without  a  thorough  recon- 
noissance  of  all  the  suspected  points  on  the  river,  and,  so  far  as  it  is 
possible  to  judge,  I  think  there  is  no  reason  to  apprehend  for  some 
time  any  serious  movements  that  might  disturb  this  satisfactory  state 
of  affairs. 

The  white  colony  1  wrote  you  about  some  time  since  is  gradually 
increasing  since  my  last.  W e  have  had  an  addition  of  five  white  men 
and  one  woman,  besides  several  blacks.  Pilot  Town  has  now  a  popu¬ 
lation  of  35  souls.  I  feel  assured  from  what  I  can  gather  from  those 
who  have  gained  this  place  of  refuge  that  there  are  numbers  of  others 
that  will  join  us  so  soon  as  circumstances  will  permit  them  to  escape. 
I  really  believe  if  a  “certainty  of  protection”  was  proclaimed  we 
would  soon  have  enough  men  to  form  a  company.  These  people  are 
generally  destitute  of  almost  everything,  as  they  leave  at  night  in 
small  boats  and  are  compelled  necessarily  to  confine  their  belongings 
to  the  smallest  amount  and  the  abandonment  of  their  other  property. 
I  furnish  them  a  certain  amount  of  food,  to  wit,  to  every  six  persons 
1  allow  four  rations  of  salt,  beef,  pork,  and  molasses;  no  bread  or 
other  part  of  the  ration.  This,  with  the  corn  some  of  them  brought 
with  them  and  the  fish  they  obtain,  has  been  enough  to  keep  these 

Eoor  people  in  sufficient  food.  If  these  people  are  sent  north  we  will 
ave  to  clothe  them.  If  the  colony  is  broken  up,  we  will  lose  the 


SOUTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


437 


advantage  of  this  nucleus  for  them  to  rally  around,  who  might  other¬ 
wise  be  compelled  to  give  their  services  to  the  rebels.  I  should  be 
greatly  obliged  to  be  informed  as  to  your  views  regarding  the  course 
to  be  pursued  toward  these  unfortunate  people. 

I  have  information  that  in  a  certain  locality  a  few  miles  above  Jack¬ 
sonville  there  is  a  large  amount  of  cotton  stored  in  bulk.  It  has  been 
thus  concealed  for  the  last  eighteen  months.  I  have  refrained  from 
going  near  the  place  till  I  can  have  the  aid  of  an  additional  small  ves¬ 
sel  to  hold  the  bar  and  lower  part  of  the  river  while  we  are  engaged 
so  far  above  the  points  necessary  to  be  guarded.  The  enterprise  will 
keep  until  you  can  coveniently  give  us  the  means  to  make  the  capture 
sure. 

There  are  numerous  salt  works  in  operation  along  the  coast  south  of 
this.  Georgia,  a  part  of  Alabama,  and  this  State  depend  principally 
on  these  works  for  the  supply  of  this  article.  I  understand  that  sait 
is  so  scarce  that  it  now  brings  in  this  State  as  high  a  price  as  $40  per 
sack,  and  by  the  slip  1  send  you,  cut  from  a  fragment  of  the  Savannah 
Daily  Morning  News  of  October  24  (found  on  shore  at  Holmes’  Mills), 
you  will  see  it  was  being  sold  at  Atlanta  at  $140  per  sack.  Nothing  I 
can  conceive  of  would  strike  a  heavier  blow  at  the  Confederate  forces 
than  the  total  destruction  of  all  salt,  works  on  the  coast  and  in  its 
neighborhood.  To  accomplish  this,  the  smallest  and  lightest  draft 
vessels  must  be  used,  as  most  of  these  salt  works  are  on  water  courses 
having  shallow  and  difficult  bars. 

All  of  which  is  submitted. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

M.  WOODHULL, 
Commander ,  U.  S.  Navy. 

Rear-Admiral  S.  F.  Du  Pont,  U.  S.  Navy. 

Comdg.  South  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron,  Port  Rogal,  S.  C.

[Slip  cut  from  Savannah  Daily  News,  October  24,  1962.] 

Progress  of  Extortion. — The  articles  which  have  advanced  so  enor¬ 
mously  in  market  are  mostly  still  on  hand,  passing  by  sale  in  large 
quantities  from  speculator  to  speculator,  each  enticed  by  the  scarcity, 
the  panic,  and  the  prospect  of  famine,  to  monopolize  the  supply,  and 
to  force  the  highest  possible  prices  from  consumers.  Thus,  salt  began 
to  ascend  in  the  speculative  scale  at  $10  per  sack,  and  thence  has  gone 
up,  leaping  $10  or  $20  per  month,  as  the  public  necessity  varied,  until 
it  has  reached  the  very  modest  figures  of  $140  per  sack  in  Atlanta,  the 
center  of  speculation  and  the  headquarters  of  those  gentry  upon  whom 
the  financial  operation  has  been  performed  of  plucking  out  their  hearts 
to  make  room  for  deposits  of  gold  within  their  iron-ribbed  chests 
while  the  country  is  bleeding  at  every  pore.  Men  equally  heartless 
are  to  be  found  in  other  places— men  who  by  trickery  stimulate  prices, 
just  as  the  bulls  and  bears  of  Wall  street  deal  in  stocks— men  who  buy 
up  certain  goods,  such  as  cotton  yarn,  and  force  it  from  $2  to  $10  per 
bunch,  osnaburgs  from  20  to  75  cents  per  yard,  boots  and  shoes  four 
or  five  times  the  common  price,  Hour  from  $10  to  $40  per  barrel,  and 
so  on  through  the  list.  These  articles  often  change  hands  in  bulk, 
without  being  open  for  retail.  They  perform  the  round  of  specula¬ 
tion,  each  step  advancing  on  supposed  consequences,  such  as  the  dim 


438 


SOUTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADKON. 


prospect  of  opening  the  channels  of  trade  in  Tennessee  and  Kentucky, 
and  the  determination  of  European  powers  not  to  intervene  for  the 
South,  so  that  any  given  production  at  home  must  be  exhausted,  and 
then  $100  for  a  side  of  bacon  or  for  a  sack  of  flour  will  complete  the 
paradise  of  speculators.  These  blood  leeches  greatly  desire  such  a 
result,  whereas  many  of  them  will  be  caught  with  large  stocks  on 
hand,  when  the  tumble  will  be  overwhelming. 

We  think  the  crisis  is  near,  and  a  just  retribution  will  follow.  JNo 
public  sympathy  need  be  expected  in  such  an  hour.  Milledgevii  e

Joint  operations  in  Sapelo  River ,  November  7,  1862. 

Abstract  log  of  tbe  U.  S.  S.  Potomska,  Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  Budd,  commanding. 

November  7,  1862.-9:55  a.  m.  stopped  at  a  plantation  on  Sapelo 
River.  At  10:40  anchored  off  King’s  plantation.  From  12  to  4  p.  m. : 
the  captain  with  ten  men,  armed,  went  on  board  the  Darlington  and 
went  up  the  river  to  a  plantation.  In  passing  a  bluff  they  were  bred 
upon  by  the  rebel  soldiers;  returned  the  fire.  At  2:20  steamer 
returned;  got  underway  and  proceeded  down  the  river,  shelling  the 
woods  as  we  went.  At  2: 05  got  aground.  Fired  36  shells  from  broad¬ 
side  guns  and  4  stands  grape;  fired  27  shells  from  Parrott.  From  4  to 
6  p.  m.:  At  4:50  floated  steamer  down  the  river;  at  5  opened  fire  on 
the  enemy’s  pickets  at  Setaliman’s  Bluff;  the  enemy  in  large  numbers 
concealed  in  rifle  pits.  At  5:30  discovered  the  buildings  on  fire  from 
our  shell. 


Report  of  Lieutenant-Colonel  Beard,  IT.  S.  Army. 

Beaufort,  S.  C.,  November  10,  1862. 

General:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  that,  as  directed  by  you,  I 
have  tried  a  portion  of  the  First  South  Carolina  V olunteers  (negro 
regiment). 

*  ****** 

Friday,  November  7,  accompanied  by  the  gunboat  Potomska,  Lieu¬ 
tenant  Budd,  commanding,  proceeded  up  Sapelo  River.  The  gunboat 
could  proceed  no  farther  than  King’s.  Lieutenant  Budd  came  on 
board  the  Darlington  and  proceeded  up  the  river  with  us  to  Fairhope. 
At  Spaulding’s  we  were  attacked  by  80  or  90  of  the  enemy,  who  were 
well  posted  on  a  bluff  behind  trees.  At  this  point  the  channel  runs 
within  50  yards  of  the  bluff.  We  killed  2  of  the  enemy  and  had  1 
colored  man  wounded.  At  bairhope  we  destroyed  the  salt  works, 
some  tan  vats,  corn,  and  other  things  that  might  be  of  use  to  the 
enemy. 

On  return  past  Spaulding’s  we  were  again  attacked  by  the  enemy  in 
greater  force.  We  effected  a  landing  and  burned  all  the  buildings  on 
the  place  and  captured  some  arms,  etc.  Five  of  the  enemy  were 
killed;  we  lost  3  wounded.  We  were  greatly  aided  here  by  the 
Potomska,  which,  from  a  bend  below,  shelled  the  woods.  Under  the 
guns  of  the  Potomska  we  landed  at  Colonel  Brailsford’s,  drove  in  a 
company  of  pickets  from  his  regiment,  and  destroyed  all  the  property 
on  the  place,  together  with  the  most  important  buildings. 


SOUTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


439 


I  am  greatly  indebted  to  Lieutenant  Budd  for  the  success  of  this  day. 

The  colored  men  fought  with  astonishing  coolness  and  bravery.  For 
alacrity  in  effecting  landings,  for  determination,  and  for  bush  fighting 
I  found  them  all  I  could  desire — more  than  I  had  hoped.  They 
behaved  bravely,  gloriously,  and  deserve  all  praise. 

I  started  from  St.  Simon’s  with  62  colored  fighting  men  and  returned 
to  Beaufort  with  156  fighting  men  (all  colored).  As  soon  as  we  took 
a  slave  from  his  claimant  we  placed  a  musket  in  his  hands  and  he 
began  to  fight  for  the  freedom  of  others. 

Besides  these  men  we  brought  off  61  women  and  children.  We 
destroyed  nine  large  salt  works,  together  with  $20,000  worth  of  horses, 
salt,  corn,  rice,  etc.,  which  we  could  not  carry  away. 

I  am,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

O.  T.  Beard, 

Lieut.  Col.  Forty-eigLtli  New  York  Vols. ,  Covidg.  Expedition. 

Brigadier-General  Rufus  Saxton, 

Military  Governor ,  Department  of  the  South. 


Letter  from  Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  Budd,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S.  S.  Potomska, 
commending  the  bravery  of  colored  troops. 

U.  S.  S.  Potomska, 

Sapelo  Diver ,  Georgia ,  November  7,  1862. 

Sir:  It  gives  me  pleasure  to  testify  to  the  admirable  conduct  of  the 
negro  troops  (First  South  Carolina  Volunteers)  under  the  command 
of  Lieutenant-Colonel  Beard,  Forty-eighth  New  York  Volunteers, 
during  this  day’s  operations.  They  behaved  splendidly  under  the 
warm  and  galling  fire  we  were  exposed  to  in  two  skirmishes  with 
the  enemy.  I  did  not  see  a  man  flinch,  contrary  to  my  expectations. 
One  of  them  particularly  came  under  my  notice,  who  although  badly 
wounded  in  the  face,  continued  to  load  and  fire  in  the  coolest  manner 
imaginable.  Every  one  of  them  acted  like  veterans. 

Very  respectfully, 

William  Budd, 

Acting  Lieutenant ,  Commanding  Potomska. 

Mr.  French, 

Chaplain ,  TJ.  S.  A. 


Report  of  Lieutenant- Commander  Davis ,  TJ.  S.  Navy ,  regarding  the

Abstract  log  of  the  U.  S.  S.  Dawn ,  Acting  Lieidenant  Barnes ,  U.  S. 

Navy ,  commanding. 

November  7,  1862. — At  11:30  a.  m.  exchanged  signals  with  the 
Wissahickon.  Were  ordered  by  Commander  Davis  to  follow  him  up 
the  Little  Ogeechee  River  to  assist  in  capturing  a  schooner  lying  below 
Coffee  Bluff  battery.  At  1  Wissahickon  ran  aground;  endeavored  to 
get  her  off;  not  succeeding,  abandoned  the  attempt  until  flood  tide. 
Captain  Davis  and  pilot  came  on  board  and  we  proceeded  up  river. 
Commenced  shelling  the  schooner,  which  had  got  underway  and  was 
trying  to  make  her  escape.  The  guns  from  the  battery  replied  to  our 
fire,  their  shot  falling  short.  The  schooner  finding  it  impossible  to 
escape  ran  ashore  under  the  guns  of  the  battery.  When  we  were 
within  miles  of  her  ran  aground  and  waited  one  hour  and  thirty 
minutes  for  tide,  to  cross  the  bar.  When  afloat  proceeded  on  up  river 
and  continued  shelling  schooner.  Battery  ceased  to  reply  to  our  fire. 
When  within  1£  miles  of  the  schooner  discovered  her  to  be  on  fire  fore 
and  aft.  After  lying  by  until  she  was  nearly  consumed,  turned  and 
steamed  down  river.  From  the  appearance  of  the  flames  and  heavy 
black  smoke  supposed  the  schooner  to  be  loaded  with  naval  stores. 
Commander  Davis  went  on  board  the  Wissahickon ;  we  then  got  under¬ 
way  and  steamed  back  to  anchorage  at  mouth  of  Hell  Gate.

Expedition  to  St.  Mary’s ,  Ga. ,  November  9 ,  1862. 

Report  of  Lieutenant-Commander  Hughes,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  TJ.  S.  S.  Mohawk. 

U.  S.  S.  Mohawk, 

Fernandina ,  Fla. ,  November  11,  1862. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  that  on  the  morning  of  the  9th 
instant  I  proceeded  with  this  vessel  on  an  expedition  to  the  town  of 
St.  Mary’s,  preceded  by  the  army  transport  Neptune ,  conveying  Colonel 
Rich  and  two  companies  of  the  Ninth  Maine  Regiment.  The  Neptune 
was  about  one  hour  in  advance,  and  as  we  were  approaching  the  place 
we  met  her  returning,  having  on  board  one  of  the  soldiers  dangerously 
wounded  from  a  shot  fired  by  a  party  of  rebels,  estimated  to  be  150 
strong.  He  was  brought  on  board  this  vessel  for  medical  attendance. 
I  proceeded  up  the  river  to  the  town,  anchoring  close  by,  and  fired 
several  shells  into  it,  when,  perceiving  two  women,  I  immediately 
ceased  firing  and  sent  a  boat  on  shore  under  a  flag  of  truce,  offering 
them  the  protection  of  our  flag  and  conveyance  to  Fernandina,  which 
they  refused.  I  then  urged  them  to  remove  to  a  place  of  safety,  and 
as  they  refused  to  do  so  I  promised  not  to  injure  the  house  in  which 
they  resided.  Not  seeing  any  more  rebels,  and  after  consultation  with 
Colonel  Rich,  I  concluded  to  return  to  this  place,  but  had  just  got 
underway  when  several  musket  shots  were  fired  at  us  from  different 
portions  of  the  town.  I  again  turned  the  vessel’s  head  toward  St. 
Mary’s,  and  came  to  anchor  before  the  town  under  a  fire  from  mus¬ 
ketry,  when  I  opened  our  battery  upon  the  place,  being  careful  not  to 
touch  the  house  occupied  by  the  women  alluded  to,  firing  shell  and 
canister,  which  drove  the  rebels  completely  out  of  the  town  and  set 
tire  to  several  buildings.  Upon  our  return  down  the  river  I  sent  a 
boat  in  charge  of  Acting  Master  George  R.  Durand  and  set  fire  to  a 
large  steam  sawmill,  completely  destroying  it. 

Yery  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

A.  K.  Hughes, 
Lieutenant-  Commander. 

Rear-Admiral  S.  F.  Du  Pont, 

Commanding  South  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron.

Report  of  Rear-Admiral  Du  Pont,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  requesting  the  views 
of  the  Department  on  proposed  destruction  of  salt  works  in  St.  John’s 
River,  Florida,  and  relative  to  valuable  timber. 

Flagship  Wabash, 

Port  Royal  Harbor ,  S.  C. ,  November  13,  1863. 
Sir:  I  have  received  a  report  from  Commander  M.  Woodhull,  senior 
officer  in  St.  John’s  River,  in  which,  after  saying  everything  was  quiet, 
he  refers  to  numerous  salt  works  along  the  coast  south  of  the  St.  J ohn’s, 
which  could  be  destroyed  by  light-draft  vessels. 

I  am  desirous  to  have  the  wishes  of  the  Department  on  this  subject 
before  taking  action. 

I  may  add  that  large  quantities  of  excellent  timber,  suitable  for 
ship’s  decks,  were  discovered  in  Nassau  River  by  Lieutenant  Snell,  of 
the  Hale ,  who  also  captured  a  small  pilot  schooner  in  the  same  locality. 
By  chartering  empty  coal  vessels,  much  of  this  timber  could  be 
removed.  It  will,  however,  have  to  be  done  with  the  aid  of  gunboats; 
but  by  the  breaking  down  of  the  Hale,  Patroon,  Wamsutta,  and  Western 
World  I  am  much  crippled  for  vessels  of  light  draft. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

S.  F.  Du  Pont, 

Rear-Admiral,  Comdg.  South  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy,  Washington.

Order  of  Commander  Wood, h  ull,  TJ.  S.  Navy ,  to  Acting  Master  Watson,

U.  S.  S.  Cimarron, 

St.  John's  River,  November  12,  1862. 

Sir:  You  will  please  proceed  with  the  Uncas  on  a  reconnoissance  of 
the  river  as  far  up  as  Trout  Creek,  and  even  to  Jacksonville,  if  you  feel 
inclined.  Be  particular  in  nearing  Jacksonville  to  examine  the  high 
ground  a  few  miles  below  it,  as  it  is  talked  about  by  the  rebels  as  a 
very  good  place  for  a  battery.  On  your  route  destroy  all  boats  and 
water  conveyances  you  discover,  give  refuge  to  all  desiring  protection, 
and  obtain  all  the  information  as  regards  the  movements  of  the  enemy’s 
forces  on  either  bank  you  possibly  can.  Be  cautious  not  to  risk  the 
lives  of  your  men  and  officers  unnecessarily.  I  have  information  that 
at  Trout  Creek,  near  its  entrance  into  the  river,  there  has  been  a  picket 
guard  of  the  enemy  at  that  point.  I  wish  you  to  examine  particularly 
this  locality. 

Respectfully,  etc., 

M.  WOODHULL,

Report  of  Commander  Woodhull,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  commanding  TJ.  S.  S. 

Cimarron,  regarding  affairs  in  the  vicinity  of  St.  John's  River, 

Florida. 

U.  S.  S.  Cimarron, 

St.  John's  River ,  Florida. ,  November  11+,  1863. 

Admiral:  1  have  the  honor  to  inform  you  that  everything  remains 
as  at  the  date  of  my  last  letter. 

I  have  had  the  river  thoroughly  examined  three  times  since  the  sailing 
of  the  Hale  as  far  up  as  Jacksonville.  The  guerrillas  have  apparently 
left  both  banks  of  the  river;  at  least  nothing  has  been  seen  of  them 
for  the  past  week. 

The  little  colony  continues  gradually  to  increase.  We  have  had 
within  the  last  week  additions  of  both  whites  and  blacks.  I  think 
something  ought  to  be  done  as  to  its  future.  If  it  is  decided  to 
remove  it,  a  transport  will  have  to  be  sent  for  the  purpose,  as  none  of 
the  gunboats  could  give  the  accommodations  necessary  for  so  large  a 
number  of  people. 

W e  will  soon  have  to  be  supplied  with  provisions,  as  we  have  only 
about  ten  days’  rations  left.  The  partial  feeding  of  so  many  mouths 
on  shore,  in  addition  to  the  crew  of  this  vessel,  will  soon  cause  the 
expenditure  of  what  is  now  on  hand. 

The  health  of  the  officers  and  crew  on  this  part  of  the  blockade  con¬ 
tinues  to  be  excellent. 

Very  respectfully,  etc.,  M.  Woodhull, 

Commander,  TJ.  S.  Navy. 

Rear-Admiral  S.  F.  Du  Pont, 

Commanding  South  Atlantic  Blockading  Sguadron.

Notes  of  Captain  Taylor ,  U.  S.  Navy,  in  regard  to  Charleston,  S.  C. , 

and  vicinity. 

Contrabands  received  from  the  Memphis,  who  escaped  from  Charles¬ 
ton  on  the  night  of  the  14th  November,  1862: 

William  King  belonged  to  Colonel  J.  D.  Hart. 

Adam  Hewbank  belonged  to  Captain  Charles  Willey. 

Henry  Dakan  belonged  to  Mrs.  Marine. 

Kento  Barton  belonged  to  Captain  Charles  Willey. 

Left  N.  E.  Railroad  wharf  in  Charleston  in  one  boat  on  evening  of 
14t-h  and  reached  Memphis  about  4  a.  m.  of  15th.  Were  not  chased 
nor  hailed. 

Henry  Dakan  is  a  fireman;  the  other  three  are  wheelmen,  and  are 
pilots  on  St.  J ohn’s  River.  AV ere  all  at  Hilton  Head  when  it  was 
taken,  and  have  been  here  ever  since  on  board  ferryboats  and 
transports. 

Provisions  are  scarce  and  high  in  Charleston.  The  troops  are  half 
fed  and  discontented;  about  two  weeks  ago  50  desertions  took  place  from 
Fort  Johnson.  General  Ripley  commands  the  forts  and  batteries; 
General  Drayton  commands  Fort  Sumter;  General  Beauregard  com¬ 
mands  at  Pocotaligo;  has  been  heard  to  express  an  opinion  that  our 
ironclads  would  deal  hardly  by  Fort  Sumter,  and  was  censured  by 
public  sentiment  for  uttering  it.  Many  of  the  residents  (especially 
women)  left  Charleston  some  time  ago,  but  some  have  since  returned, 
finding  that  no  attack  was  made. 

The  people  here  expected  an  attack  on  the  1st  instant,  and  then 
again  on  the  10th.  Troops  are  not  well  clad;  the  Herald  ran  in  about 
three  weeks  ago,  having  on  board  shoes  and  clothing. 

The  Herald,  Captain  Coxetter;  the  Hero  (captain’s  name  not  known); 
and  the  Leopard,  Captain  Peek,  are  all  inside,  loaded  with  cotton  and 
waiting  for  a  chance  to  run  out.  The  Hero  is  a  propeller;  the  others 
are  side-wheel;  all  have  masts,  the  side- wheelers  only  one,  the  propeller 
three;  no  yards.  There  are  two  ships  and  a  brig  also  inside.  The 
brig  is  loaded.  All  the  above  vessels  are  English. 

There  are  two  rams  inside,  the  Palmetto  State  and  the  Courier 
[ Chicora ];  ironclad,  plates  4  inches  thick;  about  150  or  160  feet  long; 
old  engines,  one  taken  out  of  the  Lady  Davis  and  the  other  out  of  the 
Aid;  both  small  boats.  Can  get  about  4  knots  an  hour  out  of  them; 
they  both  leak,  the  Courier  badly.  Have  four  guns  each,  smoothbore 
32  or  42  pounders.  Have  no  other  armed  vessels  afloat;  four  are  on 
the  stocks,  and  they  are  hurrying  them  along  as  fast  as  possible. 

Do  not  know  the  names  of  any  navy  officers  in  Charleston. 

No  floating  batteries. 

Castle  Pinckney  has  small  guns  and  is  garrisoned. 

Fort  Ripley  is  built  on  piles,  between  the  town  and  Fort  Sumter, 
on  starboard  side  of  the  channel  going  in;  has  four  guns,  mounted  in 
parapet  made  of  logs,  palmetto,  about  10  feet  thick,  and  masonry 
inside  of  that;  guns  of  small  size;  the  men  live  in  tents. 

Fort  Sumter. 

Fort  Johnson. 

Fort  Moultrie  is  well  garrisoned. 

Battery  Beauregard. 

Battery  at  Breach  Inlet. 

Batte^  between  the  above-named  two.

SOUTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


Fort  Beauregard  has  one  very  large  rifled  gun,  obtained  fiom  Havana. 
Fort  Sumter  has  two  rifled  guns. 

A  large  battery  near  Cumming’s  Point. 

There  are  many  batteries  all  along  the  shore  on  both  sides. 

The  City  battery  is  also  fortified,  garrisoned  by  a  regiment  of  Georgia 
troops. 

Secessionville  is  extensively  fortified  with  earthworks. 

A  row  of  stakes  run  across  the  channel  between  Forts  Sumter  and 
Ripley;  a  boom  of  heavy  logs  is  moored  between  Forts  Sumter  and 
Moultrie.

Report  of  Rear-Admiral  T)u  Pont ,  II.  S.  Navy ,  regarding  the  escape  of 
a  blockade  runner  off  Charleston ,  S.  C. ,  November  If  1862. 

Flagship  Wabash, 

Port  Royal  Harbor ,  S.  61,  November  25,  1862. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  to  the  Department  that  on  the  night 
of  the  14th  instant  a  steamer  attempted  to  run  the  blockade  of  Charles¬ 
ton  by  Maffitt’s  Channel.  She  was  first  discovered  by  the  Blunt  about 
ten  minutes  after  10,  and  was  fired  on  by  that  vessel,  whose  command¬ 
ing  officer  at  the  same  time  gave  the  usual  signal  to  the  fleet. 

The  Flag,  hearing  the  gun  and  seeing  the  signal,  stood  in  the  direc¬ 
tion  indicated  and  got  sight  of  the  steamer  and  fired  one  shot  at  her, 
when  she  appeared  to  run  seaward,  but  a  dense  fog  just  at  that  moment 
unfortunately  shut  her  out  from  view.  The  Seneca,  aroused  by  the 
previous  signal,  soon  after  perceived  the  steamer  and  fired  her  rifled 
gun,  when  she  turned,  shot  around,  and  steered  to  the  eastward,  imme¬ 
diately  after  which,  owing  to  the  fog,  she  was  lost  sight  of. 

On  the  night  of  the  15th  instant  a  steamer  again  attempted  to  run 
the  blockade  by  the  same  entrance,  and  was  again  discovered  by  the 
Blunt ,  which  vessel  she  approached  within  300  yards,  when  a  shell 
from  the  Blunt  struck  her,  exploding  on  board.  The  steamer  imme¬ 
diately  turned  to  the  northward  and  westward,  and  apparently  ran 
aground  on  the  shoal  off  Dewees  Inlet,  where,  however,  she  remained 
only  for  a  few  minutes,  in  which  time  Acting  Master  Beers,  the  com¬ 
manding  officer  of  the  Blunt,  fired  three  more  shells  at  her,  sending 
also  a  boat  to  board,  but  she  succeeded  in  getting  off  and  steering  sea¬ 
ward,  disappearing  in  the  darkness. 

The  report  of  Acting  Master  Beers  describes  her  as  a  long,  low,  side- 
wheel  steamer,  about  700  tons,  and  without  spars. 

There  is  reason  to  believe  that  the  steamer  last  spoken  of  was  the 
same  that  attempted  to  enter  the  previous  night,  on  both  of  which  occa- 


SOUTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON.  449 


sions  she  was  foiled,  and  the  impression  is  that  she  has  returned  to 
Nassau  disabled. 

V ery  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

S.  F.  Du  Pont, 

Real'- Admiral,  Comdg.  South  Atlantic  Blockdg.  Squadron. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy ,  Washington. 


Report  of  Captain  Taylor,  (J.  S.  Navy,  transmitting  reports  regard¬ 
ing  the  escape  of  a  blockade  runner  of  Charleston,  S.  C.,  November 
lk,  1862. 

U.  S.  S.  Housatonic, 

Off  Charleston,  November  15,  1862. 

Sir:  About  half  past  10  last  evening  we  were  called  to  quarters  by 
an  alarm  from  the  ships  guarding  the  entrance  to  Maffitt’s  Channel 
that  a  vessel  was  attempting  to  run  in. 

Nothing  was  seen  from  this  ship  of  the  stranger;  two  guns  were 
tired  at  her  from  the  G.  W.  Blunt,  one  from  the  Flag,  and  one  from 
the  Seneca. 

I  enclose  herewith  the  reports  of  Commander  Strong,  Lieutenant- 
Commander  Gibson,  and  Acting  Master  Beers. 

Before  11  o’clock  a  dense  fog  shut  in  and  nothing  more  was  seen  or 
heard  during  the  night.  Lieutenant-Commander  Gibson  feels  certain 
that  he  saw  the  strange  vessel,  after  he  fired  at  her,  turn  and  proceed 
to  sea  over  the  Rattlesnake  Shoal. 

A  close  examination  of  the  harbor  to-day  from  the  masthead  dis¬ 
covers  no  new  arrival  inside. 

The  Marblehead  will  be  sent  in  to-night  after  dark  to  take  position 
near  the  western  buoy  on  the  Rattlesnake;  the  vessels  guarding  that 
entrance  will  be  the  Flag,  Blunt,  Seneca,  and  Marblehead.  This  ship 
lies  within  1,300  yards  of  the  position  of  the  latter. 

The  southwest  entrance  (by  Lawford  Channel)  is  protected  by  the 
Ottawa,  Flambeau,  and  Para.  The  Keystone  State  lies  off  the  bar  of 
the  main  channel,  within  supporting  distance  of  them. 

Special  signal  has  been  made  to  the  whole  squadron  to  be  on  the 
alert. 

I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Wm.  Rogers  Taylor, 

Captain  and  Senior  Officer  Present. 

Rear-Admiral  S.  F.  Du  Pont, 

Commanding  South  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron.

U.  S.  Gunboat  Seneca, 

Off  Charleston ,  November  15,  186 2. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  that  at  about  twenty  minutes  after 
10  o’clock  last  evening  (the  14th  instant),  while  occupying  our  nightly 
berth  close  inshore,  north  of  the  west  end  of  Rattlesnake  Shoal,  the 
alarm  was  given  by  the  firing  of  guns  and  by  signals  from  the  Flag  and 
schooner  Blunt,  stationed  outside  of  us,  of  a  vessel  attempting  to  run  the 
blockade  from  seaward.  Ten  minutes  afterwards  I  saw  a  long  dark 
steamer,  bearing  E.  S.  E. ,  some  700  yards  distant  (I  judge),  but  could 
not  distinguish  her  rig,  or  whether  she  was  a  side-wheel  or  screw.  In 
the  meantime  we  had  gone  to  quarters,  slipped  the  cable,  and  turned 
our  vessel’s  head  to  the  southward  and  westward,  firing  the  rifle  gun 
at  the  stranger  as  soon  as  she  came  in  sight.  Up  to  that  time  she  was 
moving  rapidly  toward  Charleston,  but  on  our  firing,  and  she  doubtless 
catching  view  of  the  Housatonic  on  her  other  bow,  appeared  to  turn 
short  round  and  to  cross  the  Rattlesnake  Shoal,  steering  to  the  south¬ 
ward  and  eastward.  Three  or  four  minutes  afterwards  we  were  sud¬ 
denly  enveloped  in  a  thick  fog  and  we  saw  no  more  of  her. 

I  was  in  admirable  position  for  following  up  and  keeping  between 
the  stranger  and  the  snore  had  she  continued  her  course.  As  it  was, 
I  doubt  if  she  could  have  effected  her  retreat  had  it  not  been  for  the 
sudden  fog. 

I  am,  sir,  vex-y  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

William  Gibson, 

Lieutenant-  Commander. 

Captain  W.  R.  Taylor, 

Senior  Officer  Present ,  Charleston  Blockade ,  IT.  S.  S.  Housatonic.

Stettin ,  of  his  departure  for  Port  Royal,  8.  Cl ,  in  obedience  to  Depart¬

U.  S.  S'.  Stettin, 

New  York  Harbor,  November  18,  1862. 
Sir:  In  obedience  to  orders  received  ordering  me  to  proceed  with 
the  U.  S.  S.  Stettin  under  my  command  to  Port  Royal,  S.  C.,  and 
report  to  Rear-Admiral  S.  F.  Du  Pont  for  duty  on  the  South  Atlantic 
Blockading  Squadron,  I  would  most  respectfully  inform  you  that  I  this 
day  sailed  from  this  port  for  the  above  destination.

mechanics  ordered  to  report  to  Rear-Admiral  S.  F.  Du  Pont. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant,

Engagement  of  Federal  vessels  with  Confederate  batlery  in  Ogeechee 
River ,  Georgia ,  November  19,  1862. 

Report  of  Lieutenant-Commander  Davis,  D.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S.  S.  Wissahickon. 

U.  S.  Gunboat  Wissahickon, 
Ogeechee  River ,  Georgia ,  November  19,  1862. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  that  this  morning  I  moved  up  the 
river  with  this  vessel,  the  Dawn,  and  mortar  schooner  No.  5,  and 

opened  fire  on  the  battery  at  Genesis  Point  at  8 : 15. 

Advancing  from  the  first  position  about  a  quarter  of  a  mile  with  this 
vessel  and  the  Dawn,  continued  firing,  when  the  enemy  disappeared 
as  though  they  had  deserted  the  battery;  all  this  time  they  fired  no 
guns.  I  again  advanced  about  a  quarter  of.  a  mile,  with  the  Dawn  in 
company  to  the  bend  of  the  river  in  the  direction  of  the  battery  Red 
about  If  miles  from  it,  when  the  enemy  opened  fire,  at  9:45,  and  1 
regret  to  say  the  first  shot  struck  this  vessel  abreast  the  Xl-inch  gun 
and  about  4  feet  below  the  water  line,  causing  a  serious  leak;  failing 
to  gain  on  it  with  the  pumps,  and  apprehensive  of  the  necessity  of 
putting  the  vessel  ashore,  I  reluctantly  dropped  down  beyond  their 
range,  and  succeeded  in  partially  stopping  the  leak  so  that  the  pumps 
would  keep  her  free.  At  2:30  p.  m.  we  ceased  firing  and  returned  to 
our  usual  anchorages.  No  casualties  occurred  during  the  day  on  our 
side.  The  practice  of  the  vessels  was  to  all  appearances  entirely 
satisfactory. 

To-morrow  I  will  lay  the  vessel  ashore  and  with  the  means  at  my 
command  repair  the  damage. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

John  L.  Davis, 

Lieutenant-  Commander  and  Senior  Officer  Present. 

Rear-Admiral  S.  F.  Du  Pont,  U.  S.  Navy. 

Commanding  South  Atlantic  Rlockading  Squadron.

Commendatory  letter  of  Rear-Admiral  Dn  Pont,  U.  S.  Navy,  to  Lieutenant-Commander 

Davis,  U.  S.  Navy. 

Flagship  Wabash, 

Port  Royal  Harbor ,  S.  C. ,  December  11,  1862. 

Sir:  The  Water  Witch  arrived  to-day,  bringing  Charles  Cook  and 
Michael  Green.  The  former  I  shall  probably  employ  as  a  pilot;  the 
latter  will  be  sent  north. 

I  have  considered  the  report  of  your  engineer,  and  as  soon  as  possi¬ 
ble  will  relieve  you  at  Ossabaw,  so  that  the  necessary  repairs  can  be 
made  to  your  vessel. 

I  take  this  occasion  to  acknowledge  your  letters  of  the  19th  and  20th* 
of  November,  referring  to  an  engagement  with  the  battery  at  Genesis 
Point,  in  which  the  Wissahickon  accidentally  received  a  shot,  tempo¬ 
rarily  disabling  her.  I  beg  leave  to  commend  your  whole  course  in  the 
matter,  particularly  in  concealing  so  effectually  from  the  enemy  your 
injuries.  Their  official  accounts  make  no  mention  of  them. 

I  am  glad  to  learn  that  you  have  buoyed  the  channel. 

Respectfully,  etc., 

S.  F.  Du  Pont, 

Rear-Admiral. 

Lieutenant-Commander  J.  L.  Davis, 

U.  S.  S.  Wissahickon ,  Ossabaw. 


Letter/'  from  the  TJ.  S.  consul  at  Cardiff, ,  Wales ,  to  the  Secretary  of  the 
Navy,  giving  information  regarding  the  blockade  runner  Hero. 

No.  60.1  United  States  Consulate, 

Cardiff,  [  Wales\,  November  20,  1862. 

Sir:  I  have  just  ascertained  that  the  bark  Hero,  of  Yarmouth,  Nova 
Scotia,  which  is  loading  here  with  coal,  will  stop  at  Cork,  [Ireland], 
and  take  in  30  tons  of  gunpowder  and  sail  for  Nassau,  [New  Providence]. 
She  has  double  topsail  yards  and  [is]  painted  black  with  a  yellow 
streak.  Her  clearance  from  this  port  will  show  nothing  but  coal  for 
Nassau,  and  therefore  may  deceive  some  of  our  ships  that  may  over¬ 
haul  her.  But  she  is  a  Trojan  horse,  with  munitions  of  war,  if  not 
armed  men  inside. 

With  the  highest  respect,  your  obedient  servant, 

Chas.  D.  Cleveland, 

U  S.  Consul. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy.

Capture  of  the  Confederate  schooner  Annie  Dees  by  the  U.  8.  8.  Seneca, 
off  Charleston,  8.  C. ,  November  20, 1862. 

Report  of  Rear-Admiral  Du  Pont,  IT.  S.  Navy. 

Flagship  Wabash, 

Port  Royal  Harbor,  8.  C. ,  November  28,  1862. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  the  capture  of  the  rebel  schooner 
Annie  Dees  by  the  U.  S.  gunboat  Seneca  on  the  evening  of  the  7th 
[20th]  instant,  attempting  to  run  the  blockade  out  of  Charleston.  No 
papers  were  found  on  board.  The  master,  Thomas  Bennett,  acknowl¬ 
edges  that  he  threw  them  overboard  in  obedience  to  orders  from  the 
owners  in  Charleston. 


SOUTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


457 


The  schooner,  being  considered  unseaworthy,  was  sent  to  this  port. 
I  ordered  a  survey  upon  her  and  herewith  enclose  the  report,  wherein 
the  schooner  is  declared  unfit  to  proceed  north.  Her  cargo,  consisting 
of  125  barrels  of  turpentine  and  68  barrels  of  resin,  has  been  trans¬ 
shipped  to  the  U.  S.  storeship  Courier ,  which  sails  to-morrow  for  New 
York.  The  master  and  crew  go  in  the  Courier ,  as  also  three  persons, 
viz.,  John  M.  Murrey,  James  Egal  (or  Egan),  and  Arthur  Erving  (or 
Ervin),  calling  themselves  passengers. 

The  three  persons  last  named,  as  also  one  of  the  crew,  viz,  William 
Lamberton,  who  were  sent  to  this  port  in  the  Housatonic ,  are  suspected, 
from  their  conversation  when  on  board  of  that  vessel,  of  being  Charles¬ 
ton  pilots.  Pencil  sketches  of  the  coast  in  the  neighborhood  of  Law- 
ford  Channel  were  found  in  pocketbooks  belonging  to  some  of  these 
men.  I  recommend,  for  reasons  previously  stated,  that  these  men  be 
closely  scrutinized  and,  if  necessary,  confined. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

S.  F.  Du  Pont, 

Hear- Admiral ,  Comdg.  South  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Nary ,  Washington. 


Report  of  Captain  Oodon,  U.  S.  Navy,  senior  officer  off  Charleston,  S.  C. 

U.  S.  S.  Powhatan, 

Off  Charleston ,  November  21,  1862. 

Admiral:  Last  evening  at  8  o’clock  (very  dark  and  rainy)  an  attempt 
was  made  by  a  schooner,  the  Annie  Dees ,  to  escape  from  Charleston 
by  Maffitt’s  Channel.  She  was  brought  up,  however,  by  the  Seneca , 
Lieutenant- Commander  Gibson,  whose  report*  I  enclose. 

Three  shots  were  fired,  one  shell  bursting  over  the  vessel  and  some 
pieces  of  it  striking  her. 

At  9  o’clock  another  attempt  seemed  to  be  made.  The  Ilousatonic 
slipped  and  chased  eastward  and  south  for  50  miles,  but  saw  nothing 
more  of  the  vessel,  and  returned  this  morning  to  her  anchorage. 

This  ship  also  slipped,  ready  to  chase,  but  nothing  was  seen.  I 
hope  it  may  prove  a  false  alarm.  The  night,  however,  was  so  dark 
that  a  vessel  may  have  passed  out. 

I  send  the  Annie  Dees  to  Port  Royal.  Her  cargo  consists  of  140 
barrels  of  turpentine  and  a  quantity  of  resin,  and  is  a  valuable  one. 

As  the  vessel  draws  but  4  feet  (intended  for  inside  trade  entirely),  I 
do  not  feel  justified  in  sending  her  north.  She  had  a  crew  of  four  men 
and  also  three  passengers,  all  of  which  I  shall  keep  until  one  of  the 
vessels  leaves  hence  for  Port  Royal.  She  lost  both  anchors,  and  I 
have  none  to  supply  her  with.  The  captain  threw  overboard  his 
papers  by  order  of  his  owners. 

I  earnestly  request  that  the  prize  officer  and  crew  may  be  sent  back 
as  early  as  possible. 

I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

S.  W.  Godon, 

Captain  and  Senior  Officer  Present. 

Rear-Admiral  S.  F.  Du  Pont, 

Comdg.  South  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron ,  Port  Royal.

Report  of  Commander  Beaumont ,  U.  S.  Navy,  forwarding  informa¬ 
tion  received  from  contraband  regarding  Confederate  battery. 

U.  S.  Gunboat  Sebago, 

Off  Georgetown ,  S.  C .,  November  *21,  1863. 
Sir:  I  would  respectfully  inform  you  that  nothing  of  importance 
has  transpired  at  this  station  since  the  departure  of  the  Norwich.  The 
number  of  contrabands  on  North  Island  now  amounts  to  59,  8  having 
arrived  since  the  departure  of  Commander  Duncan.  One  of  them, 
who  arrived  yesterday,  informs  me  that  he  was  employed  in  the  battery 
on  Marion’s  plantation,  and  that  it  consists  of  four  rifled  cannons. 
From  his  description  I  judge  them  to  be  30-pounders,  and  that  two 
large  guns  are  expected  from  Charleston.  He  further  states  that  the 
rebels  intend  to  erect  a  battery  on  Santee  River. 

I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

J.  C.  Beaumont, 

Commander. 

Rear-Admiral  S.  F.  Du  Pont, 

Commanding  South  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron.

U.  S.  S.  Stettin, 

Port  Royal,  S.  C. ,  November  2f  1862. 
Sir:  In  accordance  to  orders  received  by  me  from  you  under  the  date 
of  October  29,  I  would  most  respectfully  report  that  I  have  this  day 


SOUTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON.  461 

arrived  at  this  port,  and  have  reported  to  Rear-Admiral  S.  F.  Du  Pont 
for  duty  on  the  South  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron. 

I  have  not  been  able  to  get  more  than  7  knots  out  of  the  Stettin  under 
the  most  favorable  circumstances,  but  trust  she  may  prove  faster.  As 
to  her  qualities,  as  far  as  regards  being  a  good  seaboat  goes,  I  have  the 
honor  to  inform  you  she  has  proved  herself  one  of  the  best  seaboats  I 
ever  saw. 

The  passage  down  has  been  very  stormy,  having  had  a  strong  gale 
with  a  high  head  sea  from  the  S.  S.  W. 

I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  yourobedient  servant, 

Edward  F.  Devens,

Report  of  Commander  Woodhull ,  U  S.  Navy,  commanding  TJ.  S.  S. 

Cimarron ,  regarding  affairs  in  St.  John's  River ,  Florida. 

U.  S.  S.  Cimarron, 

St.  John’s  River,  Florida,  November  1862. 

Admiral:  I  have  the  honor  to  acknowledge  the  receipt  of  yours  of 
the  20th  instant.  I  feel  much  gratified  that  my  services  in  this  locality 
meet  with  your  approval. 

Everything  remains  as  at  the  date  of  my  last  letter.  The  guerrillas 
occasionally  show  themselves  in  the  neighborhood  of  Jacksonville,  but 
not  in  numbers  sufficient  to  occasion  any  anxiety  or  interfere  with  the 
use  of  the  river  as  we  may  desire. 

The  colony  at  Pilot  Town  now  contains  nearly  100  men,  women,  and 
children,  white  and  black,  and  the  number  is  gradually  on  the  increase; 
every  fresh  arrival  brings  the  information  that  desertions  are  of  daily 
occurrence  among  the  Florida  troops.  Some  go  to  Fernandina,  others 
[to  St.]  Augustine  and  to  this  point.  I  am  assured  that  if  a  permanent 
post  were  established  at  this  place,  protected  by  half  of  a  company  of 
soldiers,  so  as  to  give  confidence  to  those  people  escaping  (from  “  unwil¬ 
ling  service”)  of  safety  from  recapture,  there  would  be  a  rapid  melting 
away  of  the  armed  men  composing  the  whole  military  strength  of  this 
part  of  Florida,  which,  so  far  as  1  can  ascertain,  does  not  average  over 
400  men.  The  Georgia  troops  are  all  being  recalled,  and  it  is  not 
likely  they  will  soon  be  permitted  to  return.  The  people  along  the 
river  bank  are  well  disposed  to  us,  and  I  am  satisfied  from  their  con¬ 
versation  that  they  are  very  tired  with  the  war;  that  discontent  and 
discouragement  are  very  prevalent  among  the  masses.  The  destitution 
in  this  region  of  country  is  very  great,  and  the  want  of  clothing  of  all 
kinds  is  their  greatest  need;  such  is  the  existing  state  of  affairs  up  to 
this  time. 

1  have  the  men  of  Pilot  Town  Colony  engaged  as  a  guard.  All  the 
avenues  of  approach  from  Cedar  Point  and  Trout  Creek  are  perfectly 
blockaded  with  a  heavy  abatis,  and  if  moderate  vigilance  is  observed  it 
will  be  difficult  for  the  enemy  to  assail  it.  As  you  are  aware,  there  are 
no  means  of  support  for  the  people  on  the  island,  save  what  is  obtained 
from  the  vessels  in  the  river.  I  am  consequently  compelled  to  furnish 
food  for  them.  I  presume,  under  the  circumstances,  this  is  all  right; 


462  SOUTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 

still,  I  should  very  much  like  to  have  your  views  for  my  future  gov¬ 
ernment,  and  also  as  to  the  future  of  these  people. 

X  shall  be  very  nearly  out  of  coals  by  the  first  of  the  month,  as  will 
also  be  the  Uncos.  Can  we  have  a  small  coal  vessel  dispatched  to  us  ? 
We  could  easily  accommodate  200  tons. 

The  Cimarron  is  really  in  a  very  bad  state,  and  should  be  repan  ed 
without  further  delay.  She  must  be  placed  in  a  dock  and  shored  up 
to  bring  her  into  shape  again.  She  is  evidently  spreading,  and  the 
safety  of  her  engine  is  critical. 

I  am  very  happy  in  being  permanently  attached  to  }mur  command, 
and  it  will  be  my  study  to  execute  all  your  orders  to  the  utmost  of  my 

ability.  . 

The  health  of  the  officers  and  crews  of  the  vessels  composing  this 
part  of  the  blockade,  I  am  pleased  to  inform  you,  is  excellent. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

M.  WOODHULL, 
Commander ,  TJ.  S.  Navy. 

Rear-Admiral  S.  F.  Du  Pont,  U.  S.  Navy, 

Comdg.  South  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron ,  Port  Royal ,  S.  C.

Letter  from  Rear-Admiral  Du  Pont ,  U.  S.  Navy,  to  Brigadier- 

General  Saxton ,  U.  S.  Army ,  requesting  his  views  regarding  the 

colonies  in  the  Department  of  the  South. 

Flagship  Wabash, 

Port  Royal  Harbor ,  S.  C. ,  November  26,  1862. 

General:  I  beg  to  call  your  attention  to  the  colonies  in  the  Depart¬ 
ment  of  the  South. 

There  are  at  present  60  contrabands  on  North  Island,  near  Georore- 
town. 

There  are  nearly  100  colonists  on  an  island  in  the  St.  John’s  River 
under  the  protection  of  our  gunboats,  but  of  this  number  there  are  a 
good  many  white  persons,  refugees.  Commander  Woodhull,  of  the 
Cimarron,  in  his  last  communication,  writes  as  follows: 

The  colony  at  Pilot  Town  now  contains  nearly  100  men,  women,  and  children, 
white  and  black,  and  the  number  is  gradually  on  the  increase.  Every  fresh  arrival 
brings  the  information  that  desertions  are  of  daily  occurrence  among  the  Florida 
troops. 

As  you  are  aware,  there  are  no  means  of  support  for  the  people  on  the  island,  save 
what  is  obtained  from  the  vessels  in  the  river,  and  I  am  consequently  compelled  to 
furnish  food  to  them. 

These  colonists  are  all  much  in  want  of  food  and  clothing,  the  latter  of  which  it  is 
entirely  out  of  my  power  to  supply.  I  have  been  doing  the  former  out  of  my  lim¬ 
ited  means  from  the  gunboats.  These  poor  people  can  not  be  allowed  to  starve. 

I  should  be  glad  to  hear  from  jmu  in  reference  to  this  matter  at  your 
earliest  convenience. 

I  am,  general,  respectfully,  etc., 

S.  F.  Du  Pont, 

Rear-Admiral. 

Brigadier-General  R.  Saxton, 

Beaufort,  S.  C. 


Letter  from  Brigadier-  General  Saxton,  U.  S.  Army,  to  Rear-Admiral 
Du  Pont,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  regarding  provision  for  the  colonists  at  Pilot 
Town,  Fla. 

Beaufort,  S.  C. ,  November  28,  1862. 
Admiral:  I  have  the  honor  to  acknowledge  the  receipt  of  your 
letter  of  the  26th  instant. 

I  will  send  a  steamer  to  North  Island  for  the  contrabands  at  that 
point  as  soon  as  I  can  procure  one. 

With  regard  to  the  colonists  at  St.  John’s  River  and  Pilot  Town,  I 
regret  that  I  have  no  place  to  put  them  except  in  tents;  every  building 
I  have  is  filled.  I  am  now  building  houses  at  St.  Helenaville,  S.  C., 
for  refugees,  but  they  will  not  be  ready  for  occupancy  for  several 


464  SOUTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 

weeks.  I  expect  that  our  forces  will  soon  be  enabled  to  occupy  Edisto 
Island:  in  that  event  I  shall  have  room  for  2,000  people. 

If  the  colonists  can  remain  in  their  present  position  until  the  arrival 
of  General  Hunter,  I  shall  be  able  then  to  provide  for  them  all. 

I  am,  sir,  with  great  respect,  your  obedient  servant, 

R.  Saxton, 
Brigadier-  General.

if  any  changes  have  occurred  since  your  last  visit.  While  at  Jackson¬

Benedict  to  the  North  you  will  facilitate  his  wishes.

admiral  makes  a  strong  point  of  it  in  his  orders  and  instructions  to  me.

Cimarron,  regarding  affairs  in  St.  JohvJs  Biver,  Florida. 

U.  S.  Gunboat  Cimarron, 

St.  John's  Biver,  Florida,  December  1,  1863. 

Admiral:  Enclosed  you  will  find  a  letter  recently  received  from  a 
Mr.  Burritt,  of  Jacksonville,  complaining  of  the  strict  supervision  I 
have  thought  proper  to  pursue  in  this  locality  (since  the  taking  of  the 
battery  at  St.  John’s  Bluff),  and  a  copy  of  my  answer  to  that  gentle¬ 
man.  It  is  very  true  what  he  therein  states,  that  I  have  rigorously 
maintained  our  occupancy  of  the  river,  and  in  doing  so  I  have,  among 
other  precautions,  invariably  destroyed  “all  the  boats  and  water  craft” 
of  whatever  description  met  with,  deeming  this  course  the  best  and 
easiest  means  of  putting  an  end  to,  or  at  least  in  a  great  measure 
obstructing,  “  military  operations  ”  of  the  enemy.  That  it  has  been 
so  far  successful  and  produced  the  very  inconvenience  aimed  at  by  me 
is  without  doubt  the  “pinching  cause ’’that  elicited  Mr.  B.’s  letter, 
whose  desire  evidently  is,  under  the  guise  of  a  private  communication, 


SOUTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


467 


to  obtain  an  official  recognition  and  consent  to  his  wishes  (meaning  I 
have  reason  to  believe,  the  “Confederate  officers  of  Jacksonville,”  with 
i  i1111  cred!bly  informed,  he  is  in  constant  and  close  confidence). 

Ihis  Mi.  Burritt  is  a  lawyer  by  profession,  and  rather  a  prominent 
man  m  these  parts.  \  ou,  no  doubt,  know  something  of  his  anteced- 
ents.  He  is  represented  to  me  as  having  been  at  the  outbreak  of  the 
rebellion  a  secessionist.  After  your  conquest  of  this  part  of  the  coun¬ 
try  he  took  quite  a  showy  part  as  a  Union  man.  Since  then  he  has 
returned  to  his  “secession  proclivities,”  and  now,  to  guard  against 
accidents,  he  is  trying*  to  be  a  u  go-between  ” — in  other  words,  a 
“waiter  on  Providence.”  He  never  will  be  useful  to  us,  but  will  be 
just  what  v  ill  most  conduce  to  his  own  purposes  and  contribute  the 
most  toward  the  preservation  of  his  large  property  at  Jacksonville  and 
parts  contiguous.  1  have  been  thus  particular  in  my  description  of 
the  gentleman  that  you  may  draw  the  right  conclusions  as  to  the  tenor 
of  his  letter  to  me. 

I  know  from  positive  information,  gathered  in  conversation  from  a 
number  of  people  along  the  river  bank,  that  the  course  I  pursued  in 
“  destroying  boats  ”  has  been  in  the  main  satisfactory,  as  it  has  guarded 
indirectly  the  quiet  and  inoffensive  part  of  the  inhabitants  from  “  rob¬ 
bery  and  plunder”  of  these  irresponsible  rascals,  who,  in  small  bands, 
infest  this  region  of  country,  calling  themselves  “  regulators,”  besides 
interfering  greatly  with  the  “foraging  parties”  of  the  guerrillas  and. 
other  “military  organizations.” 

We  have  destroyed,  from  first  to  last,  perhaps  a  thousand  boats. 
They  were  so  numerous  on  our  first  appearance  in  the  river  it  might 
almost  be  said  to  be  “bridged  over,”  and  you  can  well  conceive  how 
easy,  with  such  facilities,  it  was  to  concentrate  rapidly  forces  at  any 
given  point  on  either  bank  of  the  river;  also  give  them  large  means  of 
transportation  of  provisions,  plunder,  and  all  other  matters  necessary 
to  guerrilla  warfare. 

I  submit  the  above  statement,  hoping  my  course  will  meet  with  your 
approval. 

I  am,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

M.  WoODHULL,

Jacksonville,  Fla.,  November  29,  1862. 

Dear  Sir:  I  venture  to  avail  myself  of  the  opportunity  afforded  by 
the  visit  of  the  Tineas  to  saj"  to  you  that  in  a  conversation  I  had  with 
Captain  Steedman,  of  the  Paul  Jones,  while  he  was  here  in  the  early 
part  of  October,  he  intimated  to  me  that  although  General  Brannan’s 
forces  were  about  to  leave  he  would  still  continue  with  his  naval  force 
to  hold  the  river,  but  that  he  should  molest  none  of  the  inhabitants 
unless  they  molested  him.  My  intercourse  with  Captain  Steedman  was 
not  official  (as  I  am  only  a  private  citizen  of  this  place),  and  of  course 
this  was  not  understood  to  be  a  pledge  or  engagement  on  the  part  of  this 
officer,  but  only  an  expression  of  what  1  understood  to  be  his  intention. 
Whether  Captain  Steedman  continued  to  command  in  the  river  for 
any  time  after  this  I  have  had  no  means  of  knowing,  but  I  have  sup¬ 
posed  not,  because  the  policy  indicated  by  him  has  not  been  pursued.

It  is  unnecessary  to  say  that  the  use  ot  the  river  to  the  inhabitants 
alone-  the  St.  John’s  for  all  purposes  has  been  wholly  interdicted  by 
the  destruction  of  their  boats  and  everything  in  the  shape  of  water 
craft.  This  condition  of  things  has  resulted,  as  it  is  supposed,  from 
the  attempt  of  the  military  authorities  in  Florida  to  construct  (not  to 
maintain)  a  battery  at  St.  John’s  Bluff,  a  matter  in  which  the  people 
along  the  river  and  in  all  this  region  were  not  only  not  consulted,  and 
of  which  many  of  them  had  no  knowledge  at  the  time  it  was  being 
erected,  but  in  which  they  had  no  sort  of  participation  m  any  way. 
It  is  not  to  be  presumed  that  these  facts  were  fully  known  to  the  fed¬ 
eral  forces  in  the  river,  because  as  a  measure  of  retaliation  the  injuries 
might  as  well  have  been  inflicted  upon  the  citizens  of  any  other  locality. 
Whether  the  erection  of  a  formidable  battery,  such  as  General  Bran  nan 
and  Captain  Steedman  informed  me  the  one  at  St.  John  s  Bluff  was, 
and  the  prompt  abandonment  of  it  to  your  forces  without  a  struggle, 
was  a  suitable  subject  of  retaliation  against  even  those  who  devised 
and  constructed  it  may  be  a  question.  But  surely  those  who  had  noth¬ 
ing  to  do  with  it  ought  not  to  be  held  responsible,  and  yet  these  are 
the  only  ones  who  have  suffered.  I  beg  to  submit  to  you  whether 
these  facts  being  so,  as  they  incontestably  are — this  view  of  the  subject 
is  not  worthy  your  consideration,  and  whether,  in  your  judgment,  it 
would  be  inconsistent  with  the  interests  of  your  service  to  relax  some¬ 
what  the  rigor  which  has  hitherto  been  practiced.  It  must  be  obvious 
that  the  small  boats  and  canoes  used  by  our  people  in  fishing  and  in 
crossing  the  river,  and  in  passing  occasionally  up  and  down,  can  not 
be  made  available  for  any  military  purpose,  and  indeed  it  is  hardly 
possible  that  they  could  be  used  for  any  offensive  or  objectionable  pur¬ 
pose  whatever. 

Were  it  known  that  I  made  this  communication  to  you  my  motives 
would  be  misconstrued  by  many  and  would  doubtless  subject  me  to 
inconvenience.  The  people  along  the  river  would  be  very  grateful. 
In  other  quarters  I  suppose  I  should  be  censured.  I  particularly 
request,  therefore,  that  it  may  be  regarded  as  confidential.  You  will 
please  regard  it  as  the  application  of  a  private  individual  on  behalf  of 
the  quiet  and  unoffending  inhabitants  of  the  river,  many  of  them  sim¬ 
ple,  unlettered,  and  uninformed,  who  have  no  power  to  speak  for 
themselves,  and  if  they  had  would  not  dare  to  exercise  it, 

I  am,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

S.  L.  Burritt. 

Flag-Officer  Maxwell  Woodhull, 

Steamer  Cimarron ,  Commanding ,  etc. ,  St.  John's  River.
