Letter  from  Rear-Admiral  Du  Pont ,  U  S.  Navy,  to  Captain  Wise, 
U.  S.  Navy ,  regarding  general  matters ,  and  referring  to  the  Confed¬ 
erate  steamers  Fingal  and  Nashville  ( Rattlesnake ). 

Wabash, 

Port  Royal,  S.  C. ,  January  16,  1863. 

My  Dear  Wise:  1  received  your  kind  note,  with  the  drawing  and 
specification  of  the  ingenious  machine  for  sawing  piles,  of  which  you 
spoke  to  me  when  1  was  north.  Many  thanks  for  both.  The  latter 
may  be  very  useful  for  burrowing  into  Charleston  or  Savannah. 

In  reference  to  the  former  it  would  appear,  if  we  can  rely  upon 
recent  statements,  what  I  cared  as  much  for  and  more  than  forts 
(obstructions),  we  are  in  a  measure  behind.  The  depth  of  water,  a 
gale  or  two,  and  some  spring  tides  have  removed  the  great  mass  of 
them,  well  constructed  as  they  were — five  14-inch  timbers,  hooped 
with  iron,  with  iron  points  in  heel  to  sink  them,  then  fastened  together 
by  a  chain  cable  about  10  feet  apart,  with  a  torpedo  hung  to  the 
festoons. 

They  are  still  at  work  on  the  defenses,  however,  and  the  number  of 
forts  and  guns  is  simply  fabulous.  My  comfort  and  hope  is  that  with 
our  experience  and  study  of  eighteen  months  on  the  coast,  we  can 
apply  whatever  means  are  furnished  for  the  ends  desired  about  as  well 
as  most  people. 

W  e  are  threatened  now  by  the  ironclads:  The  Fingal  is  more  for¬ 
midable  than  Merrimack,  having  a  much  stronger  engine,  and  I  expect 
to  hear  she  has  fanned  out  the  gunboats  from  W assaw  and  Ossabaw, 
and  got  the  Nashville  to  sea,  now  fitted  as  a  privateer.  Then  the}-  are 
at  work  deepening  Wappoo  Cut  to  let  the  Charleston  rams  on  the 
vessels  holding  Stono. 

I  commenced  last  July  writing  on  this  subject;  was  promised  the 
Ironsides,  but  Fox  does  not  believe  a  word  of  it,  and  we  have  to  take 
what  comes,  like  men,  that’s  all. 

One  thing  J  must  believe,  there  is  more  patriotism  among  Southern 
mechanics  than  with  ours,  or  they  could  not,  with  their  crippled  cir¬ 
cumstances,  turn  off  the  work  as  they  do.  The  Charleston  ironclads 
have  been  done  two  months;  they  miscalculated  the  displacement  and 
have  weak  engines,  but  thoroughly  built  of  6-inch  iron,  heavily  armed, 
having  two  guns  less  only  than  Merrimack /  but  for  the  above  defects 
they  would  have  cleaned  out  the  blockaders  off  Charleston  without 
trouble  long  ago. 

The  loss  of  the  Monitor  gave  us  a  “sick  turn,”  as  Fox  calls  it;  we 
get  oui  news  by  the  rebel  pickets;  rather  tough  in  such  times,  having

Report  of  Captain  Green ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  proposing  the  obstruction  of 

Romerly  Marshes ,  to  prevent  the  escape  of  Confederate  steamer  JSash- 

ville  ( Rattlesnake ). 

U.  S.  S.  Canandaigua, 

Off  Ossahaw ,  January  16,  1863. 

Sir:  I  have  respectfully  to  inform  you  that  I  arrived  at  this  anchor¬ 
age  on  the  evening  of  the  11th,  in  obedience  to  your  order  of  the  9th 
instant,  and  to  acknowledge  the  receipt  of  two  communications  from 
you  dated  the  13th  instant,  one  relating  to  a  coal  vessel  about  to  be 
dispatched  to  supply  the  vessels  at  this  station,  and  the  other  to  a  sup¬ 
ply  schooner  towed  down  by  the  Water  Witch,  and  also  your  note  of 
the  same  date. 

No  reliable  information  has  reached  me  in  regard  to  the  manner  or 
means  the  rebels  design  employing  to  rescue  the  Nashville,  but  I  think 
it  probable  if  an  attempt  is  made  it  will  be  at  the  next  high  tides  with 
an  ironclad  steamer  of  light  draft  through  the  Romerly  Marshes. 

Our  force  in  Ossabaw  is  insufficient,  in  my  opinion,  to  cope  with  an 
ironclad  vessel  that  might  be  and  possibly  may  have  been  constructed, 
as  rumor  says,  for  the  purpose  of  navigating  throug’h  the  marshes, 
and  the  ship’s  draft  and  length  render  her  unsuitable  for  inside  work. 
I  would  therefore  suggest  the  expediency  of  obstructing  the  passage 
through  the  marshes  by  sinking  there,  when  the  tides  next  meet,  an 
old  hulk  loaded  with  stones.  Under  present  circumstances  the  services 
of  another  gunboat  is  very  much  needed  to  watch  the  Nashville  and 
guard  Adams  Creek. 

The  Nashville  lays  a  little  above  the  fort  on  the  Ogeechee,  appar¬ 
ently  ready  for  sea. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

J.  F.  Green, 

Captain. 

Rear-Admiral  S.  F.  Du  Pont, 

Comdg.  South  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron ,  Port  Royal ,  S.  C.

[Subenclosure.] 

Running  the  Blockade. — Arming  of  the  Nashville. 

The  celebrated  steamer  Nashville  has  now  for  a  considerable  time 
been  waiting  to  run  the  blockade  with  a  cargo  of  cotton  at  Ogeechee 
[River,  Ossabaw]  Sound,  but  has  been  prevented  from  doing  so  by  the 
vigilance  of  the  Federal  blockading  squadron.  From  information  we 
received  yesterday,  we  learn  that  this  steamer  has  been  sold  for 
$120,000  to  a  company  consisting  of  several  private  merchants,  who 
have  recently  made  some  considerable  [change]  in  her  appearance. 
She  has  been  cut  down  and  her  houses  on  deck  have  been  completely 
removed.  She  has  also  been  armed  with  two  splendid  guns,  one  of 


516  SOUTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 

them  being  100-pounder  rifled,  She  will  only  use  these  guns  in  self- 
defense,  if  attacked,  as  she  has  been  purchased  solely  for  the  purpose 
of  conveying  cotton  from  the  Confederate  States  to  a  Biitish  poit.

Destruction  of  the  Confederate  steamer  Tropic  (. formerly  Huntress ),  off 
Charleston,  S.  C.,  January  18,  1863. 

Report  of  Rear-Admiral  Du  Pont,  U.  S.  Navy. 

Flagship  Wabash, 

Port  Royal  Harbor,  S.  C.,  January  26,  1863. 

Sir:  1  had  not  time  by  the  last  mail  to  give  any  particulars  of  the 
destruction  of  the  rebel  steamer  Tropic,  formerly  the  Huntress,  of 
Charleston. 

On  the  morning  of  the  18th  instant,  between  3  and  4  o’clock,  an  alarm 
was  given  from  the  south  side  of  the  blockade;  soon  after  a  bright  light 
was  seen  to  the  southward,  and  the  Quaker  City ,  Commander  Frailey, 
immediately  steamed  to  the  spot  and  found  the  steamer  in  flames,  but 
whether  she  was  fired  intentionally  or  not  does  not  yet  appear. 

Commander  Frailey  at  once  sought  to  pick  up  the  passengers  and 
crew,  who  had  taken  to  their  boats,  but  before  being  taken  on  board 
the  Quaker  City,  they  managed  to  destroy  most  of  their  papers;  some, 
however,  were  found,  which  are  herewith  transmitted  (marked  No.  1). 

One  of  the  passengers,  a  Mr.  Vernon,  is  an  Englishman,  and  was  at 
the  time  proceeding  to  Europe  to  carry  out  a  contract  with  the  rebel 
Secretary  of  War  to  supply  the  Confederate  Government  with  medi¬ 
cines,  clothing,  arms,  powder,  etc. ;  this  contract  is  among  the  papers. 
Another  personage,  Mr.  T.  Steers,  was  apparently  engaged  in  the  same 
business;  he  says  he  is  from  Pennsylvania.  Most  of  the  officers  are 
citizens  of  the  Southern  States,  and,  by  the  shipping  articles,  most  of 
the  crew,  but  how  far  this  is  so  I  have  no  means  of  ascertaining. 

I  have  transferred  to  the  Circassian  the  captain,  passengers,  and  six¬ 
teen  of  her  crew,  directing  Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  Eaton  to  com¬ 
municate  with  Rear-Admiral  Paulding  as  to  their  disposition.  The 
second  mate  (Black),  the  Nassau  pilot  (Spatches),  the  pa}Hnaster  (Bee¬ 
son),  and  Johnson,  the  Charleston  pilot,  and  four  of  the  crew,  go  north 
in  the  Restless,

May  X  ask  the  Department  to  give  the  necessary  orders  to  Rear- 
Admiral  Paulding  before  the  Circassian  and  Restless  arrive  at  New

Report  of  Captain  Godon,  U.  S.  Navy,  senior  officer  off  Charleston,  S,  C.,  commanding 

U.  S.  S.  Powhatan, 

U.  S.  S.  Powhatan, 

Off  Charleston ,  January  18,  1863. 

Sir:  This  morning,  between  3  and  J  o’clock,  signal  rockets  and  a 
gun  from  the  south  section  of  the  blockade  gave  an  alarm;  the  night 
moderately  dark.  Shortly  after  a  bright  light  to  the  southward  indi¬ 
cated  a  lire,  and  the  Quaker  City,  Commander  Frailey,  steamed  to  the 
spot  and  found  the  steamer  Tropic ,  formerly  the  Huntress ,  of  Char¬ 
leston,  in  flames.  This  vessel  in  attempting  to  break  the  blockade, 
loaded  with  326  bales  of  cotton  and  a  quantity  of  turpentine,  had 
taken  fire  and  was  rapidly  burning  to  the  water’s  edge. 

Commander  Frailey  at  once  sought  to  pick  up  the  passengers  and 
crew,  who  had  taken  to  their  boats,  and  whom,  on  finding  themselves 
rescued  by  us,  at  once  threw  overboard  all  the  papers  they  had 
secured  but  such  as  related  to  their  own  matters.  These  papers  I 
send  3Tou. 

You  will  find  that  Mr.  Vernon  is  engaged  in  supplying  the  rebel- 
lionists  with  all  sorts  of  military  matters;  has  an  engagement  to  fur¬ 
nish  the  rebel  Government  with  engines  and  steam  boilers,  and  in  all 
ways  diligently7  employed  in  aiding  and  abetting  the  enemies  of  our 
Government.  His  letters  to  and  from  the  Secretaries  of  the  Navy 
and  W ar  are  distinct  on  this  point.  A  Mr.  T.  Steers  is  also  engaged 
in  the  same  way. 

Some  of  the  papers  give  some  useful  and  curious  information,  and 
I  have  filed  them  so  as  to  be  convenient  for  you  to  look  over. 

I  hope  if  there  are  means  of  preventing  damage  being  done  to  our 
cause  by  such  agents,  you  will  call  the  attention  of  the  Government  to 
their  cases.  The  pilot,  Johnston,  or  Johnson,  should  be  cared  for. 

About  the  time  the  Tropic  was  endeavoring  to  evade  the  blockade 
outward  another  steamer  attempted  to  pass  in.  Her  entrance  was 
prevented,  although  she  escaped  in  the  darkness,  and  probably  had 
Commander  Frailey  disregarded  the  calls  of  humanity  to  save  the 
crew  of  the  burning  delinquent,  he  might  have  caught  a  glimpse  of 
the  second  offender,  who,  of  course,  did  not  stop  to  help  his  fellow 
blockade  breaker,  although  given  to  the  flames.

[Enclosure.] 

U.  S.  Steam  Frigate  New  Ironsides, 

Port  Royal,  January  19,  1863. 

Admiral:  On  my  arrival  in  Hampton  Roads,  after  my  second  pas¬ 
sage  to  that  place  from  Philadelphia,  the  honorable  Secretary  addressed 
me  a  letter  expressive  of  his  surprise  that  I  had  not  reported  the 
behavior  and  performance  of  this  ship  on  her  passage  around;  he  will 
doubtless  expect  a  report  from  me  on  the  subject  in  my  passage  to  this 
place.  I  have  the  honor  to  make  it  to  you. 

I  left  Hampton  Roads  on  the  11th  instant  with  fine  weather  and  a 
N.  W.  wind,  which  I  held  until  about  50  miles  to  the  southward  of  Cape 
Hatteras,  when  the  wind  hauled  to  the  S.  W. ,  increasing  tc  a  smart  gale 
with  a  very  rough,  short  sea.  I  sent  down  lower  and  topsail  yards  and 
steamed  against  it  with  very  poor  progress,  the  ship  being  able,  under 
those  circumstances,  barely  to  hold  her  own. 

I  adhere  to  all  the  opinions  I  expressed  in  regard  to  her  capacity  as 
a  seaboat  in  my  communication  to  him  of  October  5, 1862.  Away  from 
land,  where  I  could  use  her  fore-and-aft  sails,  assisted  by  the  propel¬ 
ler,  I  consider  her  safe  and  seaworth}^  in  any  gale,  but  if  it  became 


SOUTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


519 


necessary  to  carry  her  directly  off  a  lee  shore  against  a  heavy  sea  and 
high  wind  she  is  unable  to  do  it  with  her  present  steam  power,  and 
nothing  could  save  her  but  her  anchors.  Instead  of  carrying  sixteen 
days’  coal,  burning  daily  25  tons,  as  was  supposed,  she  burns  nearly 
40  tons  a  day,  and  carries,  all  full,  only  ten  days’  coal;  consequently  I 
should  consider  it  unsafe  to  send  her  to  sea  on  any  passage  that  would 
require  more  than  four  or  live  days  to  perform  it,  unless  accompanied 
by  a  steamer  that  would  be  able  to  give  her  assistance  in  case  she 
should  need  it,  which  would  be  the  case  if  she  were  met  by  a  succes¬ 
sion  of  adverse  gales. 

After  the  gale  from  S.  W.,  of  which  I  have  spoken,  the  wind  hauled 
again  to  the  N.  W.,  and  carrying  courses  and  topgallant  sails  she  pro¬ 
gressed  at  the  rate  of  about  6i  knots,  never  being  able  to  exceed  that 
with  steam  and  sails  combined. 

I  reached  here  and  anchored  inside  the  light-ship  at  9  o’clock  p.  m. 
on  the  evening  of  the  17th,  having  then  only  79  tons  of  coal  on  board, 
having  made  the  passage  in  six  days  and  live  hours. 

Had  I  again  encountered  a  heavy  adverse  gale  at  this  end  of  the  pas¬ 
sage  her  situation  for  want  of  coal  would  have  been  very  critical. 

Her  motions,  rolling,  and  pitching  in  a  seaway,  are  as  easy  as  any 
ship  I  ever  sailed  in;  indeed,  I  may  say  that  they  are  even  graceful  and 
playful,  so  buoyant  is  she,  and  taking  in  as  little  water  as  any  frigate 
in  service.  Were  her  steam  power  greater  and  her  capacity  to  carry 
coal  increased  I  should  consider  her  as  safe  a  vessel  at  sea  as  I  could 
desire  to  be  on  board  of;  I  should  have  no  fear  of  anything  but  a 
direct  lee  shore.  Her  drift  in  a  seaway,  ahead  or  abeam,  is  necessa¬ 
rily,  from  the  formation  of  her  hull,  very  great. 

My  last  passage  verified  all  the  favorable  opinions  I  had  expressed 
in  relation  to  her  steerage.  As  I  had  no  opportunity  of  scudding  her, 
I  can  as  yet  express  no  opinion  upon  that  subject.  When  steaming 
against  a  head  sea  she  comes  down  with  great  violence  upon  her  coun¬ 
ters  as  the  sea  catches  her  there,  whilst  forward  she  is  buoyant  and 
rising. 

Very  respectfullv,  your  obedient  servant, 

"  ‘  T.  Turner, 

Captain.

Flagship  Wabash, 

Port  Royal  Ilarbor ,  8.  C. ,  January  20,  1863. 
Sir:  The  tempestuous  weather  would  render  it  improper  to  expose 
the  Akontauk  at  sea  again  until  there  has  been  some  change.  At  this 
moment  an  inside  blockading  force  is  holding  Ossabaw  Inlet,  coast  of 
Georgia,  consisting  of  two  regular  Xl-inch  gunboats,  with  the  Dawn 
and  a  mortar  vessel.  The  Canandaigua,  a  formidable  ship,  is  also 
lying  off  the  bar.  The  Nashville  is  up  the  Great  Ogeechee,  having 
been  fitted  as  a  privateer,  and  is  lying  under  a  five  or  seven-gun  battery, 
waiting  to  run  to  sea. 

Wo  have  report  that  the  Finqal  (now  called  the  Atlanta),  an  iron¬ 
clad,  will  attempt  to  aid  the  Nashville  in  escaping. 

As  the  most  important  operations  on  this  coast  must  be  delayed 
until  other  vessels  arrive,  and  until  those  now  here  can  be  made  ready, 
it  strikes  me  a  very  important  and  handsome  thing  may  be  done  by 
capturing  this  fort  on  the  Ogeechee  and  in  destroying  the  Nashville, 
and,  should  matters  go  well,  in  burning  the  railroad  bridge  which  the 
gunboats  can  lay  alongside  of. 

Will  you  please,  then,  get  ready  for  this  service  with  the  least  delay 
possible?  Pilots  will  be  provided,  and  if  the  Canandaigua  remains 
outside,  the  gunboats  will  be  necessarily  under  your  orders  as  senior 
officer.

Report  of  Commander  Duncan ,  U.  S.  Navy,  regarding  affairs  in  St. 

John’s  River ,  transmitting  additional  report. 

U.  S.  S.  Norwich, 

St.  John’s  River ,  Florida ,  January  21,  1863. 

Sir:  I  have  to  acknowledge  the  receipt  per  steamer  Bibb  of  dis¬ 
patches  for  this  vessel  and  the  Uncos,  and  as  the  Bibb  leaves  to-morrow 
for  Fort  Royal,  I  send  by  her  a  (blind)  white  refugee,  named  Jackson, 
who  was  sent  on  board  of  this  vessel  last  Sunday  under  a  flag  of  truce 
from  Jacksonville,  by  Colonel  Finegan,  and  as  Mr.  Jackson  is  very 
desirous  of  going  north,  he  being  a  Northern  man,  I  send  him  to  Fort 
Royal.  1  also  send  you  Colonel  Finegan’s  letter. 

1  send  the  steamer  Uncos  up  the  river  every  day  to  reconnoiter  and 
believe  the  river  to  be  free  from  rebels,  as  she  sees  but  few  of  them. 
Mr.  Jackson  gave  me  some  important  information  in  regard  to  a  rebel 
man  of  war  mounting  eight  guns,  on  the  Cattahoochee  River;  also  of 
the  steamer  Cuba ,  loaded  with  cotton,  on  the  Suwanee  River,  and  as 
the  light-house  schooner  was  going  to  Key  West,  I  sent  a  letter  with 
all  the  information  furnished  me  by  Mr.  Jackson  to  Rear-Admiral 
Bailey. 

On  Sunday  last  two  refugees,  named  Jacob  Gillespie  and  John  Con¬ 
nor,  went  over  to  Mayport  Mills  for  the  purpose  of  fishing,  as  was 
supposed,  but  without  my  permission,  and  have  not  been  heard  from 
since.  Their  families  reside  about  20  miles  from  Jacksonville.  They 
have  been  waiting  some  time  here  in  hopes  of  getting  them,  but  as  we 
had  no  opportunity  we  could  not  do  it. 

1  regret  to  report  a  sad  accident  occurred  on  board  of  the  steamer 
Uncas  to-day  while  on  her  way  up  the  river,  whereby  Acting  Ensign 
William  L.  Pavy  was  seriously  wounded  while  in  the  act  of  firing  the 
rifled  Parrott  gun  at  some  pickets  at  Cedar  Creek.  The  gun  burst  and 
shattered  his  left  arm  so  badly  that  amputation  was  necessary.  The 
doctors  have  advised  me  to  send  him  to  Fort  Royal,  which  I  shall, 
to-morrow  morning,  in  the  steamer  Bibb. 

The  gun  burst,  thowing  the  whole  main  body  and  half  of  the  ring 
overboard,  the  cascabel,  half  of  the  ring,  and  the  muzzle  from  the  trun¬ 
nions  out  remaining  on  board;  the  carriage  is  unfit  for  further  use, 
and  the  only  wonder  is  that  all  of  the  gun’s  crew  were  not  killed.  I 
enclose  Captain  Watson’s  report  of  the  accident.  If  it  is  possible,  I 
would  like  to  have  a  30-pounder  sent  down  to  replace  the  other,  as  it 
is  the  most  useful  gun  we  have,  going  up  and  down  the  river. 

As  there  is  but  one  officer  left  on  board  of  the  Uncas ,  I  have 
ordered  Acting  Master’s  Mate  George  M.  Smith,  of  this  vessel,  to  her 
on  temporary  service,  until  I  hear  from  you. 

I  have  one  white  family  residing  here  at  Pilot  Town,  and  will  send 
them  to  Fernandina  the  first  opportunity.

present  condition. 

Verv  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant,

Capture  of  the  schooner  Etiwan  by  the  U  S.  S.  Ottawa ,  off  Charleston , 

S.  C. ,  January  21,  1863. 

Report  of  Rear-Admiral  Du  Pont,  U.  S.  Navy. 

No.  38.]  Flagship  Wabash, 

Port  Royal  Harbor ,  S.  C. ,  January  26,  1863. 
Sir:  By  the  last  mail  I  had  only  time  to  inform  the  Department  of 
the  capture  of  the  rebel  schooner  Etiwan ,  off  Charleston. 

She  was  taken  by  the  Ottawa,  Lieutenant-Commander  William  D. 
Whiting,  on  the  night  of  the  21st  instant,  attempting  to  pass  out  by  the 
Swash  Channel.  Lieutenant-Commander  Whiting  allowed  her  to 
approach  near  enough  to  prevent  her  return  and  then  steamed  in 
chase.  On  coming  within  close  range  he  fired  a  shot  which,  striking 
on  her  port  bow,  made  her  heave  to.  The  schooner  has  been  sur¬ 
veyed  and  condemned  as  unfit  to  go  north.  Her  cargo,  said  to  consist 
of  99  bales  of  cotton,  will  be  transshipped  to  the  beef  schooner  Simp¬ 
son  and  sent  shortly  to  New  York. 

The  master,  A.  O.  Stone  of  Charleston,  will  go  north  in  the  Simpson. 
The  rest  of  the  crew,  viz,  Walter  Stiner,  John  Day,  Charles  Poole, 
Andrew  Jackson,  and  George  Cunningham,  I  have  transferred  to  the 
Water  Witch,  directing  her  commander,  Lieutenant-Commander  Pen- 
dergrast,  to  report  to  the  commandant  of  the  New  York  yard  as  to  their 
disposition. 

Will  the  Department  give  the  necessary  orders  to  Rear-Admiral 
Paulding?  Her  papers  will  be  forwarded  to  the  United  States  prize 
commissioners.  They  show  her  to  be  a  rebel  vessel. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

S.  F.  Du  Pont, 

Rear-Admiral ,  Comdg.  South  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy ,  Washington ,  D.  C. 


Report  of  Captain  Godon,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S.  S.  Powhatan. 

U.  S.  S.  Powhatan, 

Off  Charleston,  January  22, 1863. 

Sir:  1  have  the  honor  to  report  that  last  night  about  10  o’clock  the 
schooner  Etiwan ,  in  endeavoring  to  pass  out  of  Charleston  Harbor 
through  Maffitt’s  Channel,  was  brought  to  and  captured  by  the  Ottawa, 
Lieutenant-Commander  W hiting. 

The  Ottawa  put  a  shot  through  the  schooner’s  bow,  but  even  without 
that  damage  she  would  not  be  seaworthy  to  send  north  at  this  season. 
I  therefore  sent  her  to  Port  Royal  for  your  action. 

Her  cargo,  as  reported  by  the  master,  A.  O.  Stone,  consists  of  99 
bales  of  cotton  and  a  few  barrels  of  turpentine  and  resin.  The  only 
bill  of  lading  found  on  board,  however,  calls  for  but  91. 

1  enclose  herewith  the  vessel’s  papers,  a  letter  to  Messrs.  Adderly 
&  Co.,  of  Nassau,  New  Providence,  with  bill  of  lading  from  shipper, 
and  report  of  capture  from  Lieutenant-Commander  Whiting,  to  the 
judge  of  the  court  of  the  district  to  which  you  may  see  fit  to  order  the 
cargo  of  the  Etiwan  sent.

Report  of  Lieutenant-Commander  Whiting,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S.  S.  Ottawa. 

U.  S.  Gunboat  Ottawa, 

Off  Charleston  Bar ,  January  22,  1863. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  that  last  night  at  about  10  : 40  p.  m., 
while  at  anchor  off  the  Swash  Channel,  a  schooner  was  made  standing 
out  between  us  and  the  bar. 

Being  in  readiness  to  slip,  I  allowed  her  to  approach  so  as  to  draw 
her  out  from  the  channel  way.  When  underway  I  steamed  toward 
her,  cutting  off  the  retreat  which  was  attempted.  She  was  brought 
to  with  a  shot  from  the  20-pounder  Parrott,  which  struck  in  the  port 
bow,  bursting  and  doing  some  damage. 

On  boarding  she  proved  to  be  the  schooner  Etvwan,  of  Charleston, 
S.  C.,  just  out  from  there.  The  master,  A.  O.  Stone,  reports  the 
cargo  to  be  99  bales  of  cotton  and  2  barrels  of  resin.  She  has  a  crew 
of  five  men.  I  enclose  a  report  to  the  district  judge,  with  the  papers 
found  on  board. 

I  would  respectfully  report  that  while  in  chase  of  the  Etiwan  and 
nearing  her  the  Ilousatonic  fired  across  our  bows,  I  suppose  intended 
for  the  schooner.  I  sent  up  a  rocket  and  showed  the  red  light  on  the 
side  toward  her.  A  second  shot  was  fired  from  her  about  the  time 
our  shot  was  fired  at  the  schooner,  which  passed  over  our  mastheads.. 
I  immediately  hoisted  the  running  night  signal  lights.  A  few  minutes 
after,  while  lowering  a  boat  to  board  the  prize,  a  third  shot  was  fired 


526  SOUTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


* 

from  the  Ilousatonic,  which  passed  directly  over  the  quarter-deck, 
abaft  the  mainmast.  A  blue  light  was  then  burned  to  show  the  posi¬ 
tion  of  the  vessels,  finding  that  the  regular  running  lights  were  not 
sufficient. 

At  the  time  we  were  fired  upon  the  Powhatan  and  Quaker  City  were 
visible  with  the  glass  in  their  stations  and  the  Housatonic  distinct  with 


the  naked  eye. 

It  is  to  be  supposed  that  our  identity  was  not  sufficiently  marked  to 
protect  us  from  the  fire  of  a  blockading  vessel,  which  I  hardly  need 
add  might  have  proved  exceedingly  disastrous;  but  as  I  employed  all 
the  preconcerted  signals,  I  could  do  no  more. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Wm.  D.  Whiting,

Reconnoissance  in  Stono  River  to  Wappoo  Creek ,  South  Carolina ,  by 
boat  f  rom  TJ'.  S.  S.  Commodore  McDonough ,  January  21,  1862. 


Report  of  Lieutenant-Commander  Bacon,  U.  S.  Navy. 

U.  S.  S.  Commodore  McDonough, 

Stono  Inlet ,  South  Carolina ,  January  26,  1863. 

Sir:  I  respectfully  state  that  on  the  evening  of  the  21st  I  sent  the 
dingey  with  four  men  and  Acting  Ensign  Whitman  Chase,  of  the 
Isaac  Smith ,  and  Acting  Master’s  Mate  Daniel  B.  Hallett,  of  this  ship, 
up  Stono  River  on  a  reconnoissance.  The  object  of  the  reconnoissance 
was  to  discover  whether  the  enemy  had  placed  any  obstruction  in  the 
river,  to  sound  across  the  mouth  of  Wappoo  Creek,  and  to  discover 
whether  any  new  fortifications  or  batteries  had  been  thrown  up.  They 
passed  by  Fort  Pemberton,  went  up  Wappoo  Creek,  sounded  and 
found  3  feet  of  water  on  the  bar,  it  being  two  hours  before  low  water. 
No  obstructions  were  found  in  the  river  from  the  inlet  to  the  creek. 
No  vessels  of  any  kind  were  discovered  except  a  small  canal  boat  on 
the  west  side  of  the  entrance  to  Wappoo  Creek.  No  batteries  or  for¬ 
tifications  except  Fort  Pemberton  were  seen.  The  reconnoissance 
was  a  success,  and  reflects  credit  upon  those  who  were  engaged  in  it. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Geo.  Bacon, 

Lieutenant-  Commander  and  Senior  Officer  Present. 

Rear-Admiral  S.  F.  Du  Pont,  U.  S.  Navy. 

Commanding  South  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron.

Ensign  W.  Chase.  The  reconnoissance  was  made  chiefly  on  account

of  a  rumor  that  the  rebels  were  deepening  the  channel  at  the  mouth  of

U.  S.  S.  Isaac  Smith, 

Stono  Inlet ,  South  Carolina ,  January  22,  1863. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  submit  the  following  report  of  a  reconnois- 
sance  up  Stono  River  to  Wappoo  Creek,  made  January  21,  1863: 

Started  from  the  ship  at  7:30  p.  m.,  in  a  boat  from  the  U  S.  S. 
Commodore  McDonough ,  with  Acting  Master’s  Mate  Hallett,  and  pro¬ 
ceeded  up  the  river.  W e  saw  no  signs  of  rebels  until  we  had  passed 
Tom  Grimball’s  plantation,  when  we  saw  a  light  below  us  on  James 
Island,  and  soon  after  heard  the  beat  of  a  drum.  We  proceeded  cau¬ 
tiously  along,  examining  the  banks,  both  sides,  crossing  and  recrossing 
as  we  advanced,  and  when  about  2  miles  above  Tom  Grimball’s  heard 
voices  a  short  distance  ahead,  and  on  turning  a  point  discovered  a 
number  of  lights  and  fires  in  the  bend  of  the  river  on  James  Island, 
and  from  the  noise  and  talking  should  think  the  rebels  were  at  work 
there. 

On  the  opposite  bank  saw  a  flagstaff  and  a  lookout,  but  no  other 
signs  of  fortifications  or  encampments  on  that  side  of  the  river. 

Entered  Wappoo  Creek  and  sounded  across  the  mouth  in  3  feet 
of  water;  landed  and  examined  the  bank,  and  I  should  judge  the  tide 
had  ebbed  5  or  6  feet.  A  barge  was  lying  alongside  the  bank  near  the 
entrance,  but  could  see  no  one  on  board.  Started  to  return,  and 
arrived  back  to  the  ship  at  4  o’clock  this  morning. 

1  am,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Whitman  Chase, 

Acting  Ensign ,  U.  S.  Navy. 

F.  S.  Conover, 

Acting  Lieutenant,  Commanding .

[Enclosure.] 

U.  S.  Ironclad  Passaic, 

Port  Royal ,  January  £8,  1863. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  that  1  arrived  here  last  evening  from 
Beaufort,  N.  C.,  which  I  left  at  sunset  on  the  17th,  in  tow  of  the  Rhode 
Island ,  and  in  company  with  the  Montauk. 

The  wind  had  been  blowing  for  several  days  from  the  southward, 
but  after  a  severe  storm  cleared  off  with  a  northwester,  giving  thus 
every  promise  of  a  continuation  of  fine  weather;  this,  however,  did  not 
last,  but  shortly  after  our  getting  outside,  changed  to  the  northeast  and 
very  thick.  At  1  p.  m.  of  the  19th,  we  made  the  light  vessel  off  here, 
but  the  commander  of  the  Rhode  Island  not  being  willing  to  run  in 
while  the  weather  was  so  thick,  and  the  sea  then  breaking  over  my  ves¬ 
sel  so  heavily  that  had  I  been  so  inclined  I  could  not  have  unshackled 
the  hawsers,  it  was  determined  to  try  anchoring  under  Martin’s  Indus¬ 
try,  the  Passaic  continuing  to  ride  by  her  fasts  under  the  stern  of  the 
other  vessel.  On  swinging  head  to  sea,  however,  it  became  at  once 
evident  that,  the  former  could  not  long  bear  the  terrific  shock  of  the 
waves  on  her  bow  without  something  giving  way.  I  consequently 
directed  Commander  Trenchard  to  at  once  raise  his  anchors  and  stand 
out  again.  During  the  remainder  of  that  day  and  all  the  following, 
it  blew  so  very  hard  that  we  could  not  make  the  light  vessel  until  late 
in  the  afternoon  of  the  21st,  when,  as  stated  above,  I  anchored  here  at 
7  p.  m. 

As  while  at  Beaufort  I  had  cleared  out  the  limbers  and  put  the 
pumps  in  good  working  order,  although  the  vessel  made  a  great  deal 
of  water,  there  was  no  difficulty  in  keeping  her  free,  although  to  do 
this  in  the  heaviest  weather,  in  addition  to  the  bilge  pump,  it  was 
necessary  to  use  one  of  the  donkeys  for  two  hours  out  of  every  four. 
The  leak  in  the  bow  has  increased  a  great  deal,  and  although  I  took  the 
precaution  to  remove  much  of  the  iron  ballast  from  forward,  particu¬ 
larly  that  which  most  inconsiderately  had  been  placed  inside  of  the 
false  bow,  I  think  that  before  doing  so,  while  on  my  way  down  from 
Hampton  Roads,  this  part  of  the  vessel  was  so  seriously  strained  that  a 
little  more  heavy  weather  would  render  the  full  working  of  all  the 
pumps  necessary  to  keep  the  water  down.  W  hen  the  sea  is  at  all 
forward  of  the  beam,  the  blows  on  the  bow  projection  are,  I  think, 
more  violent  than  I  have  ever  known  in  my  experience. 

Very  little  water  entered  through  the  lower  part  of  the  turret,  as 
before,  having  managed  this  time  to  get  it  down,  which  I  now  know 
to  be  absolutely  necessary  for  safety  before  going  outside;  over  the 
top,  the  sea  would  have  regularly  broken  with  the  wind  as  far  forward 
as  abeam,  had  it  not  been  for  the  weather  cloth  and  curtains;  as  it  was, 
the  water  found  its  way  in,  but  not  in  large  quantities. 

The  windlass  seemed  to  have  so  completely  rusted  together  in  the 
joints,  from  the  quantity  of  water  which  had  been  pouring  over  it  for 
five  days,  that  I  had  great  difficulty  in  getting  it  to  work,  and  had  I 
been  in  a  narrow  channel  the  vessel  must  have  gone  ashore,  notwith¬ 
standing  the  many  alterations  it  has  undergone.  I  do  not  now  con¬ 
sider  it  as  very  reliable,  and  am  afraid  it  will  yet  get  me  into  some 
trouble.  At  no  time  was  there  a  greater  pressure  on  the  boilers  than

25  pounds;  with  this,  and  forty  revolutions,  there  ?v&s  no  foaming  of 
consequence,  and  everything  worked  well  and  smoothly. 

I  am,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

P.  Drayton,

U.  S.  S.  Montauk, 

Port  Royal ,  S.  C. ,  January  20,  1863. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  that  this  ship  left  the  bar  of  Beau¬ 
fort,  N.  C.,  at  5:30,  p.  m.  on  the  17th  instant;  weather  clear,  wind 
northerly,  and  a  little  of  the  old  S.  W.  sea  still  rolling;  continued 
clear  and  moderate  until  sunrise  of  the  18th,  when  the  wind  hauled  to 
the  northward  and  eastward,  with  cloudy,  threatening  weather;  at 
times  it  breezed  up  quite  strongly,  with  the  sea  rising  until  sunset, 
when  it  partially  cleared  and  the  wind  backed  into  N.  by  W.  and  so 
continued  until  midnight;  sea  rather  increasing  and  confused.  Toward 
the  morning  of  the  19th  the  wind  hauled  again  to  the  N.  E.,  weather 
thickening  and  sea  rising  and  more  confused.  At  10  o’clock  a.  m. 
crossed  the  S.  E.  channel  bar  of  Port  Royal  entrance,  and  at  11:45 
came  to  at  this  anchorage.  Average  speed  down,  about  knots, 
ship’s  motion  easy  both  ways;  on  one  occasion  the  stern  overhang 
struck  quite  heavily  five  or  six  times,  as  reported  by  the  engineer  of 
the  watch,  but  no  unusual  shock  was  felt  on  the  turret  at  the  time; 
soon  after,  the  port  overhang  limber  began  to  deliver  a  small  stream, 
indicating  either,  firstly,  that  water  had  made  its  way  more  than 
usual  around  the  rudder-hatch  packing;  or  secondly,  that  water  had 
made  its  way  up  through  the  rudderhead  packing;  or  thirdly,  that  she 
had  sprung  a  small  leak  in  the  overhang. 

During  the  whole  passage  considerable  water  forced  its  way  into  the 
forward  overhang  and  thence  through  the  joints  of  the  overhang  bulk¬ 
head  into  the  windlass  room;  she  leaked  a  great  deal  about  the  decks, 
deadlights,  and  hatch  covers.  In  rolling,  the  shock  of  the  impact  of 
side  overhang  was  very  perceptible  all  over  the  vessel.  The  sea  some¬ 
times  broke  over  the  deck  as  much  as  2£  or  3  feet  deep.  In  a  small, 
slow  sea  she  is  quite  buoyant  and  lively;  to  a  quick,  heavy  sea,  the 
extent  of  experience  thus  far  shows  little  disposition  to  give  to  or 
recover  from.  She  steers  well  and  steadily  as  long  as  she  has  good 
wa}r  on,  especially  in  running  before  the  wind;  on  the  whole,  she  has 
behaved  so  far  very  well  with  the  moderate  test  she  has  had,  but  gives 
positive  indication  that  if  forced  end  on  into  a  sea  will  strain  both 
overhangs  greatly;  and  if  she  gets  into  the  trough  of  the  sea  will  wal¬ 
low  very  heavily,  to  such  an  extent  indeed,  as  to  render  the  breaking 
of  a  tolerably  high  sea  over  the  turret  almost  certain. 

Respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

John  L.  Worden, 

Commander. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy,  Washington,  I).  C.

Statement  of  deserters  regarding  the  defenses  of  Charleston,  8.  C. 

[January,  — ,  1863.] 

Statement  of  Thomas  Carnes,  private. 

Have  served  twelve  months  as  private  in  the  rebel  army.  Passed 
one  day  a  week  before  last  Christmas  in  Fort  Sumter.  There  are  104 
guns  mounted  on  the  fort.  On  North  Channel  side,  battery  of  12 
X-inch  columbiads  on  ramparts.  No  guns  in  middle  tier,  except  one 


532  SOUTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 

* 

for  officers’  drill;  afraid  to  use  guns  in  this  tier,  the  arches  being 
cracked  and  weak.  Lower  tier  battery  on  North  Channel  side  consists 
of  12  VIII- inch  Dahlgrens.  On  the  side  of  sallyports  no  guns  mounted, 
except  on  ramparts,  where  there  are  12  32-pounder  light  guns.  Under¬ 
neath  this  part  are  the  officers’  quarters.  The  North  Channel  battery 
will  train  down  Lawford  Channel.  On  Lawford  Channel  side  there  is 
1  X-inch  columbiad.  No  guns  in  lower  tier;  magazine  is  under  Law¬ 
ford  Channel  corner.  Only  24  guns  bear  on  North  Channel.  Ihe 
main  magazine  in  angle  of  fort  facing  Lawford  Channel  is  vulnerable 
from  the  North  Channel,  it  being  protected  only  by  a  granite  wall 
independent  of  the  walls  of  the  fort  built  outside  and  on  the  western 
side  of  the  angle.  The  wall  outside  is  1 0  feet  high  and  8  feet  thick. 
Another  magazine  is  in  the  angle  facing  Fort  Johnson.  There  are  4 
rifled  guns  in  Sumter,  but  they  are  not  considered  safe,  and  they  do 
not  use  them.  On  Moultrie  face  there  are  12  X-inch  columbiads  on 
rampart,  and  12  Vlll-inch  Dahlgrens  in  lower  tier.  On  city  face  there 
are  6  Vlll-inch  on  rampart  and  12  Vlll-inch  in  lower  tier.  The  balance 
of  guns  in  Sumter  are  32-pounders,  on  city  side,  and  are  not  in  good 
condition.  These  are  being  replaced  as  rapidly  as  manufactured  by 
X-inch  guns.  Four  large  Armstrong  guns  are  daily  expected  from 
Nassau.  Fort  Ripley,  H  miles  from  city,  between  Sumter  and  city, 
has  2  X-inch  columbiads  mounted;  is  intended  for  four.  Four  case¬ 
mates  in  Johnson,  with  2  Vlll-inch  Dahlgrens  and  2  32-pounder  rifles. 
Morris  Island  battery  contains  2  VUI-inch  Dahlgrens  and  1  X-inch 
columbiad  on  the  sea  face,  mounted;  3  VUI-inch  Dahlgrens  in  case¬ 
mates,  which  can  not  ’be  trained  seaward.  No  other  battery  on  the 
island. 

On  the  point  of  the  city  (that  is  the  city  battery)  there  are  6  VUI- 
inch  Dahlgren  guns  and  2  8-inch  rifles,  en  barbette,  commanding  the 
approach  from  Stono.  The  old  floating  battery  is  good  for  nothing. 
They  are  digging  out  Wappoo  Creek  to  get  gunboats  to  Stono.  The 
ironclads  carry  4  guns;  draft,  9  to  10  feet;  speed,  1  mile  per  hour.  It 
is  rumored  they  are  to  be  stationary  to  assist  lower  battery  on  Stono. 
There  are  two  building,  one  framed;  the  other,  the  materials  being 
collected;  are  to  be  larger  than  the  others;  no  machinery  on  hand  for 
them;  some  expected  from  Nassau.  There  is  no  quantity  of  iron  or 
composition  on  hand;  have  used  all  but  three  bells  in  the  city.  No 
other  armed  vessels  in  harbor,  excepting  rams.  There  are  six  months’ 
provisions  and  water  in  Sumter,  kept  locked  up.  There  are  no  clothes 
or  stores  in  any  quantity,  except  the  provisions  in  Sumter. 

Statement  of  Corporal  Woodstock. 

Magazine  on  Morris  Island  earthworks  built  of  sand  and  logs;  sand 
caving  in  constantly;  square  in  form;  15  feet  in  size.  Morris  Island 
battery  mounts  on  sea  face  5  32-pounders,  so-called,  but  marked 
“8-inch”  on  trunnions;  1  rifled  gun,  throwing  a  70-pound  projectile; 
land  face,  5  32-pounders,  marked  same  as  on  sea  face;  one  or  two  may 
be  lighter.  More  heavier  guns  are  to  be  mounted.  No  guns  on  Cum- 
ming’s  Point;  iron  battery  dilapidated;  iron  removed.  There  are  2 or 
3  guns  by  Light-House  Inlet.  Carnes  says  there  are  none.  Each  ram 
has  2  IX-inch  Dahlgren  and  2  7-inch  rifles.  The  plating  is  about  4 
inches  thick,  strongly  backed  with  wood.  The  roof  extends  under 
water,  and  is  vertical,  with  ports.  Maximum  speed,  3  knots;  draft, 
8  feet.  The  channel  of  Stono  River  obstructed;  not  more  than  2  feet

Flagship  Wabash, 

Port  Royal  Harbor ,  S.  C. ,  January  22,  1863. 

Sir:  The  Rhode  Island  takes  up  the  two  pilots.  I  desire  you  to 
give  her  a  station  nearest  to  the  bar,  that  a  system  of  reconnoissance 
and  sounding  may  be  commenced  in  the  channels  over  it. 

This  must  be  done  at  night,  with  great  caution,  in  order  not  to  excite 
the  attention  of  the  enemy.  The  object  is  to  obtain  not  alone  the 
depth  of  water,  but  to  acquire  such  familiarity  with  the  features  of 
the  channels  as  to  enable  the  pilots  hereafter  to  plant  the  necessary 
buoys  in  one  night. 

You  will  please  give  Commander  Trenchard  such  assistance  as  you 
may  deem  necessary,  and  such  counsel  as  your  long  experience  off 
Charleston  may  render  desirable. 

You  had  better  come  down  yourself  and  coal  as  soon  as  you  can. 

Respectfully,  etc., 

S.  F.  Du  Pont, 

Rear-Admiral. 

Captain  S.  W.  Godon, 

U.  S.  S.  Poivhatan,  off  Charleston.

Confidential  report  of  Rear-Admiral  Du  Pont ,  U.  S.  Navy,  urging 
an  increased  force  of  ironclads  for  operations  against  Charleston , 

S.  Cm 


No.  36.]  Flagship  Wabash, 

Port  Royai  Harbor,  S.  C. ,  January  1863. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  acknowledge  the  receipt  of  the  Department’s 
confidential  dispatch  of  the  15th  instant. 

The  Department  has  been  informed  through  my  private  letters  to 
the  Assistant  Secretary  of  the  general  character  and  extent  of  the 
defenses  of  Charleston.  I  shall  endeavor  to  execute  its  wishes  with 
such  force  as  it  may  deem  necessary  for  this  purpose. 

The  Department  is  aware  that  I  have  never  shrunk  from  assuming 
any  responsibility  which  circumstances  called  for  nor  desired  to  place 
any  failure  of  mine  on  others;  but  the  interests  involved  in  the  success 
or  failure  of  this  undertaking  strike  me  as  so  momentous  to  the  nation 
at  home  and  abroad  at  this  particular  period  that  I  am  confident  it  will 
require  no  urging  from  me  to  induce  the  Department  to  put  at  my  dis¬ 
posal  every  means  in  its  power  to  insure  success,  especially  by  sending 
additional  ironclads,  if  possible,  to  those  mentioned  in  your  dispatch. 

The  army  is  not  ready  even  for  the  limited  cooperation  it  can  give, 
though  anxious  to  render  every  assistance. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

"  ‘  S.  F.  Du  Pont, 

Rear-Admiral,  Comdg.  South  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy.

Letter  from  Captain  Green ,  U.  8.  Wavy,  to  Commander  _  Worden, 

U  8.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S.  8.  Montauk,  giving  information 

obtained  from  contraband  regarding  the  steamers  Nashville  {Rattle¬ 
snake)  and  Fingal. 

U.  S.  S.  Canandaigua, 

Off  Ossabatv  Bar,  January  25,  1863. 

Dear  Worden:  I  have  just  finished  catechising  a  contraband  who 
left  Savannah  last  Friday  night,  and  who  worked  on  the  Fingal  from 
the  time  work  was  commenced  upon  her  to  fit  her  as  an  ironclad  until 
she  was  finished. 

He  is  very  intelligent,  and  gives  so  coherent  and  apparently  truth¬ 
ful  statement  in  regard  to  that  vessel  that  I  think  it  of  sufficient 
importance  to  communicate  the  substance  of  the  information  obtained 
from  him  to  you. 

The  Fingal  dropped  down  to  [St.]  Augustine  Creek  last  Monday 
for  the  purpose  of  taking  advantage  of  the  high  tides  and  going 
through  that  creek  if  possible,  otherwise  by  Fort  Pulaski  and  pro¬ 
ceed  by  sea  to  rescue  the  Nashville.  For  some  unknown  reason  she 
did  not  attempt  it,  as  the  contraband  saw  her  off  the  mouth  of  the 
creek  last  Friday. 

She  draws  18  "or  19  feet  of  water.  Roofing  extends  from  midships 
forward  and  aft  to  within  20  or  30  feet  of  bow  and  stern;  eaves  cal¬ 
culated  to  be  1  foot  under  water;  top  of  roof  flat,  about  12  feet  wide, 
in  which  is  a  scuttle  forward;  smokestack  amidships  and  lookout  tur¬ 
ret  aft;  wheelhouse  on  spar  deck  abaft  the  roofing. 

She  mounts  six  rifled  breech-loading  guns  of  6- inch  caliber,  throw¬ 
ing  projectile  of  120  pounds,  one  mounted  in  each  end,  and  two  on 
each  side,  which  are  shifting;  one  pivot  forward,  one  aft,  and  four  on 
each  side.  Portholes  18  inches  square.  Guns  about  4  feet  from 
water.  Magazine  and  shell  room  on  deck  below  gun  deck;  weakest 
part  of  the  vessel,  the  stern.  She  leaks  badly. 

The  roof  is  clad  with  two  layers  of  iron  1£  inches  thick;  the  hull 
to  the  depth  of  5  feet,  with  two  layers  of  2  inches  thick;  spar  deck 
outside  of  roof,  with  l£  inch.  Speed  will  not  exceed  3  miles  per 
hour. 

Hoping  this  information  may  be  of  some  service  to  you,  and  wish¬ 
ing  you  complete  success  in  your  present  undertaking, 

I  am,  very  truly,  yours,  etc., 

J.  F.  Green. 

Commander  J.  L.  Worden, 

Commanding  II.  8.  8.  Montauk,  Ossdbaw  Bay. 

P.  S. — I  shall  probably  leave  for  Port  Royal  to-morrow  to  get  a 
supply  of  coals,  etc.

U.  S.  Gunboat  Unadilla, 

Off  Charleston ,  January  27,  1863. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  submit  to  }^ou  the  following  report: 

On  the  morning  of  the  27th  instant  at  2  a.  m.  a  blue  light  was  observed 
to  the  eastward,  supposed  to  be  on  board  the  schooner  Blunt.  Shortly 
after  a  rocket  was  sent  up,  apparently  from  the  same  position,  in  a 
southwest  direction.  I  was  prepared  to  slip,  guns  ready  for  service. 
After  waiting  for  about  ten  minutes  another  rocket  was  discharged  from 
a  boat  which  I  had  stationed  on  picket  duty  midway  between  the  ship 
and  the  shore.  The  instant  this  last  rocket  was  seen  I  slipped  my 
cable  and  stood  directly  inshore  under  full  steam,  but  was  unable  to 
get  full  sight  of  the  vessel,  notwithstanding  my  every  effort.  It  is  to 
be  presumed  that  in  consequence  of  the  strange  steamer’s  great  speed 
she  escaped  athwart  my  bows  before  we  could  approach  sufficiently 
near  to  make  her  out. 

I  am,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

S.  P.  Quackenbush, 

Lieutenan  t-  Commander. 

Captain  Wm.  Rogers  Taylor, 

Senior  Comdg.  Off, err  Blockading  Fleet  off  ’Charleston ,  S.  C.

faithfully  executed  their  duties  in  that  respect,  it  is  doubtless  my 
fault  that  3rou  formed  the  impression  that  vessels  had  run  into  Charles¬ 
ton  without  a  sufficiently  prompt  effort  on  my  part  to  prevent  them, 
from  the  fact  that  my  report  to  Captain  Taylor  would  allow  you  to 
infer  that  I  had  been  too  dilatory  in  my  movements.  I  confess  that  I 
was  not  as  explicit  as  1  should  have  been  had  I  supposed  my  report 
would  have  been  sent  to  you.  What  m}T  report  lacked  in  detail  was 
communicated  verbally  and  entirely  to  the  satisfaction  of  Captain 
Taylor.  In  order  to  relieve  my  officers  from  any  imputation  of  want 
of  vigilance,  permit  me  to  detail  in  full  the  circumstances  of  a  steamer 
having  succeeded  in  reaching  Charleston  after  the  warning  and  guid¬ 
ing  signals  had  been  made  from  the  schooner  Blunt. 

On  the  morning  of  the  27th  January,  1863,  at  1:45,  the  Blunt 
burned  a  blue  light  and  shortly  afterwards  threw  up  a  rocket  to  the 
westward.  I  had  at  the  time  a  picket  boat  out,  stationed  to  the  north¬ 
ward  and  eastward,  and  was  between  this  vessel  and  the  shore.  The 
officer  in  the  boat  had  directions,  in  the  event  of  seeing  a  vessel,  to 
throw  up  a  rocket  in  the  direction  she  appeared  to  be  steering,  after 
the  vessel  had  passed,  then  to  show  his  light,  to  prevent  our  firing  into 
the  boat  or  running  over  her;  also  orders,  in  case  the  vessel  turned  to 
run  out,  to  flash  the  light.  Immediately  after  the  Blunt  made  her 
signals,  the  shackle  bolt  was  knocked  out  and  we  had  only  to  raise  the 
compressor  to  be  free  to  move.  A  few  minutes  elapsed,  perhaps  five, 
and  it  may  have  been  ten,  when  the  rocket  was  discharged  from  the 
boat;  instantly  the  vessel  was  underway  and  standing  in  toward  the 
shore.  I  had  proceeded  some  distance  when  it  was  reported  that 
the  boat  was  flashing  her  light,  and  as  that  was  a  signal  indicating  a 
change  of  course  of  the  vessel  I  put  my  helm  to  port  and  steered  in 
toward  the  boat.  It  is  to  be  considered  that,  notwithstanding  there 
were  at  least  thirty  persons  on  the  lookout,  no  vessel  had  yet  been 
discovered  from  tliis  vessel.  As  soon  as  we  had  approached  within 
hail  of  the  boat  I  enquired  where  the  strange  vessel  was,,  and  was  told 
she  had  passed  in.  In  answer  to  my  enquiry  why  the  light  had  been 
flashed  from  the  boat,  that  officer  stated  that  it  had  not  been  flashed; 
this  was  doubtless  so,  but  the  motion  of  the  boat  made  it  appear  so.

» 

I  do  hope  this  explanation  will  be  satisfactory  to  you,  as  it  was  to  Cap¬ 
tain  Taylor,  and  will  have  the  effect  of  relieving  my  officers  from  the 
suspicion  of  want  of  vigilance  and  attention.  The  blame,  whatever  it 
may  be,  must  be  attached  to  me,  and  it  was  in  a  great  measure,  feel¬ 
ing  conscious  that  I  had  done  all  that  mortal  man  could  do  in  the  dis¬ 
charge  of  my  duty,  that  I  failed  to  consider  that  I  should  be  more 
particular  in  my  report  than  I  was.  I  do  beg,  sir,  you  will  on  the 
receipt  and  perusal  of  this  statement  relieve  my  officers  from  blame, 
for  they  surely  do  not  deserve  it.  In  regard  to  the  officers  of  the 
Unadilla  considering  their  pecuniary  interests  greater  than  the  duty 
they  owe  to  their  country,  I  must  say  their  pride  in  capturing  prizes 
and  rendering  the  Unadilla  a  credit  to  the  squadron  under  your  com¬ 
mand  has  been  their  first  and  highest  motive.  On  the  occasion  of  the 
capture  of  the  Princess  Royal  I  know  that  pecuniary  interests  were 
never  thought  of;  on  the  contrary,  I  heard  the  officers  remark  that  the 
taking  of  that  vessel  was  more  gratifying  to  them  than  untold  wealth. 
Subsequent  events  induced  them  to  enter  a  protest  in  regard  to  other 
vessels  sharing  which  they  conceived  had  no  claim,  basing  their  opin¬ 
ion  on  certain  facts  derived  from  signalizing. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant,

Capture  of  the  schooner  Emma  Tuttle  off  Charleston,  S.  C.,  by  the  U.  S. 
schooner!'  Hope,  January  27,  1863. 

Report  of  Rear-Admiral  Du  Pont,  U.  S.  Navy. 

No.  61.]  Flagship  Wabash, 

Port  Royal  Harbor,  S.  C. ,  February  6,  1863. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  the  capture  of  the  schooner  Emma 
Tuttle ,  flying  the  English  flag,  on  the  morning  of  January  27,  off 
Charleston,  by  the  U.  S.  schooner  Hope,  Acting  Master  John  E. 
Rockwell,  commanding,  under  the  following  circumstances: 

At  daylight  on  the  morning  of  the  27th  the  Hope,  when  in  5  fathoms 
water  and  off  the  east  end  of  Rattlesnake  Shoal,  discovered  the  schooner 
Emma  Tuttle  about  2  miles  distant,  apparently  steering  S.  E.  The 
Hope  tacked  and  bore  down  upon  her,  and  the  stranger  immediately 
kept  off  to  the  east,  evidently  trying  to  escape,  but  was  soon  over¬ 
hauled,  and  after  a  shot  was  tired  across  her  bow,  she  hove  to,  hoist¬ 
ing  the  English  flag.  A  boat  was  sent  aboard  and  her  captain  was 
brought  on  [board]  the  Hope,  bringing  her  papers,  viz,  her  manifest 
of  cargo,  her  registry  and  list  of  crew,  and  log  book,  not  written  up. 

She  purported  to  be  from  Nassau,  [New  Providence],  and  bound  to 
Baltimore,  though  at  the  time  she  was  captured  she  was  steering  S.  E. 

The  schooner  was  brought  to  Port  Royal,  where  a  survey  was  held 
upon  her  (herewith  enclosed,  marked  u  No.  1”),  which  pronounced  her 
unseaworthy,  and  an  inventory  of  her  cargo  taken,  most  of  which  was 
contraband,  consisting  of  a  number  of  bags  of  saltpeter. 

The  cargo  was  transshipped  to  the  schooner  R.  W.  Dillon.  Acting 
Master’s  Mate  [James  B.]  Williamson,  of  the  Hope,  went  north  to  the

port  of  Philadelphia  in  charge  of  the  cargo  (much  of  which  was  dam¬ 
aged).  The  master  of  the  Emma  Tuttle ,  William  Florence,  and  one 
of  the  crew  were  sent  to  Philadelphia  on  the  Dillon.  The  rest  of  the 
crew  will  he  sent  by  the  first  opportunity. 

I  may  add  that  the  schooner  was  taken  once  before,  but  her  crew

Report  of  Captain  Taylor,  U.  S.  Navy,  senior  officer  present. 

U.  S.  S.  Housatonic, 

Off  Charleston ,  January  87,  1863. 

Sir:  Acting  Master  Rockwell  reported  to  me  at  2  p.  m.  to-day  that 
he  captured  the  schooner  Emma  Tuttle  A  8  o’clock  this  morning  about 
10  miles  E.  N.  E.  of  this  anchorage.  She  has  on  board  an  assorted 
cargo.  Amongst  the  articles  are  salt,  hardware,  and  saltpeter.  The 
weather  being  thick,  he  fell  in  with  the  ships  at  the  lower  end  of  the 
line,  and  having  anchored  his  prize  near  the  Keystone  State ,  ran  down 
to  this  ship  for  instructions.  He  states  that  she  is  leaking  and  as  being- 
in  a  bad  condition  generally.  Commander  LeRoy  has  rendered  such 
assistance  as  was  necessary. 

As  the  prize  is  lying  from  4  to  5  miles  dead  to  windward,  the  weather 
thick  and  wind  fresh,  1  directed  Acting  Master  Rockwell  to  return  to 
her  without  waiting  for  written  instructions,  and  whenever  the  wind 
and  weather  would  permit,  to  proceed  with  her  to  Port  Royal. 

The  Para  will  go  down  to-morrow  if  the  weather  should  be  suitable 
and  convey  this  report.  I  presume  she  will  arrive  as  soon  as  the  Hope. 

I  am,  very  respectfully,  you  obedient  servant, 

AVm.  Rogers  Taylor, 
Captain  and  Senior  Officer  Present. 

Rear-Admiral  S.  F.  Du  Pont, 

Comdg.  South  Atlantic  Blockdg.  Squadron,  Port  Royal ,  S.  C. 


Report  of  Acting  Master  Rockwell,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S.  schooner  Hope. 

U.  S.  Schooner  Hope, 

Port  Royal ,  S.  C. ,  February  1863. 

Admiral:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  the  capture  of  schooner  Emma 
Tuttle ,  under  the  English  flag,  and  under  the  following  circumstances: 

There  can  be  no  doubt  of  her  intention  to  get  into  Charleston  if  she 
could  have  done  so.  She  is  the  same  vessel  that  was  recaptured _ by  her 
original  crew  from  prize  crew  and  taken  to  Nassau,  New  Providence.

On  the  morning  of  Januanary  27,  while  returning'from  Georgetown, 
S.  C.,  toward  this  port,  and  when  in  5  fathoms  water  off  the  east  end 
of  Rattlesnake  Shoal,  it  being  then  daylight,  I  made  said  schooner 
bearing  S.  E.  some  4  or  5  miles  distant;  wind  at  the  time,  S.  S.  W. 
When  first  seen,  appeared  to  be  steering  S.  E.  Haying  been  under 
easy  sail  with  the  Hope ,  I  tacked  to  S.  E.  and  set  mainsail.  The  stran¬ 
ger  immediately  kept  off  to  about  east,  evidently  trying  to  run.  The 
Hope  soon  overhauled  him,  and  after  firing  a  shot  across  his  bow,  he 
hove  to,  hoisting  the  English  flag.  When  within  hail  the  captain 
replied  he  was  from  Nassau.  I  sent  an  officer  on  board,  requesting 
the  captain  to  come  on  board  the  Hope  with  his  papers  (the  accompany¬ 
ing  are  all  he  produced,  list  of  cargo  and  of  crew);  said  he  was  from 
Nassau,  bound  for  Baltimore;  expressed  much  dissatisfaction  at  being 
detained,  as  she  was  leaking  badly  and  partially  disabled.  From  the 
nature  of  his  cargo,  his  position  when  first  seen,  and  his  own  admis¬ 
sion  that  his  vessel  had  been  captured  before  and  rescued,  I  deter¬ 
mined  to  bring  her  to  this  port.  With  a  view  to  communicate  with 
the  senior  officer  off  Charleston,  I  detained  the  captain  on  board  the 
boat,  leaving  an  officer  and  four  men  on  board  the  prize.  Took  her  in 
tow  and  ran  in  W.  S.  W.  about  2^  hours,  when  I  made  the  steamer 
Keystone  State.  It  being  somewhat  thick  at  the  time,  could  not  make 
out  the  flagship.  Anchored  near  the  Keystone  State  and  reported  to 
Commander  Le  Roy,  asking  of  him  the  assistance  of  six  men  as  the 
prize  numbered  nine  men  all  told.  Captain  Le  Roy  kindly  furnished 
me  the  men  and  an  officer  to  assist  me. 

The  weather  having  cleared,  I  then  ran  up  to  and  went  on  board  the 
Housatonic ,  reporting  to  Commander  Taylor.  He  advised  me  by  all 
means  to  stop  by  the  prize  under  the  circumstances  and  convoy  her 
down.  Evening,  anchored  near  the  prize,  took  out  four  of  her  crew, 
and  replaced  them  with  four  of  the  Hope's,  retaining  those  from  the 
Keystone  State  on  board  the  Hope. 

28th.  Strong  gale  from  S.  S.  W.  At  7  p.  m.  parted  chain  and  set 
two  reefed  foresail;  stood  offshore.  Midnight,  blowing  heavy.  Car¬ 
ried  away  foregaff  while  wearing  ship.  Morning  of  29th,  moderating. 
Worked  up  to  prize  and  anchored.  Wind  still  too  far  to  S.  W.  to 
attempt  working  to  S.  and  westward  in  disabled  condition  of  prize. 

30th.  Proceeded  to  get  underway  and  worked  to  S.  and  westward. 
At  sunset,  off  Stono.  The  IT.  S.  S.  Bibb  having  come  along,  Captain 
Boutelle  kindly  took  charge  of  mail  and  dispatches,  and  relieved  me 
of  the  charge  of  four  prisoners.  I  then  took  the  prize  in  tow  again, 
and  at  daylight,  31st  January,  was  10  miles  S.  S.  W.  from  North  Edisto. 
Left  prize  to  proceed,  and  stood  in  for  the  purpose  of  delivering  mail 
and  express  to  steamer  South  Carolina.  The  wind  failing,  could  not 
reach  Edisto  until  evening;  7  p.  m.  ran  in  to  inner  buoy,  when  a  boat 
from  the  South  Carolina  came  alongside  for  mail.  Having  delivered 
them,  and  received  mail  and  dispatches  from  them,  proceeded  to  get 
underway  an  d  beat  out,  clearing  the  fair-way  buoy  at  10  p.  m.  Have 
had  light  winds  and  calms,  arriving  at  this  anchorage  p.  m.,  February 
2,  1863,  the  prize  having  arrived  first. 

Hoping  my  acts  will  meet  your  approval,  I  am,  very  respectfully, 
your  obedient  servant, 

John 

Acting  Master, 

Rear-Admiral  S.  E.  Du  Pont, 

Commanding  South  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron.

Attack  upon  Fort  McAllister ,  Ga. ,  by  the  U  A.  ironclad  Montauk  and 
wooden  vessels ,  January  27,  1863. 

Report  of  Rear-Admiral  Du  Pont,  U.  S.  Navy,  giving  information  gained  in  the  attack. 

No.  41.]  Flagship  Wabash, 

Port  Royal  Harbor ,  S.  C. ,  January  28,  1863. 

Sir:  Considering  it  desirable  to  test  in  every  way  the  efficiency  of 
the  ironclads  that  had  arrived,  and  to  avail  l^^self  of  their  presence 
until  others  come,  I  sent  Commander  Worden  down  to  Ossabaw  to 
operate  up  the  great  Ogeechee  River  and  capture,  if  he  could,  the  fort 
at  Genesis  Point,  under  cover  of  which  the  Nashville  was  lying,  now 
fitted  as  a  privateer  and  waiting  to  run  the  blockade,  and  in  case  of 
success  the  railroad  was  also  accessible. 

I  enclose  a  copy  (marked  No.  1)  of  Commander  Worden’s  report, 
received  at  midnight  by  the  hands  of  Ensign  [Mortimer  L.]  Johnson, 
one  of  my  aids,  who,  in  one  of  our  armed  tugs,  witnessed  and  partici¬ 
pated  in  the  attack.  He  informs  me  that  the  fort  was  a  very  formid¬ 
able  casemated  earthwork  with  bombproofs,  and  mounting  nine  guns, 
the  firing  from  which  was  excellent. 

We  have  obtained  valuable  information  in  the  success  of  the  working 
of  the  XV- in  eh  gun,  and  although  the  Montauk  was  struck  thirteen 
times  she  received  no  injury.  My  own  previous  impressions  of  these 
vessels,  frequently  expressed  to  Assistant  Secretary  Fox,  have  been 
confirmed,  viz,  that  whatever  degree  of  impenetrability  they  might 
have,  there  was  no  corresponding  quality  of  aggression  or  destructive¬ 
ness  as  against  forts,  the  slowness  of  fire  giving  full  time  for  the  gun¬ 
ners  in  the  fort  to  take  shelter  in  the  bombproofs. 

This  experiment  also  convinces  me  of  another  impression,  firmly  held 
and  often  expressed,  that  in  all  such  operations  to  secure  success  troops 
are  necessary.  The  distance  at  which  Commander  Worden  was  com¬ 
pelled  to  engage — not  far  from  his  extreme  range  — may  modify  to 
some  extent  the  above  views.  The  Department,  however,  will  observe 
how  difficult  if  not  impossible  it  will  be  to  remove  sunken  obstruc¬ 
tions  and  piling  in  shallow  water  under  fire — very  different  from  rafts 
or  booms,  floating  chains,  etc. 

The  Fingal  left  Savannah  and  has  got  to  the  mouth  of  St.  Augustine 
Creek,  whether  to  try  Pulaski  and  run  by  it  to  sea,  or  to  Wassaw  on 
her  way  to  Ossabaw  to  convoy  the  Nashville,  I  know  not,  but  most 
probably  the  latter.  I  am  waiting  for  the  weather  to  moderate  to  get 
the  Passaic  towed  to  Wassaw  in  order  to  intercept  the  Fingal  and  pro¬ 
tect  the  blockading  force  there,  but  these  monitors  are  so  unsafe  at 
sea  and  so  helpless  in  themselves  that  the  weather  must  be  narrowly 
watched. 

I  had  the  smokestack  of  the  Ironsides  taken  down  and  ordered  a  trial 
trip  to  be  made  without  it,  but  the  result  proved  so  unfavorable,  in 
consequence  of  the  escape  of  gas,  particularly  in  the  engine  room,  that 
I  had  it  replaced.  I  then  directed  a  board  of  officers  to  examine  into 
the  practicability  of  removing  the  turret  forward,  where  it  should  have 
originally  been  placed,  but  the  board  has  reported  that,  though  in 
every  way  desirable,  yet,  on  account  of  its  great  weight  (18  tons)  it  is 
impracticable,  with  the  means  at  our  command,  to  move  it.  Where 
there  are  no  means  of  feeling  one’s  way  with  the  lead  it  is  of  the  utmost 
importance  that  the  view  should  be  clear  ahead.  A  greater  blunder  in 


SOUTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


544 

a  matter  of  so  much  moment  1  do  not  remember  to  have  met  with 
before,  as  the  vessel  may  be  ashore  before  she  is  half  in  action. 

Enclosed  is  Captain  Turner’s  report  of  the  elfect  of  cutting  down  the 
smokestack,  which  further  illustrates  what  I  have  written  (enclosure,

Report  of  Commander  Worden,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S.  S.  Montauk. 

U.  S.  S.  Montauk, 

Great  Ogeechee  River ,  January  2 7 ,  1863. 

Sir:  1  have  the  honor  to  report  that  this  vessel,  in  tow  of  the  U.  S.  S. 
James  Adger ,  arrived  off  the  bar  at  Ossabaw  Sound  at  1:50  p.  m.  on 
Saturday,  24th  instant.  I  reported  immediately  to  Captain  Green,  and 
on  returning  to  this  vessel  a  thick  fog  set  in.  At  3:  27  p.  m.  it  lifted 
so  that  I  was  enabled  to  proceed  up  the  channel  under  the  pilotage  of 
Mr.  Godfrey.  At  5:10  p.  m.  the  fog  compelled  us  to  anchor.  The 
fog  remained  with  us  all  day  Sunday,  being  so  dense  that  we  were 
unable  to  proceed.  On  Monday  the  fog  hung  with  us  most  of  the 
morning,  during  which  time  I  called  the  commanding  officers  of  the 
Seneca ,  Wissahickon ,  Dawn ,  and  O.  P.  Williams  together  and  arranged 
our  plans  of  attack.  At  1:  30  p.  m.  I  got  underway,  with  Mr.  Murphy 
as  pilot,  and  stood  up  the  river,  anchoring  just  outside  of  the  range  of 
Fort  McAllister.  During  the  afternoon  the  Seneca ,  Wissahickon ,  the 
Dawn  towing  the  C.  P.  Williams ,  came  up  and  anchored  in  line 
astern.  At  8  o’clock  one  boat  from  the  Seneca  and  one  from  the  Wis¬ 
sahickon  ^  both  in  charge  of  Lieutenant-Commander  Davis,  proceeded 
up  the  river  to  reconnoiter  and  destroy  the  ranges  of  the  enemy’s 
guns,  which  were  placed  near  Harvey’s  Cut.  This  service  was  per¬ 
formed  well,  and  Lieutenant-Commander  Davis  reported  to  me  just 
before  midnight.  He  went  within  a  short  distance  of  the  obstructions 
of  spiles  and  from  appearances  came  to  the  conclusion  that  the  obstruc¬ 
tions  were  protected  by  torpedoes. 

At  7  o’clock  this  morning  I  got  underway,  followed  by  the  vessels 
enumerated,  taking  up  a  position  about  150  yards  below  the  obstruc¬ 
tions  at  a  point  designated  by  a  flag  placed  there  by  Lieutenant-Com¬ 
mander  Davis  last  night.  The  other  vessels  anchored  in  line  about  1£ 
miles  astern. 

At  7:  35  a.  m.  we  opened  fire  on  the  fort.  After  firing  our  XI  and 
XV-inch  guns  once  the  enemy  opened  a  brisk  fire  upon  us.  In  less 
than  an  hour  we  had  obtained  our  ranges,  the  enemy’s  fire  slackening. 
Their  practice  was  very  fine,  striking  us  quite  a  number  of  times, 
doing  us  no  damage.  Most  of  their  shot  struck  inside  of  15  feet 
from  us.  Our  practice  was  good,  the  enemy  replying  only  at  intervals. 

At  11:15  a.  m.,  all  our  shells  being  expended  and  finding  our  solid 
shot  not  seriously  affecting  the  enemy,  I  ordered  the  firing  to  cease 

*  See  p.  550.

and  stood  down  the  river.  A  rain  storm  and  thick  weather  setting  in, 
the  other  vessels  were  withdrawn  out  of  range. 

The  enemy  have  a  very  strong  position.  I  send  the  Daffodil  with 
this  report,  and  shall  await  your  further  orders.  I  have  no  casualties 
to  report  from  any  of  the  vessels.  If  another  attempt  is  to  be  made 
upon  the  fort,  I  shall  require  more  ammunition.  The  gunboats  also 
require  a  supply  of  ammunition. 

Yei’y  respectfully,  yours,  etc.,

Commander.

Report  of  Second  Assistant  Engineer  Stephens,  U.  S.  Navy. 

Engine  Dept.,  U.  S.  Ironclad  Steamer  Montauk, 

Off  Fort  McAllister ,  Ga. ,  January  £7,  186S. 

Sir:  Respectfully  I  make  the  following  report: 

With  hatch  and  air  port  battle  covers  on,  heavy  banked  tires  in 
boilers,  and  25  pounds  of  steam,  we  remained  in  condition,  during  the 
night,  to  move  at  short  notice.  All  hands  were  called  at  5:30  a.  m. 
At  6 :  20  spread  tires.  Engines  having  been  reported  read}^  for  motion 
all  hands  went  to  general  quarters,  stationed  as  follows: 

Second  Assistant  Engineer  Robert  Potts  in  engine  room  at  engine 
starting  bars. 

Acting  Second  Assistant  Engineer  William  D.  Eorbes  in  engine 
room  at  engine  starting  bars. 

Third  Assistant  Engineer  Daniel  P.  McCartney,  with  three  men,  in 
turret  room  at  the  fan-blower  engines  and  turret  engines. 

Third  Assistant  Engineer  George  M.  Greene  detailed  as  Captain’s 
aid. 

Second  watch  of  firemen  and  coalpassers  on  duty,  remained  at  fires. 

Third  watch  was  sent  to  report  to  officer  in  command  of  powder 
division  forward. 

First  watch  were  divided  as  follows:  One  man  placed  with  hand 
lantern  in  each  passageway  communicating  fore  and  aft  the  vessel; 
one  man  placed  in  each  coal  bunker;  one  at  bilge  pump  strainers  with 
orders  to  report  any  accident  or  damage  at  once. 

The  oilers  took  positions  about  each  side  of  engines. 

Storekeeper  was  ready  with  tools  in  case  they  were  called  for. 

Fire  hose  were  attached  to  port  steam  pump  and  coiled  in  port  pas¬ 
sage,  ready  for  use. 

At  6:45  a.  m.  started  engines  ahead  fast  (forty-eight  revolutions). 
At  7:17  a.  m.  stopped,  ship  anchored  in  range  of  the  fort;  kept  low 
fires  with  from  25  to  30  pounds  of  steam.  At  7:  30  our  first  gun  fired. 
At  7:35  a  rebel  shot  struck  the  vessel.  At  8:05  a.  m.  a  shot  struck 
lower  section  of  smokepipe  with  force,  making  an  indentation,  but 
causing  no  material  injury  to  it.  The  firing  from  turret  seemed  slow 
and  deliberate  to  those  in  engine  room;  the  smoke  from  guns  was 
forced  rapidly  into  fireroom  at  each  discharge,  but  was  well  diluted 


N  w  r— vol  13 - 35 


546  SOUTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 

* 

with  air  by  the  fans,  and  rapidly  passed  out  through  furnaces  and 
smokepipe,  causing  no  unusual  discomfort.  The  temperature  during 
the  action  did  not  exceed  104°;  average  for  whole  time  of  action  (four 
hours),  103°  Fahrenheit.  The  sound  or  report  of  our  guns  was  not 
acute,  as  when  standing  by  during  a  discharge  on  the  open  deck,  but 
was  heavy  and  dull.  The  concussion  of  air  seemed  insignificant,  except 
when  the  guns  were  fired  aft,  then  deck  and  boilers  seemed  to  spring 
up  an  inch  or  more,  causing  apprehensions  of  leakage  from  the  numer¬ 
ous  tube  joints  of  the  boilers.  We  were  aware  of  this  vessel  being- 
struck  many  times  by  the  rebels’  shot,  but  could  not  distinguish  where 
except  when  striking  overhead,  and  could  not  then  realize  any  danger 
from  them. 

At  10:15  and  10:20  a.  m.  started  ahead  slow  for  a  few  minutes 
each  time.  At  11:50  all  hands  were  “piped  down,”  then  called  to 
“up  anchor.”  At  12:05  noon  started  ahead  slow  until  12:45  p.  m. 
Stopped,  anchored,  then  removed  air  port  battle  covers  from  over 
fireroom  and  cleaned  fires  and  machinery. 

There  was  no  increase  of  water  in  the  bilge  more  than  usual  during 
the  action,  neither  has  there  been  any  damage  discovered  in  boilers, 
engines,  or  department,  excepting  the  breakage  of  glass  articles  by 
the  concussion,  such  as  lamps,  thermometers,  etc.  Considering  the 
performance  of  the  boilers,  engines,  and  machinery  of  this  vessel  sat¬ 
isfactory  during  the  action,  I  beg  leave  to  submit  this  as  my  report 
for  the  day. 

Thos.  A.  Stephens, 

.Senior  Engineer. 

Captain  John  L.  Worden. 


Congratulatory  letter  of  Rear-Admiral  Du  Pont,  U.  S.  Navy,  to  Commander  Worden,  U.  S. 

Navy. 


Wabash, 

Port  Royal ,  January  2 8 ,  1863. 

My  Dear  Captain:  You  have  managed  everything  judiciously  and 
we  have  acquired  valuable  information.  Further  success  depended  in 
my  mind  upon  the  character  and  distance  of  the  obstructions  from  the 
fort. 

I  am  sending  home  for  more  ammunition.  I  recommend  your  pre¬ 
venting  any  ill-considered  reports  reaching  the  press  and  magnifying 
your  attack  into  a  repulse. 

Please  give  my  regards  to  your  clever  associates,  Gibson,  Davis, 
and  Barnes. 

I  will  acknowledge  your  report,  of  course,  in  a  more  official  form 
than  by  the  letter  which  goes  with  this.  The  only  fault  I  find  is  the 
tremendous  amount  of  ammunition  consumed  by  gunboats,  particu¬ 
larly  by  Barnes  with  his  rifle  gun. 

With  thanks  to  Him  who  overrules  all  these  things  that  you  are  all 
spared,  I  am,  most  truly,  yours, 

S.  F.  Du  Pont. 


Commander  J.  L.  Worden, 

Montauk.

Abstract  log  TJ.  S.  S.  Montauk,  Commander  Worden,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding. 

January  25,  1863.- — Getting  ship  ready  for  action. 

January  26. — Atl:30p.  m.  started  up  the  Ogeechee  River.  At  7 
saw  a  light  over  the  marsh  in  the  direction  of  Coffee  Bluff.  At  7:45 
two  boats  on  expeditionary  duty  passed  up  from  the  fleet, 

January  27 . — At  6:30  a.  m.  got  underway  and  stood  up  the  river. 
At  7:30  anchored  below  the  battery  about  1,600  yards,  on  the  Big 
Ogeechee  River,  about  700  yards  below  the  obstructions.  At  7:25 
beat  to  quarters  and  opened  tire  with  shell,  which  was  immediately 
answered  by  the  enemy  with  eight  heavy  guns.  Continued  the 
engagement  until  11:55,  when  we  ceased  firing  on  account  of  not  hav¬ 
ing  proper  ammunition  to  continue  the  engagement.  At  this  time  the 
enemy  had  but  two  guns  mounted,  and  were  firing  at  intervals  of 
about  twelve  minutes.  At  12:10  lifted  our  anchor  and  steamed  back 
to  our  former  moorings,  where  we  anchored  at  12:30  p.  m.  The  fol¬ 
lowing  projectiles  were  expended  during  the  action:  XV-inch  gun — 
2  hollow  shot,  2  5-second  shell,  16  7-second  shell,  5  10-second  shell,  1 
15-second  shell,  35  cartridges.  From  Xl-inch  gun — 5  solid  shot,  3 
5-second  shell,  24  10-second  shell,  3  15-second  shell.  During  the 
action  we  were  struck  by  the  enemy’s  shot  as  follows:  Four  times  in 
turret,  once  in  smokestack,  four  times  on  deck,  three  times  in  side 
plating,  once  in  boat  spars,  sinking  second  cutter,  also  a  number  of 
times  by  fragments  of  shell.  The  Wissahickon,  Seneca ,  Pawn ,  and 
mortar  schooner  C.  P.  Williams  participated  in  the  engagement;  no 
casualties.

Letter  from  Rear-Admiral  Dn  Pont,  IJ.  S.  Navy,  to  Commander  Worden,  U.  S.  Navy,  regard¬ 
ing  newspaper  reporters. 

Flagship  Wabash, 

Port  Royal  Harbor,  S.  C. ,  January  30,  1863. 

Sir:  A  long  and  detailed  account  of  your  operations  against  the 
battery  in  the  Ogeechee,  written  by  Mr.  Osbon,  was  received  this 
morning  too  late  to  go  by  the  Circassian. 

I  was  of  course  aware  that  Mr.  Osbon  was  on  board  the  Montauk , 
but  1  did  not  intend  that  he  should  be  there  as  a  reporter  for  his  paper 
until  after  the  operations  on  Charleston,  having  refused  to  permit 
other  reporters  at  Hilton  Head  to  go  on  this  expedition. 

This  communication  of  Mr.  Osbon’s  is  objectionable  for  the  follow¬ 
ing  reasons,  and  can  not,  therefore,  be  forwarded  by  mail: 

1.  Because  it  is  written  from  the  ship  and  would  naturally  be  sup¬ 
posed  to  come  from  one  of  the  officers,  and  is  therefore  in  direct  vio¬ 
lation  of  my  General  Order  No.  8,  which  I  have  enforced  vigorously  in 
this  squadron. 

2.  Because  it  gives  information  which  would  be  of  the  greatest  value 
to  the  rebels  on  many  material  points,  particularly  in  enabling  them  to 
perfect  their  defenses  at  Charleston. 

3.  That  it  magnifies  the  object  of  the  expedition,  predicts  successes 
which  were  not  borne  out  by  results. 

I  have  alwa3rs  been  liberal  to  reporters,  but  I  can  not  permit  all  our 
preliminary  experiments  in  view  of  the  attack  upon  Charleston  to  be 
made  public — experiments  of  the  utmost  value  to  us,  which,  however, 
would  be  neutralized  if  published  to  the  enemy  beforehand. 

It  is  my  purpose  when  the  attack  on  Charleston  is  made,  and  when 
definite  results  must  happen,  to  permit  all  the  members  of  the  press 
who  desire  it  and  can  be  accommodated  to  be  present,  but  even  in  this 
case  their  letters  must  show  that  they  are  written  by  reporters  and 
not  by  officers  of  the  Navy. 

Respectfully,  etc., 

S.  F.  Du  Pont, 

Rear-Admiral. 

Commander  John  L.  Worden, 

U.  S.  S.  Montauk.
