P.  S. — Excuse  me,  but  I  could  not  but  smile  at  your  grand  plan  of 
sailing  in  silently  on  our  friends.  There  is  no  question  what  the  result 
would  be,  and  be  as  you  say  it  would;  but,  my  friend,  you  have  to  get 
there.  We’ll  do  it  if  it  can  be  done.  I  would  like  to  make  you  happy. 
I  think  we  shall  have  to  batter  and  pound  beyond  any  precedent  in 
history. 

I  hope  you  will  publish  my  dispatch  about  the  Nashville. 


Report  of  Commander  Raich ,  II.  S.  Navy ,  commanding  U.  S.  S.  Paw¬ 
nee. ,  of  a  reconnoisance  of  John’s  Island  through  Iliawah  River. 

U.  S.  Steam  Sloop  Pawnee, 

Stono  Inlet ,  South  Carolina ,  March  0,  1863. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  all  quiet  on  this  station,  nor  have 
we  been  able  to  discover  any  movements  of  the  enemy  leading  to  the 
belief  that  new  batteries  were  being  erected.  The  soldiers  of  the  Sev¬ 
enty-sixth  volunteers  have  been  employed  as  pickets  on  Cole’s  Island, 
but  the  vessels  are  anchored  so  close  to  that  island  as  to  preclude  the 
possibility  of  the  enemy  doing  damage,  either  by  batteries  or  riflemen. 

For  the  purpose  of  ascertaining  if  it  be  possible  for  the  rebels  to 
erect  batteries  on  John’s  Island  that  could  annoy  us  at  this  anchorage, 
I  proceeded  on  the  28th  ultimo  in  the  Unadilla ,  piloted  by  Lieuten¬ 
ant-Commander  Bacon  in  the  Commodore  McDonough ,  up  Kiawah 
River  some  5  miles,  but  we  discovered  no  signs  of  any  such  batteries. 

We,  however,  established  the  fact  that  none  could  be  placed  on  the 
eastern  end  of  John’s  Island  from  which  we  could  not  readily  drive 
the  rebels.  The  schooner  K  W.  Gardner ,  with  coal,  arrived  on  the 
25th  ultimo  and  was  discharged  on  the  27th.  I  have  been  employed 
ballasting  her,  and  she  sailed  yesterday. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Geo.  B.  Balch, 

Commander  and  Senior  Officer  Present. 

Rear-Admiral  S.  F.  Du  Pont,  • 

Comdg.  South  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron ,  Port  Royal  S-  G-

Letter  from  Rear-Admiral  Du  Pont ,  U.  S.  Nary ,  to  Captain  Turner , 
TJ.  S.Navy ,  regarding  the  proposed  withdrawal  of  the  U.  S.  S.  New 
Ironsides. 

Unofficial.]  Flagship  Wabash, 

Port  Royal  Harbor ,  S..  C. ,  March  3 ,  1863. 
My  Dear  Turner:  I  have  your  letters,  public  and  private.  The 
item  in  one  of  the  latter  which  gives  me  most  concern  is  your  belief 
that  the  New  Ironsides  must  come  here  before  being  ready  for  action.  I 
thought  we  had  done  all  when  she  was  here  that  required  a  harbor 
anchorage  to  accomplish. 

On  the  other  hand,  I  do  not  wish,  as  you  may  well  conceive,  to  throw 
obstacles  in  the  way  of  promoting  the  efficiency  of  a  ship  which  must 
have  so  important  a  share  in  pending  operations. 

Should  a  second  raid  be  attempted  in  the  absence  of  the  only  iron 
vessel  which  can  lay  outside,  and  be  more  or  less  damaging,  the  account- 


SOUTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


715 


ability  would  not  be  light.  I,  therefore,  desire  that  you  give  the  mat¬ 
ter  very  serious  consideration  and  see  what  Godon  says  at  your  with¬ 
drawal.  If  you  are  coming,  you  must  come  soon,  and  the  time  named 
by  you  as  necessary  to  have  will  have  to  be  much  shortened. 

1  am  glad  you  smoothed  down  the  English  officer.  There  is  no  use 
making  more  sore  places  than  we  can  help. 

Issue  all  such  orders  as  you  may  deem  necessary,  but  please  do  not 
call  them  general  orders;  this  has  a  technical  significance  and  inter¬ 
feres  with  a  regular  sequence  of  such  in  the  squadron.  Also,  please 
do  not  endorse  your  letters  on  the  back,  as  this  disarranges  our  files, 
and  the  Department  does  not  like  it. 

Yours,  most  truly, 

S.  F.  Du  Pont. 

Captain  T.  Turner.

SOUTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 

Attack  on  Fort,  McAllister  by  monitors  under  the  command  of  Captain 
Drayton ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  March  3,  1863.  • 

Report  of  Rear-Admiral  Du  Pont,  U.  S.  Navy,  transmitting  additional  reports. 

No.  113.]  Flagship  Wabash, 

Port  Royal  TIarbor ,  S.  C. ,  March  6,  1863. 

Sir:  The  Department  has  already  been  informed  of  my  desire,  before 
entering-  upon  more  important  operations,  to  subject  the  various 
mechanical  appliances  of  the  ironclads  to  the  fullest  test  of  active 
service  and  to  give  the  advantage  of  target  practice  to  the  officers  and 
men  with  their  new  ordnance.  For  this  purpose  I  had  ordered  a  con¬ 
centration  in  the  Ogeechee  of  such  of  these  vessels  as  were  readv  to 
attack  Fort  McAllister  and  secure  or  destroy  the  Nashville. 

Before  this  concentration  could  take  place,  the  Nashville  was 
destroyed  by  Commander  Worden,  in  the  Montauk,  the  particulars 
of  which  occurrence  I  reported  to  the  Department  by  the  last  mail. 
The  ironclads  having,  however,  arrived  in  Ossabaw,  I  directed  Captain 
Drayton,  of  the  Passaic,  to  go  on  with  the  attack  on  the  fort,  accom¬ 
panied  by  the  Patapsco  and  Naliant;  the  Montauk  having  been  three 
times  under  fire  of  the  fort  and  sufficiently  tested,  was  not  to  join  in. 

,  I  received  last  evening  Captain  Drayton’s  detailed  report  of  his 
eight  hours’  bombardment,  with  a  statement  of  the  damage  done  to  his 
vessel,  and  also  the  reports  of  Commanders  Ammen  and  Downes  to 
him,  all  of  which  are  enclosed  (marked  Nos.  1,  2,  3),  and  I  think  will 
be  read  with  great  interest  by  the  Department,  for  it  will  not  fail  to 
perceive  that  valuable  information  has  been  elicited  and  most  impor¬ 
tant  data  obtained,  and  I  feel  thankful  that  this  I  have  done  without 
any  loss  of  life.  Except  that  the  fort  might  possibly  protect  another 
blockade,  runner,  its  capture  was  of  no  special  practical  importance. 

The  injury  to  the  Montauk  from  the  torpedo  is  the  most  serious  that 
has  occurred,  and  will  require  some  ten  days  to  repair,  but  the  Depart¬ 
ment  .will  remember  the  invaluable  service  she  performed  while 
receiving  it. 

I  think  it  worthy  of  mentioning  that  this  bombardment,  so  fruitful 
in  giving  us  experience,  was  witnessed  by  Brigadier-General  Seymour 
the  chief  of  artillery,  and  Captain  Duane,  the  chief  engineer  of 
this  military  department,  and  I  shall  be  able  to  receive  from  these 
gentlemen  the  result  of  their  observation,  which,  representino-  as  they 
do,  special  branches  of  the  military  service,  will  be  interesting  and 
important.  & 

I  can  not  close  this  communication  without  speaking  of  Captain 
Drayton,  who  has  been  one  of  my  commanding  officers  since  October 
1861.  He  has  performed  this  service  with  that  ability,  judgment,  and 
calm  courage  which  have  ever  marked  his  execution  of  my  orders. 

Very  respectfully^  yrour  obedient  servant, 

D  .  ,  .  7  S.  F.  Du  Pont, 

Rear-Admiral ,  Comdg.  South  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy,  Washington ,  D.  C.

Detailed  report  of  Captain  Drayton,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding'  D.  S.  S.  Passaic. 

U.  S.  Ironclad  Passaic, 

Ogeechee  River ,  March  1863. 

Sir:  I  wrote  a  short  report  last  evening  after  my  return  from  the 
attack  on  Fort  McAllister,  and  will  now  make  one  more  in  detail.  A 
list  of  the  ammunition  expended,  of  the  injuries  to  the  vessel,  and  an 
extract  from  the  log  I  enclose  with  this,  from  which  latter  you  will 
perceive  that  my  vessel  was  under  fire  just  eight  hours.  1  was  directly 
in  front  of  the  fort,  the  guns  being,  as  we  looked  at  them,  in  the  center 
between  high  traverses  of  earth,  which  were  on  each  side.  These,  how¬ 
ever,  as  we  were  placed  had  no  effect  in  protecting  either  guns  or 
men.  The  latter  never  exposed  themselves  to  our  fire,  usually  dis¬ 
charging  their  pieces  either  while  we  were  loading  or  just  as  our  ports 
came  in  line  and  before  the  guns  were  quite  ready,  the  turret  being 
painted  black  not  deceiving  them  any  more  than  a  different  color  had 
done  in  the  first  attack  of  the  Montauk.  I  was  as  close  to  the  fort  as 
the  pilot,  who  is  the  best  on  the  river  (as  was  proved  in  this  case  by 
my  being  the  only  one  whose  vessel  was  not  aground  when  the  tide 
fell),  would  take  me,  and  as  high  as  the  Montauk  had  been  except  on 
her  second  attack,  but  only  for  an  hour,  when,  being  in  12  feet,  as  I 
understand,  Captain  Worden  was  obliged  to  drop  down  to  a  position 
below,  where  I  was  yesterday — a  rather  risky  operation,  too,  in  so 
narrow  a  channel,  where,  had  the  vessel  grounded,  she  must  have  been 
exposed  below  the  side  armor.  This  being  the  case,  I  am  satisfied  that 
12  feet  can  not  be  carried  when  a  vessel  is  to  anchor  above  where  I  was. 
The  channel  is  close  to  the  marsh  opposite  the  fort,  and  as  the  piles 
were  only  about  400  yards  beyond  where  I  was  lying  I  don’t  see  how 
more  than  200  yards  can  be  gained  nearer  to  the  fort  by  being  against 
them,  as  the  river  can’t  be  crossed,  and  is  very  wide;  certainly,  after 
discussing  the  matter  with  the  pilot  on  the  spot,  I  doubt  being  able  to 
get  nearer  than  a  thousand  yards  without  going  above  the  piles,  where 
the  channel  crosses  over.  My  distance  I  judged  to  be  1,200  yards  from 
the  following  data:  The  Xl-inch  gun  was  very  carefully  elevated  by 
a  spirit  level  to  a  little  less  than  six  degrees;  this  is,  by  Ordnance 
Manual,  1,500  yards,  axis  of  bore  10  feet  above  the  water;  mine  was 
about  4,  which  requires  a  deduction  of  130  yards.  Then  the  parapet 
of  the  fort  was  at  least  20  feet  above  the  water,  which,  requiring  about 
half  a  degree  more,  will  bring  the  distance  about  what  I  have  stated  it. 
Their  shot  were  always  less  than  five  seconds  in  reaching  me  from  the 
flash— generally  four— which  would,  considering  their  greater  initial 
velocity,  about  agree  with  my  calculation.  My  five-second  fuzes, 
however,  usually  burst  just  before  reaching,  the  seven  after  striking. 
The  pilot  called  the  distance  a  thousand  yards. 

The  fort  is  very  solidly  built,  with  high  traverses  between  the  guns, 
and  raised  at  least  20  feet  above  the  river,  and  contained  seven  guns 
and  a  Xl-inch  mortar.  One  of  these  guns  was,  I  think,  destroyed,  the 
others  used  until  we  were  out  of  range.  Immense  holes  were  cut  into 
the  earth,  the  traverses  and  face  much  cut  away,  but  still  no  injury 
done  which,  1  think,  a  good  night’s  work  would  not  repair,  and  I  do 
not  believe  that  it  can  be  made  untenable  by  any  number  of  ironclads 
which  the  shallow  water  and  narrow  channel  will  permit  to  be  brought 
into  position  against  it.  The  guns  are  one  X-inch,  a  shot  from  which 


718  SOUTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 

lodged  on  the  top  of  our  turret,  one  heavy  rifle,  about  a  hundred- 
pounder,  and  the  remainder,  1  should  judge,  32s,  with  a  light  gun 
throwing  bolts,  which  would  be  aimed  at  anyone  showing,  himself 
on  the  deck.  These,  with  the  mortar,  were,  however,  nothing,  as  a 
defense  to  the  river,  comparable  to  the  shallow  water  and  piles,  as  was 
proved  by  my  being  exposed  to  their  tire  for  eight  hours  without 
serious  injury,  but  they  answer  the  purpose,  which  is  simply  to  pre¬ 
vent  the  channel  being  cleared  of  obstructions.  Our  three  mortar 
schooners  kept  up  a  tire  during  the  day  from  about  4,000  yards  dis¬ 
tance,  but,  so  far  as  I  could  observe,  without  the  least  effect,  the  shells 
generally  falling  short. 

The  firing  from  this  vessel  was  quite  good,  and  1  think  very  few 
shots  missed  striking  about  the  parapet  after  the  first  hour,  as  I  had 
carefully  corrected  each  one,  up  to  that  time,  from  outside  of  the  tur¬ 
ret  on  deck,  where  the  effect  could  be  well  followed.  Although  the 
attack  was  an  unsuccessful  one,  it  was  certainly  not  owing  to  any  want 
of  zeal  and  attention  to  duty  on  the  part  of  either  officers  or  men,  and 
I  am  greatly  indebted  to  Lieutenant-Commander  J.  N.  Miller,  the 
executive  officer,  as  well  as  to  Acting  Master  S.  Huse,  who  attended 
under  him  to  the  management  and  pointing  of  the  guns,  and  whose 
energy  and  zeal  was  very  marked  on  this  occasion,  as  it  has  been  on 
several  others. 

1  feel  very  much,  of  course,  the  failure,  to  a  certain  extent,  of  the 
attack,  which  you  had  entrusted  to  my  direction,  but  am  satisfied  that 
the  natural  obstacles  are  such  as  to  render  another  just  as  little  likely 
to  succeed.  The  experience  obtained  is  worth  something  in  future 
operations.  I  only  withdrew  when  all  my  shell  with  fuzes  long  enough 
to  reach  (or  over  five  seconds)  had  been  expended,  and  when  the  crew 
were  almost  beyond  further  work,  having  been  occupied  for  eight  hours 
at  the  guns  without  even  an  intermission  to  eat,  and  then  I  should  have 
remained  had  I  seen  the  least  sign  of  faltering  or  slackness  of  fire  on 
the  part  of  the  enemy;  but,  on  the  contrary,  I  think  that  it  was,  if  any¬ 
thing,  more  rapid  toward  the  last. 

The  gunboats  Seneca ,  Lieutenant-Commander  Gibson;  WissahicJcon , 
Lieutenant-Commander  Davis,  and  Dawn,  Lieutenant  Barnes,  were 
anchored  near  the  mortar  schooners  in  signal  distance  of  us,  and  pre¬ 
pared  to  give  assistance  had  any  been  required. 

Everything  about  the  guns  and  carriages  worked  to  my  satisfaction, 
except  that  the  box  around  the  XV-inch  gun,  on  examination  was 
found  to  be  almost  detached  from  the  side,  owing  to  the  breaking  of 
the  bolts  which  secure  it  to  the  turret.  From  its  appearance  this 
morning,  I  should  think  that  it  could  scarcely  stand  a  dozen  more 
shots.  My  deck  having  been  very  badly  injured,  will  require  some 
repairs  before  I  could,  1  think,  safely  go  outside.  The  mortar  shell 
which  fell  on  deck  over  the  bread  room,  would  undoubtedly  have  gone 
through  had  it  not  struck  on  a  beam;  as  it  was,  it  has  completely 
crushed  in  the  planking  at  the  side  of  the  beam,  opening  quite  a  hole 
through,  and  had  it  been  loaded  with  powder  instead  of  sand,  might 
have  set  the  vessel  on  fire.  I  have  measured  a  piece  of  it,  and  it  does 
not  seem  to  have  been  larger  than  X-inch;  this  certainly  does  not  say 
much  for  the  strength  of  the  deck,  the  injury  to  which  has  been  so 
much  more  serious  than  to  that  of  the  Montauh ,  that  I  must  attribute 
it  to  a  worse  class  of  iron,  unless  heavier  guns  have  been  mounted 
since  the  attack  made  by  Commander  Worden.

I  have  omitted  to  mention  that  my  pilot  was  the  same  one  who  had

have  to  thank  Commanders  Ammen  and  Downes  for  the  hearty  sup¬ 
port  which  they  gave  me.

Report  of  Lieutenant-Commander  Miller,  U.  S.  Navy,  executive  officer  of  the  U.  S.  S.  Pas¬ 
saic,  regarding  injuries  sustained  by  that  vessel. 

U.  S.  Ironclad  Steamer  Passaic, 

Ogeechee  River ,  Georgia ,  March  h,  1863. 

Sir:  I  submit  the  following  report  of  the  injuries  we  received  in  the 
attack  on  Fort  McAllister: 

We  were  struck  nine  times  on  the  port  side  armor.  Three  of  these 
were  about  50  feet  from  the  bow  and  within  the  distance  of  3  feet  from 
each  other.  They  made  indentations  of  2  inches,  carried  away  several 
bolts,  and  raised  the  adjoining  deck  plating  1  inch.  The  other  shots 
in  side  armor  made  indentations  of  about  1  inch  without  injuring  the 
bolts. 

On  deck  plating  we  received  thirteen  shots;  one  over  wardroom  store 
room  raised  the  plating  and  carried  away  several  of  the  bolts;  one 
struck  over  the  hammock  room,  near  the  turret,  crushing  in  the  plating 
and  deck  planking,  causing  the  deck  to  leak  when  covered  with  water. 
Two  shots  struck  over  the  engine  room,  breaking  a  number  of  bolts  in 
the  plating,  which  it  also  broke  through  and  raised  the  ends.  A  X- 
inch  mortar  shell,  loaded  with  sand,  struck  over  the  bread  room,  crush¬ 
ing  in  the  deck  plating  and  planking;  it  struck  partly  on  a  beam  and 
the  angle  iron  which  supports  it,  but  as  far  as  we  can  see  these  are  not 
injured.  The  remaining  shots  on  deck  did  not  seriously  injure  the 
plating.  Five  shots  struck  the  turret,  making  indentations  varying 
from  one-half  inch  to  1  inch;  one  of  these  is  6  inches  below  the  XV- 
inch  port.  Two  shots  struck  the  pilot  house,  carrying  away  three  of 
the  bolts,  and  m'aking  indentations  of  about  1  inch.  One  shot  struck 
the  roof  of  the  turret  and  broke  one  of  its  beams  of  railroad  iron.  The 
lower  part  of  the  smokestack  was  struck  once  close  to  the  deck,  making 
an  indentation  of  li  inches,  and  carrying  away  one  of  the  boltheads. 

The  concussion  of  the  XV-inch  gun  broke  all  of  the  bolts  holding 
the  sides  of  the  box  to  the  turret,  and  I  have  no  doubt,  unless  the  bolts 
are  replaced,  that  a  few  more  fires  would  destroy  the  box,  one  side  of 
which  is  much  bulged  out.  The  bolt  holding  one  of  the  rollers  of  the 


720 


SOUTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


sliding  plate  in  concussion  box  parted  during  the 'action;  but  as  we 
always  tired  at  the  same  elevation  the  plate  was  lashed  so  that  we  could 
run  the  gun  in  and  out. 

During  the  action  we  were  struck  thirty-four  times,  nine  of  which 
were  on  side  armor;  thirteen  on  deck;  five  on  turret;  two  on  pilot  house; 
one  on  roof  of  turret;  one  on  smokestack;  one  carried  away  pennant 
staff  on  pilot  house;  one  carried  away  boat  spar  aft,  and  one  the  out¬ 
rigger  forward. 

I  am,  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

J.  N.  Miller,

Abstract  log  of  the  U.  S.  S.  Passaic,  Captain  Drayton,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding. 

March  3,  1863. — Ossabaw  Sound:  At  7:45  a.  m.  secured  fighting 
hatches,  got  underway,  and  steamed  up  the  river  with  the  ironclads 
Eatapsco  and  Nahant  following  astern.  At  7  the  three  mortar  schoon¬ 
ers  were  towed  near  us  in  a  position  for  firing.  At  8:40  anchored  off 
Fort  McAllister  at  a  distance  of  1,200  yards.  Immediately  after  the 
Patapsco  did  the  same,  about  200  yards,  a  little  to  our  port  quarter, 
we  riding  to  the  ebb,  and  the  Naliant  about  the  same  distance  on  the 
starboard  quarter.  Immediately  on  anchoring  the  fort  opened  fire  on 
us,  which  was  returned  by  us  and  the  other  two  vessels.  From  merid¬ 
ian  to  4  p.  m. :  Firing  still  upon  the  fort,  which  was  returned.  At 
1:20  p.  m.  the  pulley  that  supported  the  chain  of  the  sliding  shut¬ 
ter  of  the  XV -inch  gun  broke  and  the  gun  could  not  be  fired  for  half 
an  hour  in  consequence.  At  3:30  p.  m.  made  private  signal  to  stop 
fire  and  retire,  which  was  soon  after  obe}red  bj^  the  Nahant ,  but  could 
not  be  by  the  Patapsco,  as  she  was  aground.  She,  however,  got  off 
and  started  down  the  river  at  4:10,  followed  by  us  at  4:30.  As  we 
got  underway  we  fired  a  shot  from  each  gun  and  then  ceased  firing. 
The  fort  continued  to  fire  as  long  as  we  were  in  range,  which  was  ten 
or  fifteen  minutes  after  we  were  underway.  I  could  not  observe  that 
their  fire  was  much  slackened  from  the  morning.  At  5 : 30  anchored 
at  the  place  we  had  left  in  the  morning,  the  Nahant  and  Patapsco 
having  done  so  before  us.  Expended  during  the  action  with  the  forts: 
XV-inch  gun,  2  shell,  5-second  fuze;  37  shell,  7-second  and  10-second 
fuze;  2  cored  shot;  total,  41  projectiles,  41  charges  of  35  pounds  pow¬ 
der.  Xl-inch  gun,  4  shell,  5-second  fuze;  36  shell,  7-second  and  10- 
second  fuze;  2  canister;  1  shrapnel,  Boormann  fuze;  9  solid  shot;  total, 
52  projectiles,  52  charges  15  pounds  powder.  From  8  to  midnight, 
mortar  schooners  firing  at  intervals. 

March  It.. — Ossabaw  Sound:  From  meridian  to  4  p.  m.  saw  large 
bodies  of  men  at  work  repairing  Fort  McAllister. 


Report  of  Commander  Ammen,  U,  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S.  S.  Patapsco. 

Ironclad  Patapsco, 

Ogeechee  Rimer,  March  3,  1863. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  that,  in  obedience  to  signal  at  8  a.  m. 
of  to-day,  the  Patapsco  was  got  underway,  preceded  by  the  Passaic 


SOUTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON.  721 

and  followed  by  the  Nahant ,  and  at  about  8:30  a.  m.  anchored  below 
Fort  McAllister. 

The  enemy  immediately  opened  lire  and  had  established  a  target  for 
range  on  a  marsh  near  the  spot  where  the  three  vessels  anchored  as 
near  each  other  as  was  possible  to  swing  clear  on  a  turn  of  tide.  Seven 
guns  were  visible  on  the  face  of  the  work,  protected  by  heavy  trav¬ 
erses,  and  in  an  adjoining  wood  one  or  two  mortars  and  a  rifle  were  in 
position  and  directed  their  Are  against  us. 

The  difficulty  of  approach  through  a  narrow  channel  and  the  shoal¬ 
ness  of  the  water  evidently  left  you  without  a  choice  of  position. 
We  followed  your  movements,  and  after  firing  a  few  shell  found  the 
distance  from  the  battery  greater  than  had  been  supposed.  We  fired 
deliberately,  and  finding  the  XV-inch  gun  required  more  elevation 
than  is  desirable,  confined  ourselves  for  some  time  to  the  use  of  the 
rifle.  The  time  fuzes  of  the  rifle,  except  those  made  by  the  Ordnance 
Department,  did  not  appear  general^  to  explode  the  shells,  and  the 
percussion  shells  did  not  explode  with  the  ordinary  percussion  musket 
cap.  By  filing  the  nipple  so  as  to  receive  an  ordinary  cap  few  failed, 
even  when  striking  in  the  sand.  Fourteen  XV-inch  and  forty-six  150- 
pound  rifle  shell  were  expended  by  us  against  the  enemy. 

No  injury  was  sustained  b}rthis  vessel,  and  only  one  shot  was  knojvn 
to  have  struck  the  deck.  Much  the  greater  part  of  the  firing  of  the 
enemy  was  directed  against  the  Passaic. 

The  works  of  the  enemy  appeared  very  much  cut  up;  the  parapet 
was  breached  in  several  places  and  three  of  the  traverses  very  much 
injured. 

When  the  Passaic  and  the  Nahant  swung  to  the  flood  at  about  3  p.  m. 
we  remained  across  the  tide,  and  I  saw  at  once  that  we  were  aground, 
owing  to  having  anchored  a  few  yards  on  the  port  quarter  of  the 
Passaic  as  she  rode  to  the  ebb;  a  rising  tide  and  working  the  engine 
enabled  us  to  swing  about  3:40  p.  m. 

The  signal  by  whistle  to  get  underway  was  not  understood  by  us, 
and  the  flag  was  not  seen.  After  seeing  the  Nahant  leave,  and  learn¬ 
ing  verbally  the  order,  I  got  underway,  as  directed,  and  proceeded  to 
this  anchorage. 

I  am,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Daniel  Ammen, 

Commander. 

Captain  Percival  Drayton, 

Ironclad  Passaic. 


Report  of  Commander  Downes,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S.  S.  Nahant. 

Ironclad  Nahant, 
Ossabaw  Sound ,  March  T  1863. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  submit  the  following  report  of  the  par¬ 
ticipation  of  this  vessel  in  the  attack  yesterday  upon  Fort  McAllister: 

Weighing  anchor  at  7:30  a.  m.,  the  commencement  of  ebb  tide,  in 
compliance  with  signal,  we  steamed  up  the  river,  preceded  by  the 
Passaic  and  Patapsco ,  and  at  8:30  grounded  in  close  vicinity  to  our 
subsequent  anchorage,  and  after  the  two  leading  vessels  had  anchored, 
but,  by  backing  our  engines,  fortunately  got  afloat  again  before  the 
tide  had  receded  sufficiently  to  make  us  a  fixture  until  the  next  high 

n  w  R — vol  13- - 46 


722  SOUTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 

water.  At  8:50,  whilst  still  aground,  we  commenced  action,  about 
1,700  yards  from  the  fort,  the  enemy  having  opened  tire  about  ten 
minutes  previously  and  continued  it  subsequently  at  the  reduced  dis¬ 
tance  of  about  1,500  yards  until  ordered  by  signal  to  discontinue  and 
drop  out  of  action,  at  near  4  p.  m.,  during  which  time  we  tired  thirty- 
two  XY-inch  shell  and  twenty-nine  Xl-shell.  After  tiring  ten  charges 
of  35  pounds  from  the  XY-inch,  with  all  the  elevation  1  could  give 
the  gun,  the  shell  falling  short  of  the  parapet,  and  not  being  able  to 
reduce  my  distance  from  the  fort,  I  considered  it  necessary  to  increase 
my  charge  of  powder  to  38  pounds,  after  which  the  practice  from  this 
vessel  was  very  satisfactory  and  the  effect  upon  the  earthwork  opposed 
to  us  apparently  very  damaging,  tearing  away  the  parapet  and  trav¬ 
erses  and  bursting  the  shells  with  great  certainty  inside  the  work,  and 
very  often  in  close  vicinity  of  the  guns. 

I  can  find  no  trace  of  this  vessel  having  been  struck  by  shot  during 
the  action;  indeed,  the  leading  vessel,  the  Passaic ,  seemed  to  attract 
the  attention  of  the  battery  almost  exclusively,  they  giving  us  only  an 
occasional  shot,  which  generally  passed  over.  A  mortar  planted  under 
cover  of  the  woods  in  the  vicinity  of  the  fort  and  a  small  rifled  piece 
or  two,  aimed  apparently  at  persons  exposing  themselves  upon  the 
de.ck,  paid  us  particular  attention,  but  without  effect. 

At  various  times  during  the  action  the  compressor  arrangements  of 
the  XY-inch  gun  became  disarranged,  the  gun  twice  recoiling  so  far 
in  that  it  was  with  great  difficulty,  and  once  only  with  the  assistance 
of  a  jackscrew,  that  we  forced  it  out  again;  and  at  the  twentieth  fire 
the  rivets  of  the  brass  guides  on  the  after  part  of  the  carriage  broke, 
the  guides  falling  down  into  the  turret  chamber  below,  without,  how¬ 
ever,  disabling  the  gun.  At  the  thirty-ninth  fire  of  the  Xl-ineh  gun 
the  cast-iron  yoke  snapped  at  the  outer  edge  of  the  port  trunnion, 
thereby  effectually  disabling  the  gun  until  another  yoke  is  supplied 
to  us. 

I  estimated  the  armament  of  the  fort,  on  the  water  faces,  at  seven 
guns,  a  large  rifle,  and  the  remainder  Vi-inch,  VIII-inch,  and  X-inch 
guns,  besides  one  or  two  smaller  rifles,  not  apparent  to  us  except  from 
their  execution,  and  the  one  mortar  previously  mentioned. 

The  bearing  of  the  officers  and  crew  was  everything  I  had  expected 
of  them,  entirely  satisfactory,  and  assuring  to  me  that  under  any  cir¬ 
cumstances  they  will  perform  their  duties  thoroughly. 

Enclosed  please  find  returns  of  the  expenditure  of  ammunition  and 
the  quantity  still  on  board. 

I  am,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

John  Downes, 

Commander. 

Captain  Percival  Drayton, 

Comdg.  Ironclad  Passaic ,  Senior  Officer  Present ,  Ogeechee  River.

Order  of  Rear-Admiral  Du  Pont,  U.  S.  Navy,  to  Captain  Drayton,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding 
U.  S.  S.  Passaic,  for  the  withdrawal  of  that  vessel  and  others  from  Ossabaw  Sound. 


Flagship  Wabash, 

Port  Royal  Harbor ,  S.  C. ,  March  1863. 

Sir:  I  have  received  your  communication  of  yesterday,  giving  the 
particulars  of  your  attack  on  Fort  McAllister. 

The  results  have  been  of  great  service  in  testing  not  only  the  resist¬ 
ing,  but  the  aggressive,  powers  of  the  ironclads,  which  wilfbe  of  much 
use  in  future  operations. 

As  nothing  will  be  gained  b}"  renewing  the  attack,  you  will  therefore 
withdraw  the  Passaic  and  all  the  other  vessels  from' Ossabaw,  return¬ 
ing  to  this  anchorage,  leaving  only  the  Seneca  and  Dawn ,  which  will 
assume  such  positions  as  may  be  the  most  judicious  in  the  blockade  of 
those  waters,  and  which  the  long  experience  of  Lieutenant-Commander 
Gibson  and  Acting  Lieutenant  Barnes  will  enable  them  to  do. 

The  Ericsson  is  still  off  Ossabaw,  ready  to  tow  the  mortar  schooners 
or  other  vessels  here. 

Respectfully,  etc. , 


S.  F.  Du  Pont, 

Rear-Admiral. 


Captain  P.  Drayton, 

U.  S.  S.  Passaic,  Senior  Officer,  Ossabaw. 


Report  of  Captain  Drayton,  D.  S.  Navy,  to  the  Chief  of  Bureau  of  Ordnance,  giving  experi¬ 
ence  gained  by  the  bombardment. 

F.  S.  Ironclad  Passaic, 

Port  Royal,  March  8 ,  1863. 

Sir:  I  beg  leave  to  offer  to  the  Bureau  the  experience  gained  during 
the  eight  hours  that  this  vessel  was  under  the  fire  of  Fort  McAllister, 
on  the  Ogeechee,  on  the  3d  of  March,  particularly  that  which  especially 
belongs  to  ordnance. 

The  distance  from  the  fort  I  judged  to  be  about  1,200  yards  from 
the  following  data:  The  platform  on  which  the  gun  is  placed  being 
level,  I  elevated  the  bore  to  a  iittle  less  than  6  degrees  for  the  Xl-inch. 
This  threw  a  shell  with  15  pounds  of  powder  (ordinary  cannon)  onto 
and  over  a  parapet  25  feet  above  the  water  line,  the  axis  of  trunnion 
being  a  little  less  than  4  feet  from  the  water.  This  would,  I  consider, 
make  the  distance  between  1,200  and  1,300  yards.  In  addition,  the 


726  SOUTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 

* 

V 

shot  from  the  fort  struck  me  in  four  seconds  from  the  flash,  and  nearly 
a  second  after  the  report.  I  am  particular  in  mentioning  these  facts, 
as  the  distance  is  so  important  an  element  in  the  endurance  of  the 
vessel. 

Both  guns  worked  well,  and  I  could  see  no  signs  of  giving  away  in 
the  carriages.  That  part  of  the  fixtures,  however,  which  I  always  said 
was  too  weak — the  box  round  the  muzzle  of  the  XV-inch  gun — would 
have  been  down  in  six  more  fires,  as  every  bolt  in  the  angle  irons  hold¬ 
ing  it  to  the  turret  was  broken  off  in  that  part  attached  to  the  turret. 
The  slide  also  became  useless,  except  for  one  elevation  after  the  twen¬ 
tieth  fire.  The  guns  were  fired  immediately  after  each  other,  and  I 
do  not  see  that  the  greater  rapidity  in  loading  the  smaller  one  can  be 
taken  advantage  of,  owing  to  the  delay  caused  from  so  frequent  turn¬ 
ing  of  the  turret,  and  thereby  exposing  the  ports  to  be  entered  by  shot, 
which  is  an  important  consideration,  as  the  enemy,  from  all  experience 
so  far,  almost  invariably  waits  for  the  port  to  be  opened  to  him  before 
firing,  no  coloring  of  the  turret  deceiving  him  as  to  the  side  on  which 
the  port  is,  the  only  way  to  do  which,  I  am  satisfied,  is  to  have  an 
outer  covering  of  some  light  material  simply  to  obstruct  the  light  and 
shade. 

The  XV-inch  gun  was  fired  at  an  elevation  of  rather  less  than  5 
degrees  and  recoiled  so  as  to  bring  the  muzzle  just  clear  of  the  con¬ 
cussion  box.  In  making  the  rammers  light  enough  to  handle,  they 
have  been  made  with  very  short  heads  and  horns  to  keep  them  in  posi¬ 
tion.  These  last  invariably  break  off,  and  require  to  be  much  stronger. 
The  front  part  of  the  head  is  also  very  liable  to  splitting. 

In  only  two  cases  did  the  small  projection  on  the  XV-inch  cartridge 
enter  the  chamber,  and  the  primer,  in  consequence,  will  not  explode 
the  charge  unless  priming  powder  is  used,  and  the  only  case  in  which 
there  was  a  failure  to  do  so  occurred  from  the  captain  of  the  gun 
omitting  it. 

Some  kind  of  a  rammer  which  can  be  used  with  a  closed  port  is,  I 
think,  very  important.  While  I  was  firing  at  the  fort  several  rifle¬ 
men  came  into  the  marsh  and  opened  fire  on  the  side  to  which  we 
turned  our  guns  to  be  loaded,  and  had  I  not  driven  them  away  with 
some  canister  it  might  have  been  necessary  to  keep  the  shutters  closed, 
which,  with  the  present  rammers,  is  inconvenient.  A  rammer  of 
Lieutenant-Commander  Jeffers’  invention  is,  I  think,  very  good. 

Our  fire  was  slower  than  it  would  otherwise  have  been,  owing  to  the 
necessity  of  changing  fuzes.  Almost  all  of  our  shells  had  only  one  fuze 
hole,  and  in  it  was  usually  a  5-second  fuze.  This  I  had  not  changed, 
being  told  that  the  distance  would  not  be  over  a  thousand  yards.  I 
also  ran  out  of  7-second  and  10-second  fuzes.  In  view  of  the  very 
limited  shell  room  and  the  difficulty  of  handling  these  large  shells,  I 
would  recommend  that  those  with  one  fuze  hole  be  withdrawn.  When 
we  commenced  the  action,  I  had  up  thirteen  shells  for  the  XV-inch. 
These  were  fired  away  in  ninety  minutes,  and  I  consider  this  to  be  about 
as  fast  as  it  will  be  found  they  can  be.delivered  to  advantage.  The  aver¬ 
age  of  the  whole  was  ten  minutes;  that  of  the  Montauh  in  her  three 
actions  the  same;  of  the  Nahant  thirteen,  and  of  the  Patajpsco  thirty 
minutes. 

The  pointing  was  done  for  both  guns  with  the  Xl-inch,  the  port  of 
the  other  being  entirely  closed  by  the  concussion  box.  This  answered, 
however,  very  well,  and  after  the  range  was  once  obtained  the  shot 
fell  most  uniformly  and  with  scarce  any  variation  at  the  desired  spot.

The  deck  plating  and  planking  is  too  weak;  both  were  broken  and 
the  latter  pushed  through  in  four  places.  The  X-inch  mortar  shell, 
weight  without  sand  87  pounds,  would  have  gone  clean  through  the 
deck  and  into  the  bread  rooms  had  it  not  struck  partly  on  the  beam 
and  directly  where  it  was  supported  by  an  iron  knee.  As  it  was,  there 
being  a  little  sea,  the  bread  was  all  spoiled  from  water  rushing  over 
the  deck  above  the  hole. 

Judging  from  the  blows  on  the  side  armor,  I  should  say  that  at  400 
yards  it  would  be  entirely  penetrated,  and  I  am  satisfied  that  it  will  be 
shown  on  the  first  occasion  of  a  nearer  approach  to  heavy  guns  par¬ 
ticularly  that  the  turret,  pilot  house,  and  smokestack  have  alone  suf¬ 
ficient  resisting  power. 

One  of  our  pilots,  an  Englishman,  deserted  from  Fort  McAllister 
two  months  ago.  The  battery  was  then  an  Vffl-inch  and  six  32s.  A 
few  days  before  he  left,  after  a  visit  from  Genei*al  Beauregard,  two 
rifles  and  a  mortar  were  sent  down,  which  were  about  being  mounted, 
and  since  then  a  X-inch  has  been  added,  as  we  have  the  shot  which  struck 
the  pilot  house,  making  an  indentation  of  1  inch,  and  being  caught  on 
the  rebound  by  the  rim  of  the  turret.  A  second  one,  which  struck  on 
the  opposite  side  just  as  we  were  getting  underway,  was  broken  into 
small  pieces  without  sensibly  jarring  the  pilot  house,  as  1  could  observe, 
from  being  at  the  time  on  top  of  the  turret,  outside  and  leaning  against 
it,  to  shelter  myself  from  the  enenry’s  shot.  The  two  indentations 
are  exacthr  alike  as  to  depth  and  curve.  The  whole  shot  is  only 
flattened  rather  less  than  a  quarter  of  an  inch. 

As  we  were  swinging  to  the  flood  tide,  both  the  guns  were  fired  so 
as  just  to  clear  the  smokestack,  and  the  engineers  who  were  watching 
the  effect  report  that  there  was  no  injurious  disturbance  to  the  boilers. 
It  was  thought  on  board  of  the  Montauk  that  tying  the  cartridge  at  both 
necks  had  the  effect  of  causing  the  small  projection  to  enter  the  cham¬ 
ber.  Such  was  not,  however,  the  case,  nor  do  the  blocks  serve  any 
better  purpose. 

There  was  no  inconvenience  in  the  turret  from  either  smoke  or  noise, 
at  least  that  was  not  quite  bearable,  and  even  less  in  the  pilot  house. 

Below  deck  the  chimneys  of  two  lamps  were  broken,  but  no  light 
was  extinguished  nor  any  particular  jar  felt  when  the  deck  was  struck 
or  our  own  guns  fired  over  it,  nor  was  the  atmosphere  below  particu¬ 
larly  oppressive,  although  at  times  the  smoke  was  quite  disagreeable. 

The  conclusion  I  have  come  to,  both  from  my  attack  and  that  of  the 
Montauk  on  Fort  McAllister  is,  that  if  we  expect  to  reduce  heavy 
earthworks,  it  must  be  done  as  in  the  attack  of  fortified  places  on  shore, 
by  a  continuous  fire  by  day  to  destroy,  and  at  night  to  stop  repairs, 
and  this  seems  to  be  the  opinion  of  the  army  officers,  some  of  whom 
witnessed  the  affair  of  the  3d.  They  also  state  that  enfilading  works 
with  such  heavy  traverses  is  not  more  favorable  than  acting  on  the 
front.  This  being  the  case,  the  only  question  that  seems  to  remain  is 
one  of  distance,  and  except  for  the  increased  chance  of  hitting  the 
guns,  I  rather  doubt  whether  the  effect  of  the  shells  would  not  be  as 
great  at  1,200  as  at  600  yards.  In  the  case  of  Fort  McAllister,  there 
is,  however,  no  opportunity  of  testing  the  question,  as  just  beyond 
where  I  was  anchored  the  river  becomes  too  shoal  to  permit  a  vessel 
drawing  near  12  feet  to  remain  after  quarter  ebb,  and  to  retire  with  a 
falling  tide  in  a  narrow  channel,  by  dropping  down,  was  more  risk 
than  I  was  inclined  to  take  without  a  more  important  object  than  the 
one  in  view  at  the  time,  and,  indeed,  the  pilot  would  not  have  taken 


728  SOUTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 

me  higher  without  a  positive  order  on  my  part  to  absolve  him  from 
censure.  No  one  except  myself  is  possessed  of  an}r  information  on 
which  to  base  the  distance  from  the  fort,  but  1  send  you  a  statement, 
given  me  by  Commander  Worden,  which  shows  the  time  he  was  under

tauk ,  with  reference  to  a  target  which  was  on  the  river  bank,  I  should 
say  that  I  was  nearer,  decidedly,  when  his  estimated  distance  was  1,500 
yards,  slightly  so  at  the  place  of  his  1,400,  and  50  yards  short  of  where 
he  supposed  ‘it  to  be  1,200  yards.  From  the. report  of  Commander 
Downes,  of  the  Nahant ,  you  will  see  that  he  used  3  pounds  more 
powder  than  the  regular  charge  of  the  XV-inch,  as  his  carriage  only 
allows  an  elevation  of  6  degrees,  and  he  tells  me  that  there  was  quite 
a  list  on  the  side  of  fire.  Five  degrees  must  have  been  the  full  prac¬ 
ticable  elevation,  and  the  JVahant  being  some  distance  farther  off  than 
the  Passaic ,  would  about  make  an  agreement  with  my  supposed  ranges. 

The  injury  done  to  my  deck  and  side  armor  is  so  very  much  more 
serious  than  any  which  the  Montauk  has  suffered  that  I  am  at  a  loss  to 
account  for  it.  '  The  distance  so  nearly  agreeing  leaves  only  two  modes 
of  explanation,  one  that  the  iron  used  on  the  Passaic  is  of  an  inferior 
quality,  the  other  that  the  size  of  the  shot  was  greater  than  any  which 
struck  the  Montauk.  Out  of  the  four  guns  of  the  Passaic  and  JVahant , 
two  were  used  up,  as  regarded  a  continuance  of  fire,  my  XY-ineh  from 
the  breaking  loose  of  the  box,  the  Xl-inch  of  the  JVahant  owing  to 
the  yoke  giving  way.  The  XV-inch  of  the  Patapsco  was  only  fired 
fourteen  times  and  was  consequently  not  much  tried.  The  200-pounder 
rifle,  however,  which  was  discharged  forty-six  times,  stood  well.  This 
certainly  looks  as  if  our  gun  fixtures  were  not  to  be  depended  on  for 
long  firing,  and  I  consider  it  very  fortunate  that  in  my  case  the  dis¬ 
covery  was  made  before  going  into  Charleston  Harbor.

Fort  Monroe,  Va.,  March  11 ,  1863 — 5 p.  m. 

I  bring  dispatches  from  Admiral  Du  Pont.  Charleston  not  yet 
attacked.  Our  experience  against  Fort  McAllister  on  the  3d  instant 
demonstrates  that  we  must  have  more  guns  to  be  successful  against 
Charleston. 

I  have  told  Admiral  Du  Pont  that  we  can  get  th &  Nantucket,  Sanga¬ 
mon,  and  Keokuk  at  work  upon  Charleston  in  the  first  week  in  April. 
I  came  in  the  Ericsson ,  which  can  carry  back  iron  for  reinforcing  the 
docks  and  prospective  repairs.  I  wish  to  get  another  raft.  Weeha/wken 
steers  better  with  than  without  one  attached  to  her  bow.  A  X-inch 
mortar  shell  struck  the  deck  of  Passaic  without  going  through.  Injury 
to  bottom  of  Montauk  by  the  torpedo  is  not  serious;  repairing  at  Port 
Royal.  W as  on  board  Passaic  during  eight  hours’  action  with  fort. 
Everything  worked  admirably.  Will  be  in  Washington  to-morrow 
morning. 

Alban  C.  Stimers, 

Chief  Engineer.

Report  of  Major  Harris,  C.  S.  Army,  chief  engineer  of  the  district  of  Georgia. 

Savannah,  Ga.,  March  9,  1863. 

General:  In  compliance  with  my  instructions,  Captain  McCrady 
has  made  a  report  in  detail  of  the  engagement  of  the.  enemy  with  the 
battery  at  Genesis  Point  (Fort  McAllister)  on  the  3d  instant,  which  I 
have  the  honor  to  hand  you  herewith. 

This  interesting  report  is  based  upon  information  furnished  by 
Assistant  Engineer  J.  W.  McAlpin,  to  whose  admirable  conduct  on 
this  and  previous  attacks  upon  Fort  McAllister  I  respectfully  invite 
the  attention  of  the  general  commanding. 


780 


SOUTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 

* 

I  have  visited  the  battery  since  the  engagement  and  found  it  in  a 
good  condition  in  every  respect. 

It  would  appear  that  the  ironclads'  are  not  such  formidable  monsters 
after  all,  particularly  against  sand  batteries.  Where  crushing  effect 
is  desired,  as  against  vessels  and  brick  or  other  walls,  the  XV-inch 
shell  and  solid  shot  could  be  used  to  advantage,  but  for  the  reduction 
of  sand  batteries  the  same  amount  of  metal  thrown  from  VIII  and 
X  inch  guns  in  the  same  time  would,  I  think,  have  treble  the  effect. 
The  firing  of  the  ironclads  was  not  as  accurate  as  it  should  have  been 
under  the  circumstances.  The  fire  of  our  battery  having  been  directed 
against  one  of  them  alone,  the  others  ought  to  have  fired  with  all  the 
deliberation  and  care  requisite  to  insure  accuracy.  I  am  therefore  at 
a  loss  to  account  for  their  wild  firing.  The  most  of  their  shots  passed 
over  the  battery.  The  mortars  were  fired  at  a  distance  of  at  least 
miles,  without,  as  usual,  any  damaging  effect  upon  the  battery. 

I  am  fully  persuaded  the  turret  of  No.  1  ( Montauk *)  was  injured 
during  the  engagement. 

The  result  of  this  engagement  ought  to  make  us  feel  quite  comfort¬ 
able.  When  the  grand  affair  with  which  the  abolitionists  have  been 
so  long’  threatening  us  shall  come  off,  if  it  ever  does,  I  am  sure  our 
sand  batteries  will  give  a  good  account  of  themselves. 

Mr.  McAlpin  thinks  the  ironclads  did  not  pass  over  the  torpedoes  in 
the  river.  I  have  directed  an  examination  to  be  made  to  ascertain  if 
the3r  are  in  the  position  in  which  they  were  anchored  in  the  stream. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  general,  yours,  very  respectfully, 

*  D.  B.  Harris, 

Major  and  Chief  Engineer1. 

Brigadier-General  Thomas  Jordan, 

Chief  of  Staff. 


Report  of  Captain  McCrady,  C.  S.  Army. 

C.  S.  Engineer  Office, 

Savannah ,  March  <§,  1863. 

Major:  The  following  report  of  the  engagement  with  three  of  the 
enemy’s  monitor  fleet,  which  occurred  at  Fort  McAllister  on  Tuesday, 
March  8,  is  founded  upon  the  notes  and  observations  of  Assistant 
Engineer  McAlpin  and  the  statements  of  Captain  [G.  W.]  Anderson, 
Captam  [J.  L.]  McAllister,  Lieutenant  [E.  A.JElarbee,  and  Mr.  Motte 
Middleton. 

Three  of  the  monitor  fleet  took  position  off  the  battery  at  8:45  a.  m. ; 
opened  fire  at  8:54  a.  m.,  and  ceased  at  4:15  p.  m.,  the  action,  so  far 
as  these  vessels  were  concerned,  lasting  seven  hours  and  twenty-four 
minutes.  Another  monitor  lay  near  the  bend  of  the  river  below  Har¬ 
vey’s  Cut,  but  took  no  part  in  the  action.  She  was  accompanied  by 
one  river  steamer  and  one  ocean  steamer,  besides  two  mortar  schooners 
m  plain  view  and.  one  which  was  not  seen,  but  which  threw  mortar 
’  ^°£f®hher  with  the  other  two,  during  the  whole  engagement. 

I  he  three  ironclads  were  drawn  up  in  line  of  battle  at  distances 
varying  from  1,400  to  1,900  yards  from  the  battery.  At  these  dis- 
tances  they  appeared  to  be  all  so  nearly  of  the  same  model  as  to  render

it  impossible  to  distinguish  them  by  differences  of  form  or  proportion. 
Each  carried  a  single  turret,  nearly  amidships,  and  in  front  of  smoke¬ 
stack.  They  could  only  be  distinguished  from  each  other  by  their  dif¬ 
ferences  of  color,  which  are  given  in  the  enclosed  table.  One  of  them 
lay  above  the  target,  the  other  two  below  it.  Calling  that  above  the 
target  and  nearest  the  battery  No.  1 ,  No.  2  lay  about  300  yards  below 
it,  and  No.  3  about  50  yards  below  No.  %.  Their  position  was  in  the 
channel  about  200  yards  from  the  marsh,  on  the  opposite  side  of  the 
river.  Assistant  Engineer  Posted,  stationed  at  Rosedew,  states  that 
only  one  of  the  three  carried  a  Hag  upon  her  turret.  This  was  prob¬ 
ably  the  Montauk*  which  in  previous  engagements  carried  such  a  flag. 
The  plates  on  the  hull  of  No.  1  were  distinguishable  from  the  battery 
and  were  thought  by  Mr.  McAlpin  to  be  from  18  to  21  inches  square. 

The  tables  attached  to  this  report  will  show  the  differences  of  color, 
armament,  etc,,  of  the  three  ironclads,  as  well  as  the  number  of  shot 
fired  by  each  and  the  number  which  took  effect  upon  the  battery.  The 
whole  number  fired  was  221,  and  of  these  not  more  than  50  struck  any 
part  of  our  works.  Of  the  27  which  struck  the  traverses  and  superior 
slope  only  12  shells  exploded,  and  they  did  no  serious  damage.  The 
greatest  injury  inflicted  by  a  shot  was  the  destruction  of  the  carriage 
of  the  Ylll-inch  gun. 

The  tire  of  our  battery  was  concentrated  exclusively  on  monitor 
No.  1.  No  shots  whatever  were  fired  at  Nos.  %  and  3.  The  men  on 
No.  3  watched  the  engagement  from  the  deck  of  their  vessel  without 
fear  of  being  fired  at.  Captain  Anderson  reports  that  he  attempted 
firing  by  battery,  but  did  not  succeed  for  want  of  a  signal  which  could 
be  heard  in  all  the  gun  chambers  at  once.  He  reports  that  the  stroke 
of  the  bass  drum  was  not  sufficient  for  this  purpose. 

The  firing  of  the  X-inch  mortar,  Captain  Martin,  was  very  accurate, 
all  the  shells  falling  near  No.  7,  and  one,  filled  with  sand,  striking  her 
deck  and  breaking  to  pieces.  The  32-pounder  rifled  gun,  with  charges 
of  7  pounds  of  powder,  did  well,  all  the  bolts  and  most  of  the  shells 
being  thrown  satisfactorily.  The  VUI-inch  gun  fired  with  its  usual 
accuracy  until  dismounted  at  11  o'clock.  The  firing  of  the  42-pounder, 
alwavs  accurate,  was  only  interrupted  for  thirty  minutes,  when,  the 
traverse  wheel  being  broken  by  a  fragment  of  shell,  it  required  that 
time  to  replace  it.  The  gun  was,  however,  fired  several  times  with 
the  broken  wheel,  but  at  last  gave  way.  The  X-inch  gun  was  served 
with  an  elevation  of  6°  30'  and  generally  shot  over  the  turret;  it  is 
thought,  however,  that  several  of  its  shot  struck  the  vessel.  1  he  32- 
pounders  were  fired,  I  suppose,  for  the  purpose  of  dividing  the  enemy’s 
attention.  It  will  be  thus  seen  that  the  42-pounder  and  the  rifle  gun 
were  those  which  principally  maintained  the  action  on  our  part,  the 
VlIRinch  gun  having  been  disabled  at  11  o’clock  and  the  X-inch 
generally  overshooting  the  mark. 

The  following  are  the  circumstances  which  have  caused  a  belief  that 
No.  1  was  injured  in  the  engagement :  The  last  shot  fired  at  her  was 
from  the  42-pounder.  It  was  reported  to  have  struck  near  the  turret 
and  low  down  toward  the  water  line.  Immediately  after  she  was  struck 
a  volume  of  smoke  or  steam  issued  from  her  side  in  a  manner  not  wit¬ 
nessed  in  previous  engagements,  and  which  caused  a  remark  that  she 
was  on  fire.  At  the  same  time  three  men  rushed  out  of  her  turret  and 
shortly  returned.  She  then  blew  her  whistle  three  times,  when  No.

for  volunteers  for  that  purpose.  They  attained  a  position  from  200  to 
250  yards  from  monitor  No.  1.  On  the  officer  stepping  out  of  the 
turret  to  ascertain  the  effect  of  his  shot,  one  rifle  was  tired  at  him, 
but  missed,  upon  which  he  immediately  turned  to  reenter  the  turret, 
but  was  shot  in  the  act,  stumbling  forward,  and  at  last  only  enter¬ 
ing  with  difficult}^.  No.  1  fired  grape  or  canister  at  the  men  in  the 
marsh  immediately  after  this,  and  once  subsequently,  but  without 
hurting  one  of  them.  Lieutenant  Elarbee,  from  his  position,  had  a 
nearer  view  of  No.  1  than  anyone  has  yet  had  of  one  of  the  monitor 
fleet.  No.  1  is  supposed  to  be  the  Montauk .*  He  reports  that  her  ports 
are  always  open ;  that  her  guns  run  in  and  out  of  battery,  and  that 
they  are  loaded  from  the  muzzle.  He  could  distinctly  hear  the  words 
of  command,  “In  battery,”  etc.,  and  saw  the  hands  of  the  men  and  the 
staff  of  the  rammer  protruding  through  the  port  in  loading.  He  also 
reports  that  in  No.  1  the  muzzle  of  the  gun  when  in  battery  protrudes 
about  6  inches  from  the  port.  He  could  see  nothing  of  the  same  kind 
in  Nos.  2  and  3.  He  could  observe  no  injury  done  by  our  shot  to  the 
turret,  the  only  observable  effect  being  a  whitish  streak  on  the  iron. 
The  shot  either  glanced  or  were  broken  to  pieces.  One  of  our  shot  is 
reported  to  have  struck  about  6  inches  from  the  port.  According  to 
Lieutenant  Elarbee’s  observations,  and  also  Mr.  McAlpin’s,  the  turret 
oi  No.  1  during  this  engagement  turned  only  one  way,  the  revolutions 
being  to  an  outsider  uniformly  from  left  to  right.  Lieutenant  Elarbee 
also  observed  that  the  motion  of  revolution  was  not  even  and  continu¬ 
ous,  but  effected  by  a  marked  trip  at  regular  intervals.  The  turret 
appeared  to  be  sometimes  arrested  temporarily  in  its  revolutions, 
whether  from  design,  imperfect  machinery,  or  injury  from  our  shot 
could  not  be  ascertained. 

The  mortar  fire  of  the  enemy  did  no  damage  to  the  works  during 
the  day.  They  resumed  firing  at  6  p.  m.,  and  continued  their  bom¬ 
bardment  until  6  a.  m.  the  next  day.  Only  one  shell  struck  any  part  of 
the  works,  and  that  opened  a  crater  of  about  4  feet  in  diameter  and  2 
feet  deep  in  the  top  of  the  covered  way  leading  from  the  main  work  in 
the  mortar  battery.  To  sum  up  the  effects  of  the  seven  hours’  bom¬ 
bardment  on  Fort  McAllister  by  three  ironclads,  carrying  each  two 
guns  of  the  heaviest  caliber,  and  three  mortar  boats,  carrying  each 
one  X  or  XV  inch  mortar,  I  make  the  following  statement  of  damage: 

Earthwork.—  No  material  damage,  nor  any  that  could  not  be  repaired 
in  one  night. 

Guns—  One  gun  carriage  scattered;  two  traverse  wheels  broken. 


*  The  U.  S.  S.  Montauk  was  not  in  action. 


SOUTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


733 


Men. — Two  men  slightly  wounded. 

On  account  of  the  continued  bombardment  the  negroes  could  not  be 
worked  during  the  night,  and  a  working  party  was  detailed  for  that 
purpose  from  the  sharpshooters.  With  these  men  and  the  assistance 
of  their  officers.  Assistant  Engineer  McAlpin  had  all  the  damage 
repaired  by  morning,  the  Vlll-inch  columbiad  remounted  on  a  spare 
carriage  sent  from  Savannah,  and  the  broken  traverse  wheel  of  the 
32-pounder  replaced  by  a  new  one.  The  broken  traverse  wheel  of  the 
42-pounder  had  been  replaced  during  the  action  by  Lieutenant  Quinn, 
of  the  Emmett  Rifles,  commanding  the  gun,  the  spare  traverse  wheel 
having  been  brought  from  the  rear  of  the  battery  in  the  midst  of  the 
flying  shells  by  one  of  the  gun  detachment,  who  being  unable  to  lift  it 
the  whole  way,  rolled  it  along  the  ground  by  holding  the  fork. 

A  fresh  supply  of  ammunition  was  received  from  Savannah  during 
the  night,  and  the  following  morning  the  garrison  were  as  well  pre¬ 
pared  to  renew  the  fight  as  the}^  had  been  to  begin  it;  but  the  enemy 
did  not  come  up  to  time.  The  battery  will  be  in  all  respects  complete 
by  Tuesday  night  should  nothing  untoward  prevent. 

I  desire  to  make  special  mention  to  the  general  commanding  of  the 
coolness,  courage,  and  presence  of  mind  of  Assistant  Engineer  J.  W. 
McAlpin,  who,  while  under  fire,  sketched  the  positions  of  the  vessels, 
and  kept,  with  the  assistance  of  others,  a  tally  of  the  shots  fired  by 
the  enemy,  besides  taking  notes  and  collecting  the  principal  facts  upon 
which  this  report  and  the  annexed  tables  are  founded. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

John  McCradt, 

Captain  and  Chief  Engineer ,  State  of  Georgia. 

Major  D.  B.  Harris, 

Chief  Engineer  South  Carolina ,  Georgia ,  and  Florida , 

Charleston ,  S.  C.

Order  of  the  Secretary  of  the  Navy  to  Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant 
West ,  U  S.  Navy ,  commanding  17.  S.  S.  Massachusetts ,  to  proceed 
to  the  South  Atlantic  Squadron  for  the  delivery  of  mails,  passengers, 
an  d  provision  s. 


Navy  Department,  March  f  1863. 

Sir:  On  the  10th  instant  you  will  proceed  with  the  U.  S.  S.  Massa¬ 
chusetts  to  the  South  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron  and  deliver  the 
mails  and  passengers  for  the  vessels  of  that  squadron  and  supply  them 
with  fresh  provisions,  etc.  The  limits  of  the  squadron  are  the  divid¬ 
ing  lines  of  the  Carolinas  on  the  north  and  Cape  Canaveral  on  the 
south.  The  headquarters  of  Rear-Admiral  Du  Pont,  with  whom  you 
will  communicate,  are  at  Port  Royal. 

It  will  be  your  duty  to  communicate  with  all  the  vessels  on  the  coast 
belonging  to  this  squadron  unless  Rear-Admiral  Du  Pont  should 
otherwise  direct,  and  to  deliver  their  mails  and  passengers  and  receive 
mails,  passengers,  and  invalids  to  be  brought  north.  Your  mails 
should  be  properly  assorted,  each  vessel’s  mail  to  itself,  so  that  it  may 
be  ready  for  immediate  delivery ;  also  any  other  packages  or  parcels 
for  officers  and  men.  Much  complaint  has  heretofore  been  made  of 
the  loss  of  such  packages  or  of  serious  damage  to  them. 

On  }rour  homeward  trip  you  will  communicate  with  the  vessels  of 
the  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron  off  Beaufort  [and]  Wilming¬ 
ton,  and  receive  any  mails  or  passengers  to  be  sent  north.  You  will 
also  touch  at  Hampton  Roads  and  communicate  with  Acting  Rear- 
Admiral  Lee.  From  this  point  you  will  mail  your  dispatches  for  the 
Department,  to  go  via  Baltimore,  by  which  they  will  reach  here  earlier 
than  if  mailed  at  New  York  after  your  arrival  there. 

Notwithstanding  the  special  service  assigned  to  the  Massachusetts , 
she  is  to  exercise  all  the  rights  pertaining  to  a  cruiser  of  the  United 
States  in  time  of  war.  The  unquestioned  belligerent  right  of  search 
is  to  be  exercised,  and  you  will  be  vigilant  to  detect,  seize,  and  send 
into  port  for  adjudication  any  vessel  engaged  in  carrying  contraband 
of  war  to  the  insurgents  or  in  violating  the  blockade  that  you  may  fall 
in  with  in  your  cruise.  Enclosed  is  a  circular  letter  in  reference  to 
visiting  and  searching  vessels  and  several  of  the  recent  general  orders 
issued  by  the  Department. 

Before  sailing  from  New  York  transmit  to  the  Department  a  list  of 
passengers  going  out  in  the  Massachusetts ,  designating  the  vessels  to 
which  they  are  respectively  destined,  and  on  your  return  to  New  York 
the  following  lists,  viz: 

1.  Of  passengers  brought  home,  from  vessel  received,  and  cause  of 
return. 

2.  Similar  list  of  seamen. 

3.  Similar  list  of  prisoners. 

4.  Of  vessels  supplied  with  provisions,  stating  date  and  locality. 

5.  Of  vessels  spoken  or  boarded  at  sea  during  the  trip,  with  the 


usual  remarks. 

I  am,  respectfully,  etc., 


Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy. 


Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  Wm.  H.  West,  U.  S.  Navy, 

Commanding  U.  S.  S.  Massachusetts ,  New  York.

Flagship  Wabash, 

Port  Royal  Harbor ,  S.  C.,  March  5 ,  1863. 

Sir:  You  will  proceed  \Vith  the  Wissahickon  under  your  command 
to  Georgetown,  and  assume  temporarily  the  charge  of  the  blockade 
there. 

You  wdll  direct  Lieutenant-Commander  Eastman  to  proceed  to  the 
Santee  and  endeavor  to  get  off  the  steamer  Queen  of  the  Wave,  ashore 
there,  or  if  this  is  impracticable,  to  save  from  the  wreck  such  parts  of 
her  cargo  and  machinery  as  are  worth  preserving.  It  is  reported 
vaguely  that  there  is  an  engine  packed  in  her  forehold,  which,  of 
course,  should  be  obtained,  as  well  as  the  engine  of  the  steamer  itself. 
You  will  direct  Lieutenant-Commander  Eastman,  in  case  he  can  not 


get  the  vessel  off,  to  destroy  her. 

This  being  accomplished,'  you  will  repair  off  Charleston,  leaving  the 
Gonemaugh  in  charge  at  Georgetown,  and  report  to  the  senior  officer 
present  for  blockading  duty. 

Respectfully,  etc., 

S.  F.  Du  Pont, 

Rear-  Admiral.

force  of  ironclads,  therefore,  will  be  the  Montauk ,  Weehawken,  New 
Ironsides,  Passaic ,  Nahant,  Patapsco,  Catskill,  Nantucket,  and  Keokuk.

Assuming  that  these  vessels  escape  from  loss  in  contemplated  move¬ 
ments,  you  will,  immediately  after  your  attack  upon  Charleston  and 
Savannah  is  completed,  send  to  Hampton  Roads  the  Passaic ,  Montauk , 
and  Keokuk. 

Let  all  others  proceed  without  delay  to  Pen.sacola.  The  condition  of 
affairs  in  the  Gulf  requires  a  force  of  ironclads  to  be  sent  there  with¬ 
out  delay,  but  you  may  retain  two  of  the  monitors  destined  for  the 
Gulf,  unless  the  attack  upon  Savannah  results  in  the  destruction  of 
the  ironclads,  in  that  port.  Even  in  that  event  the  Department  leaves 
it  to  your  judgment  to  send  the  six  remaining  ironclads  south,  or  only 
four;  only  impressing  upon  you  that  the  exigencies  of  the  public  service 
are  very  great  in  Rear-Admiral  Farragut’s  squadron. 

Very  respectfully, 

Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy.

Report  of  Commander  Rodgers ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  covvmandvng  U.  S.  S.

direct  from  New  York. 

U.  S.  Ironclad  Catskill, 

Port  Royal ,  March  5,  1863. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  inform  the  Department  that  I  have  arrived 
here  in  four  and  three-quarters  days  direct  from  New  York.  The 
weather  has  been  boisterous,  with  heavy  sea  at  times,  which,  on  several 
occasions,  went  over  the  awning  on  the  turret.  Through  the  care 
taken  in  securing  the  vessel  for  sea  and  the  vigilance  of  the  officers, 
in  connection  with  the  judgment  and  seamanship  displayed  by  Com¬ 
mander  Mullany,  of  the  Bienville ,  I  have  been  enabled  to  carry  out 
the  wishes  of  the  Department  in  proceeding  direct  to  my  destination. 

The  ship  upon  her  arrival  was  reported  ready  for  service. 

I  am,  verv  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

G.  W.  Rodgers, 

Commander .

Report  of  Commander  Mullany,  U.  S.  Ncvoy ,  commanding  U.  S.  ffi. 
Bienville,  of  the  arrival  of  that  vessel  at  Port  Royal ,  S.  C.,  towing

U.  S.  S.  Bienville, 

Port  Royal  Harbor ,  S.  C. ,  March  6,  1863. 
Sir:  For  the  information  of  the  Department  I  have  the  honor  to 
state  that  I  arrived  here  to-day  with  this  ship  under  my  command  and 
the  [ironclad]  Catskill  in  tow,  the  passage  from  New  York  direct  hav¬ 
ing  been  accomplished  in  five  days.  The  weather  was  boisterous  and 
the  sea  quite  rough  during  the  greater  portion  of  the  time,  but  the 
Catskill ,  under  the  judicious  management  of  Commander  Rodgers, 
stood  it  very  well,  and  is  apparently  in  as  good  condition  for  service 
as  when  she  left  New  York. 

I  am,  sir,  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

J.  R.  M.  Mullany, 

Commander. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles,

Port  Royal  Harbor ,  S.  C. ,  March  7,  1863. 

Sir:  1  regret  to  inform  the  Department  that  I  am  forced  to  send  the 
Quaker  City  to  New  York,  as  she  is  disabled  and,  as  a  blockading  ves¬ 
sel,  useless.  Enclosed  is  the  survey  (marked  No.  1). 

In  addition  to  invalids  and  men  whose  terms  of  service  have  expired 
I  have  sent  in  her  William  Perry,  captain  of  the  prize  schooner  Glide , 
who  is  a  Charleston  and  Savannah  pilot,  and  considered  a  dangerous 
man;  also  George  A.  Luce,  a  pilot  for  these  Southern  waters,  taken  on 
the  same  prize.  All  such  men  are  most  useful  to  the  rebels,  and  I 
have  written  to  Rear-Admiral  Paulding  to  retain  them  on  board  of  the 
North  Carolina  until  the  determination  of  the  Department  is  known. 
The  former,  William  Perry,  may  be  required  in  Philadelphia  as  a 
witness  when  the  case  of  the  Glide  is  taken  up  there  by  the  United 
States  district  judge. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

S.  F.  Du  Pont,

Capture  of  the  schooner  Lightning  by  the  U.  S.  S.  Bienville ,  March 

'9,  1863. 

Report  of  Rear-Admiral  Du  Pont,  TJ.  S.  Navy. 

No.  130.1  Flagship  Wabash, 

Port  Royal  Harbor ,  S.  C. ,  March  15,  1863. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  forward  herewith  (marked  No.  1)  the  report 
of  Commander  J.  R.  M.  Mullany,  of  the  Bienville ,  detailing  the  cir¬ 
cumstances  of  the  capture  by  that  vessel  of  the  schooner  Lightning. 

After  she  was  brought  into  this  port  I  ordered  a  survey.  The 
report  of  the  board  is  enclosed  (marked  No.  2),  condemning  the  vessel 
as  unfit  to  go  north,  appraising  her  value  at  $400,  and  giving  an  inven¬ 
tory  of  the  cargo.  The  latter  was  transshipped  to  the  bark  Alander- 
son ,  bound  to  Philadelphia,  under  the  charge  of  Acting  Ensign  Frank 
H.  Wilkes,  of  the  Bienville.

Report  of  Commander  Mullany,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S.  S.  Bienville. 

U.  S.  S.  Bienville, 

Port  Royal  Harbor ,  S.  C. ,  March  9 ,  1863. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  that  after  coaling  I  left  this  port 
to-day  for  Key  West. 

About  3:30  p.  m.,  16  miles  south  of  the  light-boat  stationed  off  this 
port,  I  fell  in  with  and  captured  the  schooner  Lightning  (supposed  to 
be  English),  having  reason  to  believe  she  intended  to  violate  the  block¬ 
ade  of  the  Southern  coast  instituted  by  the  authorities  of  the  U nited 
States. 

On  account  of  her  small  burden,  her  being  badly  found  in  rigging 
and  sails,  and  my  proximity  to  this  port,  I  deemed  it  prudent  to  bring 
her  in  here,  where  1  have  just  arrived,  and  submit  the  case  to  the  rear- 
admiral  commanding  for  his  action,  in  preference  to  putting  a  prize 
crew  on  board  and  running  the  risk  of  sending  her  north  at  this  season 
of  the  year. 

The  circumstances  under  which  the  capture  was  made  are  these: 
When  the  schooner  was  first  seen  she  was  steering  north,  but  subse¬ 
quently  steered  various  courses  as  we  approached  her,  failing,  how¬ 
ever  to  show  her  colors,  although  ours  were  hoisted  some  time  before. 
She  was  boarded  by  an  officer  from  this  ship  about  3:30  p.  m.,  who 
ascertained  that  she  was  from  Nassau,  New  Providence,  and  that  she 
was  cleared  for  Beaufort,  N.  C.  When  the  master  was  asked  for  his 
papers  he  replied  that  he  had  none,  but  subsequently  produced  an 
English  register  and  clearance.  The  former  records  the  schooner  as 
being  of  10  tons,  although  apparently  much  larger.  The  latter  has 
recorded  on  it  a  portion  of  the  cargo,  consisting  of  coffee,  salt,  and  tin. 

There  was  no  regular  manifest  of  the  cargo  nor  crew  list  to  be  found. 

The  persons  on  board  were  five  in  number,  one  of  whom,  calling 
himself  Boothbey,  claims  to  be  the  master.  Another  of  the  party — 
Charles  Henry-says  that  he  is  from  Connecticut.  On  his  person  was 
found  $260.25  in  gold,  which  I  directed  the  paymaster  to  take  charge 
of,  but  subsequently  it  was  turned  over  to  Fleet  Paymaster  Cunning¬ 
ham,  in  obedience  to  an  order  from  Rear-Admiral  S.  F.  Du  Pont,  a 
receipt  for  the  same  having  been  taken. 

The  proximity  of  the  vessel  to  the  coast  of  Georgia  and  South  Caro¬ 
lina,  the  nature  of  her  cargo,  and  the  fact  that  she  was  entirely  out  of 
her  course  if  bound  to  Beaufort,  N.  C.,  and  that  there  was  no  endorse¬ 
ment  on  her  papers  by  our  consul  at  Nassau,  New  Providence,  con¬ 
vinced  me  that  it  was  my  duty  to  seize  her. 


SOUTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


745 


After  we  had  taken  possession  of  the  prize  the  master  hoisted  Eng¬ 
lish  colors,  but  previously  had  given  as  a  reason  for  not  doing  so  before 
that  the  halliards  were  out  of  order,  which  was  not  the  case.  All  the 
papers  found  on  board  were  transmitted  to  Rear-Admiral  Du  Pont. 

I  enclose  a  correct  list  of  the  officers  and  crew  of  this  ship,  together 
with  a  list  of  the  cargo,  as  far  as  it  could  be  ascertained.  There  were 
no  other  public  vessels  in  sight  at  the  time  of  the  capture. 

Since  writing  the  above,  the  admiral’ having  determined  to  have  the 
vessel  appraised  here  and  transship  the  cargo  into  another  vessel  for 
conveyance  north,  Acting  Ensign  Frank  IT.  Wilkes  has  been  detailed 
to  take  charge  of  it. 

I  shall  sail  for  Key  W est  to-morrow  morning. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

J.  R.  M.  Mullany, 

Commander. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy ,  Washington.  I).  C.

Report  of  Commander  Duncan ,  U.  S.  Navy,  regarding  the  occupation 

of  Jacksonville,  Fla. 

U.  S.  S.  Norwich, 

Off  Jacksonville,  Fla.,  March  1J+,  1863. 

Admiral:  I  beg  leave  to  report  the  arrival  here  of  the  transports 
from  Port  Royal  on  the  8th  instant,  with  a  force  of  colored  troops  on 
board,  under  the  command  of  Colonel  [T.  W.]  Higginson.  _ 

On  the  morning  of  the  10th  instant  I  convoyed  them  with  this  ves¬ 
sel  and  the  TJncas  up  the  river  to  this  place,  and  on  our  arrival  the 
command  of  Colonel  Higginson  was  thrown  on  shore  and  quiet  pos¬ 
session  taken  of  the  town.  The  two  gunboats  uncler  my  command 
were  placed  in  position  to  render  any  assistance  that  might  be  called  for. 

In  the  afternoon  of  that  day  some  skirmishing  took  place  outside  of 
the  town,  upon  which  I  threw  several  shell  in  the  supposed  direction 
of  the  enemy,  which  very  soon  dispersed  them.  During  the  next  day 
another  skirmish  took  place  with  the  like  result. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

J.  M.  Duncan, 

Commander. 

Rear-Admiral  S.  F.  Du  Pont, 

Comdg.  South  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron,  Fart  Royal,  S  6.

Steamship  Ericsson  arrived  Fortress  Monroe,  Port  Royal  dates  to 
8th  March.  Passengers,  Chief  Engineer  Stimers,  with  dispatches  to 
Government;  Chief  Engineers  Robie  and  Newton  and  C.  C.  Fulton,  of 
American.  Monitor  Catskill  arrived  Port  Royal  5th;  fine  condition. 
Repairs  to  Montauk  completed.  Charleston  papers  say  rebels  on  Red 
River  have  captured  ram  Queen  of  the  West  and  gunboat  Indna/nola. 


746  SOUTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 

Gunboat  Quaker  City  left  Port  Royal  Sunday  for  Philadelphia. 
Ericsson  passed  her  off  Wilmington  in  chase  of  propeller  with  English 
ffag  flying;  overhauled  and  boarded  her  and  was  lying  alongside  when 
last  seen.  Propeller  seemed  to  have  lost  one  of  her  masts.  English 
steamer  Queen  of  the  Wave ,  with  valuable  cargo,  driven  ashore  at 
mouth  of  North  Santee,  abandoned  by  crew,  who  escaped  to  George¬ 
town,  S.  C.,  first  attempting  to  blow  her  up,  but  only  slightly  dam¬ 
aged.  Gunboat  Conemaugh  took  possession  of  her,  capturing  lieuten¬ 
ant  and  five  soldiers,  who  came  from  shore.  Admiral  Du  Pont  has  dis¬ 
patched  vessels  to  try  and  get  her  off'  or  if  not  save  cargo,  consisting 
of  ammunition  and  clothing.  Said  to  be  new  and  magnificent  ves¬ 
sel.  Whole  monitor  fleet  have  returned  from  Ossabaw  and  now  at 
Port  Royal,  six  in  number.  Ossabaw  Sound,  March  5th,  monitors 
Passaic ,  Patapsco,  and  Nahant ,  with  three  mortar  schooners,  com¬ 
menced  combined  attack  on  Fort  McAllister  at  8  o’clock  on  Tuesday 
morning.  Cannonading  conti  nued  all  day  with  slight  intermission  and 
mortar  schooners  kept  up  a  fire  on  the  fort  all  night.  On  Wednesday 
morning  fight  was  not  renewed.  Commander  Drayton,  senior  officer, 
finding  that  rebels  had  repaired  fort  during  night,  ordered  cessation  of 
attack.  It  was  found  impossible,  on  account  of  obstruction  in  river, 
to  get  in  full  range  of  fort.  One  rebel  gun  was  dismounted  and  shat¬ 
tered  and  portions  of  parapets  broken  away,  but  being  unable  to  get 
past  the  fort  it  was  impossible  to  take  it  without  a  cooperating  land 
force.  Beauregard  was  there.  The  monitors  were  struck  by  scores  of 
balls,  but  none  of  them  were  damaged,  and  all  proved  impregnable 
except  a  few  holes  through  upper  portion  smokestacks.  Not  less  than 
300  shot  and  shell  were  fired.  The  attack  will  not  be  resumed,  having 
been  mostly  intended  for  a  test  of  strength  of  vessels. 

C.  C.  Fulton. 

Captain  G.  V.  Fox.

Flagship  Wabash,

of  Surgeon  Mayo. 


SOUTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


747 


To  carry  out  the  recommendation  of  the  medical  officers,  I  have  to 
detach  you  from  the  command  of  the  Powhatan ,  and  you  will  take 
passage  for  New  York  in  the  U.  S.  transport  Arago ,  which  leaves 
to-morrow.  Report  by  letter  to  the  honorable  Secretary  of  the  Navy. 

1  need  hardly  add  how  much  I  regret  the  necessity  which  impera¬ 
tively  compels  this  course,  for  I  know  the  zeal  and  determination 
which  you  have  evinced  to  serve  throughout  the  war,  and  this  imme¬ 
diately  following  the  wear  and  tear  of  a  coast  of  Africa  cruise. 

I  have  to  thank  you  for  your  valuable  services  on  this  station  while 
under  my  command  and  for  many  months  ;  for  your  ceaseless  vigilance 
in  conducting  the  blockade  of  Charleston  as  senior  officer,  a  service 
which  few  understand,  but  which  has  been  as  thoroughly  done  as  the 
number  of  vessels  covering  it  could  accomplish,  and  at  great  hazard 
of  losing  the  ships.  In  this  arduous  work,  with  the  long  services 
which  preceded  it,  you  have  lost  your  health,  but  I  trust  that  the  rest 
you  have  so  fairly  and  honorably  earned  will  restore  it  and  you  to 
active  service. 

I  enclose  a  copy  of  my  leter  to  the  Department. 

Respectfuilv,  etc., 

S.  F.  Du  Pont, 

Pear- Admiral. 

Captain  S.  W.  Godon, 

U.  S.  S.  Powhatan ,  Port  Royal.

Report  of  Commander  Frailey ,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S.  S. 
Quaker  City ,  of  the  arrived  of  that  vessel  at  New  York ,  having 
captured  the  British  steamer •  Douro  en  route  from  Port  Royal,  S.  C. 

U.  S.  S.  Quaker  City, 

Navy  Yard ,  New  York ,  March  1%,  1863. 
Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  the  arrival  of  this  steamer  under 
mv  command  off  this  yard,  four  days  from  Port  Royal,  S.  C.,  under 
instructions  from  Rear-Admiral  S.  F.  Du  Pont  to  proceed  north,  a 
copy  of  which  is  herewith  enclosed,  marked  “A.”  On  the  same  day, 
March  8,  1  communicated  with  the  commanding  officer  off  Charleston, 
S  C.  and  thence  continued  on  toward  Beaufort,  N.  C.,  to  land  Cap¬ 
tain  Howell,  aid  to  General  H.  M.  Naglee,  “if  feasible,  but  without 
unnecessary  delay.” 


748  SOUTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 

* 

Oil  reaching  the  vicinity  of  that  port  I  found  a  dense  fog  prevailing, 
which  continued  for  sixteen  hours.  During  the  time  I  remained 
cruising  off  and  on,  at  the  expiration  of  which  I  deemed  it  prudent  to 
proceed  on  my  course  north,  having  but  a  limited  supply  of  coal  and 
provisions  on  board,  and  bringing  Captain  Howell  to  this  city,  which 
decision  I  trust  may  meet  your  approval. 

Previous  to  my  departure  from  Port  Royal  I  received  on  board  a 
large  number  of  invalids  for  transfer  to  the  naval  hospital,  besides  7 
Confederate  prisoners  of  war,  a  number  of  men  from  vessels  of  the 
squadron  whose  terms  of  service  had  expired  and  to  be  discharged,  7 
prisoners,  officers  and  crew  of  the  prize  schooner  Glide ,  etc.,  lists  of 
all  of  which  are  also  annexed,  marked  “B.” 

I  have  also  on  board  the  body  of  Assistant  Surgeon  Charles  H.  Pile, 
late  of  the  U.  S.  gunboat  Paul  Jones ,  and  subject  to  the  order  of 
Charles  M.  Pile,  Philadelphia. 

I  am  gratified  to  inform  you  that  on  the  9th  instant,  in  latitude  33° 
35'  N.,  longitude  77°  01'  W.,  I  had  the  good  fortune  to  capture  the 
English  iron  screw  steamer  Douro ,  of  Liverpool,  which  had  sailed 
from  Wilmington,  N.  C.,  the  night  previously,  and  having  on  board 
a  cargo  of  upward  of  420  bales  of  cotton,  bound  to  Nassau,  New 
Providence.  This  steamer  was  discovered  about  6:30  a.  m.  of  the 
9th,  standing  to  the  southward.  I  immediately  gave  chase,  causing 
her  to  alter  her  course  to  the  northeast  and  making  every  effort  to 
escape.  At  noon  she  was,  however,  in  our  possession,  when  a  prize 
crew  of  23  men  was  sent  on  board,  under  charge  of  Acting  Ensign 
T.  F.  De  Luce,  assisted  by  Acting  Master’s  Mates  George  C.  Sanborn 
and  E.  W.  Hale,  also  Acting  Assistant  Engineers  William  Craig  and 
James  Barnes  and  Henry  Wauklin,  with  orders  to  Mr.  De  Luce  to 
proceed  with  the  prize  to  New  York.  To  insure  her  safety,  I  deemed 
it  necessary  to  remove  her  master,  second  officer,  second  engineer,  and 
two  passengers,  as  also  16  of  her  crew  to  this  vessel.  A  list  of  their 
names  also  accompanies  this  letter. 

The  prize  steamer  is  in  sight,  following  this  vessel  up  the  bay. 

T  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Jas.  Madison  Frailey, 
Commander ,  U.  S.  Navy. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy ,  Washington ,  I).  C.
