Flagship  Wabash, 

Port  Royal  Harbor ,  S.  C. ,  March  13,  1863. 

Sir:  I  have  to  request  that  the  blockading  line  be  closed  in  a  little 
more — where  it  has  generally  been.  If  additional  space  be  required 
for  the  heavy  vessels  to  maneuver,  in  case  the  rams  come  out,  it  is  the 
more  necessary  that  the  channels  should  be  better  covered  by  the 
smaller  ones,  which  can  slip  and  run  out  with  the  information  of  their 
approach  while  watching  the  blockade  runners. 

If  the  latter  once  get  inside  of  a  line  that  is  well  out,  they  have  it 
all  their  own  way  in  finding  the  channels  and  crossing  the  bars, 
whereas  when  the  vessels  are  closer  in,  even  if  the  runners  evade 
them,  they  often  get  on  shore  and  are  lost,  fearing  to  be  reached  by 


shot  or  shell. 

Respectfully,  etc., 


S.  F.  Du  Pont, 


Rear-Admiral.

Letter  from  Colonel  Barton ,  U.  8.  Army ,  to  Lieutenant-  Colonel  Hal- 

pme,  U.  8.  Army ,  giving  information  obtained  from  deset'ters  from

Headquarters  U.  S.  Forces  on  the  Savannah  River, 

Fort  Pulaski ,  Go,. ,  March  13,  1863. 

Colonel:  I  have  the  honor  to  advise  you  that  I  forward  herewith 
to  Department  headquarters  three  deserters  from  the  vicinity  of 
Savannah,  who  came  to  this  post  yesterday. 

The  following  is  a  brief  summary  of  the  information  they  bring, 
which  I  state  in  order  that  you  may  compare  it  with  the  statements 
they  may  hereafter  make: 

The  Atlanta  (ram)  is  lying  some  half  mile  from  the  Georgia ,  and  nearer  Fort  Jack- 
son.  A  third  ironclad  is  so  far  completed  as  to  be  ready  for  her  armament,  and  one 
or  two  more  are  commenced.  A  large  earthwork  is  in  process  of  erection  near  Caus- 
ton’s  Bluff,  which  Beauregard  pronounces  the  key  to  the  possession  of  the  city.  But 
seven  guns  are  as  yet  mounted  on  it.  It  is  proposed  to  mount  twenty-seven  to  thirty. 
A  new  line  of  obstructions  is  also  commenced.  Great  fear  is  felt  that  the  city  will  be 
attacked  and  taken.  The  troops  which  were  massed  there  during  the  attack  on  Fort 
McAllister  have  been  sent  to  Charleston  and  North  Carolina. 

I  would  mention  the  man  James  Bowen  as  the  most  intelligent  of 
the  three. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  colonel,  with  great  respect,  your  obedient 
servant, 

William  B.  Barton, 

Colonel  Forty-eighth  New  York  Volunteers,  Commanding  Post.

Assistant  Adjutant-  General,  Tenth  Army  Corps.

Wabash, 

Port  Royal,  S.  C. ,  March  If,  1863. 
My  Dear  Turner:  I  have  your  note.  It  makes  it  hazardous  to 
withdraw  the  Unadilla  from  the  Stono,  for  with  the  Isaac  Smith  now, 


*  See  Series  I,  volume  2,  page  74. 


752 


SOUTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


in  addition  to  the  two  ironclads,  two  vessels  will 'be  hardly  enough 
there.  Still,  the  Bibb  goes  off  at  daylight  with  orders  for  her  to  join 
you. 

One  matter  I  want  you  to  understand:  Every  other  station  on  this 
line  of  coast  is  kept  to  the  very  lowest  figure  in  order  to  keep  up  the 
Charleston  blockading  force,  and  the  commanding  officers  at  all  those 
points  are  writing  me  for  more  vessels  or  informing  me  that  they  are 
helpless  from  broken  engines. 

You  have  at  this  moment  eleven  steamers  and  two  sailing  vessels  off 
Charleston.  The  difference  of  draft  is  very  little  between  the  Unadilla 
and  the  Huron  and  Wismhickon. 

If  we  had  twenty-four  vessels  off  Charleston  instead  of  twelve  or 
thirteen  the  running  in  and  out  would  be  reduced  one-half,  and  if  we 
could  muster  thirty-six  it  would  about  close  up  the  port,  except  of  a 
foggy  night.  This  is  what  the  Navy  Department  and  the  people  at 
home  do  not  understand. 

But  for  all  this  we  must  not  fail  to  do  what  we  can,  and  the  ships 
must  be  drawn  closer  in. 

My  squadron  is  regularly  diminishing,  and  I  have  written  and 
implored  for  more  vessels,  but  they  do  not  come. 

The  St.'  John’s  is  threatened;  North  Edisto  likewise. 

The  only  excuse  for  a  paymaster  to  come  to  Port  Royal  is  that  he 
attends  to  his  accounts  and  receipts.  Mr.  Russell  went  awa}7  without 
giving  the  latter,  and  the  paymaster  of  the  Powhatan  did  the  same. 

Yours,  truly, 

S.  F.  D.  P. 

Captain  T.  Turner, 

U.  8.  8.  New  Ironsides ,  off  Charleston ,  8.  C.

Your  communications  have  been  duly  received  and  are  always  inter¬ 
esting.  I  will  acknowledge  them  in  due  form  when  I  am  less  pressed. 
Write  always  when  you  can,  as  your  communications  are  always

Respectfully,  etc.,

Extracts  from  consular  dispatches. 

Liverpool,  February  1-i:  The  steamer  Gibraltar ,  late  pirate  Sumter, 
arrived  here  last  night  from  Gibraltar. 

A  steamer  called  the  Czar  cleared  from  this  port  yesterday  for  Ali¬ 
cante;  Stoddard  &  Bro.  are  her  consignees;  Captain  T.  Lawson  com¬ 
mands  her;  715  tons  burden,  and  a  very  suspicious  craft.  This 
steamer  was  built  at  the  same  yard  and  at  the  same  time  the  Bermuda 
was  built,  and  at  that  time  was  regarded  as  a  sister  ship  to  the 
Bermuda. 

The  Minna  cleared  9th  February  for  Nassau.  Among  the  articles 
of  her  manifest  are  over  100,000  pairs  boots  and  shoes,  27,457  ditto 
gaiters,  large  number  of  blankets,  army  cloth,  woolen  and  cotton 
goods  in  large  quantities,  medicines,  hardware,  brandies,  teas,  etc. 
Valuable  cargo. 

The  Dolphin  cleared  same  day  for  Nassau,  with  assorted  cargo. 
Among  the  entries  on  manifest  are  7  cases  cutlery,  7  cases  swords,  7 
cases  rifles,  35  ditto. 

Falmouth,  February  14,  1863:  The  Dolphin  (side-wheel  steamer) 
arrived  last  evening;  Eustice,  master.  I  have  been  informed  on  good 
authority  that  the  captain  states  openly  that  his  object-  is  to  run  the 
blockade,  in  which  he  has  succeeded  before.  Has  two  masts  without 
yards;  one  funnel,  rather  long  and  painted  white;  hull  black;  has 
scarcely  any  bowsprit.  [Reports  her  departure  in  subsequent  letter, 
February  15.] 

Liverpool,  February  17,  1863:  The  steel  ship  Banshee ,  so  often 
referred  to  in  this  correspondence,  built  for  E.  Lawrence  &  Co.  as  a 
dispatch  boat  to  run  the  blockade,  entered  yesterday  at  the  customs  to 
load  for  Nassau  via  Madeira.  There  is  no  doubt  about  the  character 
or  destination  of  this  vessel.  She  is  216  tons  burden  and  has  great 
speed. 

The  steamer  Sumter ,  now  called  the  Gibraltar ,  is  in  the  river  oppo¬ 
site  Liverpool.  I  understand  her  object  in  coming  is  to  repair — to  put 
in  new  boilers  and  machinery. 

The  bark  Otto ,  referred  to  in  previous  dispatches,  sailed  on  Satur¬ 
day  last.  She  cleared  for  Tampico  and  Matamoras.  I  understand  she 
is  to  run  into  some  one  of  the  blockaded  ports  if  she  can. 

1  am  informed  that  Fawcett,  Preston  &  Co.  are  making  three  marine 
engines  for  gunboats  that  are  to  be  shipped  from  Liverpool  to  Nassau,

Steamer  Banshee :  Arrival  reported  at  Queenstown  February  25;

Has  boiler-iron  topgallant  forecastle  for  about  20  feet  forward.  Steers

sea.  Draft  10  feet  loaded  and  coaled.  Two  masts. 

Steamer  Georgiana:  Consul  at  Teneriffe  writes  13th  February,  1863: 
English  screw  steamer  Geoi'giana ,  Captain  A.  B.  Davidson,  left  this 
port  yesterday  for  Nassau.  *  *  *  From  her  appearance  and  the

fear  that  she  is  an  armed  vessel,  intended  for  a  cruiser  against  our 
merchantmen.  Powerful  screw  steamer  of  407  tons  and  150  horse¬ 
power,  two  masts,  with  yards  on  both,  one  stack  ahead,  with  bowsprit 
and  jibboom,  painted  black;  smokestack  also  black;  evidentlv  a  very 
swift  vessel.

Report  of  Rear-Admiral  Du  Pont ,  P.  A.  Navy ,  regarding  the  suspen- 
•  sion  from  duty  of  certain  officers  for  violation  of  orders. 

No.  134.]  Flagship  W  abash, 

Puri;  Royal  Harbor ,  A.  C. ,  March  15,  1863. 

Sir:  I  have  to  inform  the  Department  that  I  have  deemed  it  my 
duty  to  suspend  from  duty  Assistant  Paymaster  G.  W.  Beaman,  of 
the  Seneca ,  and  Acting  Assistant  Pa}'inaster  A.  W.  Kelsey,  of  the 
IWssPzieZuw,  for  violating  my  General  Order  No.  8,  that  of  the  Navy 
Department  dated  April  22,  1862,  and  the  third  clause  of  the  Depart¬ 
ment’s  order  of  December  12,  1862. 

These  gentlemen  plead  ignorance  and  express  regrets;  had  they 
belonged  to  any  other  grade  I  should  have  sent  them  both  home,  but 
the  confusion  in  accounts  and  the  liability  of  loss  in  clothing  and  pro¬ 
visions  by  the  sudden  removal  of  a  paymaster  deterred  me.  & 

The  information  conveyed  was  important  to  a  wily  enemy.  The 
correspondents  generally  have  done  their  best  to  point  out  the  weak 
points,  as  they  thought,  of  the  ironclad  vessels,  and  the  last  tiring  from 
kort  McAllister  showed  how  quick  the  rebels  Avere  in  improving  on 
such  information. 

But  a-s  I  care  more  to  prevent  the  repetition  of  misconduct  than  to 
punish  it,  if  the  Department  will  express  its  displeasure  by  letter  to 
these  gentlemen  I  think  it  will  be  sufficient. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

„  .  S.  F.  Du  Pont, 

Rear-Admiral,  Comdg.  South  Atla/ntic  Blockading  Squadron .

Report  of  Captain  Turner ,  TJ.  S.  Navy ,  regarding  the  position  of 
vessels  on  the  Charleston  blockade. 

U.  S.  S.  New  Ironsides, 

Off  Charleston ,  S.  C. ,  March  15,  1863. 

Admiral:  I  have  the  honor  to  acknowledge  your  letter  requesting 
that  the  blockading  line  be  made  closer. 

The  positions  occupied  by  the  various  vessels  of  this  blockading 
force  were  given  them  in  full  consultation  with  and  by  the  advice  of 
Captain  Godon,  with  whom  I  looked  over  the  chart  most  carefully  to 
define  them  as  they  should  be,  because  of  his  superior  knowledge  from 
long  experience  of  the  entire  ground  and  his  familiarity  with  the  gen¬ 
eral  aims  and  action  of  vessels  endeavoring  to  violate  the  blockade. 

1  was  not  here  prior  to  the  raid  of  the  rams,  but  Captain  Green,  of 
the  Canandaigua, ,  and  Captain  Watmough,  of  the  Memphis,  inform 
me  that  the  vessels  to  the  north  on  the  line  are  lying  a  little  nearer 
now  than  they  were  before  the  raid.  They  of  course  have  to  be  gov¬ 
erned  by  their  draft  of  water.  I  have,  however,  issued  an  order,  a 
copy  of  which  is  herewith  enclosed,  to  require  of  them  a  still  closer 
position  if  possible. 

The  Row  hat  an1  s  position  was  the  one  I  was  dissatisfied  with,  because 
she  lay  too  far  out,  I  thought,  and  was  a  sort  of  beacon  for  vessels  to 
run  in  by;  and  I  had  sent  for  Captain  Godon  the  day  I  discovered  him 
to  be  so  ill  to  request  him  to  take  up  a  position  nearer  in,  and  in 
returning  to  his  place  that  night  I  gave  my  orders  to  his  first  lieuten¬ 
ant  to  that  effect.  My  own  position  is  taken  without  any  reference  to 
distance  from  the  point  the  rams  might  come  out,  but  directly  oppo¬ 
site  the  point  where  they  came  out  before;  and  I  am,  by  measurement 
on  the  chart  made  at  this  moment  by  the  master,  just  a  mile  and  three- 
eighths  from  the  outer  edge  of  the  bar.  I  should  think  it  unsafe  to  be 
nearer  with  this  ship,  for  in  the  event  of  snapping  a  chain  it  requires 
some  time,  with  banked  fires,  to  move  so  large  a  body  as  quickly  as 
might  be  necessary. 

Persons  passing  or  tarrying  for  a  few  hours  at  this  anchorage  are 
constantly  conveying  false  information,  from  a  want  of  proper  knowl¬ 
edge  of  the  positions  of  the  squadron  and  things  on  shore,  sometimes 
discovering  batteries  where  there  are  none,  and  at  others  denying 
their  existence  where  I  know  them  to  be. 

1  spare  no  pains  to  convey  to  you  such  accurate  information  as  you 
should  be  furnished  with  of  everything  within  the  region  of  my  com¬ 
mand.  I  think  you  will  do  me  the  justice  to  award  that  it  is  likely  to 
be  more  reliable. 

Verv  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

T.  Turner, 

Captain. 

Rear-Admiral  S.  F.  Du  Pont, 

Commanding  South  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron.

Report  of  Commander  Batch,  U.  S.  Navy,  senior  officer  in  Stono  Inlet, 
regarding  a  second  reconnoissance  to  John"! s  Island  through  Kiawah 
River. 

U.  S.  Steam  Sloop  Pawnee, 

Stono  Inlet ,  South  Carolina ,  March  16,  1863. 
Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  all  quiet  on  this  station.  I  went  up 
the  Kiawah  River  some  6  miles  in  this  ship  on  the  morning  of  the  10th 
instant,  remaining  at  anchor  all  day,  but  could  discover  no  batteries 
nor  any  of  the  enemy’s  troops  on  John’s  Island. 

On  the  11th  instant  four  contrabands  succeeded  in  getting  down  the 
river.  They  represented  that  they  had  lately  been  employed  boiling 
salt  near  a  camp  on  the  mainland  on  the  other  side  of  Stono  River. 
They  also  state  that  there  are  a  number  of  batteries  along  the  banks 
of  the  Stono. 

I  have  already  given  an  opinion  as  to  the  propriety  of  their  putting 
up  batteries  in  that  direction.  If  a  division  of  the  army  is  to  advance 
by  Folly  Island,  batteries  placed  on  the  Stono  can  do  us  no  harm,  and 
they  should  be  encouraged  in  rendering  that  river  as  strong  as  they 
can  desire,  for,  by  so  doing,  they  will  take  away  guns  and  troops 
which  might  be  made  available  on  the  real  point  of  attack.  My  move¬ 
ments  have  all  been  directed  to  the  John’s  Island  side,  and  it  was  with 
this  view  that  I  took  the  Pawnee  up  the  Kiawah,  having  already  had 
the  TJnadilla  and  Commodore  McDonough  up  that  river. 

The  contrabands  report  that  troops  have  been  going  south  to  Savan¬ 
nah  from  Charleston. 

I  have  sent  the  paymaster  of  the  Comrnodore  McDonough  to  Port

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  acknowledge  the  receipt  of  your  communi¬ 
cation  of  16th  instant,  enclosing  copy  of  a  letter  from  Captain  J.  F. 
Green,  of  the  Canandaigua,  dated  March  15,  in  which  he  states  he 
discovered  a  strange  steamer  to  the  northward  and  westward,  astern 
and  near  the  Housatonic. 

At  daylight  I  hoisted  what  1  supposed  was  my  number,  and  as  soon 
as  I  discovered  one  of  the  blockading  squadron,  1  steered  directly  for 
her  and  on  coming  up  close  to  her  I  immediately  slowed  the  engine, 
hailed  her,  and  asked  where  the  New  Ironsides  lay  and  was  informed 
where  she  was.  I  was  then  asked  what  vessel  was  that,  and  replied 
“The  Massachusetts. ”  Captain  Taylor  said:  “How  are  you,  Captain 
West?  You  have  the  wrong  number  up.”  I  ordered  it  hauled  down 
and  hoisted  what  1  supposed  was  215,  and  was  given  me  in  New 
York  as  such.  I  ran  within  speaking  distance  of  the  Canandaigua 
and  was  hailed  by  an  officer  aboard  her,  “What  ship  is  that?’  I 
replied,  “The  Massachusetts .”  I  then  understood  him  to  say,  “If  you 
do  not  haul  that  number  down  I  will  tire  into  you.”  I  ordered  the 
number  hauled  down,  and  a  few  minutes  after  a  shot  passed  over 
mv  quarter-deck.  I  did  not  hear  the  order  to  heave  to  or  would  have

done  so.  I  then  spoke  the  Powhatan  and  proceeded  to  the  New  Iron¬

General  order  of  Rear-Admiral  Du  Pant ,  IT.  S.  Navy ,  to  commanding 
officers  _  of  vessels,  for  the  expeditious  transfer  of  supplies  from  the 
storeship. 

Flagship  Wabash, 

Port  Royal  Harbor,  S.  C,  March  17, 1863. 
The  U.  S.  S.  Massaclmsetts,  Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  West,  com¬ 
manding,  has  been  assigned  by  the  Navy  Department  the  duty  of  run¬ 
ning  to  the  South  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron  as  a  supply  "ship  and 
with  the  authority  of  a  cruising  vessel  besides. 

On  her  arrival  at  the  different  naval  stations  on  the  coast,  I  have  to 
request  that  the  senior  officer  present,  and  each  and  every  commandino- 
officer,  will  give  immediate  attention  to  obtaining  their  supplies  and 
mails  from  this  vessel,  doing  all  in  their  power  to  expedite  her  depar¬ 
ture  for  her  next  point  of  destination. 

A  sufficient  numbci  of  boats  must  be  sent-  to  receive  the  supplies, 
with  proper  officers  to  sign  receipts,  and  these  officers  must  be  given 
to  understand  that  they  go  on  duty  and  not  to  attend  to  private  affairs ; 
other  officers,  if  the  commanding  officers  deem  fit,  may  go  on  board  for 
such  purposes. 

The  paymasters  of  the  different  vessels  will  give  their  personal  atten¬ 
tion  to  receiving  the  supplies  in  their  department  and  not  depute  this 
duty  to  their  clerks  and  stewards  alone. 

It  will  add  to  the  efficiency  and  comfort  of  the  whole  squadron  if,  bv 
system  and  quick  dispatch,  this  vessel  can  be  accelerated  in  her  round 
trips,  and  I  have  to  request  the  senior  officer  wherever  she  stops  not 
to  permit  her  to  be  delayed  except  from  unavoidable  causes,  which 
are  to  be  reported  to  me  by  letter. 

Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  West  will  be  instructed  to  do  all  in  his 
power  to  meet  the  above  requirements  by  a  systematic  arrangement  of 
his  supplies  and  a  ready  mode  of  delivery.

Report  of  Captain  Turner ,  U  S ?  Navy,  regarding  an  attack  upon ,  and 
the  escape  of,  a  vessel  passing  in  through  Maffitfs  Channel. 

U.  S.  S.  New  Ironsides, 

Of  Charleston,  S.  C.,  March  18,  1863. 

Admiral:  Under  the  impression  that  the  James  Adger  will  be  here 
to-day,  when  I  shall  be  obliged  to  send  off  the  Augusta  to  Port  Royal, 
I  am  writing  this  letter  to  go  by  her. 

Last  night  about  half  past  8  o’clock,  having  perceived  sharp  firing 
along  the  northern  line  of  the  blockade,  I  got  underway  immediately 
with  this  ship  and  proceeded  to  the  neighborhood  to  the  south  of 
Rattlesnake  Shoal.  As  I  could  not  go  inside,  I  anchored  there  for  the 
night.  This  morning  the  Memphis  Came  down  to  inform  me  that  a 
steamer  endeavored  to  get  in  through  Maffitt’s  Channel.  She  was 
attacked  by  the  Memphis,  Wissahickon,  Blunt,  and  America ,  and  for 
some  minutes  was  under  a  very  sharp  fire,  but  being  under  full  head 
of  steam,  and  passing  very  rapidly,  evidently  a  fast  vessel,  she  got  by 
and  went  in. 

This  morning  she  was  seen  passing  between  the  forts',  a  large  Con¬ 
federate  flag  flying  at  the  fore,  English  ensign  at  her  flagstaff.  Cap¬ 
tain  Watmough  informs  me  that  atone  time  so  closely  was  she  pressed 
that  they  thought  they  had  her.  She  doubtless  has  been  considerably 
injured.  Unfortunately  I  had  sent  the  Huron  to  Port  Royal,  with 
which  vessel,  Captain  Watmough  thinks,  they  would  have  secured 
her.  I  am  of  the  opinion  that  the  reception  this  vessel  met  lest  night 
will  drive  them  to  another  point  in  their  next  attempt. 

They  prefer  the  Northern  Channel,  from  being  able  to  make  Cape 
Romain  and  shape  their  course  in  along  down  the  land.  If  they  con¬ 
tinue  their  attempts  upon  the  blockade  at  that  point,  with  two  more 


762

gunboats  I  hope  to  be  able  to  catch  or  drive  them.  back,  should  they 
attempt  it  again. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

T.  Turner, 

Captain.

Letter  from  Captain  Turner ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  to  Rear-Admiral  Du  Pont , 

U.  S.  Navy ,  requesting  to  be  informed  as  to  the  distinguishing  fag 
for  the  rank  of  commodore. 

U.  S.  S.  New  Ironsides, 

Off  Charleston ,  S.  G. ,  March  18,  1863. 
Admiral:  In  an  unofficial  conversation  with  you  on  my  first  arrival 
at  Port  Royal,  speaking  of  the  flag  which  would  be  worn  by  an  officer 
holding  the  rank  of  commodore,  which  1  was  daily  expecting  to  be 
promoted  to,  I  understood  you  to  say  that  it  was  a  matter  upon  which  , 
your  mind  was  not  made  up,  and  that  you  would  endeavor  to  ascertain 
from  the  Department  what  its  views  were  upon  that  point. 

As  I  presume  I  shall  receive  my  commission  in  that  grade  in  a  few 
days,  I  shall  be  glad  to  know  if  you  have  any  instructions  to  give  me 
on  the  subject,  or  what  your  wishes  are  in  relation  to  it. 

I  can  not  but  think  that  something  to  designate  that  grade  in  an 
officer,  placed  as  I  am  at  this  moment  in  command  of  a  large  division 
of  ships,  would  be  to  the  advantage  of  the  service;  whilst,  on  the  other 
hand,  as  a  mere  matter  of  opinion,  I  would  say  that  with  a  single 
command  or  in  the  presence  of  a  superior  officer  it  would  be  of  little 
importance  how  the  cpiestion  was  settled,  beyond  the  mere  personal 
pride  and  feelings  of  the  officer,  who,  in  our  service,  is  certain  to  be 
far  past  the  meridian  of  life,  and  naturally  feels  a  pride  in  being  recog¬ 
nized  by  his  flag  in  a  rank  superior  to  one  he  has  held  as  a  captain  and 
beyond  which  he  may  never  arrive. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

T.  Turner, 

Captain. 

Rear-Admiral  S.  F.  Du  Pont, 

Commanding  South  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron.

[Enclosure.] 

U.  S.  Ironclad  Nahant, 

Port  Royal,  March  18,  1863. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  acknowledge  the  receipt  of  a  communica¬ 
tion  from  Mr.  Ericsson,  addressed  to  Rear-Admiral  Dahlgren,  and 
forwarded  b}T  him  to  you,  at  Mr.  Ericsson’s  request,  who  has  written 
it,  I  presume,  in  response  to  my  communication  of  the  20th  ultimo  to 
the  Ordnance  Department,  though,  upon  a  careful  revision  of  that 
letter,  1  can  find  nothing  therein  calculated  to  elicit  such  imputations 
of  ignorance  and  professional  prejudice  as  Mr.  Ericsson’s  letter  implies. 

I  confess  that  I  was  not  aware  that  Mr.  Ericsson  had  planned  his 
vessels  with  the  view  that  their  guns  should  be  fought  exclusively 
over  the  bow  in  a  seaway,  and  in  reference  to  this  point,  I  beg  leave 
to  offer  a  proposition,  based  upon  my  professional  experience.  What 
if  we  become  engaged  with  an  ironclad  of  superior  activity  to  our¬ 
selves,  who  will  not  permit  us  to  keep  our  bow  pointed  toward  him, 
an  event  which  seems  quite  practicable  to  me,  particularly  as  my 
experience  of  this  class  of  vessel  leads  me  to  believe  them  easily 
affected  and  rendered  unmanageable  in  a  seaway  ?  I  quite  concur  with 
Mr.  Ericsson,  however,  in  his  suggestion  that  our  floating  antagonists 
should  be  fought  bows  on,  if  possible,  but  the  idea  had  occurred  to 
me  before  the  receipt  of  his  communication.  But  I  beg  leave  to  dif¬ 
fer  with  him  in  opinion  as  to  the  proper  manner  of  laying  these  ves¬ 
sels  to  meet  the  tire  of  Fort  Sumter  or  other  batteries,  and  again  1 
base  my  opinion  upon  experience.  ^  Gunners  find  it  an  easy  matter  to 
make  good  line  shots,  the  great  difficulty  being  to  avoid  overreaching 
or  falling  short  of  the  object.  The  decks  of  these  monitors  are  their 
weakest  points  exposed  to  fire,  and,  as  proven  the  other  day  at  Ogee- 
chee  River,  are  not  invulnerable  to  heavy  shot.  I  therefore  submit, 
that  by  la}dng  the  length  of  your  deck  to  the  enemy,  instead  of  the 
breadth,  you  are  the  more  completely  exposing  you/ weakest  point  of 
resistance  to  him. 

Mr.  Ericsson  says  that  I  will  do  well  to  reflect  further  on  the  sub¬ 
ject  before  I  assert  that  my  guns  are  practically  useless.  Such  was 
not  my  intention,  as  I  had  no  idea  that  the  monitors  of  this  class  were 
intended  to  engage  in  a  seaway.  My  hints  were  intended  to  apply  to 


SOUTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


765 


the  use  of  the  heaxy  XV-inch  guns  in  the  other  seagoing  vessels,  such 
as  the  Roanoike ,  etc.,  but  if  this  class  of  monitor  is  intended  for  fight¬ 
ing  in  a  seaway,  undoubtedly  my  letter  will  bear  this  construction— that 
the  XV-inch  guns,  mounted  as  mine  is,  are  practically  useless  in  a  sea¬ 
way,  and  I  can  offer  an  addititional  reason  for  asserting  them  to  be  so, 
viz,  the  impossibility  of  sighting  them  correctly.  The  sight  hole 
through  the  turret  purports  to  enable  one  to  point  the  gun  within  3 
feet,  horizontally,  of  the  object  aimed  at,  but  the  elevation  or  depres¬ 
sion  of  the  piece  is  almost  a  matter  of  chance;  and  these  vessels  are 
intended  to  mount,  in  both  ports,  XV-inch  guns,  the  lire  from  which, 
under  these  circumstances,  must  be  very  ineffective.  Mr.  Ericsson 
does  not,  in  his  letter,  credit  his  vessels  with  one  good  quality  which 
they  certainly  possess — that  of  steadiness  in  the  trough  of  a  sea;  they 
never  roll  heavily  and  their  pitching  motion  is  nearly  as  great  as  their 
rolling.  But  other  causes  than  motion  would  prevent  these  vessels 
from  fighting  in  weather  when  vessels  constructed  upon  the  ordinary 
model  could  use  their  guns  without  difficulty.  The  volume  of  water 
which  would  pour  into  their  ports  and  under  the  raised  turret,  flood¬ 
ing  the  turret  chamber  below  and,  as  one  of  the  consequences,  by  wet¬ 
ting  the  belts  of  the  blowers  stop  the  breath  and  kill  the  steam  of  the 
vessel,  would  be  a  serious  obstacle  to  their  being  fought  at  all  in  any¬ 
thing  approaching  heavy  weather.  But  I  have  no  desire  to  give  Mr. 
Ericsson  ground  for  complaint  of  me  for  the  entertainment  of  profes¬ 
sional  prejudice  against  the  monitor  class  of  vessel  as  I  am  not  con¬ 
scious  of  the  existence  in  my  mind  of  any  such  prejudice,  neither  can 
I  find  anything  in  my  letter  referred  to  above  which  will  bear  that 
interpretation,  unless,  indeed,  he  considers  my  statement,  based  not 
upon  experiment,  but  upon  observation,  that  1  believe  it  to  be 
impracticable  to  work  the  XV-inch  gun  in  a  seaway,  or,  as  Mr.  Erics¬ 
son  st3Tles  it,  “upon  an  oscillating  plane,”  upon  the  present  carriage 
and  with  the  present  arrangement  of  the  compressor,  as  the  result  of 
prejudice,  whereas  it  is  based  solely  upon  the  experience  gained  on 
board  this  vessel.  My  professional  experience  enabled  me  to  see  many 
defects  in  the  monitor  class  of  vessels  as  seagoers,  which,  as  the  result  has 
proved,  do  actually  exist  and,  if  I  am  not  misinformed,  enabled  others 
to  make  suggestions  of  additions  and  improvements  which  have  been 
ultimately  adopted  and  yet  were,  at  the  time,  attributed  to  the  pre¬ 
judice  rather  than  to  the  experience  of  the  proposer. 

Perhaps  my  suggestions  are  worthless;  they  are  mere  suggestions, 
offered  for  the  consideration  of  the  Ordnance  Department,  but  I  must 
state  that  one  auxiliary  for  the  working  of  the  gun,  which  Mr.  Erics¬ 
son  states  that  we  possess,  does  not  to  the  best  of  my  knowledge,  or 
that  of  any  officers  whom  I  have  consulted,  exist.  No  mechanism  is 
supplied  for  locking  the  iron  rollers  of  the  carriage,  if  by  the  iron  rollers 
is  meant  the  trucks  upon  which  it  runs  in  and  out. 

In  conclusion  I  beg  leave  to  state  that  whilst  I  believe  this  to  be  the 
most  perfect  combination  of  the  elements  of  offense  and  defense  afloat 
in  smooth  water  and  when  opposed  to  vessels  or  forts  of  masonry,  I 
have  by  no  means  the  same  confidence  in  their  defensive  or  offensive 
powers  in  rough  water  or  when  opposed  to  earthworks  where  rapidity 
of  fire  is  to  a  certain  degree  of  greater  importance  than  weight  of 
metal.  In  a  word,  I  do  not  consider  the  invention  yet  perfected,  and 
think  that  any  suggestions  intended  for  the  increase  of  their  efficiency 


SOUTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


766 

ought  to  be  received  as  emanating  from  a  laudable  motive  rather  than 
one  of  detraction  from  the  merits  of  the  invention. 

I  am,  verv  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

John  Downes, 

Commander. 

Rear-Admiral  S.  F.  Du  Pont, 

Comdg.  South  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron,  Port  Royal,  S.  C. 


Private  letter  from  Rear-Admiral  Du  Pont,  U.  S.  Navy,  to  the  Assist¬ 
ant  Secretary  of  the  Navy,  regarding  affairs  in  general. 

Flagship  Wabash, 

Port  Royal  Harbor,  S.  C. ,  March  19, 1863. 

My  Dear  Sir:  I  can  not  take  the  time  I  once  had  to  write  you 
unofficially,  but  I  thought  you  would  like  to  hear  [a]  few  words. 

We  are  hard  at  work  on  the  ironclads.  They  require  so  much,  and 
the  injury  of  the  Montauk  is  very  great.  I  crawled  on  “all  fours”  to 
see  for  myself.  We  are  afraid  to  beach  one  of  these  vessels,  and  yet  it 
seems  a  difficult  job  without  so  doing. 

The  Patapsco’s  pumps  are  not  yet  in  order.  I  had  dispatched  the 
Weehawken  to  Edistothis  morning  to  establish  our  base  of  operations, 
but  an  equinoctial  g:jle  sent  her  back.  I  may  send  her  to  Savannah 
River  in  lieu.  A  boat  and  crew  from  the  Georgia  deserted  three  days 
since,  taking  the  midshipman  prisoner.  Their  information  is  of  interest 
and  I  have  sent  for  them. 

I  am  anxiously  looking  for  the  Keokuk.  Her  less  draft  than  the 
others  is  very  important.  I  think  these  monitors  are  wonderful  con¬ 
ceptions,  but,  oh,  the  errors  of  details,  which  would  have  been  cor¬ 
rected  if  these  men  of  genius  could  be  induced  to  pa}'  attention  to  the 
people  who  are  to  use  their  tools  and  inventions. 

Much  to  my  regret  I  was  forced  to  take  the  TJnadilla  out  of  Stono 
and  send  her  to  the  Rattlesnake,  off  Charleston,  so  fierce  is  the  block¬ 
ade  running  now,  when  she  got  aground  on  Stono  Bar  and  had  to  be 
towed  in,  a  lame  duck. 

If  George  Sanders’  cruising  iron  vessels  come  over,  we  shall  be 
swept  from  one  end  of  the  coast  to  the  other. 

The  most  important  thing  in  view  of  your  proposed  work  for  the 
ironclads  I  have  not  mentioned,  but  intend  to  write  officially  on  the 
subject.  I  mean  the  life  given  to  that  XV-inch  gun  by  Dahlgren. 
There  is  not  an  ironclad  captain  who  does  not  believe  it  will  be  exceeded 
at  Charleston  alone.  The  memorandum  I  sent  you  was  drawn  up  by 
John  Rodgers  from  the  different  reports. 

Please  let  the  Massachusetts  run  to  Philadelphia.  We  shall  never 
see  her  again  from  New  York. 

In  haste,  yours  truly, 

Hon.  Gr.  Y.  Fox, 

Assistant  Secretary  of  the  Navy,  Washington, 


S.  F.  D.  P.

Report  of  Captain  Rodgers,  U.  S.  JVcrny,  transmitting  abstract  of  state¬ 
ments  of  deserters  f  rom  the  Confederate  transport  Savannah. 

Flagship  Wabash,  March  19,  1863. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  herewith  to  submit  the  result  of  an  exami¬ 
nation  of  five  deserters  from  the  Confederate  transport  Savannah,  who, 
being  on  picket  duty,  secured  the  arms  of  their  officer,  a  master’s  mate, 
and  brought  him  prisoner  to  Fort  Pulaski. 

These  men,  all  foreigners,  were  sent  off  by  the  military  authorities 
on  Hilton  Head  to  the  Wabash  for  examination. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

John  Fodders, 

Captain. 

Admiral  S.  F.  Du  Pont, 

Comdg.  South  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron ,  Port  Royal. 

Lieutenant  Mackenzie  kindly  acted  as  amanuensis  and  thus  condensed 
the  testimony  of  the  crew. 

[Enclosures.  ] 

Abstract  of  statements  of  deserters. 

The  crews  of  the  various  vessels  appear  to  be  poorly  fed  and  not 
well  clothed  and  somewhat  discontented.  Their  pay  is  very  irregular. 
The  personal  treatment  is  not  very  harsh  on  board  of  the  efficient 
vessels,  namely,  the  Atlanta,  ram  Savannah ,  and  Isondiga. 

The  efficient  vessels  for  active  movements  are  three,  the  ironclads 
Atlanta  and  Savannah  and  the  wooden  gunboat  Isondiga.  The  entire 
battery  of  these  three  vessels,  ten  or  eleven  guns,  is  comprised  of  6 
and  7-inch  rifles.  The  Atlanta  is  said  to  be  much  the  fastest,  and 
will  probably  steam  8  knots.  Her  draft  is  about  16  feet,  and,  as  far 
as  can  be  ascertained,  she  is  slow  to  mind  her  helm.  The  discipline  of 
this  vessel  is  said  to  be  good  under  the  present  captain. 

The  Georgia  lies  at  the  Elba  Island,  [Savannah  River],  in  cribs  com¬ 
posed  of  logs,  kept  in  their  places  by  stones  thrown  into  them;  she 
has  warps  out  by  which  her  broadside  can  always  be  turned  on  either 
the  north  or  south  channel. 

The  Atlanta  lies  inside  of  the  Georgia. 

The  old  Savannah  is  moored  head  and  stern  with  her  gun  pointed 
down  the  channel.  The  ram  Savannah,  had  not  moved  down  from  the 
city  [Savannah]  at  the  time  these  men  deserted.  The  whole  naval 
forces  are  under  the  command  of  Commodore  Tattnall,  whose,  flag  is 
upon  the  Fingal,  although  he  resides  in  the  city.  The  second  in  com¬ 
mand  is  Captain  Sinclair,  of  the  Fingal.  The  vessels  are  descibed  as 
having  no  means  of  ventilation;  when  the  hatches  are  on  they  are 
almost  hermetically  sealed,  the  only  opening  being  the  ports.  There 
are  no  blower  engines  in  these  vessels.  One  of  the  deserters  heard 
Commodore  Tattnall  say,  while  pulling  down  the  Thunderbolt,  about 
three  weeks  ago,  that  when  the  ironclads  move  upon  Charleston  he 
would  attack  this  place.  This  was  said  to  his  son,  who  was  formerly 
in  the  Marine  Corps,  and  to  other  officers  of  the  Fingal  who  accom¬ 
panied  him.  Another  one  has  heard  him  say  that  he  would  destroy 
the  vessels  in  Wassaw  Sound  if  the  ironclads  were  to  leave  that  place. 

With  regard  to  moving  these  vessels  past  the  obstructions  at  the 
head  of  Elba  Island,  one  of  the  deserters  who  assisted  in  blowing 


768  SOUTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 

% 

them  up  some  weeks  ago,  when  it  was  intended  to  rtiake  a  movement, 
says  that  now  it  could  be  easily  done  in  one  day  by  using  heavier 
charges  of  powder,  although  it  then  took  them  a  week  to  remove 

them. 

All  the  stores  in  Savannah  are  said  to  be  filled  with  cotton  belonging 
to  an  English  agent  named  Low,  who,  in  buying  the  cotton,  gives  the 
price  as  regulated  by  Confederate  currency  in  orders  on  the  Bank  of 
England  for  gold. 

The  Nashville  was  intended  not  for  a  man-of-war,  but  for  a  priva¬ 
teer.  She  had,  according  to  one  witness,  four  guns;  according  to 
another  she  had  only  two,  a  24-pounder  and  32-pounder,  the  rest  to 
be  obtained  at  Nassau.  She  had  on  board  700  bales  of  cotton,  40  bar¬ 
rels  of  tobacco,  and  some  turpentine.  She  had  been  entirely  deserted 
by  her  crew  before  blowing  up. 

There  is  said  to  be  much  drunkenness  among  the  officers  of  these 
vessels. 

The  navy  ration  is  IT  pounds  meat,  14  ounces  bread,  and  some 
sweet  potatoes. 

The  commodore  is  cheerful  and  popular. 

The  army  appears  to  have  much  poorer  fare. 


Flagship  Wabash,

Chasing  ashore  of  the  British  steamer  Georgiana  by  the  U.  8.  8.  117*- 
sahickon,  March  19,  1863 ,  and  her  subsequent  destruction. 

Report  of  Rear-Admiral  Du  Pont,  U.  S.  Navy. 

No.  140.1  Flagship  Wabash, 

Port  Rayed  Harbor,  8.  G.,  March  21,  1863. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  to  the  Department  that  about  mid¬ 
night  of  the  18th  instant  the  English  iron  steamer  Georgiana  attempted 
to  run  into  Charleston  through  Maffitt’s  Channel. 


N  W  R — VOL  13 - 49 


770 


SOUTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


The  alarm  had  been  given  by  the  U.  S.  yacht  Argefica,  Acting  Mas¬ 
ter  J.  Baker,  who  also  tired  into  her,  and  the  U.  S.  S.  Wissahickon ,  Lieu¬ 
tenant-Commander  J.  L.  Davis,  soon  after  perceiving  her,  opened  so 
heavy  a  fire  upon  her  that  her  commander  hailed  to  say  that  he  surren¬ 
dered.  Upon  this  the  Wissahickon  ceased  firing,  but  the  captain  of 
the  ship,  taking  advantage  thereof,  pointed  his  vessel  toward  the  shore, 
which  was  quite  near,  and  succeeded  in  running  her  aground,  and, 
with  all  on  board  of  her,  escaped  on  the  land  side. 

Captain  Davis  being  of  opinion  that  the  vessel  could  not  be  saved, 
determined  to  destroy  her,  which  he  did  by  setting  her  on  tire. 

The  cargo  was  a  very  valuable  one,  and,  according  to  late  statements 
in  the  papers,  the  vessel  itself  was  pierced  for  fourteen  guns,  but  as 
I  have  not  received  any  report  as  yet  from  Lieutenant-Commander 
Davis,  I  am  not  certain  that  this  was  the  case. 

I  shall  be  able  to  give  further  particulars  by  the  next  mail. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

S.  F.  Du  Pont, 

Rear-Admiral ,  Comdg.  South  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy ,  Washington ,  D.  C. 


Report  of  Captair  Turner,  U.  S.  Navy,  senior  officer  off  Charleston,  S.  C. 

U.  S.  S.  New  Ironsides, 

Off  Charleston ,  S.  C. ,  March  19 ,  1863. 

Admiral:  I  endeavored  to  get  a  letter  on  board  of  an  army  schooner 
passing  this  morning,  but  it  was  blowing  too  heavi^  to  effect  it.  I  am 
writing  this  in  hopes  of  being  able  to  overhaul  some  vessel  in  passing 
here  to-morrow,  as  I  am  not  expecting  to  send  any  vessel  from  here 
to  Port  Royal  soon,  unless  it  should  be  for  provisions,  as  they  are  all 
well  supplied  with  coal  at  present,  excepting  this  ship  only. 

I  have  the  pleasure  to  communicate  to  you  the  following  intelligence: 
Last  night,  about  half  past  12  o’clock,  the  English  iron  steamer  Geor- 
giana  attempted  to  run  in  through  Maffitt’s  Channel.  The  Wissahickon 
fortunately  happened  to  lay  in  her  path,  and  immediately  opened  upon 
her  so  heavy  a  lire  as  to  cripple  her.  Her  commander  hailed  to  say 
that  he  surrendered,  and  at  the  same  time,  by  an  act  of  the  most  con¬ 
summate  treachery,  pointed  his  ship  toward  the  shore,  which  they 
were  very  near  to,  and  grounded  her  in  14  feet  of  water,  himself  and 
everybody  on  board  of  her  escaping  on  the  land  side. 

Captain  Davis  at  the  time,  not  knowing  that  she  was  aground,  had 
ceased  his  fire,  because  of  the  summons  to  surrender  having  been 
assented  to.  She  is  a  very  large  steamer,  filled  with  the  most  valuable 
assorted  cargo;  among  other  articles,  rifled  guns.  As  it  was  then 
calm,  Captain  Davis,  very  wisely,  fearing  that  the  rams  might  come 
out  to  rescue  her,  set  fire  to  her  in  three  different  places,  and  when  he 
came  down  here  to  report  to  me  this  morning  she  was  burning,  and  I 
suppose  by  this  time  she  is  entirely  destroyed.  It  has  been  blowing 
so  heavily  here  all  day,  and  so  high  a  sea  running,  that  I  am  unable  to 
go  to  the  scene  to  ascertain  further  particulars,  which  I  shall  do  as 
soon  as  the  weather  clears  up. 

As  soon  as  I  can  get  the  Huron  back,  and  the  Unadilla,  if  she  can 
be  sent,  with  these  three  gunboats  I  think  I  can  effectually  close  that 


SOUTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


771 


passage  (except  in  fogs)  to  vessels  coming  in;  not  so  easily  to  those 
going  out.  as  they  have  the  advantage  of  a  fresh  departure,  within  a 
mile  of  the  entrance. 

The  Wissahickon  performed  this  whole  work  alone.  I  had  placed 
the  Memphis  just  to  the  north  of  the  Rattlesnake  Shoal.  The  steamer 
got  by  her  unperceived  (at  least  I  suppose  so),  and  her  draft  of  water 
would  have  been  too  great  to  have  gone  to  the  spot. 

Some  one  of  the  three  vessels  lying  to  the  north  of  Rattlesnake 
Shoal  gave  the  alarm,  which  gave  the  Wissahickon  the  opportunity  to 
be  ready  when  the  steamer  came  up. 

I  wish  two  more  pilots.  These  young  officers  commanding  gun¬ 
boats  require  skillful  pilots  on  board,  to  enable  them  to  take  up  their 
positions  close  in. 

My  own  pilot  is  on  board  of  the  Wissahickon ,  doing-  invaluable  service 
there. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

T.  Turner, 

Captain 

Rear-Admiral  S.  F.  Du  Pont, 

Commanding  South  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron. 

P.  S. — Captain  Davis  thinks  that  he  had  put  so  many  shot  in  the  hull

steamer  Georgiana. 

U.  S.  S.  New  Ironsides, 

Off  Charleston ,  S.  C. ,  March  21, 1863. 
Admiral:  I  have  the  honor  to  inform  you  that  a  boat  was  picked  up 
last  night  with  a  sergeant  and  eight  men  belonging  to  the  rebel  service. 
He  represents  that  he  was  sent  to  the  Georgiana  to  look  after  her,  but 
got  lost  last  night  in  the  dark. 

I  shall  send  them  north  by  the  Massachusetts. 


772 


SOUTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


In  consultation  with  Lieutenant-Commander  Davis,  of  the  Wissa¬ 
hickon,  I  have  ordered  the  wreck  of  the  Georgiana  to  be  destroyed. 
It  might  suggest  the  idea  to  the  rebels  of  planting  a  battery  there, 
which  would  give  us  great  trouble;  besides,  being  within  three-fourths 
of  a  mile  from  the  shore,  any  attempt  to  raise  or  discharge  her  would 
be  met  by  resistance,  and  batteries  once  planted  on  that  beach  might 
become  fixtures,  to  our  great  annoyance  in  chasing  vessels  trying  to 
run  the  blockade  at  that  point. 

March  22. 

I  see  a  vessel,  which  is  supposed  to  be  the  Circassian ,  coming  in, 
and  I  close  my  letter  in  hopes  of  being  able  to  send  it  by  her.  I  have 
not  heard  from  the  scene  of  the  wreck  since  yesterday  morning,  but  a 
large  explosion  took  place  last  night  in  that  direction,  which  I  suppose 
was  the  wreck.  Another  explosion  took  place  this  afternoon,  which  I 
suppose  was  another  batch  of  powder  on  board  of  her. 

The  Wissahickon  and  the  Huron  yesterday  afternoon,  by  my  orders, 
set  her  on  fire  with  their  shells. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

T.  Turner, 

Captain. 

Rear-Admiral  S.  F.  Du  Pont, 

Commanding  South  Altantic  Blockading  Squadron.

into  Charleston  to  receive  her  officers,  to  be  fitted  out  as  a  cruiser 
there.  She  had  110  men  on  board,  with  an  armament  of  guns  and  gun 
carriages  in  her  hold,  commanded  by  a  British  naval  retired  officer.

Letter  from  Rear-Admiral  Du  Pont,  U.  S.  Navy,  to  Commodore  Turner,  U.  S.  Navy,  approving 
his  course  in  the  destruction  of  the  steamer. 

Flagship  Wabash, 

Port  Royal  Harbor ,  S.  C. ,  March  2k,  1863. 
Sir:  I  have  your  several  communications  in  reference  to  the  inter¬ 
ception,  running  on  shore,  and  ultimate  destruction  of  the  steamer 
Georgiana  while  attempting  to  run  the  blockade. 


SOUTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON.  773 

I  he  course  pursued  in  destroying  her  was  the  best  under  the  circum¬ 
stances,  and  1  approve  of  it.  I  was  aware  of  the  character  of  this 
vessel,  and  consider  her  capture  of  the  utmost  importance. 

In  your  communication  of  the  21st  you  inform  me  of  your  intention 
of  sending  home  by  the  Massachusetts  the  sergeant  and  eight  men  who 
were  picked  up  in  a  boat  and  who  had  come  out  of  Charleston  Harbor. 
If  you  have  done  so,  which  1  hope  still  you  may  not,  I  have  to  express 
my  regrets,  no  one  having  authority  to  dispose  of  prisoners  but  myself. 
It  would  have  been  of  great  interest  to  have  had  these  men  here  to 
undergo  the  systematic  examination  we  are  in  the  habit  of  giving 
such,  and,  besides,  we  are  not  sending  prisoners  north  now,  having- 
some  of  our  own  people  in  Savannah  for  whom  they  could  have  been 
exchanged. 

If  1  had  any  Charleston  pilots  I  would  send  them  up  with  pleasure, 
but  since  the  blockade  was  established,  now  nearly  two  years,  we  have 
never  had  any;  occasionally  a  coast  pilot  has  been  on  board  some  of 
the  vessels,  but,  as  a  general  rule,  the  commanders  of  light  vessels, 
by  their  superior  knowledge  of  charts,  soon  become  quite  proficient  on 
the  outside  work.  I  had  a  buoy  put  on  the  Rattlesnake  to  help  them, 
and  I  can  do  no  more. 

Respectfully,  etc.,  S.  F.  Du  Pont, 

Rear-Admiral. 

Commodore  T.  Turner, 

TJ.  S.  S.  New  Ironsides ,  off  Charleston.

Report  of  Lieutenant-Commander  Davis,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S.  S.  Wissahickon. 

U.  S.  Gunboat  Wissahickon, 

Off  Charleston  Bar ,  S.  C. ,  March  19 ,  1863. 
Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  that  at  half-past  12  o’clock  last  night' 
I  discovered  a  steamer,  which  had  been  fired  at  by  the  blockading  ves¬ 
sels  lying  outside  of  my  position,  running  in  for  Charleston.  1  at 


774  SOUTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 

* 

once  opened  my  battery  upon  her,  and  with  such  effect  as  to  cause  the 
stranger  to  stop  and  show  a  light,  when  I  ceased  firing,  understanding 
a  hai  1  that  he  surrendered.  U pon  approaching  him,  he  had  changed  the 
direction  of  the  vessel’s  head  and  started  off  to  the  northward,  intend¬ 
ing  to  run  in  along  the  beach.  I  headed  him  off,  using  all  the  guns  I 
could  bring  to  bear,  pressing  him  hard,  and,  no  doubt  disabled,  he  ran 
aground  about  2  miles  to  the  eastward  of  Breach  Inlet,  and  displayed  a 
bright  white  light.  I  stopped  firing,  and  dispatched  boats,  in  charge 
of  Lieutenant  S.  Casey,  with  orders  for  all  on  board  to  come  immedi¬ 
ately  to  this  vessel.  When  Mr.  Casey  reached  the  steamer  all  hands 
had  deserted  her  in  their  boats.  Preparations  were  at  once  made  to 
get  the  vessel  off.  She  proved  to  be  a  large  iron  steamer,  the  Georgiana , 
last  from  Nassau,  New  Providence. 

Having  made  signal  for  assistance,  boats  from  the  Canandaigua , 
Ilousatonic ,  Memphis ,  and  America  reported  themselves.  Every  effort 
was  made  by  hedging  and  towing  with  this  vessel  to  get  the  steamer 
afloat,  but  without  success.  Before  she  was  deserted  every  means  was 
adopted  under  the  precipitate  flight  of  the  deserters  to  ensure  her  fill¬ 
ing  with  water,  and  I  have  reason  to  suppose  the  vessel’s  hull  had  sus¬ 
tained  material  injury  from  our  shot.  Lieutenant  M.  S.  Stuyvesant, 
of  the  Hemsatonic ,  reported  the  fact  that  the  vessel  was  rapidly  filling. 
Having  exhausted  every  effort  to  keep  her  free,  and  not  knowing  how 
near  she  was  to  the  rebel  batteries,  I  directed  him  to  secure  all  the 
property  he  could,  and  set  fire  to  the  steamer.  Just  at  daylight  the 
boats  shoved  off,  the  vessel  having  about  14  feet  of  water  in  her  hold 
and  being  on  fire.  There  was  not  much  property  saved.  The  officers 
commanding  the  boats  were  directed  by  me  to  take  an  inventory  of 
the  articles  they  had  secured,  and  hand  to  me  the  lists.  As  soon  as 
they  are  rendered  I  will  forward  them  to  you. 

I  think  it  quite  probable  when  the  weather  moderates  there  may  be 
obtained  some  of  her  cargo  and  machinery.  The  character  of  the 
cargo  is  not  known,  except  what  was  lying  on  top,  such  as  small  rifled 
guns,  projectiles,  and  Enfield  rifles,  as  no  manifest  was  found. 

I  would  respectfully  state  that  I  ceased  firing  on  both  occasions  when 
the  light  was  displayed,  understanding  it  to  be  a  signal  of  surrender, 
and  to  continue  firing  would  have  been  in  violation  of  the  rights  of 
helpless  creatures  and  barbarous,  but  from  the  conduct  of  those  in 
authority  on  board,  it  is  evident  they  disregarded  honorable  principles 
by  taking  advantage  of  my  humanity,  for  after  surrendering  they 
attempted  to  escape  with  the  vessel.  I  was  in  doubt  as  to  continue 
firing  on  her  after  she  got  aground,  although  a  light  was  shown,  but 
1  gave  them  the  benefit  of  a  doubt,  supposing  that  they  would  not  repeat 
their  first  offense,  if  such  a  slight  expression  could  be  applied  to  their 
cases. 

With  this  communication  I  send  the  report  of  Acting  Assistant  Pay¬ 
master  Kelsey  and  accompanying  papers,  who  was  instructed  to  collect 
and  preserve  all  found  on  board. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

John  L.  Davis, 
Lieutenant-  Commander. 

Rear-Admiral  S.  F.  Du  Pont,  U.  S.  Navy, 

Commanding  South  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron.

Report  of  Captain  Kinzie ,  TJ.  S.  Army,  to  Major-General  Hunter, 
TJ.  S.  Army ,  regarding  the  defenses  of  Savannah,  Ga. 

Hdqrs.  Department  of  the  South, 

Hilton  Head,  Port  Royal,  8.  C. ,  March  W,  1863. 
General:  I  have  the  honor  to  submit  for  your  consideration  the 
following  facts  regarding  the  defenses  of  Savannah  and  the  condition 
of  the  troops  composing  its  garrison:  The  ironclad  battery  Georgia 


776 


SOUTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


lies  just  within  and  close  up  to  the  obstructions,  commanding'  both  the 
North  and  South  channels.  The  Georgia  is  only  afloat  after  half-flood 
tide;  her  portholes  are  open,  four  on  each  side  and  one  on  each  end;  she 
can  not  move  unless  she  is  towed  by  some  other  vessel.  When  she  was 
launched  one  of  the  cross  pieces  of  the  ways  stuck  to  her  bottom  and 
is  fast  there  still.  There  are  no  obstructions,  such  as  torpedoes,  etc., 
in  the  North  Channel  this  side  of  the  Georgia.  This  I  regard  as  true, 
for  it  came  from  three  New  Yorkers  who  belong  to  the  Georgia  and 
are  anxious  to  desert;  it  is  also  corroborated  by  the  pilot  of  the  rebel 
steamer  Ida ,  who  is  not  a  rebel  at  heart,  and  who  also  told  the  pilot 
of  the  Mattano  that  there  were  no  torpedoes  this  side  of  the  obstruc¬ 
tions.  Colonel  Barton,  of  Fort  Pulaski,  agrees  to  go  up  the  river  and 
satisfy  you  of  this  last  fact  by  personal  investigation,  if  you  wish  it. 
The  pilot  of  the  Mattano ,  who  has  been  up  on  every  flag  of  truce  and 
has  never  let  the  opportunity  pass  without  finding  out  something  from 
the  pilots  who  come  down  on  the  rebel  boats,  and  who  are  old  friends 
of  his,  assures  me  that  the  torpedoes  are  all  inside  of  the  obstructions 
and  that  he  can  take  one  of  our  ironclads  within  150  yards  of  the 
Georgia.  The  Weehawlcen  and  another  of  the  monitors  have  not  yet 
been  tried.  From  personal  observation,  and  from  information  that  I 
regard  as  reliable,  I  am  confident  that  two  of  our  ironclads  could 
destroy  the  Georgia  in  two  or  three  hours.  The  North  Channel  runs 
close  under  Elba  Island,  so  that  our  ironclads  could  lie  within  800 
yards  of  the  Georgia ,  having  their  hulls  thus  protected  from  the  fire 
of  Fort  Jackson  and  the  batteries  on  Causton’s  Bluff.  The  troops 
designed  for  the  defense  of  Savannah  have  mostly  been  withdrawn  to 
Charleston,  leaving  from  5,000  to  7,000  in  and  around  Savannah.  The 
fortifications  at  Causton’s  Bluff  are  quite  formidable,  but  are  not  yet 
completed.  I  saw  the  Fingal  (or  Atlanta )  up  near  Fort  Jackson,  and 
the  unfinished  “turtle”  is  up  at  the  city.  The  obstructions  are  made 
of  large  wooden  crates  or  boxes  filled  with  stone  and  then  sunk 
between  two  rows  of  piles.  The  people  of  Savannah  have  no  confi¬ 
dence  in  the  defenses  of  the  city  and  are  ready  at  anjr  moment,  if  we 
make  a  vigorous  attack,  to  seek  safety  in  flight. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Arthur  M.  Kinzie, 
Captain  and  A.id-de-  Camp.

Hdqrs.  Department  of  the  South,

Deport  of  Commander  Steedman ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  commanding  U.  S.  S. 

Paul.  Jones ,  regarding  a  reconnoissance  in  St.  John's  River  to  Jack¬ 
sonville ,  Fla. 

U.  S.  Gunboat  Paul  Jones, 

Off  Jacksonville,  Fla.,  March  W,  1863. 

Admiral:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  that  on  my  arrival  at  the  mouth 
of  this  river  [St.  John’s],  I  immediately  pushed  on  to  this  place,  which 
I  found  upon  my  arriving  in  the  quiet  possession  of  Colonel  Higginson, 
with  his  command  of  colored  troops,  who  two  days  previously,  under 
convoy  of  the  gunboats  Norwich  and  TJncas ,  Commander  Duncan,  sen¬ 
ior  officer  in  command,  had  come  up  in  his  transports  and  landed  his 
forces  in  the  town  without  meeting  with  the  slightest  resistance. 

Herewith  I  transmit  Commander  Duncan’s  report.  I  was  informed 
by  Judge  Stickney,  on  the  day  of  his  leaving  here  in  the  steamer 
Boston,  that  it  was  his  intention  to  obtain  a  large  reinforcement  of 
troops  for  the  purpose  of  holding  this  place  permanently.  I  have  been 
obliged  to  remain  here  to  give  protection  to  the  force  now  in  possession 
of  the  town,  as  I  did  not  think  it  adequate  to  hold  it  without  our 
assistance. 

The  Boston,  with  reinforcements,  is  now  coming  up  the  river. 

As  there  are  but  some  30  tons  of  coal  at  Fernandina  I  have  decided 
not  to  send  the  Norwich  there  for  a  supply,  but  will  endeavor  to  pro¬ 
cure  from  the  army  transports  enough  to  last  for  a  couple  of  weeks. 
Should  I  not  be  able  to  do  this,  I  will  have  to  supply  her  from  this 
vessel. 

So  soon  as  the  expected  reinforcements  have  arrived  I  will  make  a 
reconnoissance  up  the  river  as  far  as  Palatka;  having  done  this,  and 
tinding  that  the  presence  of  this  vessel  is  no  longer  necessary,  I  will 
return  to  my  station  agreeably  to  your  instructions. 

I  am  happy  to  inform  you  that  I  have  learned  from  reliable  sources 
that  there  is  no  foundation  for  the  report  that  the  steamer  St.  Mary's 
has  been  raised  or  moved  from  the  place  where  she  was  sunk  some 
time  since.

Letter  from,  Rear-Admiral  Du  Pont ,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  to  Brigadier-  General 
Van  Vliei,  TJ.  S.  Army,  requesting  that  army  transports  be  restricted 

from  approaching  the  blockading  fleet  off  Charleston. 

Flagship  Wabash, 

Port  Royal  Harbor,  S.  G. ,  March  23,  1863. 

Sir:  The  senior  officer  off  Charleston  informs  me  that  army  trans¬ 
ports  on  their  way  south  frequently  approach  the  blockading  fleet  at 
night,  even  getting  within  the  lines,  and  on  several  occasions  have 
narrowly  escaped  being  fired  into,  at  the  great  risk  of  loss  of  life  and 
danger  to  the  vessel. 

May  I  ask  you  to  warn  the  captains  of  army  transports  not  to 
approach  the  blockading  fleet  off  Charleston,  particularly  at  night? 

Respectfully,  etc., 

S.  F.  Du  Pont, 

Rear-Adm  iral. 

General  Van  Vliet, 

Chief  Quartermaster,  New  fork.

Letter  from  lion.  Ira  Harris,  to  the  Secretary  of  the  Navy,  transmit¬ 
ting  letter  from  Nassau,  New  Providence,  regarding  the  movements 
of  blockade  runners  between  that  place  and  Southern  ports. 


Albany,  March  2JH  1863. 

My  Dear  Sir:  I  have  just  received  the  enclosed  letter  which  I  deem 
of  sufficient  importance  to  place  it  in  your  hands.  It  discloses  a  state 
of  things  which  few  would  be  prepared  to  believe.  Did  I  not  know 
the  writer  so  well  I  should  at  once  say  the  statement  was  exaggerated; 
but  coming  as  it  does  from  Judge  Bosworth,  now  the  chief  justice  of 
the  superior  court  of  New  York,  I  am  forced  to  believe  every  word 
of  it.  Whether  anything  more  can  be  done  than  is  already  being  done 
to  break  up  this  regular  and  frequent  communication,  by  which  the 
rebels  are  evidently  receiving  much  aid  and  comfort,  is  a  question  for 
you  to  consider. 

Yours,  with  esteem, 

Ira  Harris. 


Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy. 


[Enclosure.] 

Nassau,  New  Providence,  March  16,  1863. 

Dear  Sir:  I  have  been  at  this  port  since  the  evening  of  the  6th 
instant  and  shall  remain  until  the  13th  of  April. 

I  write  in  haste  and  but  a  word.  I  can  not  think  that  our  Govern¬ 
ment  begins  to  know  what  is  going  on  here.  There  are  over  twenty 
swift,  light-draft  steamers  running  regularly  between  this  and  Charles¬ 
ton  and  Wilmington,  mostly  to  and  from  Charleston.  From  nine  to 
eleven  days  is  the  passage  to  and  from.  Over  one  million  of  rifles  and 
any  quantity  of  cannon  and  ammunition  have  gone  from  this  port,  the 
steamers  bringing  back  cotton  and  other  cargo.  Any  quantity  of  gun 
carriages  lie  here,  for  which  there  is  no  present  demand  in  Dixie. 


782 


SOUTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


Three  steamers  left  here  Saturday  and  two  arrived  Saturday  night 
and  Monday  morning. 

We  need  three  or  four  fleet  steamers  off  Abaco  light.  Our  gunboat 
which  is  about  there  is  too  slow,  and  can  be  run  around  and  away  from 
by  the  blockade  runners. 

They  are  now  shipping  grain  largely  from  this  port  to  Charleston, 
whether  for  seed  or  consumption  1  am  not  advised.  There  is  abundance 
of  coal  here,  and  the  steamers  took  enough  for  a  passage  out  and  back. 
The  passage  is  made  in  about  sixty  hours  to  Charleston. 

It  is  known  here  when  the  steamers  are  to  leave  and  are  expected 
back,  as  well  as  when  steamers  leave  New  York  for  Europe  and  are 
expected  to  return. 

This  information  meagerly  detailed  may  not  be  useful,  but  I  think 
that  these  steamers  run  so  confidently  that  the3T  might  be  taken  and 
the  business  broken  up  if  some  swifter  steamers  could  surprise  them. 


Yours,  very  sincerely, 


Hon.  Ira  Harris. 


J.  S.  Bosworth.

Sir:  On  being  relieved  by  the  Conemaugh ,  Commander  Werden,  in 
charge  of  the  blockade  of  Georgetown,  you  will  return  to  Port  Royal

After  diligent  enquiry  I  am  induced  to  believe  that  it  will  be  to  the

to  direct  that  you  will  take  them  on  board  and  bring  them  to  Port

Report  of  Rear- Admiral  Du  Pant,  U.  S.  Navy ,  requesting  the  appoint¬ 
ment  as  acting pnaster  of  the  executive  officer  of  the  U.  S.  Coast- Sur¬ 
vey  steamer 1  Bibb . 

No.  153.]  Flagship  Wabash, 

Port  Royal  Harbor ,  8.  C.,  Afar  eh  26,  1863. 
Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  inform  the  Department  that  I  have 
appointed  Robert  Platt,  at  present  executive  officer  of  the  U.  S.  Coast 
Survey  steamer  Bibb ,  as  acting  ensign  in  the  U.  S.  Navy  from  the 
1st  of  March,  this  being  the  highest  appointment  I  can  confer.  I 
would,  however,  recommend  that  the  Department  should  give  him  the 
appointment  of  acting  master  from  the  same  date.  Mr.  Platt  has 
been  of  great  service  in  this  squadron,  is  an  educated  and  thorough 
seaman,  and  is,  moreover,  [competent]  to  pilot  the  fleet  into  Charleston 
Harbor,  as  I  have  reason  to  believe  that  his  knowledge  of  the  channels 
exceeds  that  of  any  of  the  few  pilots  we  have  here,  and  for  which 
perilous  service  he  has  patriotically  volunteered. 

I  may  add  that  there  are  two  other  pilots  in  the  squadron  holding 
the  position  of  acting  master,  which  is  a  further  reason  for  making 
the  appointment. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

S.  F.  Du  Pont,

Letter  from  the  Secretary  of  the  Navy  to  the  Secretary  of  State,  respond¬ 
ing  to  enquiry  regarding  permits  for  British  subjects  to  load  cotton  in 
Savannah  River. 


Navy  Department,  March  27,  1863. 


.  Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  acknowledge  the  receipt  of  your  letter  of 
the  24th  instant,  enclosing  a  copy  of  a  note  addressed  to  you  by  Lord 
Lyons,  who  desires  to  be  informed  if  British  subjects  will  be  permitted 
to  load  ships  with  cotton  in  the  Savannah  River,  below  the  Confeder¬ 
ate  obstructions. 

In  reply  I  would  state  that  I  am  aware  of  no  authority  to  grant  per¬ 
mits  for  shipment  of  cotton  in  the  blockaded  region.  Port  Royal  is 
the  only  place  in  the  vicinity  of  Savannah  from  which  such  shipments 
can  legally  be  made. 

Very  respectfully,  etc., 

Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy. 


Hon.  William  H.  Seward, 

Secretary  of  State. 


Letter  from  the  Secretary  of  the  Navy  to  Rear- Admiral  Du  Pont,  U.  S. 

Navy,  regarding  prize  cases  pending  in  the  Supreme  Court. 

Washington,  March  27,  1863. 

My  Dear  Sir:  I  duly  received  yours  in  regard  to  the  prize  cases 
pending  before  the  Supreme  Court  at  the  time  your  letter  was  written, 
but  which  had  been  argued  and  submitted  to  the  court  when  it  came  to 
hand.  Mr.  Davis  would  have  been  authorized  to  appear  in  your  behalf 
had  it  been  known  that  you  desired  it. 

The  disposition  of  the  cases,  you  will  have  learned,  was  favorable  on 
every  point.  It  has  gone  abroad  that  the  court  stood  five  to  four,  but 
I  have  been  informed  that  Judge  Catron,  counted  as  one  of  the  four, 
abstained  from  giving  an  opinion,  not  having  made  himself  sufficiently 
familiar  with  the  law  and  facts. 

I  congratulate  you  on  the  result,  though  late. 

We  are  all  looking  with  great  earnestness  and  confidence  to  your 
squadron  at  this  time.  This  is  natural  and  to  be  expected.  I  offer  no 
suggestions  or  opinion  or  wishes  which  I  would  have  control  your 
action.  It  is  and  has  been  my  aim  to  strengthen  and  assist  you  so  far 
as  in  me  lay,  and  trust  to  your  courage,  skill,  and  sagacity  for  the  rest. 

The  country  is,  as  usual,  impatient  with  us  all,  but  the  fault-finders 
are  less  reckless  and  abusive  than  in  the  earlier  periods  of  the  war. 
But  were  they  as  censorious  as  ever  they  should  not  he  permitted  to 
precipitate  inconsiderate  action. 


SOUTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


787 


I  am  inclined  to  believe  the  rebels  are,  and  for  some  time  havebeen^ 
strengthening  their  defenses  quite  as  vigorously  as  we  are  preparing 
for  the  offensive.  You,  however,  are  better  informed  than  we  are,  I 
presume,  on  these  subjects. 

There  has  been  a  marked  improvement  in  the  tone  and  feeling  of  the 
country  during  the  last  few  weeks,  which  at  times  surprises  me,  for 
there  have  been  no  great  successes  to  inspire  the  change.  It  indicates, 

I  think,  persistency  and  high  resolve  in  this  great  struggle,  and,  I  flat¬ 
ter  myself,  increasing  confidence  in  our  heroic  leaders. 

Nothing  decisive  is  yet  received  from  Farragut  and  Porter,  though 
expectation  in  that  direction  almost  equals  that  toward  Charleston. 

My  heart  and  best  wishes  are  with  you.  God  grant  you  a  great 
success.  It  always  gives  me  pleasure  to  hear  from  you  officially  and 
unofficially,  and  I  hope  you  will  often  gratify  me. 

Yours,  truly, 

Gideon  Welles. 

Rear-Admiral  Samuel  F.  Du  Pont,

U.  S.  Steam  Battery  Keokuk, 

Port  Royal,  March  26,  1863. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  the  arrival  of  this  vessel.  We  left 
Hampton  Roads  on  Sunday  evening  at  9  o’clock,  after  a  detention 
of  several  hours  by  fog.  On  the  passage  down,  in  tow  of  steam  tug 
Governor ,  we  had  rough  weather  after  passing  Cape  Lookout  Shoals. 
In  a  heavy  sea  the  vessel  rolls  deeply,  but  easily.  I  consider  her  a 
good  and  safe  vessel  at  sea.  The  convoy  steamer  E.  B.  Hale  was  lost 
sight  of  on  Tuesday  evening  in  a  heavy  squall.  When  the  engines  are 
worked  more  and  in  good  order  the  Keokuk  will  be  able  to  go  without 
convoy,  and  I  think  will  attain  a  speed  of  over  9  knots  in  smooth  water. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

A.  C.  Rhind, 

Commander.

Report  of  Commander  Batch ,  II.  S.  Navy ,  senior  officer  in  Stono  Inlet , 
South  Carolina ,  regarding  naval  cooperation  extended  in  a  military 
reconnoissance  on  Colds  Island. 


U.  S.  Steam  Sloop  Pawnee, 

Stono  Inlet ,  South  Carolina ,  March  27,  1863. 

Sir:  The  One  hundredth  Regiment,  Colonel  Dandy,  has  just  been 
landed  on  Cole’s  Island.  I  have  furnished  him  with  everything  in  my 
power  to  effect  their  landing.  In  coming  in  yesterday  the  Expounder 
struck  on  the  North  Breaker,  and  I  immediately  proceeded  in  the 
Commodore  McDonough  to  her  assistance,  and  in  "the  effort  to  aid  the 
Expounder  the  McDonough  struck,  remaining  on  shore  till  9  p.  m.,  when 
she  came  off,  uninjured,  as  far  as  we  can  judge.  The  Paionee's  boats 
rendered  all  the  assistance  possible.  At  daylight  this  morning  Captain 
Bacon  led  in  and  anchored  near  Cole’s  Island;  the  troops  were  landed, 
and  I  accompanied  Colonel  Dandy  in  a  reconnoissance  over  the  island, 
pointing  out  the  different  localities.  I  received  by  the  army  transports 
your  order  in  reference  to  Lieutenant-Commander  Bacon’s  buoying  the 
Stono  entrance,  and  as  soon  as  we  can  get  the  buoys  from  the  trans¬ 
ports  and  the  weather  permits  he  will  proceed  on  that  duty.  I  have 
nothing  of  importance  to  report  in  regard  to  the  enemy  in  this  locality. 
Captain  Garfield  arrived  to-day  at  11  a.  m.  and,  in  obedience  to  orders 
to  him,  I  hasten  to  dispatch  him  to  Port  Royal  by  this  tide. 

He  would  be  very  useful  in  the  event  of  sending  more  transports 
into  Stono. 

I  am  happy  to  report  all  well  on  this  station. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Geo.  B.  Balch, 

Commander  and  Senior  Officer  Present. 

Rear-Admiral  S.  F.  Du  Pont, 

Comdg.  South  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron.

Report  of  Rear-Admiral  Du  Pont,  U.  S.  Navy,  transmitting  report  of  the  commanding 

officer  of  the  U.  S.  S.  Stettin. 

No.  162.1  Flagship  Wabash, 

Port  Royal  Harbor ,  S.  C.,  March  31 ,  1863. 
Sir:  I  herewith  forward  (marked  No.  1)  the  report  of  Acting  Master 
Edward  F.  Devens,  of  the  Stettin ,  detailing  the  circumstances  of  the 
capture  of  the  English  steamer  Aries,  on  the  28th  instant,  in  attempt¬ 
ing  to  run  the  blockade  off  Bull’s  Bay. 

Acting  Master  Devens  brought  the  steamer  into  this  port,  and  I  have, 
after  supplying  him  with  a  crew,  directed  him  to  proceed  to  Boston, 
in  accordance  with  the  order  of  the  Department. 

Acting  Master  Devens’  health  is  not  good,  and  as  the  prize  is  valu¬ 
able,  and  her  cargo  consists  largely  of  liquor,  I  deemed  it  best  to 
send  him  home  in  charge  of  her.  He  has  been  detached  from  the 
Stettin ,  and  that  vessel  will  be  put  in  command  temporarily  of  some 
acting  master. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

S.  F.  Du  Pont, 

Rear-Admiral ,  Comdg.  South  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy ,  Washington,  D.  C. 


Report  of  Acting  Master  Devens,  D.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S.  S.  Stettin. 

Prize  Steamer  Aries, 

Port  Royal  Harbor ,  March  29,  1863. 

Sir:  I  would  most  respectfully  make  the  following  report  in  regard 
to  the  capture  of  the  English  steamer  Aries,  while  endeavoring  to  run 
the  blockade  off  Bull’s  Bay: 

At  12:45  a.  m.  of  the  28th  instant  a  steamer  was  discovered  stand¬ 
ing  to  the  westward.  I  immediately  got  all  ready  and  slipped  my 
anchor,  and  when  the  steamer  was  inside  of  me  and  near  shoals  in  this 
place  commenced  firing  at  him,  at  the  same  time  following  him  as  fast 
as  possible.  Finding  the  water  to  shoal  very  fast,  I  anchored  in  3 
fathoms.  At  early  daylight  saw  the  above  steamer  ashore  on  the 
south  end  of  Petrel  Bank.  I  immediately  armed  and  equipped  the 
boats’  crews,  and,  taking  command  in  person,  I  went  on  board  and 
took  possession  of  her  as  a  prize  to  the  U.  S.  Government. 

Found  her  to  be  aground  astern;  commenced  shifting  cargo  forward. 
At  7  a.  m.  she  came  off.  1  proceeded  to  Charleston  with  her,  and  was 
ordered  by  Commodore  T.  Turner  to  report  to  you  at  Port  Royal, 
Lieutenant  Robeson  taking  command  of  the  Stettin. 

I  am,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Edward  F.  Devens, 

Acting  Master ,  Commanding. 

Rear-Admiral  S.  F.  Du  Pont, 

Commanding  South  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron.

No.  163.1  Flagship  Wabash,

Sir:  In  a  previous  dispatch  (No.  162)  I  have  informed  the  Depart¬ 
ment  of  the  capture  of  the  prize  steamer  Aries. 

As  it  is  impossible  to  furnish  the  prize  with  engineers  and  firemen 
to  take  her  north  without  great  detriment  to  the  public  service,  1  have 
made  an  arrangement  with  two  engineers,  William  Curkipp  and  Wil¬ 
liam  Maud,  and  six  firemen,  John  F.  King,  Edward  Crook,  Harry 
Warner,  John  L.  Samuels,  William  Chadwick,  and  Joseph  Colwood, 
of  the  captured  vessel,  to  pay  the  former  $3  a  day  and  the  latter  $2 
per  day  from  the  30th  day  of  March,  instant,  until  the  arrival  of  the 
Aries  in  Boston. 

I  have  also  made  an  arrangement  with  the  cook,  Joseph  Alphonse, 
to  pay  him  at  the  rate  $1  per  day  from  the  30th  of  March  until  the 
arrival  of  the  prize  in  Boston. 

Commodore  J.  B.  Montgomery  has  been  informed  of  this  arrange¬ 
ment,  but  may  I  request  the  Department  to  authorize  him  by  telegraph 
to  make  the  above  payments  ? 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

S.  F.  Du  Pont,

Petition  of  captured,  passengers  to  be  sent  to  Savannah  or  Charleston  under  flag  of  truce. 

On  Board  of  the  Aries, 

Port  Royal , - , - . 

Sir:  We,  the  undersigned,  passengers  in  the  ship  and  Spanish  sub¬ 
jects,  beg  of  you,  with  all  attention,  to  allow  us  to  be  sent  to  Savannah 
or  Charleston  under  flag  of  truce,  so  as  to  relieve  the  anxiety  of  our 
families  and  to  be  able  to  see  them. 

As  under  word  of  honor  we  all  can  say  that  none  of  us  has  at  present, 
neither  had  before,  anything  to  do  with  regard  to  help  in  any  way  the 
South  or  North  in  this  unfortunate  war,  and  that  under  this  true  promise 
and  conviction  we  take  the  liberty  to  beg  of  you  the  mentioned  par¬ 
ticular  favor. 

If  you  are  kind  enough  to  accept  our  petition,  we  will  take  another 
liberty,  as  the  allowance  to  take  with  us  and  with  our  baggage  some 
cigars  and  other  trifles  that  we  carry  in  our  rooms  for  our  exclusive 
use  and  our  families,  which  things  are  not  in  the  manifest  of  the  ship. 
If  it  is  not  in  your  power  the  allowance  we  beg  to  be  sent  under  flag 
of  truce,  then  we  beg  to  be  transshipped  to  the  next  mail  boat  to 
North,  as  here  now  is  very  uncomfortable  to  leave. 

Trusting  that  you  will  attend  our  just  petitions,  and  assuring  you 
that  will  ever  find  out  anything  contrary  to  our  statement  to  regret, 
we  send  you  anticipated  thanks  and  obligations.

Letter  from  Rear-Admiral  Du  Pont,  U.  S.  Navy,  to  the  captured  passengers  of  the  prize, 

declining  to  grant  their  petition. 


Flagship  Wabash, 

Port  Royal  Harbor,  S.  C '.,  March  29,  1863. 

Gentlemen:  Your  request  to  be  sent  to  Savannah  or  Charleston,  I 
regret  to  inform  you,  can  not  be  granted. 

You  have  been  engaged  in  an  attempt  to  violate  the  law  of  the 
blockade,  and  you  can  not  expect  to  escape  the  inconveniences  conse¬ 
quent  thereto.  You  will  be  sent  north  by  the  first  convenient  oppor¬ 
tunity. 

If  you  desire  to  write  to  your  families  in  either  Charleston  or  Savan¬ 
nah,  I  will  forward  the  letters,  of  course  unsealed,  by  the  first  flag  of 
truce. 


Private  effects  which  you  have  had  in  your  rooms  intended  for  your 
own  use  and  not  for  trade  you  will  be  permitted  to  take  with  "you, 
subject  to  the  discretion  of  Captain  Devens. 

Respectfully,  etc., 

S.  F.  Du  Pont, 

Rear-Admiral.

U.  S.  gunboat  Stettin ,  among  the  crew  of  which  [  observe  the  name 
of  Simpson  Adkins,  reputed  to  be  one  of  the  most  expert  pilots  upon 
the  Southern  coast,  believing  it  a  part  of  my  duties  to  aid  and  assist 
in  bringing  to  justice  all  offenders  against  the  laws  of  my  country,  I 
beg  leave  to  inform  you  that  this  man  Adkins  is  an  old  offender,  he 
having  once  before  been  taken  in  the  same  capacity  and  brought  to 
this  port,  and  by  my  order  confined  in  Fort  Taylor  for  blockade  run¬ 
ning;  but  upon  representations  being  made  of  his  good  character  and 
reliability,  I  released  him,  upon  his  giving  his  parole  of  honor  not  to 
leave  the  island,  allowing  him  the  limits  of  the  same.  He  broke  his 
parole  and  escaped  from  the  island  during  the  night,  and  when  next 
heard  from  was  on  the  mainland.  Thinking  the  above  information 
might  be  of  importance  to  you  in  dealing  with  his  case,  I  have  taken 
the  liberty  of  forwarding  the  same  to  you  for  your  consideration. 

I  have  the  honor,  admiral,  to  be,  most  respectfully,  your  obedient 
servant, 

Jos.  S.  Morgan,

Report  of  Commando r  Duncan,  TJ.  S.  Navy ,  regarding  the  evacuation 

of  Jacksonville,  Fla.,  by  the  TJ.  S.  Army  forces  March  39,  1863. 

U.  S.  S.  Norwich, 

St.  John’s  River,  March  30,  1863. 

Admiral:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  that  on  Sunday,  the  29th, 
the  troops  evacuated  the  city  of  Jacksonville.  Before  leaving  they 
destroyed  the  greater  part  of  the  city,  including  two  of  the  churches, 
the  Catholic  and  Episcopal,  also  warehouses,  etc.  We  arrived  here  on 
the  evening  of  the  same  day,  and  the  transports  have  been  detained 
here  on  account  of  the  weather,  which  has  been  such  as  to  prevent 
them  from  going  out;  they  will  leave  as  soon  as  the  weather  will 
permit. 

The  Paul  Jones  arrived  on  the  12th  to  allow  me  to  go  to  Fernandina 
for  coal,  but  as  I  learned  that  there  was  not  sufficient  there  for  me  I 
took  from  the  Pond  Jones  30  tons  of  coal,  of  which  1  let  the  army  trans¬ 
port  John  Adams  have  8  tons. 

By  order  of  Captain  Steedman,  the  John  Adams  went  to  Fernandina 
and  got  38  tons  of  navy  coal.  On  her  return  she  let  the  Uncas  have 
12  tons,  leaving  a  balance  of  34  tons  due  the  navy  from  the  army. 

We  have  on  board  of  this  vessel  about  25  tons  of  coal  on  hand. 

1  shall  keep  both  vessels  at  the  mouth  of  the  river  for  the  future. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

J.  M.  Duncan, 

Commander  and  Senior  Officer  Present.
